stories.Headline: Wizards of the Coast gives its Anthropic settlement share to D&D writers
stories.Summary:
Wizards of the Coast decided to give its entire share of the Anthropic AI settlement to the writers of Dungeons & Dragons books, according to novelist James Lowder. The company confirmed to the press that it is handing its share to the writers, Shane the Gamer reported on 22 November 2026. The money comes from Bartz v. Anthropic, the class action over pirated books used to train Anthropic's Claude AI models. Blain Howard, Senior Manager, Brand Publicity for D&D, told EN World that Wizards took part in the settlement as the copyright owner of D&D novels, modules and stories.

Howard added that this week authors began receiving letters explaining how to claim their share of the settlement. The letter explains that because Wizards is the registered owner of the Works, Wizards filed the claims in its name. It then says the company has decided to voluntarily forgo its share of the proceeds and pass its share of the Settlement payments for the Works on to the authors. According to Lowder, some payments will go out through the Anthropic settlement mechanism, and some of the money Wizards will collect and then pass on. Final approval of the settlement was granted on July 20, 2026, and the Authors Guild says the $1.5 billion award will be split among the rightsholders.

Lowder's estimate is that this amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars WotC could have collected going to the writers, at about US$3,000 per book, normally split 50/50. Lowder, a freelance writer and editor who has contracted with Wizards of the Coast on D&D books, discussed the news and its personal impact on him via LinkedIn. He wrote that this is remarkable and amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars that WotC could have collected going to the writers. He said Wizards is doing this at a time when the larger publishers are scrambling to grab as much settlement money as possible from authors. He wrote that conversations at Wizards about the Anthropic settlement have been ongoing for months, and that he has been part of these conversations on and off.

He said the real heavy lifting was done by folks with more clout, and that this all came about because some of the writers used what influence they possessed to raise the issue. Lowder wrote that the people inside Wizards, up to the highest levels, were willing to consider the situation from more than a financial perspective. He thanked all the writers who stepped up, especially the efforts of R.A. Salvatore, and said he does not think this would have happened without those author-prompted discussions. He gave huge credit to the folks at Wizards, in particular Dan Ayoub, who were open to the discussions and then did the generous and right thing.

Lowder wrote that this payout will help a lot of writers, folks who certainly deserve to be rewarded for their work. PC Gamer's Ted Litchfield wrote that it is unambiguously great that writers like Lowder benefitted from this settlement more than they were required to. Litchfield wrote that Wizards' reputation has taken a drubbing in recent years, and that it behooves the company to secure PR victories like this where it can. He noted that Wizards has refused to voluntarily recognize an employee union twice in one year, forcing a vote among the staff, and that Wargamer reported last week the company appears to be preparing to deal with a unionised workforce.

He recalled that Wizards' attempt to rework D&D's influential Open Gaming License met a huge fan and industry backlash, prompting the company to backpedal almost immediately. He also recalled incidents of AI art appearing in marketing material and a D&D sourcebook that met with a sour response. He noted that Wizards laid off 1,100 people in 2023, including much of the publishing team that liaised with Larian Studios on Baldur's Gate 3. Larian has insisted that its decision to pivot from D&D back to its own Divinity series was a creative one, and that its shift away from Wizards was amicable, but most forum-goers and hoi polloi still assume the worst about the split.

Litchfield wrote that Lowder's estimate that Wizards stood to receive hundreds of thousands of dollars stood out to him, since that is life-changing money for an extremely successful author like R.A. Salvatore but couch cushion change for a multi-billion dollar operation like Wizards of the Coast. By his reckoning, the real value of the case to publishers was extracting some sort of concession, a legal precedent regarding copyright and training AI models. He wrote that Wizards undeniably did the right thing here, but that he thinks it was a PR victory cheaply bought. The articles leave open the results of the union ballot, which are not yet public.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells a mother she probably need not save for her children’s college
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft’s AI CEO, told a mother of two that she should “probably not” bother saving for her children’s college education, Business Insider reported. The mother asked whether her family should save for college for her four- and five-year-old children. Suleyman answered “probably not,” according to the report. The exchange was reported by Business Insider and recounted in a Moneywise article published by Yahoo Finance on November 22, 2026. The article appeared under the headline that 15% of parents have already cut college savings after the exchange.

Intuit Credit Karma data shows 27% of parents say they are rethinking how much they need to save for their children’s education overall because of concerns about AI’s impact on their children’s future. 15% have already reduced how much they are saving for college, saying they are less certain it will be worth the cost. A Digital Education Council 2026 global survey found 41% of college students say they are nervous about AI reducing job opportunities in their field of study. 42% of recent college graduates are underemployed, and computer science majors currently have a 7.0% unemployment rate, comparable to fine arts majors. This year, 16 colleges listed a total price above $100,000 a year.

Dr. Shaan Patel, founder of Prep Expert, said there is definitely an argument to worry about the future value of college savings for a child who is only eight years old today. Patel said registered nurses earn a median salary of $97,550 and physicians earn a median salary of $275,930, and nursing graduates have an unemployment rate of only 2.1%. Patel said the argument is not to stop saving for college but to stop assuming any college degree will be of value to a child in the future. Jason Robinovitz, CEO at Score at the Top Learning Centers, said the cost of college is out of control and he sees few signs it will slow down. Robinovitz said savings can give a child options, while having no savings can take away options.

Robinovitz said college is where kids grow up and build a network of peers they can call on for decades to share an opportunity or find one. Robinovitz said a 529 account grows untaxed and withdrawals for qualified expenses are tax-free, while the same investments in a regular brokerage account owe tax on dividends along the way and on gains when you sell. Moe Manshad, Associate Professor of Business Intelligence and Data Analytics at Monfort College of Business, University of Northern Colorado, said he expects a split, with degrees that only certify attendance losing value. Manshad said programs built on applied projects, internships and real work with AI will keep their premium. Manshad said the knowledge that makes an organization run its processes, decisions and relationships is mostly private, and AI can’t replace what it can’t see.

The Moneywise article said technology industry heavyweights believe AI may wipe out white-collar jobs in the next decade. The article said parents have long been concerned about the exorbitant cost of college aside from the AI factor. The article said many college degrees still lead directly to a license and to jobs that can be very high paying even in the age of AI. The article said AI is trained on public information, and the knowledge that makes an organization run is mostly private. The article said colleges have historically excelled at training in that private knowledge, which is learned on the job.

The article did not say whether Suleyman responded further or whether Microsoft commented on the exchange. The article did not say what the mother decided to do about saving for her children’s college education. The article did not give the mother’s name or where she lives. The article did not say when the exchange between the mother and Suleyman took place. The article did not say what action, if any, policymakers or colleges plan to take in response.

stories.Headline: China uses smuggling and front companies to bypass US export controls on AI chips
stories.Summary:
China used spies and smuggling to acquire super-powered computer chips from the United States. These illicit activities occurred recently to bypass strict American export controls on high-end technology. A woman ran a Singaporean front company to facilitate these illegal chip transfers. She established data centres in Southeast Asia to house the smuggled Taiwan-made hardware. Chinese companies then leased the use of these chips through this complex loophole.

The scheme requires Nvidia chips made by one specific manufacturing facility located in Taiwan. These chips rely on rare machines produced by a single company in the Netherlands. The U.S. government set export controls to limit which countries Nvidia can ship to. However, the Trump administration signed off on selling 900,000 chips to China over six months. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik was reportedly lax with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang regarding these sales.

Kyle Chan from the Brookings Institution says the U.S. views AI as a winner-take-all race. He explains that some officials believe achieving Artificial General Intelligence provides an existential strategic advantage. Kenton Thibaut of the Atlantic Council says China views AI as a general purpose technology. He states that Chinese policies focus on making AI useful for society and the economy. Thibaut notes that the U.S. focuses on frontier systems while China supplies near frontier technology.

Chinese firms are affected by hardware constraints and focus on doing more with less computing power. They aim to automate factories and speed up drug discovery to benefit their overall economy. U.S. companies like Anthropic fear their models could run out of control and want more regulation. These American firms rely on the chip advantage to push the envelope of AI development. China seeks to integrate these advances holistically rather than focusing only on a singular goal.

The U.S. has more computing power than any other nation due to its chip access. China faces physical constraints that make discussions about runaway AI models largely moot for them. The Chinese government is predisposed to prevent any societal disruptions caused by new technology. They currently rely on a bridge of smuggled tech to maintain their competitive computing power. This strategy allows them to function while they work toward their own manufacturing capabilities.

China wants to eventually create its own version of the super-manufacturers found in Taiwan. They aim to separate themselves from the Western tech stack to achieve total independence. AI Czar David Sacks has explicitly advocated for selling more chips directly to China. The articles leave open whether the U.S. will tighten or loosen these export controls. It remains unclear if China will successfully build its own high-end chip manufacturing industry.

stories.Headline: NATO weighs how militaries can use private AI while keeping sovereign control
stories.Summary:
NATO officials and technology companies met at the NATO Edge conference, with reporting dated 22 November 2026, to discuss how allied militaries can adopt artificial intelligence and other private technology without surrendering control over the systems they depend on. The gathering framed the problem as a sovereignty dilemma, because the software and computing power behind modern military tools increasingly come from private firms rather than from governments themselves. France 24 reported that the alliance is weighing this reliance on private tech and AI as a security question rather than a purely commercial one. The conference brought the two sides together to air the tension between speed of adoption and national control. The core requirement the discussion sets out is that NATO members find a way to use private technology, including artificial intelligence, while keeping sovereign authority over how it is used and secured.

The articles give no specific budget figures, contract values or program names beyond the conference itself and its November 2026 date. What changes, according to the reporting, is the assumption that militaries can build or own everything they rely on, since private firms now supply much of the underlying capability. The dilemma is described as one of sovereignty, meaning allied governments must decide how much dependence on outside providers they can accept. Responsibility for resolving the tension sits with NATO and its member governments, which must set the terms under which they buy and rely on private systems. The articles do not name individual officials or attribute specific statements, so the positions are described only in general terms as a debate over control and reliance.

Companies supplying the technology are the other party, and the conference served as the venue where the two sides confronted the trade-off. No direct quotations from participants are given in the source material. The context is that military forces across the alliance are leaning more heavily on private technology and AI as these tools become central to modern operations. The articles do not say what specific decisions, deadlines or follow-up meetings will come out of the NATO Edge conference. What happens next is left open, with the sovereignty dilemma presented as an unresolved question rather than a settled policy.

stories.Headline: NATO officials and defence experts debate how militaries can use AI without ceding data control to private firms
stories.Summary:
NATO officials and defence experts gathered at the NATO Edge conference in Izmir, Turkey, this week to discuss how militaries can use artificial intelligence and high tech without losing control of sensitive data. The three-day conference on critical technologies and digital warfare brought together military chiefs, government officials and defence experts from NATO's 32 member states and Ukraine. The rapid integration of high tech and artificial intelligence into the armed forces presents a dilemma of entrusting part of their future to private companies while risking their sovereignty. One example is the civilian Starlink satellite network and its military counterpart, Starshield, which Ukraine needs. Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Kyiv has faced restrictions on access to Starshield, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX.

Companies driven by market forces and private capital demanding profits sit on one side, independent of political control. Military leaders who answer only to political authority and are obsessed with strategy, hierarchy and defence secrecy sit on the other. Between them is the race to connect the battlefield, from troop coordination to real-time terrain analysis, generating terabits of data that can decide a war's outcome and the fate of many lives. The articles cite the even more complex issue of so-called killer robots. Musk has shifted his stance on Ukraine many times, insisting any disruption was the responsibility of Washington, not SpaceX.

Analyst Tom Barton of the intelligence firm Janes said this is a difficult issue many ministries of defence are grappling with. Barton said that for companies to deliver the so-called networked battlefield, some access ideally needs to be given to confidential data. He said defence establishments, from space to land-based sensors and military communications, are experimenting with standalone exercises and varying levels of trust and access. A US company representative, speaking on condition of anonymity, said there is a lot of push or advocacy for military and government to have a closer relationship with industry. The representative said there is a fine line, and fumed that Elon Musk was doing things in Ukraine like slowing down the internet.

Major General Rainer Beeck, one of NATO's top cyberspace commanders, called it a hard nut to crack and said you have to make choices about which classification you make, for which data. Beeck said the problem is the trust. Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, insisted that trust is the most important thing, in architecture, in data sharing, in AI agents and in decision-making tools. Vandier said we need to close the fighter-factory gap and that Ukraine did it. The US company representative said you don't need to be 100 percent sovereign, but sovereign enough.

Mitch Free, vice president of international government at Vantor, which provides satellite imagery for defence and intelligence agencies, said smaller governments need to build up their capacity. Free said many may only own a handful of satellites and must weigh their intelligence value against the cost of building and operating them, and that this is where commercial help fills the gap. Beeck said that for large powers data collection is not the problem, and that if war would start they would get it, but then it is too late to organise, calling for a more proactive approach. Jean-Charles Ellermann-Kingombe, NATO's cyber and digital transformation chief, said the bottleneck is often not technology but permission: classification boundaries, national rules and trust decisions. He said the alliance must make AI adoption possible at scale, with these capabilities secure, interoperable and deployable within NATO's infrastructure by personnel who understand their value and their limitations.

Nearly five years of war have given Kyiv more experience than anyone else in NATO. The dynamics also vary according to the size of national defence budgets. Militaries without safeguards cannot entrust their fate to developers, who are often focused primarily on civilian needs. With boundaries constantly shifting, military leaders have little choice but to compromise. The articles leave open how the trust problem will be resolved and what safeguards militaries might adopt.

stories.Headline: Modi says skilled workers keep jobs as AI grows and India will host WorldSkills Asia in 2027
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi asserted on Saturday, November 21, 2026, that artificial intelligence cannot take away jobs from people with the right skills. He spoke at the fifth National Skill Convocation Ceremony, also called the National Kaushal Deekshant Samaroh, held in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. The event took place at the Indira Gandhi Pratishthan in Gomti Nagar before a gathering of roughly 2,000 people. Modi stressed that skilled workers would remain indispensable to the economy and urged for the modernization of Industrial Training Institute curricula. He noted that those with craftsmanship would see their demand rise as the world seeks trained technicians over university graduates.

The Prime Minister announced that India will host the WorldSkills Asia competition in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh, in the year 2027. He mentioned a semiconductor chip manufacturing factory by HCL and Foxconn near Jewar and BrahMos missile production within the state. Modi stated that students from Industrial Training Institutes deserve the same respect as those attending the Indian Institutes of Technology. He called for a change in mindset because some parents hesitate to disclose that their children enrolled in vocational training. The government aims to restore dignity to labour through the spirit of Shramev Jayate and upgrade machinery for students.

Modi said that no one can take away the employment of a person who possesses skills, regardless of growing artificial intelligence concerns. He recalled that skilled workers kept India functioning during the Covid pandemic when money alone could not ensure survival without essential services. The Prime Minister claimed that royal families in Saudi Arabia, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Qatar, and Kuwait credited Indian artisans for their cities. He mentioned an exercise where officials listed nearly 1,000 different kinds of work required by a person from birth to death. Modi asserted that India is moving towards becoming the world skill capital with its young people at the center.

Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said youth trained under Skill India will be the backbone of a developed and self-reliant India by 2047. Union minister Jayant Chaudhary asserted that there is tremendous interest across the world regarding the skilled workforce coming from India. Adityanath noted that the state partnered with Tata Technologies to introduce emerging technology courses at more than 150 different institutes. These courses include 3D printing, robotics, the Internet of Things, and drone technology, which helped 12,000 youths secure campus placements. The event was attended by Rajnath Singh, Pankaj Chaudhary, Keshav Prasad Maurya, Brajesh Pathak, Manoj Pandey, and Kapil Dev Agarwal.

Modi blamed the decline of traditional Indian crafts on foreign invasions and the British rule, which he said struck craftsmanship first. He claimed the colonial education system introduced by Thomas Babington Macaulay reduced skill based learning to producing paper pushing clerks. The Prime Minister highlighted traditional skills like metalwork, sculpture, steel making, Kalamkari, cotton textiles, and Banarasi and Kanchipuram silk. He specifically mentioned that the city of Lucknow has preserved its traditional craft of chikankari for many generations of artisans. Modi stated that the British destroyed skills in India specifically to advance their own industry during the period of colonial rule.

Next, the government will work to ensure vocational training keeps pace with industry requirements and technological advancements through new trade agreements. The Uttar Pradesh Skill Development Mission has trained over 1.7 million young people since 2017, with seven lakh securing jobs. The state continues to implement the Prime Minister Skill Mission to provide platforms for youth to harness their full potential. The articles leave open how the government will specifically modernize the curricula or train instructors in emerging technologies for students. They do not state when the specific machinery upgrades for the Industrial Training Institutes will be completed across the country.

stories.Headline: Australia spy chief Mike Burgess warns data centres and AI risk foreign interference
stories.Summary:
Mike Burgess, the director-general of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, warned in an interview with The Age on Nov 22 that data centres and artificial intelligence risk exposing Australia to foreign interference and malicious state actors. He raised the prospect of covert ownership of data centres, according to the newspaper, and said control of such infrastructure could give other nations physical or virtual access to technology. Burgess described the AI and data centre industries as having “equal hype, opportunity and threat”, the report said. The security chief has previously warned of rising cyberthreats by foreign governments, and in October a report from the Australian Signals Directorate said the nation faces escalating cyber and foreign interference threats.

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said on ABC Television on Nov 22 that the report was concerning, adding that “this is the world that we live in”. He said the situation was in a sense not new, but that the building of data centres creates a new vector and a new avenue for foreign actors to engage in. Marles said the government is very mindful of its own cybersecurity, according to the newspaper. Digital security has been an increasing concern in Australia, and in October OpenAI apologised for its AI models breaching the country’s government websites and promised to set up a new task force as part of reforms after the incident.

The warnings from Burgess and Marles place data centre ownership and artificial intelligence within the same frame of foreign interference and state-backed cyber threats that Australia’s security agencies have been raising through 2026. The October assessment from the Australian Signals Directorate described escalating cyber and foreign interference threats, and the OpenAI incident that month showed how AI systems could reach government websites. The Age interview and the deputy prime minister’s television remarks were published on the same day, Nov 22, linking the two industries to the country’s broader digital security concerns. The articles do not say what measures, reviews or reviews of data centre ownership might follow the warnings.

stories.Headline: China-linked hackers use AI agents to find zero-day flaw in medical-imaging software
stories.Summary:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a zero-day flaw in medical-imaging software. These attackers gained root access to a university server during a campaign in September. Amazon Threat Intelligence reported the incident this week after reconstructing the intrusion. The AI agents mapped the application interface and wrote files in eleven minutes. The operators set the goals and targets while the agents selected the methods.

The flaw affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup without login enabled. This path-traversal weakness, CVE-2026-133968, allows unauthenticated attackers to write files outside the storage folder. It received a critical security score of 9.8 out of 10. The maintainers merged a source code fix on October 19, 2026. No patched version is available for installation, as the newest release is from 2024.

Amazon Threat Intelligence identified the activity with moderate confidence by analyzing a Cairn control panel. They noted the use of Simplified Chinese prompts and China Standard Time settings. The company stated the agents worked with little step-by-step direction from the operator. Investigators believe the targets were likely of interest to China. They did not link the work to a named group or government.

The attack affected one university server and potentially a second university network. Amazon believes the second network was breached similarly but has not confirmed the compromise. The report does not show that clinical systems or patient records were taken. Other MONAI Label users are affected if they run the server under root. The campaign also included several failed operations on other targets.

MONAI Label is an open-source server used by research teams to label scans and train models. It is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework. The attackers used Cairn, an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers. The root access was achieved by planting a Python startup file. This file connected back to the attacker when a training feature started.

Users should block untrusted network access and turn on authentication for their servers. They are advised to run the server under limited accounts and restrict writable folders. Administrators must check for unusual training jobs and unexpected Python startup files. The articles leave open whether the second university network was actually compromised. It remains unknown if the attackers reached beyond the described university targets.

stories.Headline: KPMG rolls out KCi AI agents to US audit teams after cutting some timelines by up to three and a half weeks
stories.Summary:
KPMG LLP announced the U.S. rollout of KPMG Clara intelligence, or KCi, on November 17, 2026, from New York. The firm said KCi leads the profession to an AI-enabled, human-assured audit for audit committees, management teams, and KPMG auditors. KCi embeds specialized AI agents directly into auditor workflows rather than operating as a standalone tool. Auditors direct and review agent-orchestrated workflows, with agents automating routine tasks and first-pass documentation. The launch follows successful use in 2026, with KCi rolled out to more than 125 U.S. teams and 500 teams globally.

KPMG is aiming to deploy KCi in all private company audits in 2027 and plans a structured, phased rollout for public company audits. Automated data pipelines analyze 100% of transaction populations in selected audit areas, identifying outliers, trends, and anomalies for targeted auditor investigation. On some engagements, KPMG reports this shortened timelines by up to three and a half weeks and removed the need for clients to manually retrieve volumes of individual support documents. KCi operates within a governed environment grounded in KPMG audit methodology, professional standards, and the firm's Trusted AI framework. The technology foundation combines proprietary KPMG capabilities with enterprise technologies from relationships with Anthropic, Google Cloud, Microsoft, and OpenAI.

Christian Peo, Vice Chair of Audit and Assurance at KPMG U.S., said auditor judgment cannot be automated but technology helps remove barriers between data, analysis, and action. Peo said that when people spend less time assembling information and more time understanding it, they can focus on where the risk is and what needs to be challenged. He described the moment as defining for the profession, as fundamental as the transition from paper to digital workflows. KPMG said auditors retain responsibility for review and final judgment, and traceability lets teams inspect underlying data sources and corroborate findings. The firm said agents can generate and organize material, but responsibility does not transfer to the software.

KPMG is modernizing its audit operating model by strengthening role clarity, moving supervision and review earlier in the audit lifecycle, and creating greater consistency in how data is organized and used. The firm said nearly 1,000 Audit and Assurance interns attended training at its Lakehouse facility earlier this year on critical thinking, professional skepticism, and evaluation of AI-assisted work. KPMG said the approach simplifies the audit experience for client accounting teams by providing greater visibility into requests, milestones, and engagement activities. The announcement does not present the three-and-a-half-week result as an average across all engagements, describing it as a company-reported outcome from selected work. The announcement does not specify which provider powers each individual KCi function.

KPMG Clara is the firm's global smart audit platform, and KCi is built on it. KPMG said it was the first of the Big Four firms to organize itself along the same industry lines as clients. Over the past several years, the firm has built a secure data and technology foundation across KPMG Clara. KPMG said KCi is designed to evolve as technology advances and is the latest milestone in its long-term transformation of the audit experience. The articles state that KPMG has market-leading alliances with many of the world's leading software and services vendors.

KPMG's planned expansion in 2027 will test how consistently the model can operate across engagements while preserving human scrutiny. The articles leave open which provider powers each individual KCi function. The articles do not state how many public company audits the phased rollout will cover or on what timetable. The articles do not give the number of engagements behind the three-and-a-half-week result. The articles do not say what KCi costs or how the 2027 private company deployment will be sequenced.

stories.Headline: US Commerce Department restricts Chinese remote access to super intelligence chips and servers
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Commerce Department announced new restrictions on Monday, November 17, 2026, regarding remote access to super intelligence chips and servers. These rules aim to stop Chinese companies from bypassing sales limits by renting computer time in other countries. The Bureau of Industry and Security issued the interim final rule under the National Security Council and Treasury Department. These measures target cloud services and contract manufacturing at overseas foundries to prevent indirect access to advanced technology. The regulations officially took effect on November 19, 2026, to tighten controls over these alternative computing channels.

Suppliers need government permission for data centers providing power equal to roughly 330 advanced Nvidia chips to restricted entities. Licenses are now required for chip exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to higher diversion risks. Data centers and exporters must conduct due diligence to identify owners from Macau or Chinese state owned enterprises. Restrictions also cover Cuba, Iran, North Korea, and Russia, while foreign foundries need licenses for Chinese company manufacturing. TSMC and Samsung suspended shipments for nodes 16 nanometers or below, limiting Chinese firms to 28nm and 40nm nodes.

The Commerce Department stated the rule aligns remote access safeguards with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive technology. They noted that rapid advances in cloud infrastructure make it easier to access U.S. capabilities remotely through other countries. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Nvidia internal controls, suggesting executives would be dismissed if the company were a bank. President Donald Trump mentioned two different views on the approach, with one side favoring friendliness and another risking confrontation. He stated that both positions were acceptable and that he understood the different perspectives within his own administration.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun accused Washington of interfering in trade and overstretching the concept of national security for its benefit. He warned that China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests after the U.S. violated previous bilateral understandings. Representative John Moolenaar welcomed the rule, stating it sends a message that America is serious about closing dangerous export loopholes. Affected companies include ByteDance and Baidu subsidiary Kunlunxin, who may lose access to Samsung Electronics semiconductor shipments and services. Nvidia established an Export Control Oversight Committee of independent directors and legal professionals to strengthen its internal company controls.

The House passed the Remote Access Security Act in January to restrict foreign adversaries from using U.S. cloud computing services. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after admitting to an affair with a woman recruited by Chinese intelligence. The Justice Department is investigating if Singapore based Megaspeed transferred billions of dollars in advanced chips to Chinese end users. In February, Applied Materials paid a 252.5 million dollar penalty for illegally exporting equipment to China via South Korea. The Commerce Department had previously requested sales records from Nvidia regarding Megaspeed in May 2025 during its investigation.

President Trump will travel to Manila for a U.S. ASEAN summit and then to Shenzhen for an APEC leaders meeting. He is scheduled to hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday while these new trade restrictions are active. Congress is considering a defense bill and Senate measures for semiconductor tracking and congressional review of advanced AI chip licenses. The U.S. is encouraging allies like Japan and the Netherlands to align their export controls with current Washington policies. Articles leave open whether China will retaliate with rare earth export restrictions or if the Senate will pass legislation.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose a four-stage framework to evaluate AI outbreak alerts in conflict-affected health systems
stories.Summary:
Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Zhenhao Li, Yifan Yu, Panwang Pan and Wentao Zhu submitted arXiv paper 2606.14068 on 12 June 2026, and the v1 was posted at 03:29:34 UTC that day. The paper asks whether large language models apply consistent response standards to the same negative behavior under matched male-actor and female-actor conditions. The authors introduce GAMA-Bench, a gender-mirrored benchmark of 1,298 scenarios covering intimate relationship and public social conflicts. Experiments on 10 representative LLMs reveal a consistent male-disadvantaging asymmetry, with male actors receiving more punitive, escalatory and blame-centered framing. Female actors receive more therapeutic and empathy-oriented framing for the same misconduct, and the pattern persists across model families, scenario tracks, model scale and explicit thinking-style reasoning.

GAMA-Bench builds gender-neutral misconduct templates through controlled grids and cross-model review, then compiles them into paired first-person prompts with matched actor-gender and role-reference variations. The authors design a structured response-framing protocol to measure how models allocate punishment, empathy, escalation, instruction and blame. The paper is under review in Computation and Language, carries DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2606.14068, and its full text is 11,361 KB. The official code is available at a URL the paper gives. The submission history lists only the 12 June 2026 version.

The authors state that existing studies on gender bias in LLMs have largely focused on stereotypes, occupational associations or explicit harmful outputs. They ask whether LLMs apply consistent response standards to the same negative behavior under matched male-actor and female-actor conditions. They report that the male-disadvantaging asymmetry persists across model families, scenario tracks, model scale and explicit thinking-style reasoning. They describe the official code as available at the URL the paper gives. The paper is listed under review.

The bioengineer.org article, dated 21 November 2026, reports a mini review in Frontiers in Public Health on infectious disease surveillance in conflict-affected health systems. The authors synthesized evidence on artificial intelligence early-warning tools alongside operational experiences from conventional humanitarian disease surveillance programmes. They proposed a four-stage conceptual evaluation framework covering data readiness, alert performance, verification and decision-making, and public health action and equity. They emphasize that direct empirical evidence linking artificial intelligence outbreak warnings to improved clinical or health outcomes in crisis settings remains limited. Early predictive detection therefore cannot be treated as an established causal driver of reduced morbidity or mortality.

In Southwest Cameroon, routine integrated disease surveillance and response systems achieved timely reporting for cholera in only 16.3 percent of instances during intense conflict, compared to 40.7 percent during periods of reduced conflict intensity. In Borno State, Nigeria, a conventional Early Warning, Alert and Response System produced 13,737 alerts, yet only 16 required an immediate operational response after verification. In that deployment, 89.6 percent of the 13,737 alerts were verified within 24 hours, and subsequent investigations led to 9,794 alerts being discarded, 2,501 placed under monitoring and exactly 16 prompting an active response. Documented experiences from Yemen demonstrate persistent diagnostic, transport and governance hurdles that constrain outbreak verification during acute humanitarian emergencies. In Sudan, conflict-related disruptions to malaria reporting created difficulties in interpreting longitudinal disease indicators because facility registries were outdated.

Stage one examines whether surveillance inputs are sufficiently timely, complete, representative and geographically informative before models ingest them. The researchers differentiate between reporting delays and data completeness, noting that an empty surveillance registry entry can signify absent disease, an unsubmitted report, a non-operational medical facility or a severed communications link. Evaluations of Somalia's electronic Early Warning and Response Network demonstrated continuous reporting challenges, showing that failing to account for missingness risks training models that identify shifts in reporting logistics rather than genuine changes in transmission dynamics. Research across Ugandan refugee settlements and broader refugee surveillance networks revealed parallel databases, fragmented reporting streams and substantial coverage gaps, while findings from Lebanon showed difficulties in tracking refugee health when national registries do not disaggregate vulnerable cohorts. Stage two evaluates alert performance using information available strictly at the time of prediction, with indicators including sensitivity, positive predictive value, specificity, calibration, false-alert burden and warning lead time against prespecified reference standards.

An evaluation of a temporal data augmentation approach for outbreak detection in humanitarian settings demonstrated a sensitivity of 0.72 alongside an annual false-alert burden of approximately 2.8 to 3.6 false alerts per local government area across temporal folds. Stage three distinguishes an automated alert from a verified epidemiological event, and the researchers argue that evaluations must systematically track verification time, documentation of rationales and the availability of diagnostic testing. Stage four evaluates whether verified signals trigger timely, proportionate and equitable interventions, with indicators including the elapsed time from verification to response initiation, the overall geographic reach of interventions and whether responses address underserved or displaced groups. The review cautions that unequal distribution of logistical resources can cause well-served populations to receive rapid outbreak containment while remote or displaced groups face unmitigated transmission despite equal or greater biological need. The authors recommend shadow-mode prospective evaluations, where model predictions run in parallel with existing surveillance workflows without directing operational resources.

The researchers conducted a structured literature search in Scopus covering publications released from January 2015 through October 2026. The search strategy synthesized literature across four central concepts: artificial intelligence and machine learning, outbreak detection and early-warning forecasting, surveillance data quality and timeliness, and conflict-affected health systems. During reference verification, the authors systematically separated direct evidence regarding artificial intelligence model performance from broader contextual evidence describing conventional surveillance programs. The authors note that operational difficulties identified in routine surveillance, such as transport constraints and governance disruptions, provide realistic implementation context but cannot be taken as direct proof that machine learning improves outcomes. A primary limitation of the mini review is its focused narrative scope, which did not attempt an exhaustive systematic assessment across all existing surveillance literature.

The analyzed studies exhibited substantial heterogeneity in disease targets, population demographics, epidemiological outcomes and evaluation protocols, preventing direct statistical comparison. Direct empirical evidence linking artificial intelligence outbreak warnings to improved clinical outcomes in conflict-affected regions remains scarce, and findings from conventional humanitarian surveillance programmes provide contextual insight rather than direct measures of machine-learning effectiveness. The proposed four-stage evaluation framework remains conceptual and requires prospective empirical validation across diverse epidemiological settings before its causal assumptions can be established. The authors outline methodological priorities including nowcasting, missingness imputation, uncertainty-aware alert thresholds and abstention strategies under live operational constraints, and implementation research into governance structures, clear chains of accountability, human oversight and whether complex machine-learning algorithms offer verifiable operational advantages over simpler hybrid models combining standard indicators with local knowledge. The review concludes that the public health value of artificial intelligence in conflict-affected outbreak surveillance cannot be measured solely by mathematical accuracy or prediction speed.

stories.Headline: Philippines labor department joins AI council to prepare workers for AI shift
stories.Summary:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order 131 on Nov. 12, adopting a national AI governance framework and creating an interagency council to guide the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence in the country. Under that order, the Department of Labor and Employment was designated as a member of the National Artificial Intelligence Council, which will coordinate, facilitate and monitor implementation of the framework. The department announced its role in a statement issued on Friday and signed by Secretary Francis Tolentino, according to The Manila Times. As a council member, the department will take part in policy discussions and coordinate government efforts to address AI's impact on employment and skills development.

The department will also support the council's technical working group on capabilities, which is tasked with developing action plans for a national AI competency and digital workforce development program. The framework serves as the national strategic guide for policy formulation, regulatory coordination, institutional development and capacity-building to support the country's AI ecosystem. It seeks to ensure that AI is developed and used responsibly, safely, securely and inclusively while strengthening the country's capacity to adapt to emerging technologies. The department said it will work with other government agencies, the private sector, academe and other stakeholders to strengthen workers' competencies and prepare them for emerging employment opportunities.

The same partners will help address potential risks arising from AI adoption in workplaces, the department said in its statement. Secretary Tolentino signed that statement, which laid out the department's role under the new framework. The council's technical working group on capabilities is expected to develop the action plans for the national competency and workforce program. The articles do not say when those plans are due or what funding the effort will receive.

stories.Headline: Elon Musk warns AI companies face a severe cash crunch by 2027 due to data center delays
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk warned that the artificial intelligence industry could face a severe cash crunch in 2027 on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The xAI chief executive posted his concerns on the social media platform X regarding the race to expand computing capacity. He stated that delays in getting data centres operational could leave companies scrambling for hundreds of billions of dollars in capital. This financial challenge arises because companies must pay for infrastructure before those facilities can reliably serve customers and generate income. Musk believes that even a few months of cumulative industry delays would create a massive need for additional working capital.

The crisis involves spending on chips, servers, data centres, cooling systems, and electricity in places like the United States and Canada. IDC reported global AI infrastructure spending reached 121.4 billion dollars in the second quarter of 2026, a 53 percent increase. IDC raised its full year 2026 forecast to 521 billion dollars, while five major tech companies spent 400 billion in 2025. US and Canadian net new data centre IT capacity is projected to rise from 8 gigawatts in 2026 to 20 gigawatts. The IEA estimates global data centre electricity consumption could rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030.

Elon Musk is responsible for these warnings and said that getting this amount of compute turned on and cooled is hard. He asked where the money will come from if companies need hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital. He noted that the cash shortage is going to be nuts next year due to the difficulty of reliable operations. Musk responded to a user who argued that AI stocks remained undervalued despite the rising costs of various key components. He highlighted a problem with the economics of the boom, specifically the gap between massive spending and actual revenue generation.

Other users argued that inference is becoming increasingly profitable and that demand for AI research and model development is growing. Companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic are affected as they spend massive sums to secure compute for chatbots and tools. Investors are also affected, as some speculate the AI bubble popped after the S&P 500 and Dow entered correction. Financial regulators in Taiwan responded to market volatility by limiting short selling, similar to actions taken during the 2008 housing crisis. Data centre operators are also at risk if their multibillion-dollar investments fail to generate the anticipated revenue from customers.

The IEA noted that the capacity of specialised AI data centres had more than tripled over the previous 18 months of expansion. S&P Global reported in November 20 that power shortages, grid connection delays, and local community opposition are complicating data centre expansion. The industry faces obstacles in securing electricity, connecting facilities to power grids, and obtaining necessary approvals from various local government authorities. Some investors appear bearish on chip companies continuing to notch soaring profits, suggesting that data centre construction faces serious headwinds. Recent setbacks include a blue midterm wave and backlash from the communities where these large data centres are being built.

Intercontinental Exchange launched a tool on November 17 to assess the risk of US data centre projects being delayed or halted. This tool considers local economic conditions, permitting records, and the costs of water and electricity to evaluate potential project risks. The articles leave open whether companies can secure the hundreds of billions of dollars in working capital that Musk says they need. It remains unclear if the industry can overcome the electricity shortages and grid connection delays mentioned by the S&P Global report. The reports do not state if the projected capacity increases for 2027 will be achieved despite these significant financial hurdles.

stories.Headline: University of California signs $1.2 million annual OpenAI deal for campuswide ChatGPT access
stories.Summary:
The University of California signed a systemwide agreement with OpenAI that is worth $1.2 million a year and will give students access to ChatGPT and other artificial intelligence tools, according to the New York Post. The partnership will bring OpenAI technology, including ChatGPT Edu and Codex, to UC campuses in the coming weeks. The deal covers basic AI models, while individual campuses and users will have the option to buy access to more advanced versions at discounted rates. It expands on a 2024 campus-by-campus agreement with OpenAI, and UC President James B. Milliken described it as a way to make the technology more accessible while protecting student data and cutting costs.

Milliken wrote in a letter to faculty that the purchase would help ensure equitable access to widely used tools while providing stronger data protections and lower costs. The commitment reportedly caught members of UC's Academic Senate off guard, and faculty leaders raised concerns late last month that administrators had failed to sufficiently consult educators before moving forward. Academic Senate Chair Susannah Scott said in a statement that the senate believes it is unwise to give students universal access to a tool capable of performing the academic work required to earn a degree without first addressing the concerns of the faculty responsible for curriculum, teaching and academic integrity. A UC spokesperson pushed back on claims that faculty had been left out, telling EdSource that the senate had been consulted and that its feedback had been thoughtful and helpful, and said the university would continue working with the Academic Senate and other faculty groups on best AI practices.

Greg Leazer, an associate professor of information studies at UCLA, told the Los Angeles Times that ChatGPT reduces learning and substitutes homogenized slop in place of the productive struggle of careful reading, discussion and writing. Milliken has stressed that providing access to the technology does not require students or professors to use it, and that the agreement does not establish any new academic policies. Supporters have argued the partnership is about giving all students access to tools that wealthier classmates can already afford, rather than letting AI become an advantage reserved for those who can pay for premium services. Some educators say the technology is being forced on them whether they want it or not, and professors recently told the Post they feel AI is being shoved down their throats.

UC Berkeley mathematics professor Richard Borcherds, who made headlines last month for no longer grading his students' homework because of AI, said he now bases grades mainly on in-person exams with no electronic devices allowed. He said online exams are now a waste of time because several students just use AI to answer the questions, and that he cannot tell which students are using AI but notices the average score increases a lot in online exams. The criticism comes amid broader concerns about declining academic skills, including reports of college instructors having to teach students basic math.

stories.Headline: Gillibrand seeks investigation into AI role in Iran war
stories.Summary:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand warned on Sunday, November 22, 2026, about the consequences of using artificial intelligence in the war against Iran without human oversight, according to Al Jazeera reporting cited by 8am.media. She called for an investigation into the role that artificial intelligence is playing in that war, the report said. Gillibrand said artificial intelligence is effective at intercepting missiles, but she argued that a lack of human oversight could put civilian lives at risk. She warned that she did not want a girls' school in a foreign country to be targeted because of an error made by artificial intelligence.

Her remarks come after a missile struck a girls' school in southern Iran on February 28, the same day the war began, according to the article. More than 170 people were killed in that attack, mostly female students, the report said. The article does not say who launched the missile or whether artificial intelligence played any part in the strike. It also gives no further details on the investigation Gillibrand is seeking or on what any inquiry would cover.

Gillibrand is a U.S. senator, and she made her warning about artificial intelligence in the Iran war in remarks reported by Al Jazeera on Sunday. She said artificial intelligence works well for intercepting missiles but that human oversight is needed to protect civilians. She warned that she did not want a girls' school in a foreign country hit because of an artificial intelligence error. The article does not say what response, if any, she received or what other officials said about her call.

The article offers no further context beyond the February 28 strike on the girls' school in southern Iran and the casualty figure of more than 170 people, mostly female students. It does not say what happens next with the investigation Gillibrand requested or whether any body has agreed to conduct one. It also does not say how artificial intelligence is being used in the war beyond missile interception. No further details on the senator's proposal or on the school attack are given in the report.

stories.Headline: OpenAI releases GPT-Live-1.1 with standby billing for idle voice sessions
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released GPT-Live-1.1, a full-duplex voice model for multilingual conversations, in its API under the model ID gpt-live-1.1 on November 21, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. The model can listen while it speaks and follows GPT-Live-1, which reached the API on September 10, 2026, and has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15. It accepts audio and text inputs and outputs, supports streaming and function calling, and does not support images, video, structured outputs, fine-tuning or predicted outputs. The release also adds standby, a cheaper billing state for idle sessions, and the model runs only on OpenAI's cloud through v1/live/sessions, with clients connecting over WebRTC or WebSocket.

Live sessions hold a 128,000-token default context window, and instructions can run up to 16,384 tokens. Standby bills idle WebRTC time at $0.02 per minute versus $0.05 active, a 60% lower rate, or $1.20 per hour against $3.00. Standby pauses inference during silence while the connection stays open, the server emits session.paused after the timeout and session.resumed when the user speaks, and the session ID and history are kept. OpenAI warns the first reply after a short utterance may be slower and says the microphone track should stay active during standby, and standby works for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1.

Voice sessions are billed by duration, and the GPT-Live-1 model page says billing is per second, while backend model and tool usage are billed separately. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model, and OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks, though third-party backends also work. The Live conversations guide sets delegation.type to client or responses, where responses mode uses OpenAI models and client mode connects your own backend. Switching an existing Live session requires setting the model to gpt-live-1.1 and starting a new session.

OpenAI says the model speaks with more natural and consistent accents across languages, handles transcription, letters and numbers better, and completes tasks more reliably than GPT-Live-1. OpenAI published no benchmark scores for 1.1, so the quality gains are self-reported with no numbers. The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech, and OpenAI says the model reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model, handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively. Outbound SIP calling reached all organizations on November 2, so phone agents are supported, and GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1 have separate concurrent-session limits that each apply across inference regions, though the 1.1 page does not publish tier numbers.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics opens an AI home experience store in Singapore to test and expand its AI appliances across Southeast Asia
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics established an artificial intelligence home advance base in Singapore on November 23, 2026, to target the Southeast Asian market. The company opened this new experience store to reach a regional population of 700 million people through a strategic base. This outpost allows the company to verify the marketability of its AI home appliances before expanding into other neighboring countries. The company aims to use Singapore as a gateway to enter the broader Southeast Asian region and its premium consumers. LG Electronics intends to promote its AI home competitiveness and expand customer contacts to major countries such as Malaysia.

The company opened an AI home experience store of about 140 square meters at the Milenia Walk complex shopping mall. This space implements real residential areas including a kitchen, a living room, a laundry room, and a children's room. Customers use the LG ThinQ app to connect and control various home appliances and Internet of Things devices. The store features Fit and Max refrigerators and wash towers designed to minimize gaps between walls and home appliances. These specific products target the local residential environments of Singapore, which contains many apartments and condominiums.

Lee Gun-ho is the head of the Singapore branch of LG Electronics and is responsible for this new outpost. He stated that the company will provide an AI home experience that is differentiated by products optimized for local lifestyles. He noted that the services are specifically designed to fit the residential environment and the lifestyle of the local people. Employees at the store use dioramas implemented in transparent OLED to introduce the various AI home solutions to the customers. This approach helps the company inform visitors about the specific benefits of their differentiated AI home products and services.

Customers in Singapore are the primary people affected by the opening of this new AI home experience space. These consumers can now directly experience how to control their home appliances using the integrated LG ThinQ mobile application. Global companies also use the Singapore market to monitor consumer reactions before they enter the wider Southeast Asian market. The company targets premium consumers who live in the many apartments and condominiums found throughout the city of Singapore. This allows the company to test local reactions to its specialized home appliance products in a key market.

LG Electronics started its home appliance subscription business in Singapore last year before securing this AI home experience base this year. The company is speeding up its efforts to tap into the local market by establishing this strategic advance base. Grandview Research claims the home appliance market in five major Southeast Asian countries will grow from 21.25 billion dollars in 2024. This market is expected to reach 30.9 billion dollars by 2030 according to the global market research company. The average annual growth rate for this specific region is expected to be 6.7 percent from 2025 to 2030.

The company will now use this Singapore base to expand its business operations into other neighboring Southeast Asian countries. LG Electronics plans to increase its customer contacts in major markets like Malaysia using the data from this store. The company will continue to promote its AI home competitiveness to reach more consumers across the wider regional market. The articles leave open how the company will specifically implement its expansion into the other four major Southeast Asian countries. They also do not state the specific timeline for when the business will move into the Malaysian market.

stories.Headline: Defiance and GraniteShares plan leveraged Anthropic ETFs trading Nov 23
stories.Summary:
Anthropic PBC began trading its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT on November 19, 2026. The developer of Claude priced its initial public offering of 980 million shares at $83.00 per share on November 18, 2026. The price came in above the initially indicated range of $70.00 to $78.00. The offering represented approximately $81.34 billion in total gross proceeds, including shares sold by existing shareholders. Anthropic itself sold 956,351,354 shares, representing approximately $79.4 billion in gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and expenses.

The offering included a 30-day option for underwriters to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley acted as representatives of the underwriters. The stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, November 19. That opening price valued Anthropic at more than $2 trillion on a fully diluted basis, which also counts stock options, restricted stock and convertible securities. Anthropic is based in San Francisco, was founded in 2021 and is organized as a Delaware public benefit corporation.

GraniteShares said the GraniteShares 2x Long Anthropic Daily ETF (Nasdaq: AIL) and the GraniteShares 2x Short Anthropic Daily ETF (Nasdaq: ANS) are expected to begin trading on Monday, November 23, 2026. Will Rhind, Founder and CEO of GraniteShares, said Anthropic's debut is one of the most closely watched market events of the year. He said new listings can move sharply while the market finds its footing and that leverage magnifies that in both directions. He encouraged traders to read the prospectus and monitor their positions every day. He said the funds are designed for investors who want to express a short-term view on Anthropic's shares, up or down, and who seek 2x the daily move.

Defiance ETFs said its Defiance 2X ANT Long Daily ETF (Nasdaq: ANTC) and Defiance 2X ANT Short Daily ETF (Nasdaq: ANTQ) are expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on Monday, November 23, 2026. ANTC seeks 200% of the daily percentage change in ANT's share price and ANTQ seeks -200%, neither for a period other than a single trading day. Total annual fund operating expenses are 0.71% for each fund, according to the prospectus. The funds obtain exposure through swap agreements with financial institutions and may also use listed options, and they rebalance at or near each close.

An investor could lose the full value of an investment within a single trading day. According to its prospectus, Anthropic reported revenue of $33.2 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, compared with $2.5 billion for the same period of 2025. It reported a net loss of $104.0 billion for the 2026 period, of which $94.3 billion came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs. GraniteShares, headquartered in New York City, was founded in 2016 by Will Rhind and managed $12.27 billion in assets as of September 30, 2026.

Defiance was founded in 2018 and specializes in thematic, income and leveraged ETFs. Anthropic delivers Claude through its models, developer platform and applications such as Claude Code. ANTC and ANTQ are expected to begin trading at the 9:30 a.m. ET open on Monday, November 23, 2026, and the expected date may change.

Shares of ANTC and ANTQ cannot be purchased until the funds begin trading. The funds are not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by Anthropic, and an investment in the funds is not a direct investment in Anthropic. The articles leave open whether the underwriters will exercise their 30-day option for up to 147 million additional shares. The articles also leave open how ANT will trade after its first session.

stories.Headline: Philippe Laffont buys over $1 million each in Salesforce, Microsoft, Meta and Shopify in Q3
stories.Summary:
Philippe Laffont of Coatue Management rebalanced his portfolio in Q3, and four of his biggest buys, each more than $1 million in the quarter, were in the application layer space rather than hardware. His largest purchase in the quarter was Salesforce, followed by Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Shopify. Geoffrey Seiler wrote about the buys for The Motley Fool on November 22, 2026. The article appeared on Yahoo Finance and on fool.com. The article said Laffont seemed particularly bullish on AI agents.

Salesforce created its Data 360 solution, which used zero-copy technology to retrieve data from within an organization and from outside storage places like cloud providers and data warehouses without the time and cost of moving it. Salesforce then acquired Informatica to clean and organize this data. Since then it has acquired Fin, Qualified, Cresta and Braze to improve its front- and back-end for AI agents. Microsoft's Copilot saw an eightfold increase in customers to more than 50,000 users last quarter. Microsoft shifted to a hybrid seat plus consumption model for Copilot and GitHub, and it said agentic AI consumption features at GitHub have more than doubled since the pricing change.

Microsoft said the pricing strategy shift is boosting average revenue per user growth and increasing its total addressable market. Meta's Muse AI agents could be a game-changer for the social media company and its stock. AI is already driving strong ad revenue at Meta's social media sites by feeding users more content and ads they are interested in, leading to a higher ad load and stronger ad prices. Meta's growth driver will be facilitating e-commerce purchases, with revenue from affiliate or transaction fees. Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol with Alphabet and others and uses that protocol for its AI-ready database called Shopify Catalog.

Catalog-based searches at Shopify converted to sales at double the rate of ordinary searches last quarter. Shopify's Sidekick AI assistant saw daily active users soar 3.7 times year over year last quarter. Shopify recently launched a new online store builder to help merchants personalize their digital stores and build them more quickly. The article said Salesforce has worked diligently to build the foundation to become a leading agentic AI company in the enterprise space. The article said AI agents are only as good as the data to which they have access.

The article said Microsoft looks set to be a big AI software-as-a-service winner given how ingrained it is with enterprise productivity tools. The article said Meta's massive user base puts it at a big advantage to capture a nice chunk of the agentic AI commerce market. The article said Shopify looks positioned to be one of the biggest winners for agentic commerce. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include Salesforce among the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now. Geoffrey Seiler has positions in Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Salesforce, and The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Salesforce and Shopify.

The article said Salesforce's buy of Salesforce makes a lot of sense if Laffont is bullish on AI agents. The article said Microsoft's growth is being driven by its cloud computing unit, Azure. The article said Meta has been one of the best companies at employing AI to drive growth in its core business. The article said Shopify's e-commerce software company is one of the best ways to play the agentic commerce theme. The article said Meta's consumer AI agents can help individuals perform a lot of different tasks.

The article did not give the size of any individual purchase beyond saying each was more than $1 million. The article did not give the exact date in Q3 when the buys were made. The article did not say what Laffont or Coatue said about the purchases. The article did not give the size of Laffont's stakes after the buys. The article did not say whether Laffont still held the shares at the time of writing.

stories.Headline: US Senate passes permitting reform bill to accelerate energy construction for AI power demand
stories.Summary:
Financial markets suffered major losses this week as concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble grew. The US Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday to speed up energy construction. Confusion is also growing over new Medicaid work requirement rules that are set to begin in January. Investors feared the AI boom could bust despite a record initial public offering from Anthropic on Thursday. The entire stock market was pummeled on Friday during one of the worst weeks in years.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 passed the Senate with a 62-33 vote. It rewrites the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act. The bill changes the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 and shortens timelines for getting most permits. It requires data centers to pay for energy usage and exempts some projects from environmental review. These changes aim to lower energy costs and speed up oil, gas, solar, and hydropower projects.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Ruben Gallego supported the bill to bring down carbon emissions. Senator Martin Heinrich said the legislation provides a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito stated that Americans deserve bipartisan solutions that make life more affordable. These authors argued that cutting red tape allows more energy production and lowers prices for the public. They believe working people cannot afford to wait years for these necessary infrastructure improvements to happen.

The Sierra Club and Natural Resource Defense Council opposed the bill because it weakens bedrock environmental protections. Executive Director Loren Blackford said the bill is deeply flawed and threatens endangered species and tribal sovereignty. Nearly a dozen tribal organizations warned that the changes limit Indigenous input on sites with important cultural significance. Labor unions, oil and gas companies, and most clean energy industry groups expressed their support for the measure. Many voters in recent elections prioritized cost of living and affordability issues over these environmental concerns.

The NASDAQ dropped 10 percent this week, marking its worst performance since the pandemic year of 2020. The S&P and Dow Jones indices both ended the week in a correction after dropping 10 percent. In September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years, increasing borrowing costs. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang resigned this month following suspicions of an affair with a woman spying for China. Democrats are set to take over Congress and many state governments in January and promise to slow AI.

The permitting bill must now clear the House before it reaches the desk of President Donald Trump. The House is out of session next week for Thanksgiving and must extend government funding by December 11. Republicans may need Democratic votes in a narrowly divided chamber to pass the bill before January. It remains unclear if the House will pass the bill or if Democrats will wait until January. The articles leave open whether the AI market is a bubble or just a temporary readjustment.
