stories.Headline: Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Framework Calibrates Urban Traffic Fundamental Diagrams in Jordan
stories.Summary:
Transportation engineers developed and tested a hybrid calibration framework combining video trajectory analytics, mobile smartphone telemetry, and machine learning optimization to measure how vehicles move along congested urban roadways. Researcher Laith D. Alomari conducted the study, published in the Journal of King Saud University ,  Engineering Sciences, evaluating macroscopic traffic fundamental diagrams across thirty heterogeneous road segments in Irbid, Jordan. The experimental campaign gathered empirical field observations across thirty distinct locations throughout Irbid, including major arterials, intersection approaches, roundabouts, and mid-block road segments. Each site was monitored for thirty to sixty minutes during multiple weekdays, covering both peak and off-peak travel periods. In total, the field deployments produced approximately 3,000 validated observation points.

The investigation treated each monitored road segment and intersection approach as an independent link-level traffic system rather than merging all data points into a single city-wide diagram. Data collection relied on thirty high-definition video cameras recording at 1080p resolution and thirty frames per second, processed using YOLOv8 with Deep SORT. The team also gathered mobile sensor telemetry from volunteer drivers operating approximately twenty participating vehicles, logging GPS coordinates and accelerometer signals at 1 Hz. The validated microscopic trajectory records were aggregated into macroscopic traffic variables using fifteen-second observation intervals. Speed curves declined sharply once traffic density reached approximately 35 to 40 vehicles per kilometer, while flow-density plots peaked within a critical density boundary of 30 to 35 vehicles per kilometer.

The researchers implemented a sequential, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization routine pairing a Genetic Algorithm with Bayesian Optimization to refine model parameters while maintaining physical interpretability. The Genetic Algorithm conducted a global parameter search, capping free-flow speed between 40 and 120 kilometers per hour and jam density between 80 and 250 vehicles per kilometer. Bayesian Optimization then applied a Gaussian process surrogate model with exploration-exploitation acquisition functions to locate optimal basins of convergence with high numerical stability. The two-stage routine yielded parameter variance of less than 8 percent across test iterations and showed smooth convergence within fifteen to twenty-five generations. The authors emphasized that reported numerical parameters characterize link-level performance across specific road sections and roundabouts rather than serving as network-wide macroscopic fundamental diagrams or universal engineering standards.

Baseline formulations yielded free-flow speeds generally estimated between 62 and 68 kilometers per hour and jam densities clustering around 130 to 160 vehicles per kilometer. At Site S02, the baseline Underwood model achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.93 and a root mean square error of 4.9 kilometers per hour, outperforming the linear and logarithmic alternatives. The refinement process reduced root mean square errors by approximately 15 to 25 percent across the evaluated sites compared with standard baseline regression, while lifting the coefficient of determination for the Underwood formulation up to 0.96. A Support Vector Regression model with a radial basis function kernel, evaluated on a 70 percent training, 15 percent validation, and 15 percent testing split, achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.97 and a root mean square error of 3.9 kilometers per hour. The authors noted its functional black-box nature, which prevents direct physical interpretation of structural roadway indicators such as roadway carrying capacity or spatial vehicle packing thresholds.

Classical analytical expressions, originally introduced decades ago under assumptions of uniform vehicular streams and strict lane compliance, often diverge from empirical observations in rapidly growing developing cities. In these environments, mixed fleets, weak lane discipline, and volatile flow transitions complicate standard theoretical assumptions, creating an operational need for low-cost, localized calibration methods. The investigators initially fitted four canonical analytical formulations using standard nonlinear least-squares regression: the linear model proposed by Greenshields, Greenberg’s logarithmic formulation, Underwood’s exponential decay structure, and the multi-regime exponential-polynomial model introduced by Drake and colleagues. The vehicular mix mirrored standard developing urban streams, comprising passenger automobiles, minibuses, motorcycles, and light commercial vehicles. Data collection relied on a dual-modality sensing strategy designed to bypass expensive fixed roadway detectors such as inductive loops or radar systems.

The framework integrated the calibrated models into a physics-guided hybrid architecture, with the evolutionary-optimized analytical equations defining the base physical trajectory and the Support Vector Regression component acting as an adaptive residual corrector predicting localized deviations. When aggregated across all field study locations using observation-weighted metrics, the resulting empirical dataset yielded an average free-flow speed of approximately 65 kilometers per hour, a critical density of approximately 32 vehicles per kilometer, and a jam density of approximately 145 vehicles per kilometer. The field empirical trials were confined to thirty locations within a single city, excluding broader environmental variables such as inclement weather, variable geometric grades, and dynamic traffic signal splits. Because traffic density was derived through flow and speed calculations, comparative evaluations measured relative mathematical fit rather than causal transport mechanisms. The research team identified the low-cost sensing workflow and hybrid algorithmic framework as scalable and transferable tools for developing metropolitan regions, while cautioning that direct operational deployments require localized parameter recalibration.

Articles.Title: Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Framework Calibrates Urban Traffic Fundamental Diagrams in Jordan

stories.Headline: Law firm argues AI legal advice still needs a human lawyer to catch hidden risks
stories.Summary:
Michael Kyprianou & Co. LLC published an article on 20 November 2026 arguing that AI legal advice still needs a human lawyer. The article says generative AI tools like ChatGPT can draft contracts in seconds. It says speed and polish do not guarantee legal protection. It says relying on chatbots without professional oversight exposes businesses to hidden risks. It says these risks include hallucinated legal provisions and unenforceable clauses that only reveal their flaws when disputes arise.

The article says ChatGPT launched in November 2022. It cites Wolter's Kluwer's 'Future Ready Lawyer 2024' report finding that 76% of in-house lawyers use generative AI at least once a week. It says they use it for document analysis, first drafts, translation and case law searches. It says a 2024 Stanford study found popular language models hallucinating in 69-88% of legal queries. It says a 2025 Stanford RegLab and Yale study found specialised legal tools gave inaccurate answers in 17-33% of cases.

The article says no rule prohibits lawyers from using AI. It says full responsibility for the content and consequences of documents rests with the lawyer, regardless of whether a digital tool was used. It says professional bodies such as the National Chamber of Legal Advisers in Poland already issue guidance. It says law firms using AI responsibly rely on Enterprise or API versions with security certifications, anonymise data and uphold procedures against informal AI use. It says sharing personal data with a provider makes you a data controller and requires a data processing agreement (DPA).

The article says a lawyer asks about your business, what you cannot afford to lose and what the other side might do. It says a chatbot answers only what you typed, not what you forgot to mention. It says a lawyer reads the other side's drafts as an adversary would. It says a chatbot does not know your bargaining position or what you should walk away from. It says generic text can quietly breach mandatory provisions or ignore recent changes.

The article says the old rule 'garbage in, garbage out' means the quality of an answer depends on the quality of the question. It says asking the correct question requires knowing what the right answer looks like. It says AI looks cheaper because the cost of a mistake is invisible when you choose. It says if AI is wrong you may face a dispute over a clause that does not say what you intended, a payment you cannot enforce or a missed deadline. It says these costs usually exceed a consultation and occur when your options are limited.

The article says a good law firm uses AI for faster drafts, research and document analysis, then verifies every source and spends the saved time on advice. It says AI can help you prepare by explaining a term, summarising a text or listing questions for a meeting. It says AI should not decide when you are about to sign something, which may involve a significant sum of money, when a relationship is at stake, when you are in dispute with the other party, or when a deadline is approaching. It says AI is a real tool that raises the quality of legal services but does not replace judgement, accountability or someone working to solve your problem. It says use AI to prepare and rely on a lawyer when the decision matters.

Articles.Title: AI Or A Lawyer? Why Legal Advice Still Needs A Human - Legal 500

stories.headline_source: AI Or A Lawyer? Why Legal Advice Still Needs A Human

stories.Headline: Researchers find phone accelerometer models detect quakes best at higher sampling rates and tight false alarm budgets
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a comparative evaluation showing that deep learning models running directly on smartphones can detect earthquake signals from built-in accelerometers, but how well they perform depends heavily on sensor sampling rates and the allowed number of false alarms. The team tested five neural network architectures to tackle long-standing problems in crowd-sourced earthquake early warning, including severe data imbalance, limited computing power on phones, and the difficulty of modeling signals over time. Crowd-sourced warning systems use accelerometers inside everyday smartphones to widen seismic monitoring across earthquake-prone regions, yet deployment has been held back by the huge imbalance between constant human vibration and rare earthquakes. To benchmark the architectures rigorously, the investigators built a unified dataset of 35.4 million two-second windows drawn from roughly 186,000 recordings, covering broadband seismometer traces, shake-table smartphone experiments and human-activity data in a 60-gigabyte archive.

The team handled training difficulties with a stratified majority-class under-sampling approach based on a sampling index, which kept the original 60-gigabyte archive while balancing the test-set positive-to-negative ratio from 79.74 to 1 down to 1 to 1. The same method cut the number of training windows per epoch by a factor of 8.6, making training more practical. Model comparisons showed contrasting strengths: an attention-augmented network combining convolutional layers, bidirectional recurrent units and Bahdanau attention reached an area under the curve of 0.9617 with the smallest generalization gap, an absolute difference of 0.004. A dilated temporal convolutional network reached a higher overall area under the curve of 0.9688, but because broadband seismometers made up 99.99 percent of positive test windows, the researchers stratified validation by sensor provenance.

Discrimination stayed robust at 0.944 to 0.962 when seismic and non-seismic classes shared the same instrument type, but accuracy dropped to between 0.86 and 0.92 for earthquakes recorded on 50-hertz smartphones. Performance fell to chance levels on devices sampling at 25 hertz, where the crucial 0.5 to 20 hertz seismic band is only partly observable. On the deployment side, 8-bit quantized models occupied between 44 and 138 kilobytes, while built-in operator variants on Android devices needed 239 to 486 kilobytes and ran inferences in 3.2 to 6.4 milliseconds per window. Under a budget allowing 100 false alarms per device-day, the Bahdanau attention architecture detected 76 percent of seismometer-recorded events and 61 percent of smartphone-recorded events, while the dilated temporal convolutional network detected 53 percent and 33 percent respectively.

The evaluation was carried out by Şara, Almaqtari, Eken, Koç, Arslan, Kahveci and Atay, and their paper, Real-time seismic detection with edge-AI: a balanced comparison, appears in Cluster Computing, volume 30, issue 1, Article 47, with DOI 10.1007/s10586-026-06833-z. The findings show that the ranking of models by unconstrained receiver operating metrics can reverse once realistic false alarm budgets are applied, which matters for anyone choosing an architecture for a phone-based warning system. The results also indicate that sensor bandwidth sets a hard limit, since phones sampling at 25 hertz cannot reliably capture the seismic frequencies the models depend on. The articles do not say what deployment or follow-up work comes next.

stories.Headline: Futurist Silvia Leal warns quantum computing threatens current encryption methods
stories.Summary:
Silvia Leal, a futurist who has advised the European Commission for 15 years, gave a new interview on the series Tomorrow in which she warned that quantum computing poses a fundamental threat to current cybersecurity practices. In the interview she described how modern cyberattacks work, saying attackers get into a company, stay there, wait, spy and gather information, data, projects and knowledge of everything. Leal, who has also presented a technology series on RTVE, Spain's public broadcaster, said current encryption methods could become obsolete and that existing security protocols are vulnerable to attacks using the processing power of quantum computers. She explained that the speed at which quantum computers can break current encryption standards requires proactive adaptation rather than reactive damage control.

Leal's 15-year collaboration with the European Commission has recently focused on the intersection of artificial intelligence and industries such as retail, food and automotive. She argued that trust is the central issue for AI adoption, because many organizations moved quickly without putting IT governance, controls and reliable data in place. She also called for continuous professional development, noting that skills require refreshing every 15 to 18 months and that experienced professionals should embrace learning from younger colleagues. Shekhar Natarajan, host of Tomorrow, echoed that sentiment, saying life is about lifelong learning and that you never stop it.

Leal detailed how successful cyberattacks are no longer immediate extractions of data but prolonged, insidious infiltrations that let attackers accumulate comprehensive intelligence before any disruptive action. She said the threat demands a new generation of cybersecurity specialists who can adapt as the technological landscape rapidly evolves. The emphasis on adaptability is important for a workforce that must navigate constant change and secure systems against emerging quantum threats. The articles do not say what the European Commission or any other body plans to do next in response to her advice.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro signs AI ad disclosure law taking effect in December
stories.Summary:
Governor Josh Shapiro signed Pennsylvania's Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, known as SB 806, into law in late October 2026. The law takes effect December 21, 2026. Under it, an advertiser may not run an ad that uses synthetic content in a way that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of what is being sold, unless the ad carries a clear disclosure. Synthetic content covers any image, video, audio, or text that AI has significantly modified or generated.

The disclosure must say that the ad contains content modified or generated using artificial intelligence, though the law does not require any particular wording. It must be easy to notice and understand given its size, contrast, duration, and volume, it must appear in the consumer's language, and it must show the first time the content appears and in the same medium. Where technically feasible, it must be permanent or very hard to remove. The law exempts content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary, criticism, and text-only content. The Attorney General or a district attorney may seek an injunction or sue, and courts may award damages, fines of up to $3,000, and attorney fees and costs, but there is no private right of action.

The law applies to advertisers who create and disseminate an ad or cause it to be created and disseminated, and earlier drafts limiting it to knowing, reckless, or willful conduct were removed. Because it covers all advertising shown in Pennsylvania, it reaches commercials made in other states or countries as well. Commentators have noted that terms such as "significantly modified" are subjective, and the broad exemptions for parody and commentary may leave advertisers room to maneuver. Unlike California and New York laws aimed at synthetic performers, this law appears to focus more on consumer protection.

Companies will need to decide when a disclosure is needed. A strict reading suggests none is required unless AI use creates a false consumer perception, but regulators have not yet said how they will enforce that standard. Some companies may therefore adopt a conservative approach and disclose more broadly. Observers expect that Pennsylvania's law is part of a wider trend of states regulating AI in advertising.

stories.Headline: Researchers review atomic-scale imaging and AI methods for materials science
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive academic review published in the Journal of Materials Science: Composites evaluates recent technical milestones in atomic-scale characterization, establishing how modern microscopy, spectroscopy, and artificial intelligence workflows are reshaping materials science. Authored by Obinna Onyebuchi Barah, Mushabe David, and Malisaba Joseph, the study highlights how examining matter at sub-nanometer and sub-angstrom scales has become essential for unlocking structure-property relationships in energy storage systems, quantum materials, and macromolecular biological structures. The authors emphasize that static observations are increasingly replaced by multimodal platforms operating under in situ and operando conditions. By combining aberration-corrected imaging, localized chemical spectroscopies, and automated data pipelines, researchers can now interrogate transient atomic rearrangements that dictate macroscopic device behavior. The review demonstrates that atomic-scale insights directly resolve critical engineering challenges, including efficiency losses in solar cells, battery degradation mechanisms, and structural variations in additive manufacturing.

The development of modern atomic-scale microscopy traces an evolutionary path from early optical tools to twentieth-century electron and scanning probe systems that bypassed fundamental diffraction limits. The introduction of transmission electron microscopy during the nineteen thirties enabled direct nanoscale visualization, which was later complemented by scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy in the nineteen eighties. Over the past two decades, innovations in electron optics, notably spherical aberration correctors, monochromators, and direct electron detectors, have dramatically elevated spatial, temporal, and energy resolutions. These refinements allow modern transmission instruments to resolve individual atomic columns in complex crystal lattices with sub-angstrom precision. Furthermore, environmental transmission electron microscopy has extended atomic-scale imaging into dynamic gaseous and liquid settings, permitting operando observations of catalytic reactions and battery electrodes.

For example, aberration-corrected environmental cells have visualized lattice distortions and ion migration pathways in hybrid perovskite films, directly linking dynamic defect propagation to operational degradation under simulated working conditions. Scanning transmission electron microscopy enhances structural analysis by focusing an electron probe to scan specimens while collecting simultaneous signals across complementary imaging detectors and spectroscopic channels. High-angle annular dark-field detectors provide atomic number contrast, known as Z-contrast, which offers heightened chemical sensitivity for resolving atomic species across heterostructures, quantum dots, and engineered interfaces. Modern developments in four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy collect complete two-dimensional convergent beam electron diffraction patterns at every individual probe position across a raster grid. This high-density multidimensional acquisition enables quantitative mapping of local strain tensors, crystallographic orientations, and three-dimensional atomic configurations with spatial precision reaching approximately three tenths of a nanometer in battery cathodes.

Although scanning transmission electron microscopy delivers superior chemical and structural sensitivity compared to conventional scanning probe techniques, the review notes that the methodology requires significantly more elaborate specimen preparation protocols to achieve electron transparency without altering fragile native phases. Surface-sensitive and cryogenic imaging modalities complement transmission electron techniques by analyzing specimens under specialized ambient, liquid, or low-temperature environments without destructive specimen processing. Scanning tunneling microscopy precisely maps local electronic states and densities on conductive surfaces, whereas atomic force microscopy operates across both conductive and insulating substrates in varied operational modes. High-speed atomic force microscopy captures real-time conformational transitions of dynamic biomolecules under physiological buffer conditions, bridging static structural models with functional kinetic behaviors. In parallel, helium ion microscopy utilizes a focused beam of helium ions to deliver sub-nanometer surface imaging with approximately half-nanometer resolution, elevated secondary electron yields, and minimal sample charging on delicate polymers.

Meanwhile, cryogenic electron microscopy has transformed structural biology through rapid plunge vitrification, dose fractionation, and direct electron detection that preserves macromolecular assemblies in vitreous ice without chemical staining, resolving structures such as the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein at resolutions finer than two angstroms. Spectroscopic techniques provide essential chemical, vibrational, and electronic information that contextualizes structural images obtained from atomic-scale microscopy platforms. Electron energy loss spectroscopy integrated within scanning transmission electron microscopes utilizes monochromated electron sources to achieve energy resolutions below ten millielectronvolts, facilitating nanoscale vibrational spectroscopy and phonon mapping in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides. Complementary energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy leverages advanced silicon drift detectors to record high-count elemental maps across alloys and nanoparticles. For surface investigations, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy resolves quantitative chemical bonding states, particularly through near-ambient pressure instrumentation applied to heterogeneous catalysis.

Tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy couples metallic probe tips with optical excitation, circumventing conventional optical diffraction barriers to provide molecular vibrational fingerprints at spatial resolutions down to ten nanometers. Additionally, atom probe tomography applies controlled laser-assisted field evaporation to generate three-dimensional compositional reconstructions with near-atomic spatial precision around three tenths of a nanometer, exposing subtle elemental clustering and phase separation phenomena. The rapid proliferation of complex, high-dimensional datasets generated by advanced analytical instrumentation has elevated artificial intelligence from an auxiliary computational tool to a central analytical engine. Supervised machine learning algorithms, including convolutional neural networks, support vector machines, and random forests, are widely deployed to automate image segmentation, map grain boundary networks, and identify atomic vacancies with higher consistency than manual inspection. Generative adversarial networks assist training workflows by synthesizing realistic image patches and spectroscopic profiles, effectively mitigating data scarcity in resource-intensive experimental settings.

Simultaneously, unsupervised clustering algorithms, such as k-means, density-based spatial clustering, and manifold projection algorithms including t-SNE and UMAP, identify hidden correlations across high-dimensional spectral images without prior manual labeling. To counteract model vulnerabilities related to dataset noise and annotation bias, researchers increasingly incorporate Bayesian inference and Monte Carlo dropout for rigorous uncertainty quantification, ensuring algorithmic inferences remain reproducible and physically grounded against synthetic benchmarks. Multimodal data fusion and correlative workflows address the growing challenge of interpreting heterogeneous datasets that frequently encompass terabytes of raw experimental output. Modern characterization studies integrate structurally and chemically diverse information from transmission electron microscopy, electron energy loss spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to capture complete material behaviors. Advanced computational frameworks apply joint non-negative matrix factorization, canonical correlation analysis, and deep learning image registration to align disparate modalities with nanometer and sub-nanometer spatial fidelity.

These correlative workflows allow simultaneous evaluation of topographic features, vibrational modes, and elemental oxidation states across complex interfaces that appear ambiguous in isolated measurements. Furthermore, experimental observations are increasingly coupled with high-performance computing simulations, including density functional theory, molecular dynamics, and finite element analysis. These first-principles computational models establish quantitative reference benchmarks for interpreting observed spectral signatures, generating predictive surrogate frameworks that accelerate the rational exploration of advanced composition spaces. Autonomous experimentation and real-time data processing represent a transformative shift toward closed-loop laboratory ecosystems where analytical instruments function as active research collaborators. Integrated computational pipelines perform on-the-fly image denoising, pattern recognition, and feature extraction, enabling dynamic acquisition steering toward emergent defects, grain boundaries, or unexpected phase transitions.

Autonomous artificial intelligence agents guided by reinforcement learning algorithms and Bayesian optimization dynamically calibrate microscope operating parameters, optimize detector dwell times, and adapt electron dosages based on real-time feedback. In automated cryogenic electron microscopy, intelligent algorithms detect properly preserved macromolecular assemblies to trigger acquisition autonomously, while self-driving scanning transmission electron systems navigate complex specimen landscapes to capture high-value structural details while minimizing beam-induced specimen damage. This closed-loop responsiveness proves particularly vital during in situ and operando experiments, where transient electrochemical transformations and catalytic reaction pathways unfold rapidly, requiring immediate parameter adjustments to record non-equilibrium physical phenomena before structural degradation occurs. Targeted case studies documented throughout the review underscore how atomic-scale characterization directly guides performance breakthroughs in commercial energy technologies and specialized manufacturing. In photovoltaic research, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy identified lead iodide segregation along grain boundaries in methylammonium lead iodide films, guiding chemical passivation strategies that elevated single-junction perovskite solar cell ef More to follow.

stories.Headline: China uses artificial intelligence to enforce its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress
stories.Summary:
The People's Republic of China implemented the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress over four months ago. This landmark legislation aims to promote ethnic unity and forge a strong sense of community. The state uses artificial intelligence to enforce these rules through policing, learning, and producing. AI helps the government detect, delete, and report content that undermines ethnic unity. These systems also generate state-approved material and intelligence on people the state watches.

The law requires Mandarin as the basic language of instruction in classrooms. Parents cannot instill ideas not conducive to ethnic unity in the home. Article 31 requires network operators to delete and report information undermining ethnic unity. Article 15 promotes the digitalization of minority languages, while Article 52 mandates alert and reporting systems. Provisions in Articles 16, 19, 24, 61, and 63 also impact ethnic minority identities.

The state is responsible for enforcing these rules through its surveillance infrastructure. Officials aim to achieve the sinicisation of 55 ethnic minorities to adopt mainstream Chinese values. This process seeks to construct one unified national identity for the Chinese people. The government uses AI to monitor communications and shape behaviors across the country. State organs must identify and resolve major risks to maintain national security and stability.

International rights groups and critics view the law as a human rights problem. They argue the goal is han-isation, which assimilates minority identities into the Han majority. Eight UN Special Rapporteurs sent a letter to Beijing in April detailing these concerns. Minority groups are affected by the digitalization of their languages for state policing. Some AI models still write hate speech in Kazakh and Mongolian when asked.

The Cybersecurity Law has prohibited inciting ethnic hatred or discrimination since 2017. The CAC required platforms to police content undermining ethnic unity starting in March 2020. The Criminal Law has criminalized incitement to ethnic hatred for a much longer period. Interim Measures from August 2023 forbid generative AI from promoting ethnic hatred and discrimination. Hangzhou integrated DeepSeek-R1 into its City Brain in February 2025 to process data.

Network operators like Tencent, ByteDance, and Weibo use AI to handle massive censorship duties. AI is integrated into the criminal-justice pipeline, including smart courts and smart prisons. The state continues to build data to help AI understand minority languages better. It remains unclear if this progress will reach the commercial models people use. The articles leave open how AI will fully meet the law's policing demands.

stories.Headline: Delaware court sanctions lawyer over hallucinated citations but exonerates firm with AI guidelines
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery issued an order sanctioning a lawyer who signed a brief with hallucinated citations, according to an Above the Law article by Stephen Embry. The lawyer submitted fabricated quotations and mischaracterized legal authorities in a brief, and after the other side outed him he owned up to it, sort of. He filed a corrected brief that removed quotation marks from the original hallucinated citations but retained the inaccurate legal propositions. The lawyer blamed a paralegal and then tried to blame the other side for failing to meet and confer before alerting the court. The court sanctioned the lawyer under Delaware's version of Rule 11 but exonerated his law firm because it had proper AI use guidelines in place.

Delaware's Rule 11 provides that absent exceptional circumstances a law firm must be held jointly responsible for a violation committed by its partner, associate, or employee. The court also cited the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct, which require law firm leadership to make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance with ethical rules. It referenced ABA Formal Opinion 512, which calls on firms to establish clear policies on permissible AI use. The firm barred the use of unapproved GenAI tools in March 2023, formed a working group to evaluate GenAI tools and study ethical guidance in 2024, and adopted a comprehensive GenAI policy in July 2025. That policy required an experienced lawyer to review GenAI output for accuracy and completeness.

The court found the exceptional circumstances that relieved the firm of joint responsibility, determining that the firm had undertaken substantial institutional efforts to prevent the very problem at issue. The court said the firm warned of GenAI risks, established clear verification policies, and trained its personnel through a substantial, multi-layered approach. The court said the firm acted reasonably to prevent GenAI misuse and should not be sanctioned for an individual lawyer bypassing those controls. The court said there is nothing to negotiate or compromise when an attorney submits false citations to a tribunal. The judge made sure the lawyer paid the monetary sanctions out of his own pocket.

The firm developed an internal training program addressing hallucinations and the recommendations of Opinion 512, and it addressed professional obligations concerning competence, confidentiality, meritorious claims, candor, and supervision. Delaware's Commission on Continuing Legal Education accredited the program for an hour of enhanced ethics credit. Embry wrote that AI use guidelines must be a three-legged stool, with a thorough policy, training and education, and guidelines that stay evergreen. Embry wrote that lawyers are naturally skeptical and independent and most believe they are special snowflakes. Embry recalled being told to use the firm's VPN at all times when working remote, but it was slow and clunky and a pain in the ass.

Embry wrote that if the firm's approved GenAI tools are slow and clunky, lawyers will jump to tools that aren't. Embry wrote that guidelines created in 2023, for example, would be unlikely to address the use of AI agents, which is getting more and more common today. Embry wrote that firms need someone, or perhaps several someones, to keep up with AI developments, risks, and the evolving law. Embry wrote that someone must spend nonbillable time monitoring those developments and ensuring the guidelines are frequently revised. Embry wrote that the firm must have a mechanism to approve revisions that doesn't take six months and involve never-ending partner meetings.

Embry wrote that judges are growing increasingly impatient with hallucinations in court filings. Embry wrote that hallucinations could lead to embarrassment, potential malpractice claims, or at the very least, unhappy clients. Embry wrote that law firms absolutely must have AI use guidelines and must train partners, associates, paralegals, legal professionals, and everyone else in the firm about them and why they're necessary. Embry wrote that firms absolutely must keep those guidelines up to date and must have a mechanism for promptly approving needed revisions. Embry wrote that this is simply a cost of doing business in these days and times, so roll up your sleeves and get to work.

Articles.Title: AI Use Guidelines: It’s Complicated. It’s Also Not A Choice - Above the Law

stories.headline_source: AI Use Guidelines: It’s Complicated. It’s Also Not A Choice

stories.Headline: OpenAI updates security to block unauthorized reasoning extraction from its latest AI models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI strengthened the security safeguards for its latest artificial intelligence models, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, on November 22, 2026. These updates were designed to stop unauthorized reasoning extraction, which is a machine learning technique known as distillation. This process allows attackers to reproduce advanced capabilities without the original safety restrictions. The company implemented these changes after detecting multiple distillation campaigns that increased significantly over the summer.

The new defenses drastically reduced attack success rates for GPT-6.2 Astra, dropping from 54 percent to 0.2 percent for earlier interactions. For reasoning generated during current interactions, the success rate fell from 22.9 percent to 0.9 percent. The anti-distillation strategy utilizes a combination of model training, automated classifiers, and API-level restrictions. Reasoning is now tied to the specific conversation that generated it, meaning that rewriting an earlier message removes all subsequent reasoning.

OpenAI officials stated that unauthorized distillation poses significant risks in dual-use fields like biological research and cybersecurity. They warned that distilled models might provide dangerous assistance that the original systems would refuse under safety policies. The company reported disrupting an extraction campaign involving individuals from Moonshot AI in September. Additionally, OpenAI briefed the US Congress in February regarding activity that indicated DeepSeek was attempting to distill US frontier models.

The company took weekly enforcement actions affecting thousands to tens of thousands of accounts to protect national security. Internal studies showed that student models trained on exact reasoning traces performed better than those trained on summaries. These models retained an advantage across two cybersecurity benchmarks, proving that exact traces help models develop skills beyond original tasks. OpenAI continues to use input and output classifiers to identify suspicious requests and prevent potential leaks.

Articles.Title: OpenAI strengthens AI safeguards, cuts reasoning extraction attack rates

stories.headline_source: OpenAI strengthens AI safeguards, cuts reasoning extraction attack rates

stories.Headline: Huawei introduces new architecture and scaling law to build 1.4nm chips without EUV lithography
stories.Summary:
Huawei introduced the Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture on May 26, 2026, to develop semiconductor chips. The Chinese technology company aims to produce 1.4nm-class chips by the year 2031 without using EUV lithography from ASML. This new approach focuses on reorganizing chip architecture to increase computing density and reduce signal propagation time. The company plans to debut this technology in a Kirin processor for the Mate 90 series this autumn.

The LogicFolding architecture reportedly provides a 55 percent increase in transistor density without relying on expensive Western machinery. Tau Scaling moves away from traditional Moore's Law by focusing on smarter engineering to manage heat and distribute power. These changes are designed to help China reduce its dependence on foreign chip technologies amid ongoing geopolitical tensions. Such innovations could lead to faster AI processing and lower energy consumption for massive cloud infrastructure.

Huawei believes that smarter coordination between hardware and software is more important than simply shrinking transistors. The company suggests that these methods can bypass the manufacturing barriers created by current global semiconductor export restrictions. By focusing on efficient designs, they intend to create more competitive AI hardware that does not depend on a few Western firms. This strategy represents a major shift in how the company approaches the future of high performance computing.

The semiconductor industry is now exploring 3D stacking and chiplet-based designs to improve flexibility and overall performance. Experts remain cautious because managing heat and maintaining yield consistency at 1.4nm is extremely difficult. If these concepts succeed, they may influence global chip design and create alternative ecosystems across Asian markets. Future innovation will likely depend on smarter architecture to support the growing demands of large language models.

stories.Headline: From administrative reforms to AI policy to green economy, Keralam’s fifth Administrative Reforms Commission has a wide-ranging mandate
stories.Summary:
Keralam’s Congress-led United Democratic Front government constituted the fifth Administrative Reforms Commission through an order issued on October 1, 2026, and the Personnel and Administrative Reforms department published its terms of reference through a separate order dated November 19, 2026. The commission is headed by former Minister and Indian Union Muslim League leader M.K. Muneer, according to The Hindu. The panel’s mandate is more expansive than that of the fourth commission, which was headed by former Chief Minister V.S. Achuthanandan. The fifth commission is required to recommend a State artificial intelligence policy and a connected legal framework, and to examine emerging challenges that range from demographic ageing, migration, urbanisation, disaster and climate resilience and public health preparedness to the green economy, Centre-State relations and fiscal federalism.

The terms of reference require the panel to review the structure and processes of the State administration against the backdrop of policy changes, institutional developments and technological advances since the previous commission’s tenure. The commission must also update the Manual of Office Procedure and the Rules of Business of the government in line with current policy, Acts and Rules. It will assess how earlier commission recommendations were implemented, while suggesting reforms to make the State administration adaptive, citizen-centred, efficient, accountable and future-ready. In budgeting and planning, the panel should recommend agile planning and budgeting mechanisms that help the government adapt to unforeseen sectoral requirements, and it will look into barriers to inter-departmental coordination and the interface between departments and local governments.

The Personnel and Administrative Reforms department has issued orders creating 12 posts for the new commission, including those of an Additional Secretary and a Deputy Collector, and there will be four daily-wage posts in addition. The number of posts for the fifth commission and for the chairman’s personal staff will be the same as that of the fourth commission. The ARC chairman will have 12 personal staff whose appointments will be on a co-terminus basis. The commission’s wide-ranging terms of reference cover administrative reform, artificial intelligence policy and the green economy, among other areas.

Articles.Title: From administrative reforms to AI policy to green economy, Keralam’s fifth Administrative Reforms Commission has a wide-ranging mandate

stories.Headline: Seoul education chief Chung Keun-sik pushes vocational high schools and essay-based grading as AI reshapes work
stories.Summary:
Superintendent Chung Keun-sik of the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education recently proposed a plan to strengthen career education. He discussed these goals during an interview this month at the National Assembly in Yeouido, Seoul. The plan focuses on nurturing vocational high schools as artificial intelligence reshapes industry work and job structures. Chung argues that students must learn hands-on skills because AI is taking over knowledge processing. He believes direct experience and skill acquisition are becoming more important as AI technology advances.

The office will expand essay-based assessments, raising their share in semester grades to 35 percent by 2027. By 2030, more than 50 percent of regular exams will be converted to the essay format. The office will support teacher training and specialized graders by 2032 and use Chaeum AI for grading. A new five-tier school grading system will apply to the 2028 college admissions cycle for current high school sophomores. This system expands the top tier of students from 4 percent to 10 percent.

Superintendent Chung stated that the perception of college entrance as the ultimate goal of education must change. He argued that getting into Seoul National University does not guarantee a life for a student. Chung believes a child who tests well is different from a smart or fine child. He said the current admissions structure prioritizes university rankings over the actual aptitudes of the students. He noted that students often choose majors to match their scores rather than the work they want.

Parents and students are facing excessive anxiety regarding the new five-tier grading system and admission prospects. Universities are also affected because they must find new ways to distinguish among applicants in the top tier. Chung believes this anxiety is largely a psychological problem and urges a focus on everyday learning. He expressed concern that elementary students relying on digital devices may lack basic reading and writing skills. He suggested a balance between digital education and traditional methods like discussion and reading.

The articles state that a gap exists between college studies and the work people actually do in Korea. The government wants to change local education grants from 20.79 percent of domestic tax revenue to economic growth rates. Superintendents proposed a compromise to keep the tax link but use excess increases for future national investment. The state would cover one-third of the excess decrease if grants fall more than 5 percent. The Seoul office could not accommodate 965.7 billion won in requests, including 676.6 billion won for environments.

The office will continue implementing the phased transition toward essay-based assessments and the new grading system. Chung seeks social consensus before introducing the Alpha Phone to curb student overdependence on smartphones. He continues to push for stable education finances to maintain and improve conditions in schools. The articles leave open how the government will respond to the superintendents' proposed grant funding compromise. They also leave open how the office will define specific Alpha Phone regulations for different grade levels.

Articles.Title: Seoul Education Chief Pushes Vocational High Schools in AI Era - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Gomumari adds contracting authority selection to its Target List Creation AI agent
stories.Summary:
Gomumari Co., Ltd., based in Arakawa, Tokyo and led by representative director Yuta Murayama, announced on November 22, 2026 that its business AI agent "Target List Creation" now supports the selection of contracting authorities for companies selling to government agencies and local governments. The company began offering the new business development agent in October 2026, and the new function starts on November 22, 2026. If a customer sends a list of contracting authorities it has won orders from, even names alone, along with information on its products and target areas, the AI analyzes the conditions shared by the authorities that placed orders. It then lists likely contracting authorities from among those posting notices on the government procurement information portal site, with a selection reason for each authority, and returns the list together with the selection criteria. Initial setup starts at 500,000 yen over a period of four weeks or more, followed by operation from 100,000 yen per month.

The articles give the scale of the problem the function addresses. Notices for government and local government tenders exceed 300 on a single weekday, and when Gomumari pulled notices from October 1 to 30, 2026 through the portal site's search API across all 47 prefectures, it found 8,916 notices in one month, or 306 to 626 per weekday, issued by 1,055 authorities. Notices arrive by case, but sales visits are decided by authority, and filtering methods used for private companies, such as industry or employee count, do not work for contracting authorities. Among the October notices, 418 cases had "system" in the title, issued by 187 of the 1,055 authorities, so names and sizes alone do not show which authorities buy a company's products. The know-how about which authorities buy often stays only in the head of the person who has tracked tenders, and when that person is transferred, the successor starts over by reading notices from the top.

The processing runs in four stages. The customer submits its past order list, which can be names of contracting authorities alone, with product and target area information, and about 30 orders are enough to derive conditions, with no need to standardize formats in advance. The AI analyzes the conditions common to authorities that placed orders and puts into words, with reasons, why authorities meeting those conditions buy. It then selects likely authorities from among the 1,055 that posted notices in October 2026 and ranks them by priority with a reason for each. It outputs the list with reasons, an order analysis memo, the selection criteria themselves, and data in a format that can be imported into a CRM, so the company can later build lists on the same criteria internally.

The criteria are re-read each time new orders accumulate, and no dedicated system installation or operation training is required. Murayama said that strong salespeople in the public sector decide which authorities to approach before notices appear, and that this difference lies less in how they read notices than in whether they remember which authorities bought and why. He said the company added the function of selecting the next contracting authorities from a list of past orders to its existing method of reading the conditions of buyers from order records, and that it actually pulled the 8,916 notices from 1,055 authorities in one month and counted which items are usable as sales material. He said the company aims to increase sales teams where a successor can explain in his or her own words which authority to visit next even after a personnel change. The articles also describe the base service: in a customer's sales department, about 2,000 negotiations and about 2,000 activity records were read to redesign customer segments into six groups and apply them to about 4,000 clients, producing a list narrowed to about 300 sales targets.

Gomumari also counted the October notices itself, finding 1,294 notices located in Tokyo, 14.5 percent of the national total, but only 83 of them were issued by the metropolitan and ward governments, with the rest from national institutions, independent administrative agencies and national universities, so counting notices by location does not represent the number of cases a local government issues. The same Target List Creation is also offered as a specialist AI-BPO service that returns deliverables, starting at 200,000 yen and taking seven business days from the day after materials are ready, for either a one-time or monthly engagement. Customers can choose between AI agent introduction to run the process internally and the AI-BPO deliverable list, and Gomumari also offers adjacent services such as data enrichment that organizes CRM company information and assigns customer ranks. The company presents itself as an FDE company that enters customer sites and builds AI agents, providing introduction of AI agents with initial setup and monthly operation, and it says its lineup will be added in order from work refined in actual fields. The articles state that prices and periods are as of the time of release and may be revised, with the latest conditions on the company website.

stories.Headline: Vivaldi CEO Jon von Tetzchner calls much AI use not useful despite high valuations
stories.Summary:
Vivaldi CEO and co-founder Jon von Tetzchner said much of today's AI technology isn't useful, despite the enormous valuations attached to AI companies. He made the comments in an interview with technology news outlet The Tech Report. The interview was reported by Benzinga and Yahoo Finance on Sunday, November 22, 2026. Artificial intelligence has become one of the biggest investment stories in the world, with technology companies spending billions to develop new products and infrastructure. Von Tetzchner questioned whether much of that investment is going toward things people actually want.

Von Tetzchner compared the current AI excitement with the earlier rush into blockchain technology. He said there are a lot of companies that now call themselves AI, describing how businesses previously embraced blockchain and cryptocurrency. He pointed to companies rebranding themselves around popular technologies to attract investor interest, even when the connection to their existing businesses was questionable. He said he does think a lot of the AI use is not useful. He asked whether AI will prove its use over time so that people start using it in times that improve society and not ruin it.

Von Tetzchner questioned whether AI is actually improving productivity. He said companies are using AI to write longer documents, only to use another AI tool to summarize them. He raised similar concerns about AI-generated computer code being checked by other AI systems. He said the problem is that the tools supposed to be helping people be more effective are doing the opposite. He also questioned whether technology companies are paying enough attention to their customers.

Von Tetzchner pointed to an unnamed search partner that introduced AI results and subsequently asked users whether they wanted the feature. According to his recollection, roughly 80% said no. He also described browser companies adding AI features, facing backlash and eventually introducing options to turn those features off. When asked directly whether AI is in a bubble, he stopped short of predicting a crash. He said clearly valuations of companies are really high.

Von Tetzchner acknowledged that some companies with high valuations eventually justify them, while others see their valuations fall sharply. He said sometimes companies get valued very high and then shortly afterwards they are valued very low. For investors, the concern is whether companies spending heavily on AI will eventually generate enough revenue and profits to support their valuations. The central question for AI investors is whether today's spending will eventually produce products that customers use and pay for. Revenue growth, profitability and customer demand will help determine whether current valuations hold up.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Romanian lenders must align credit scoring models with GDPR and EU AI Act rules by 2026
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a 2026 compliance guide on automated lending in Romania, published by Global Advisory Experts on November 22, 2026. The guide says automated lending in Romania is a compliance exposure that sharpens in 2026. It says the EU AI Act is being applied in phases and treats credit scoring and automated lending decisions as high-risk artificial intelligence. It says the General Data Protection Regulation already governs profiling and automated decision-making. It says Romanian banks, non-bank financial institutions and credit servicers using scoring models answer to two overlapping regimes.

The guide cites the GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, and its Article 22 right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, where the decision has legal effects or similarly significantly affects the individual. It cites Article 35, requiring a Data Protection Impact Assessment where processing is likely to create high risk for individuals. It cites Articles 13 and 14 on transparency duties and the recitals on human intervention, stating a point of view and contesting a decision. It cites the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, classifying AI systems used to assess the creditworthiness of natural persons, or to establish their credit score, as high-risk. It names the Romanian Data Protection Authority (ANSPDCP), the National Bank of Romania (BNR), the European Banking Authority, the European Data Protection Board, the European Data Protection Supervisor and the National Authority for Consumer Protection (ANPC).

The guide assigns owners to its ten steps: the model owner with the DPO for mapping the use case and data flows, and Legal, Compliance and Risk for classifying the model's risk. It assigns the DPIA to the DPO with Risk, Legal and the model owner, and model governance to Risk/Model Validation and IT. It assigns explainability and transparency to Compliance, Legal and Communications, and human oversight to Credit Operations and Compliance. It assigns vendor due diligence and contracting to Procurement and Legal, recordkeeping to Compliance and IT, redress and adverse-action processes to Legal and Customer Operations, and ongoing audit and reporting to Compliance and Internal Audit.

The guide says a common mistake is to run AI governance and data protection as separate projects, and that in lending they are two sides of the same workstream. It says not every model attracts the full weight of both regimes, but most meaningful scoring systems do, and that passing one test does not excuse you from the other. It says the AI Act contains limited carve-outs, such as systems used to detect financial fraud, and that fraud-detection tools are treated differently. It says ANSPDCP has published a list of processing operations that require a DPIA, and that a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated may require prior consultation with ANSPDCP. It says supervisors expect a dated audit trail.

The guide says a single significant model takes three to four months from start to go-live, with monitoring continuing indefinitely afterwards. It says an inspection, whether by ANSPDCP on data protection or by BNR on prudential grounds, will test whether a coherent, dated set of documents can be produced. It says missing or inconsistent papers are among the most reliable triggers for escalation. It says a validation report describing a superseded version is worse than none. It lists compliance officers, data protection officers, in-house counsel, risk and model owners, and vendors supplying banks, IFNs and credit servicers in Romania as the readers it addresses.

The guide says the model file a bank keeps for prudential and data protection purposes needs to be able to support AI Act conformity as well. It says the ten steps can partly run in parallel and that for every step the owner, the minimum documentation and the sign-off dates should be confirmed. It says the minimum file for automated credit scoring in Romania is listed with the internal owner of each item, and that everything should be kept under version control and aligned with the live production model. It says the durations in its table should be treated as minimums for one model of moderate complexity, and that portfolios of models scale accordingly. It says the guide covers who should own each task, how long the work usually takes and what supervisors are likely to look for on inspection.

The guide says it contains a step-by-step checklist, a table of required documents, DPIA triggers, sample adverse-action notice wording and a vendor due-diligence checklist. It says these are mapped to the EU AI Act, the GDPR and Romanian supervisory expectations. It says the redress and adverse-action processes should be tested before go-live, and that an early internal audit should be scheduled after deployment. It says monitoring KPIs, revalidation triggers, incident procedures and reporting lines should be set. It leaves open what the supervisory file must contain beyond the items it lists, and what ANSPDCP's published DPIA list covers.

stories.Headline: Virginia Beach school leaders weigh AI guardrails as survey shows 60% of high schoolers use AI to explain concepts
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already a common part of the high school experience in Virginia Beach, and school leaders are now weighing how to make sure students use the technology responsibly while still gaining its educational benefits, according to WTKR. A survey by Virginia Beach City Public Schools found that 60% of high school students surveyed said they have used AI to explain difficult concepts, while 46% said they have used it to study for quizzes or tests. The same survey found that 36% of the students said they have used AI to check homework answers, and the district reported that 91% of high school students surveyed know their school's rules for using AI on assignments. The discussion came before the School Board as the technology becomes another tool available to students, and the district's current rules say open generative AI is not allowed for elementary or middle school students.

Under those current rules, high school students can use approved tools, including Gemini, with teacher guidance and district safeguards in place. School Board member Melinda Rogers said the conversation also needs to include the ethical boundaries surrounding AI use, noting that the technology is used a lot to deceive people in society and that an ethical standard should reflect that just because you can does not mean you should. School Board member Kimberly Melnyk asked district officials for data on the percentage of students who refuse to use AI, and a district official responded that no current data was available. That means the district has information about how surveyed students say they are using AI but does not currently have data showing how many students are choosing not to use the technology.

Kathleen Brown, of District 10, said there has been some conversation about generative AI, which she described as entering a prompt and getting a generated feedback loop, and she said families in the community are very concerned about that. The discussion reflects a broader challenge for Virginia Beach schools, which is determining how AI can help students learn while establishing clear expectations for when and how the technology should be used. The district survey and the board's questions show that leaders are still gathering information about student use, including the group of students who decline the technology. The articles do not say what specific guardrails, if any, the board will adopt or when any further action is expected.

stories.Headline: Bank of Portugal governor warns Europe lags US in AI investment
stories.Summary:
Bank of Portugal Governor Álvaro Santos Pereira warned on Friday, November 20, 2026, that Europe risks falling further behind the United States in artificial intelligence investment. He spoke at the ninth Future of Banking conference in Lisbon, organised by Jornal de Negócios at the SANA Marquês hotel. The governor said Portugal's banks enjoy stronger balance sheets and improved credit quality. He set out an agenda spanning energy risks, regulatory reform, cybersecurity and financing of technological transformation. The central bank expects growth of around 2.3% in 2026, easing to 1.8% in 2027.

The governor put the non-performing loan ratio at 2.1%, a marked contrast with double-digit levels of earlier years. He said the proportion of euro-area banks adopting generative AI rose from 46% in 2024 to 86% more recently. Around 43% of US workers were using AI at work, compared with 32% in Europe, he said. The share of companies using AI in production was approximately 7% in the United States and 4% in Europe. Six reporting requirements have already been discontinued, with another two scheduled to disappear by the end of 2026.

Santos Pereira said growth of the Portuguese economy remains "reasonable, not spectacular, but reasonable." He said, "We have to ask ourselves whether it is sustainable to continue along this path of not increasing public capital decisively." He said, "If we have a very cold winter, that will put more pressure on natural gas prices and, obviously, on electricity prices as well." He said, "I think there is clearly room for us to continue raising deposit interest rates closer to those in the euro area." He said, "The big question is who will capture the financial gains associated with this: the banks, the customers or the technology suppliers."

He said interest paid on deposits by Portuguese banks remains significantly below the euro-area average. He said public debt remains historically high and the downward trajectory must continue. He said European gas storage levels in some northern markets were below their averages of the previous decade. He cited competition with Asia, disruption in the Middle East and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz as added risks. He said the European Central Bank would continue to safeguard price stability.

He described AI as a general-purpose technology comparable to steam power, electricity, computers and the internet. He said AI is spreading more quickly than earlier general-purpose technologies. He singled out cybersecurity as a top systemic concern for the financial sector. He said the Bank of Portugal has begun work on post-quantum encryption and signed a memorandum of understanding with the Bank of Spain. He said stronger supervision introduced over the past 15 years should be preserved but unnecessary complexity can be removed.

He said the objective is to establish a single point of contact for bank reporting during the first quarter of 2027. He reported the elimination of 465 Bank of Portugal regulatory provisions in connection with the IMF's Financial Sector Assessment Program, with a further reduction of around 100 envisaged for 2027. He said the bank intends to assemble its applicable rules in a single rulebook. He said simplifying regulation will be a top priority in the coming years. He said the central bank would discuss the reporting arrangements with banks.

stories.Headline: US education unions condemn Google for tying school search access to AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Google announced earlier this month that it plans to turn off search engine access as soon as next year for K-12 schools that toggle off its AI tools, claiming the decision is necessary based on the technologies' recent fusion. Education unions in the United States strongly criticized Google's reported decision to require schools to adopt its AI tools if they wish to continue using the company's search and education services. The American Federation of Teachers condemned the move, arguing that schools should not be presented with an all-or-nothing choice. The National Education Association echoed those concerns, stressing that schools must remain free to decide whether and how AI technologies are used. The criticism follows reports that Google is pressuring schools to choose between access to its search and education ecosystem and the adoption of its AI products.

Google disclosed that it would turn off its Gemini AI program and search engine for schools until schools decide which services to enable. Google has only offered school districts more ways to interact with AI, such as AI Mode and AI Overview, which provides users with chatbot search functions and summarized results. Potential options include DuckDuckGo and Microsoft's Bing, both of which offer users the option to disable AI-generated answers. Some of the country's largest school districts, including in Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago, are considering doing away with Google altogether. A January report by the Brookings Institution's Center for Universal Education found that AI can undermine children's foundational development.

Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement that if Google doesn't reconsider their position, they will explore other search options. Samuels said they refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out. Google told the Times in a statement Wednesday that it is actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure its products support students and teachers. The AFT said it is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of children. The AFT said that instead of working with educators and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, Google throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to its tools altogether.

The NEA said educators, school districts, and parents should have the freedom to decide which AI tools are right for their students. The NEA said they deserve the time and opportunity to make sure these tools are useful, safe, fair, accessible, protect student privacy, and keep educators involved in how they are used. Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report's authors, told NPR in January that when kids use generative AI that tells them what the answer is, they are not thinking for themselves. Winthrop said they are not learning to parse truth from fiction and are not learning to understand what makes a good argument. Winthrop said they are not learning about different perspectives in the world because they are actually not engaging in the material.

Education International has consistently argued that the adoption of artificial intelligence in education must be guided by pedagogical needs and democratic governance, not by commercial profit making. EI General Secretary David Edwards said no technological product or platform can replace the trust, care, and professional judgement at the heart of teaching and the lifeblood of our societies. Edwards said we demand transparency, accountability, meaningful teacher consultation, and the right to say no to technologies that undermine professional judgement, educational quality, equity, or student privacy. The reported decision by Google also raises concerns about vendor lock-in and the growing dependence of schools on a small number of technology companies. The Google announcement comes at a time when schools around the world are grappling with how to harness new technologies while safeguarding students' rights.

The AFT has called on Google to engage constructively with educators and families and to demonstrate its commitment to protecting students by adopting stronger safeguards for privacy and data protection. Education International emphasizes that education is not a site for technological innovation and product testing. Clear public regulatory frameworks are needed to ensure transparency, accountability, data protection, human oversight, and respect for educators' professional judgement. As governments and education systems develop policies governing artificial intelligence, education unions continue to advocate for transparent regulation, meaningful consultation with education workers, strong privacy protections, and the right of schools to determine whether AI tools serve their educational mission. Studies conducted over the last several months have indicated that the risks attached to the use of AI in schools outweigh the potential benefits.

stories.Headline: Tech stocks plunge as Anthropic loses 109 billion dollars in value
stories.Summary:
Wall Street suffered its worst tech selloff in years during the week of November 22, 2026. The S&P 500 fell 8.6 percent, marking its biggest weekly drop since April 2025. The Dow lost 8 percent, its worst week since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 10 percent, also its worst week since March 2020. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged about 17 percent, its worst week since September 2001.

Anthropic hit the market this week and lost 109 billion dollars in value on Friday. The stock finished Thursday with a market cap of 1.28 trillion dollars. President Donald Trump says his administration will ban U.S. companies from building data centers overseas. Companies that build these centers will face a tremendous tax. Meta and Alphabet signed agreements worth billions of dollars to build overseas data centers.

Attorney General Rob Bonta said California is examining potential criminal violations of state law. He stated the legal framework involves prohibitions against misleading investors and the public. Analyst Michael James McDonald says extreme bearish sentiment supports a near-term rally. He noted long-term indicators suggest the correction could last three to four months. Dividend Value Investor called HP revenue growth spectacular due to AI PC demand.

Hyperscalers are worrying about data center opposition and increased costs after the Democratic midterm sweep. Nvidia is being probed for unlawfully selling advanced chips to China and misleading investors. Gen Z is expected to lead a rebound in in-store Black Friday shopping. A CivicScience survey found 41 percent of shoppers plan to shop in stores. This is the highest share of in-store shoppers since 2014.

The Nasdaq is in the red for the year. The S&P and Dow are in correction territory for the first time since Liberation Day. An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Two independent groups verified the proof, but formal recognition is still pending. HP operates on thin margins, and rising memory prices threaten its profitability recovery.

HP and Dell report earnings on Tuesday, while Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Zoom report Monday. The October core PCE price index is expected to rise 3.2 percent on Wednesday. Hyatt Hotels goes ex-dividend Monday, and Johnson and Johnson goes ex-dividend Tuesday. Newmont and S&P Global go ex-dividend Wednesday. The articles leave open whether the current market correction will end soon.

stories.Summary:
Fractal AI is described by Analytics India Magazine as a leader in artificial intelligence solutions, with work spanning sectors that include healthcare and fashion. A story dated 24 December 2025 reports that Fractal, called India's first AI unicorn, is eyeing a $500 million initial public offering. Another story from the same day says its Vaidya.ai product outperformed GPT-4 and achieved 83 percent in PG-NEET, a medical examination. A report published on 9 December 2025 says the government will select BharatGen, Fractal and Tech Mahindra in the second phase of the IndiaAI Mission.

Coverage from 3 October 2025 says Fractal's chief executive reflected on what he called the worst mistake of his life after twenty-five years. Earlier stories describe generative AI work on intelligent collections and receivables, dated 9 September 2024, and a visionary approach to transforming the fashion value chain with vision intelligence, dated 1 August 2024. A story dated 24 May 2024 says AWS and generative AI helped Fractal Analytics reduce call handling time by up to 15 percent. On 26 February 2024, the company introduced Kalaido, described as a new Indic text to image diffusion model.

Coverage dated 16 February 2024 examines how Fractal is leveraging generative AI for insurance. An interview with Chandramauli Chaudhuri, published on 29 April 2022, discusses driving successful AI transformations at the enterprise level. stories.Headline: Shift Plus adds Gemini 4 Carbon, Argon and Hydrogen to its zevo AI system for Japanese local governments
stories.Summary:
Thomas Cherickal used the Gemini 4 Argon model to generate ten billion-dollar startup ideas. This activity occurred around November 20, 2026, as reported by the TechBeat section of HackerNoon. The AI model provided insane product ideas that solve huge problems for the user. This event coincided with the broader release of new Google Gemini 4 series models. These tools are designed to help users build high-value products through advanced reasoning.

Shift Plus Co., Ltd. added Gemini 4 Carbon, Argon, and Hydrogen to the zevo system on November 19, 2026. This system serves local governments in Japan, including Miyakonojo City, and operates within the LGWAN environment. The new models feature a March 2026 knowledge cutoff and a one million token input window. They provide a 64K output window and are hosted in overseas regions for all users. These updates are available at no additional cost to the participating local government organizations.

Shift Plus CEO Yuya Nakao oversees the company based in Osaka and Miyakonojo, Japan. The company stated that the zevo system now offers more AI model options for governments. They explained that Carbon is for deep reasoning, Argon balances speed, and Hydrogen is for efficiency. The firm noted that organization administrators must enable these models since they are disabled by default. They also promoted LGTalk and eRex as integrated tools for secure communication and transcription.

Thomas Cherickal said the results from the Gemini 4 Argon model blew his mind completely. Local government employees are affected by the new zevo updates for their daily administrative tasks. These officials can now use AI for document creation, summarization, and professional analysis of materials. The system allows them to process images, audio, and PDF files for specialized government work. This technology aims to improve the overall efficiency of digital transformation within Japanese local municipalities.

Shift Plus was established in December 2006 and maintains twenty-eight offices across Japan. The company developed the LedgHOME system, which is used by over 560 municipalities as of August 2026. This specific software manages approximately fifty percent of all hometown tax donations across the entire country. The zevo system was developed jointly with Miyakonojo City to bring generative AI to governments. It integrates various models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI into a secure government network.

The zevo system will continue providing these Gemini 4 models within existing contract plans for users. Shift Plus offers a ten-account trial for LGTalk and a one-month trial for eRex. The articles do not state if other AI models will be added to zevo soon. It remains open whether Cherickal will actually build any of the ten billion-dollar startup ideas. The text does not specify the exact nature of the ten insane products generated.
