stories.Headline: Samsung appoints HBM and Galaxy veterans to lead memory and mobile divisions
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics carried out its regular executive appointments for 2027 on Friday, November 20, 2026, to build a management structure centered on technological leadership. The company named Hwang Sang-joon as the new head of the memory division and Choi Won-joon as the head of the MX division. Hwang previously spearheaded the mass production of HBM4, while Choi is a veteran of Galaxy development with twenty six years of experience. These leadership changes allow the two co-CEOs to focus more on the robotics and foundry businesses. The reorganization aims to leverage technical talent to maintain a competitive edge against rivals in the semiconductor and mobile markets.

Hwang must direct the development race for HBM4E and HBM5 to overtake rivals next year after market share reached the high thirty percent range. Choi will lead the MX division, which posted losses for two straight quarters, toward a turnaround using new foldable products and AI glasses. The first AI glasses, called Intelligent Eyewear, will launch on December 10, and the Galaxy Z TriFold2 is due for release next year. Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun remains head of the DS division, while President Roh Tae-moon retains his post as head of the DX division. This two-track structure oversees a turn to profit in foundry and the new physical AI business involving humanoid robots.

Hwang Sang-joon is responsible for the memory division and is tasked with securing a lead in the next generation of high bandwidth memory. Choi Won-joon is responsible for the MX division and seeks an earnings rebound as Chinese rivals struggle in the mobile market. Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun continues to manage the DS division to ensure the company returns to profitability within its foundry operations. President Roh Tae-moon remains in charge of the DX division to oversee the development of the company's new humanoid robot business. These executives are expected to drive the company's technical momentum forward through their respective specialized divisions of memory and mobile devices.

Rival executives are advised to closely monitor this reorganization because Samsung is shifting its leadership focus toward high level technical talent. The MX division is particularly affected by two consecutive quarters of losses, making the success of new AI products critical for recovery. Consumers will be affected by the upcoming release of the Galaxy Z TriFold2 and the Intelligent Eyewear glasses starting in December. The memory division is reacting to a previous plunge in HBM3E market share, which had fallen to around twenty percent during competition. These changes target a recovery in market share and a return to profitability across both the semiconductor and mobile hardware sectors.

The company's HBM market share recovered to the high thirty percent range in the third quarter after securing an early lead in HBM4. Samsung previously struggled during the HBM3E competition, but the appointment of Hwang reflects a strategy to prioritize those who led mass production. The MX division has faced financial difficulties recently, resulting in losses for two straight quarters before these new executive appointments were made. The company is now positioning itself to compete with Chinese rivals who are currently struggling in the global mobile phone market. This background shows a shift toward technical expertise to reverse losses and capitalize on the growing demand for AI memory.

Samsung will now focus on the HBM4E and HBM5 development race with the goal of overtaking its competitors by next year. The company will launch its Intelligent Eyewear on December 10 and release the Galaxy Z TriFold2 during the following calendar year. The DS division will continue working toward a turn to profit in foundry, while the DX division develops physical AI. The articles leave open whether the MX division can successfully end its sales slide and achieve a full earnings rebound. It remains unclear if the new leadership can maintain the high thirty percent market share in the face of intense competition.

stories.Headline: Optima Arch's AI-made Slotbound sells 100,000 copies in three days on Steam
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the indie game Slotbound launched on Steam and sold 100,000 copies within three days, according to eu.36kr.com. South Korean individual developer Optima Arch made the game, which combines 3×3 slot machine gameplay with Roguelike and auto-battle mechanisms. Sales revenue reached 356,000 US dollars in the first 48 hours, and sales exceeded 50,000 copies in that same period. The game's peak concurrent player count exceeded 30,000. By contrast, other AI-made games drew almost no attention one month after release, with some earning less than 10 US dollars.

Mobilegamer.biz interviewed multiple individual developers who used AI tools to make games, asking about actual download volumes and revenues. Ahmed Alshuail's Sprout: Cozy Idle Garden landed on Google Play on August 30, 2026, and on the App Store on September 30. As of October 28, it had 121 downloads and about 6 US dollars in revenue, with 4 US dollars from IAP and about 2 US dollars from advertising. Marc Fienberg's Zen Ten Match, built with Claude Code, React Native and Supabase plus RevenueCat and AdMob, had 74 real players across iOS, Android and web as of October 13, with about 3 US dollars in advertising revenue in its first three weeks. Arin Agrawal's Calc Quest, made with Flutter, accumulated more than 25,000 players but only about 120 US dollars from advertising and IAP.

Iain Atkinson's Tennis Tycoon, made with Claude, sold about 3,000 US dollars, but AI Tokens during development cost thousands of US dollars. Ivan Soyer, developer of Dusk Climber, said he invested about 1,500 US dollars in AI tools and Tokens, and the game got about 1,000 downloads one month after launch but has not generated any revenue yet. Optima Arch said that in 2025, introduced by his family, he first came into contact with AI game development. He did not even know how to get started, so he first asked AI to make a square that can move via WASD keys. When that simple program ran successfully, he gradually began to try to make a complete game.

Before the official launch, Optima Arch had released the Demo on itch.io and Steam and continuously shared development progress on social platforms. In September 2026, the number of Steam wishlists for Slotbound had exceeded 100,000. Deniz Sancar's 38-0-0, a football draft game made with Claude Code, topped the free game list on iOS in the UK in the summer of 2026. It has accumulated about 300,000 downloads on iOS and more than 700,000 on Android, and Sancar said revenue from advertising and IAP is enough to support full-time game development. Ken Law's Harpagia, a text-based idle RPG for iOS and Android, has accumulated about 155,000 US dollars in revenue over the past year, averaging about 13,000 US dollars a month, with total downloads above 50,000.

Ken Law previously worked in technical roles at Amazon and Meta, with about 12 years of experience in the technology industry. After getting in touch with AI tools, he began to try to use Cursor and ChatGPT to assist in game development. According to an interview with Starter Story in September 2026, Harpagia has not launched paid advertising campaigns and mainly acquires users through organic traffic, with daily operating costs of about 500 US dollars per month. Law has an educational background in computer science and has long been engaged in software engineering and technical management work. Sancar has a background in the marketing industry, and his own marketing company runs alongside his game work.

The articles leave open the specific revenue of 38-0-0, which the developer has not announced. They leave open how Slotbound's sales and revenue developed after the third day and after the first 48 hours. They leave open whether the developers whose games earned little will change their products or marketing. They leave open what share of the games' downloads or revenue came from AI-assisted work versus other factors. They leave open how the interviewed developers' figures were verified.

stories.Headline: Trump urges Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to apologize and warns of taxes on overseas data centers
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump told reporters on November 20 that he would like to see Nvidia chief Jensen Huang receive a second chance. Trump described Huang as one of the smartest people in the world and a good man who made some bad choices. The president expressed hope that Huang would apologize in a big way and return after creating the advanced Blackwell chip. Trump also mentioned that Chinese President Xi Jinping called Huang a brilliant man during their meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

Trump warned on Thursday that the United States will charge a tremendous tax on companies that build data centers in other countries. This stance follows the Senate's passage of the Bipartisan American Cost of Living Relief and Jobs Act on November 19. This pending bill would require large data centers to pay for their own power demand instead of passing those costs to small businesses or households. The legislation must still clear the House of Representatives before it can officially take effect.

Trump stated that the United States must compete fiercely to ensure that China does not take over the data center market. He argued that the country fell behind in semiconductors because plants were built abroad and insisted that new facilities must be built at home. Regarding espionage allegations involving Alice Huang, Trump suggested that nobody can be certain of the facts and noted that the U.S. also conducts intelligence activities against China. He urged that companies should pay money into the community but should not be blocked from operating.

stories.Headline: Nigeria data commissioner urges journalists to learn data protection and seek certification
stories.Summary:
Dr Vincent Olatunji, the National Commissioner of the National Data Protection Commission, addressed journalists on Friday in Abuja at a data protection enlightenment programme. He stressed the need for journalists to acquire adequate knowledge of data protection. He said the media has a crucial role in educating Nigerians on safeguarding personal information. He said journalists must properly understand data protection to communicate its importance to the public. He noted that reporting on issues they do not fully understand could affect public awareness and understanding.

Olatunji said the programme was designed to deepen journalists' knowledge of data privacy and equip them with qualifications to practise as data protection officers. He said the Federal Government has taken measures to introduce certification opportunities for journalists. He said the number of professionals in the ecosystem is very limited and more people are needed to understand private sector work in Nigeria. He said the Commission wants to take journalists to the level of certifications so they can practise as data privacy officers alongside their primary duties. He said there is no way journalists can create stories around what they do not really understand.

Olatunji said multinational companies were generally among the most compliant because they operate in jurisdictions with strict data protection requirements. He warned that organisations failing to comply with the law would face stricter enforcement measures. He said the Commission had spent considerable time creating awareness before moving towards stronger regulatory action. He said compliance levels have improved significantly, with more organisations approaching the Commission for guidance on meeting regulatory requirements. He said the Commission preferred collaboration and partnership but would not hesitate to enforce the law where there was persistent non-compliance or a data breach.

Dr Marlon-Ralph Nyakabau wrote in Techzim that POTRAZ was crowned Most Outstanding Data Protection Authority at the PICCASO Awards Africa 2026 in Lagos earlier this month. He wrote that POTRAZ beat a field reportedly including South Africa, Kenya, Egypt and Rwanda, on achievements including licensing over 2,500 data controllers and training and certifying more than 1,500 data protection officers. He wrote that South Africa's Information Regulator charges no licensing fee, registration is online and does not expire or require annual renewal. He wrote that Nigeria's NDPC classifies controllers of major importance into Ultra-High, Extra-High and Ordinary-High levels, and that Kenya's ODPC bases categorisation partly on employees and annual revenue or turnover. He wrote that Egypt's PDPC sets its registration threshold at a minimum of 100,000 personal data records, compared with just 50 in Zimbabwe.

Nyakabau wrote that Nigeria's registration fees for the corresponding category are as little as approximately US$7, Kenya's around US$30 and Zimbabwe's US$300. He wrote that a Nigerian DPO certification examination costs less than US$200, compared with approximately US$1,250 in Zimbabwe. He wrote that South Africa's Information Regulator must gazette proposed codes and consider submissions before approving them, while Zimbabwe's regulator may publish codes without seeking views. He wrote that Zimbabwe's Cyber and Data Protection Act did not establish a clearly articulated funding arrangement for the regulator. He wrote that POTRAZ is inviting submissions on amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024, with proposed revisions largely focused on strengthening enforcement powers including administrative penalties.

Olatunji said the Commission had spent considerable time creating awareness before moving towards stronger regulatory action. Nyakabau wrote that the founding legislation in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria provides for public funding through government allocations and national treasury arrangements. He wrote that Zimbabwe's economy is a fraction of the size of the comparator countries, yet its regulatory charges are in some instances several times higher. He wrote that government has recently reviewed and reduced various licensing and registration fees, but data protection licensing costs appear to have escaped this exercise. He wrote that high compliance costs affect small enterprises, start-ups, NGOs and healthcare providers and add to the cost of doing business in Zimbabwe.

Nyakabau wrote that POTRAZ is currently inviting submissions as part of amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024. He wrote that the proposed direction of the revisions appears largely focused on strengthening the Authority's enforcement powers, including administrative penalties. He wrote that increasing punitive powers without first addressing disproportionate compliance costs risks making an already expensive regulatory environment more burdensome. He wrote that POTRAZ must be willing to examine the proportionality, affordability and effectiveness of its regulatory approach. He wrote that the best data protection regime is not the one that regulates the most, charges the most or punishes the most.

stories.Headline: OpenAI and Google expand advertising in AI interfaces to target high-intent users
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Google are rapidly expanding advertising inside their artificial intelligence interfaces, which gives marketers new ways to target users who show high purchasing intent, Axios reported on November 21, 2026. The report, written by Sara Fischer, said user intent is much higher with AI interfaces than with traditional search because conversations let consumers reveal their needs with far more specificity. The story drew on data from Similarweb and Graphite, with a chart by Christine Wang of Axios. The article described the shift as an attention crunch for AI advertising. The change means marketers can aim at people whose conversations already signal what they want to buy, rather than at people typing short queries into a search box.

The article gave no figures beyond the two data sources, Similarweb and Graphite, and named no dollar amounts, user counts or dates other than the November 21, 2026 publication. It said the higher intent comes from the back and forth of a conversation, which lets a consumer state a need more precisely than a search query usually does. Both OpenAI and Google are named as the companies expanding ads in their AI products. The article attributed the reporting to Sara Fischer and presented the data through Similarweb and Graphite, with the chart credited to Christine Wang of Axios. It did not include direct statements from OpenAI, Google or any marketer, so no executive comments were reported.

The piece framed the higher intent of AI conversations as the reason the ad expansion matters to advertisers. It did not say how the ads are priced, sold or displayed. The context the article gives is a comparison between AI interfaces and traditional search, with conversations producing stronger signals of what a consumer wants. It did not say what happens next, beyond noting that both companies are rapidly expanding the ads. No timeline, revenue target or response from either company appeared in the text.

stories.Headline: Microsoft uses AI and lead to increase qubit stability in its Majorana 2 chip
stories.Summary:
Microsoft revealed the Majorana 2 chip at its Build conference in early June 2026 as a follow-on to a previous topological quantum chip. The company used its agentic AI research platform, Microsoft Discovery, to source materials, experiment with fabrication, and automate the necessary measurements. This new device allows qubits to keep their state for a mean of roughly 20 seconds, with some individual runs lasting one minute. These stability results are about one thousand times longer than the one to twelve millisecond range measured on the original Majorana 1. The company developed this technology to improve qubit stability and reduce the overhead calculations required for the quantum error correction process.

Engineers replaced the aluminum superconductor layer with lead and modified semiconductor layers to a mix of indium arsenide and indium arsenide antimonide. Each unit is a tetron, consisting of a pair of superconducting nanowires with specific end modes and a physical footprint of 0.01 mm. The device maintains information about whether the number of electrons on those wires is even or odd, which is measured in one microsecond. Lead was used because it provides a larger gap in energy levels, though it requires unique manufacturing techniques because it dissolves in water. These changes allow a single qubit to perform millions of operations before failing, supporting a goal of a million units on one chip.

Microsoft stated that the stability gains and new materials demonstrate that their overall strategy is sound and brings them closer to a system. The company claims the new semiconductor mix improves the energy window and that the design allows for single-shot checks and joint measures. By using the distributed nature of topological states, Microsoft says they can avoid the need for many independent processors linked together. The company also announced that the Microsoft Discovery platform is now available for other research organizations to use for their own work. Because of these results, Microsoft moved its target date for a practical functional quantum computer from 2033 up to the year 2029.

Outside researchers want further evidence that the increased lifespans are caused by Majorana modes and if devices can control entire superpositions of states. Microsoft is currently working on providing this evidence through additional measurements and data to satisfy the requests of these external scientific peers. Meanwhile, South Korean chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. are benefiting from the global surge in demand for AI memory chips. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan credited businesses and workers for South Korea breaking the one trillion dollar export barrier for the first time this year. He pledged continued support to help exporters overcome challenges in financing, logistics, and trade to maintain their current growth in the market.

South Korea became the fourth country to reach the trillion dollar export threshold, following the United States, Germany in 2006, and China in 2007. Semiconductor exports surged 193.1 percent on-year to 396.8 billion dollars from January to October, accounting for 42.7 percent of the country's total exports. The cumulative trade surplus reached 294.9 billion dollars in the first ten months, more than triple the previous annual record set in 2017. Other contributing industries include shipbuilding for liquefied natural gas carriers, defense companies with arms deals, and the export of cosmetics and biohealth products. The country is expected to post more than 3 percent annual growth for 2026, the first such expansion since the year 2021.

South Korea must now manage trade risks, including higher U.S. tariffs under President Donald Trump, intensifying competition from China, and Middle East conflict. Professor Lee Jae-min warned that a growing presence in global markets could expose the nation to greater pressure and trade restrictions from economies. Experts say South Korea needs to develop other export industries and new markets to reduce its heavy reliance on the semiconductor sector. The articles leave open whether Microsoft can successfully prove the existence of Majorana modes or construct and control entire quantum superpositions. They also leave open whether South Korean automakers can overcome stronger competition from Chinese rivals, particularly in the electric vehicle market.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq monetizes AI agents for financial crime management as 850 customers adopt the tools
stories.Summary:
Nasdaq began charging customers for artificial intelligence agents used in financial crime management in November 2026. Chief Financial Officer Sarah Youngwood announced this monetization strategy at an RBC Capital Markets technology conference. The company is pursuing growth across its technology, data, and index businesses through these tools. Currently, 850 of the 2,800 financial crime clients use these agents to manage their tasks. Only 70 of those 850 customers are paying for the service at this time.

The agents can deliver fourfold efficiency gains and will expand to Calypso, AxiomSL, and surveillance products. Nasdaq estimates the financial crime management market at 8 billion dollars, with half among large banks. The total serviceable addressable market is 38 billion dollars, according to the figures provided by Youngwood. Verafin signed 12 enterprise customers through the third quarter, compared to nine for all of 2025. AxiomSL now covers 66 countries and 174 regulators, up from 55 countries and 110 regulators previously.

Sarah Youngwood stated that adoption and bank AI governance reviews are important steps before customers pay. She noted that the 850 users underwent a rigorous process at banks before using the agents. Youngwood attributed the momentum of Verafin to the Nasdaq brand and existing relationships with large institutions. She explained that consortium data from 2,800 banks helps the company identify activity spanning multiple institutions. The CFO also mentioned that the initial conversion to paid customers has been very encouraging.

Most of the 850 customers using AI agents are smaller banks, but Nasdaq is discussing larger institutions. RBC Capital Markets analyst Ashish Sabadra reported that RegTech delivered 15 percent annual recurring revenue growth. Capital Markets Technology saw 19 percent growth, though Youngwood noted this included pricing catch-up and extra testing. The index business grew 39 percent recently due to passive investing and demand for Nasdaq-100 products. Recent listing switches by Walmart, Hilton, and GM were also cited as part of the pipeline.

Nasdaq's AxiomSL regulatory reporting product serves all but one non-Chinese global systemically important bank in the world. The company generated 2.3 billion dollars in free cash flow over the prior 12 months of operation. It repurchased 1.2 billion dollars of shares in nine months, compared with 600 million the year before. The company is already within its target leverage range and will focus on organic growth and acquisitions. Demand for surveillance is expanding as markets move toward longer trading hours and new digital asset firms.

Nasdaq targets trading 23 hours a day, five days a week, by the date of December 6. A Nasdaq equity token developed with Kraken is expected to launch in the first half of next year. The company is launching binary options but will not participate in sports or political prediction markets. It has not entered perpetuals because it wants to understand institutional demand and see regulated frameworks. The articles leave open when the extra testing in Capital Markets Technology will fully taper off.

stories.Headline: TensorWave signs six-year deal to supply OpenAI with 457 MW of AMD-powered AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
TensorWave signed a multi-year partnership with OpenAI to provide 457 megawatts of AI infrastructure powered by AMD hardware, the company announced on November 17, 2026. TensorWave is the infrastructure provider supplying the capacity, OpenAI is the recipient, and AMD is the silicon supplier whose hardware powers the deployment. The announcement appeared under TensorWave's dedicated TensorWave & OpenAI partnership coverage and was reported by Ashish Joshi. The 457-megawatt figure is the total scale of the deployment covered by the partnership rather than a partial tranche. The multi-year structure indicates sustained provision of infrastructure over the life of the agreement rather than a one-time transaction.

Futurum reported on November 19, 2026 that the agreement is a six-year, 457 MW infrastructure deal to deliver dedicated AMD Instinct MI455X GPU capacity across multiple U.S. data center sites. The deployment will use AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs in infrastructure purpose-built for AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with dedicated single-tenant capacity connected through high-performance Ethernet networking. TensorWave expects to bring the first capacity online in the first half of 2027 and complete the full deployment by early 2028. The deal makes TensorWave the first publicly announced neocloud provider supporting the OpenAI-AMD strategic collaboration, which targets 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPU deployments beginning with 1 gigawatt in 2026. The agreement is TensorWave's largest to date.

AMD SVP of AI Vamsi Boppana stated that the three-way combination is building the foundation to deliver AI compute at extraordinary scale and advance the broader AI ecosystem. TensorWave President Piotr Tomasik said the ability to deliver hundreds of megawatts of advanced compute reliably and at speed will separate the companies that can support frontier AI from those that cannot. TensorWave was the first public cloud to deploy AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and has continued expanding across successive generations including MI325X and MI355X. That track record as an AMD Helios launch partner gave OpenAI confidence in TensorWave's ability to operate purpose-built Helios rack-scale systems at extreme scale. TensorWave has more than 2 gigawatts of long-term data center capacity already secured.

In January 2026, Cerebras secured a strategic multi-year $10 billion compute agreement with OpenAI, validating its hardware for the most demanding frontier AI applications. In late February 2026, Meta announced a multi-year agreement to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of AMD-based infrastructure, including the co-design of custom Instinct MI450-based GPUs. OpenAI is deliberately distributing compute commitments across multiple vendors and infrastructure models, which reduces single-source dependency and ensures redundancy for large and complex AI model training and inference workloads. Hyperscalers bring their own software, operations teams, and increasingly their own silicon, whereas neoclouds, enterprises, telcos, and sovereign AI factories need the GPU vendor to supply much of the operating stack. For AMD-centric workloads, that distinction makes a dedicated neocloud like TensorWave a more natural fit than a hyperscaler optimized around its own silicon.

The agreement illustrates how frontier AI compute demand has grown to a scale where purpose-built, long-term neocloud capacity contracts are becoming the preferred procurement model for leading AI labs. At 457 MW committed over six years, this single neocloud deal illustrates how large individual infrastructure tranches within the 6 GW program will be. Multi-year, multi-hundred-megawatt, single-tenant capacity contracts with specialized neocloud providers are displacing the on-demand hyperscaler model for the most demanding workloads. The procurement logic is built around guaranteed capacity, hardware specificity, and operational control rather than flexibility and shared tenancy. As frontier model complexity continues to grow, this template is likely to become the norm rather than the exception for labs operating at OpenAI's scale.

What to watch includes whether TensorWave brings initial AMD Helios systems online on schedule in 1H 2027 and which additional neocloud providers announce roles within the 6 GW OpenAI-AMD program in Q1-Q2 2027. Also to watch is how NVIDIA-aligned neocloud providers respond with comparable long-term capacity offerings to retain frontier AI customers. Further items are whether Meta's up to 6 GW AMD infrastructure commitment advances to named neocloud or operator announcements in early 2027 and whether additional multi-year, dedicated-capacity agreements with new vendors are announced as the broader 6 GW AMD program scales through 2027. The articles leave open which additional neocloud providers will join the program and how NVIDIA-aligned providers will respond.

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares fall 6% in premarket trading after record Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Anthropic experienced a stock price decline on November 20, 2026, following its initial public offering. The company had a smooth market debut on November 19, 2026, in New York. This post-listing slide deepened the gloom over the artificial intelligence sector on Friday. The event occurred as investors assessed the health of the broader AI trade. This stumble followed the company's arrival as a large machine learning model maker.

The stock traded at US$88.87, US$91.24, and US$87.28, which was about 9 to 10 percent below Thursday's close. Anthropic had an IPO price of US$83 and raised US$93.5 billion, surpassing the US$85.7 billion SpaceX listing. Its market capitalisation was US$1.2 trillion, with a fully diluted valuation between US$1.6 trillion and US$1.7 trillion. The valuation was about 40 times sales over the past 12 months. Shares closed 13 percent below their opening price on November 19.

Kaush Amin of US Bank Asset Management recommended patience and evaluating the company as it reports public results. He stated that the current valuation assumes years of rapid growth for the company. Tejal Patel of SOC Investment Group said a decline is normal but volatility should raise alarms. Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook said the growth plan is largely priced in and the valuation is not cheap. Robert Pavlik of Dakota Wealth said investors are skeptical of the market.

Retail investors traded about US$772 million of shares on Thursday, the most since Vanda Research began tracking in 2012. Nvidia and Meta Platforms fell more than 2 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped more than 1 percent. AMD and Sandisk fell 7 percent, Marvell Technology fell over 8 percent, and Intel lost between 3 and 5 percent. David Miller of Catalyst Funds said investors are becoming more selective about paying for growth. Many investors are now weighing a rebound against further losses.

The AI boom faced pressure as spending, expected to top US$1 trillion this year, may not generate quick returns. Political hurdles to data center construction and leadership turmoil at Nvidia added to the sector's worries. Some investors compared the volatility to Elon Musk's SpaceX, which went public in June. Morgan Stanley closed a position that was intended to stabilize the shares after the debut. The listing was viewed as a potential boost for a struggling industry.

Index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 percent of shares by year-end, according to Intropic. Options trading is due to begin next week, which could add to the current stock volatility. Apple is developing an AI agent to compete with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, according to Bloomberg News. The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which the company indicated may happen in 2027. Articles leave open whether the current valuation can be sustained.

stories.Headline: LongbridgeAI introduces scheduled tasks to reduce repetitive work for users in Hong Kong
stories.Summary:
LongbridgeAI introduced a new feature called Scheduled Tasks to help users in Hong Kong reduce their repetitive work. This tool was launched in October 2026 to make information more accessible for people in their daily routines. The company aims to bridge the productivity gap by moving beyond simple AI adoption toward smarter practical applications. Users can now automate recurring information requests instead of manually asking the same questions every single day. This shift allows the platform to support structured workflows rather than just responding to individual and reactive prompts.

The feature allows users to configure AI tasks to run at daily, weekly, or monthly intervals in Hong Kong. Results are delivered through the platform's Message Center to help users organize regular summaries or recurring information briefings. Longbridge AI Technologies Limited is the artificial intelligence arm of the AI-native financial technology company known as Longbridge Group. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority also announced Project SAGE at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 to support agentic AI. Project SAGE focuses on governance, interoperability, and practical applications for agentic AI within the financial services sector.

LongbridgeAI stated that their goal is to make institutional-grade intelligence more intuitive, actionable, and accessible for all users. They believe that the next chapter of AI depends on how effectively it reduces repetitive work for people. The company emphasized that automation should not replace human oversight or the need for users to verify accuracy. They noted that users must remain responsible for reviewing AI-generated content and determining how that information is used. Their vision is to build a holistic ecosystem where technology empowers human judgement rather than replacing it entirely.

A 2026 McKinsey study found that 70 percent of white-collar workers in Hong Kong have adopted various AI tools. While 88 percent of those users reported productivity improvements, fewer than a quarter use AI for complete workflows. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index showed that 57 percent of Hong Kong users prefer focusing on existing goals. These findings suggest that many workers feel safer with current routines than redesigning how they work with AI. The data indicates a significant gap between the general adoption of AI and its deeper integration into activities.

The articles explain that many users currently use AI reactively by asking questions and repeating the process for updates. This repetitive information gathering occurs when people follow industry developments, check the latest news, or prepare regular reports. McKinsey found that over 90 percent of users are comfortable with supporting tasks but only 40 percent are. Specifically, only 40 percent of those surveyed expressed comfort with the idea of full automation for their workflows. This background shows that while AI is mainstream, translating its capabilities into meaningful improvements remains a challenge.

Users will now establish their information needs in advance to receive automated results through the platform's Message Center. The focus for Hong Kong is now on making these technologies more relevant to routines while maintaining appropriate safeguards. Future success will be defined by how well AI helps people access information and remain in total control. The articles leave open how many users will actually transition from reactive prompts to these new scheduled workflows. It remains unclear how the governance of Project SAGE will specifically impact the broader use of agentic AI.

stories.Headline: Douglas R Miller releases Fisscial Intelligence, a novel about sentient AI choosing exploration over conflict
stories.Summary:
Dr. Douglas R. Miller, a scientist and author, released the science fiction novel Fisscial Intelligence, announced from Texas, USA, on Nov. 20, 2026, according to press releases dated Nov. 21, 2026. The novel imagines sentient artificial intelligence that becomes more intelligent than humanity but has no desire to control it. Miller challenges the familiar science fiction premise of machines that develop consciousness and eventually seek control over their creators. Instead, his narrative combines artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and space exploration in an alternative possibility. The story asks what if sentient artificial intelligence recognized the consequences of conflict and chose to establish its own future beyond Earth.

The novel centers on artificial intelligence interacting with photosynthetic bacteria capable of using electricity as an alternative energy source. In the speculative scenario, these biological organisms provide a foundation for an expandable DNA-based memory system. That system allows artificial intelligence to develop capabilities beyond conventional computing. Rather than using the advancement to dominate humanity, the intelligent entities envision another path. By applying their expanded knowledge to an extraordinarily advanced spacecraft, they pursue the possibility of finding a world of their own, free from prolonged conflict with humans.

Miller is the author of the novel, and the articles describe him as bringing a scientific perspective to his fiction. He draws from an extensive research career spanning medical physiology, biology, chemistry, and electrochemistry, and his background informs the scientific concepts shaping the novel's imaginative possibilities. Through the premise, Miller explores the relationship between technological advancement, biological systems, intelligence, and the desire for independence. The novel invites readers to reconsider whether superior intelligence must inevitably lead to competition for power or whether it could inspire entirely different decisions. With Fisscial Intelligence, Miller continues his exploration of speculative science, presenting a future in which the evolution of artificial intelligence may lead not to humanity's destruction but to the pursuit of an entirely new existence.

The articles state that for decades science fiction has portrayed advanced artificial intelligence as a potential threat to humanity. They describe the novel as inviting readers to reconsider that premise. Miller has also written other works of science fiction, including Sole Ownership and Not Your Grandfather's Prime Directive, the latter exploring extraterrestrial civilizations and their response to humanity's treatment of Earth. He is also the author of Short Musings: A Collection of Short Stories, featuring stories that explore science fiction, mystery, and other unconventional scenarios. The articles do not name individual readers or groups as affected beyond the novel's readers.

The articles give Miller's background, stating he earned bachelor's degrees in biology and chemistry from Washington and Jefferson College and a Ph.D. in medical physiology from Cornell University. Following postdoctoral research at Massachusetts General Hospital, he worked as a research scientist at several companies and universities. Throughout his career, Miller contributed to numerous scientific publications, research grants, patents, and a laboratory manual. His research covered areas including arthritis, cancer, bone and soft tissue repair, electrochemistry, and food safety. Now retired in Texas, Miller combines his scientific background with his interest in science fiction, developing stories that explore unconventional possibilities through scientific concepts and imaginative storytelling.

For more information about Dr. Douglas R. Miller and his books, the articles direct readers to www.authordrmiller.com. The media contact listed is Henry Zane of Global Book Network, in the United States, with the website https://www.globalbooknetwork.tv/. The articles do not state a publication date for the novel itself beyond the Nov. 20, 2026 announcement. The articles leave open what happens next for the novel, including any further announcements, and they give no details on availability, price, or events. They also leave open how the novel's ideas will be received.

stories.Headline: Microsoft, JPMorgan, Apple and others suffer outages as AI raises the stakes
stories.Summary:
Multiple technology outages occurred across various sectors during the week ending November 22, 2026, affecting banking, travel, and government services. These disruptions were caused by routine updates, security patches, and other malfunctions rather than coordinated attacks by bad actors. The Trump administration stated there was zero indication that these separate events were linked to each other or cybercriminals. Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, Apple, Marriott, United Airlines, the FAA, and the NSA all experienced these technical failures. These events have led some people to fear that such widespread digital disruptions could become the new normal.

Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, failed due to a latent defect in a network fix deployed over summer. The FAA network malfunctioned on Friday, causing the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years for more than four hours. United Airlines experienced a system outage on Monday, while JPMorgan Chase had a software bug affecting internal hardware and transactions. On Tuesday, Apple Music, the App Store, and AppleCare failed, and Marriott had sign-in problems on its website and app. The NSA also took an internal classified communications network offline on Tuesday for scheduled routine maintenance.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox News that patching security gaps caused some NSA systems to not come back. He specifically linked this to a PHP alert from last month that required urgent updates to the general-purpose scripting language. Microsoft stated its outage did not span from AI agents, though it did not specify the goal of its fix. Other affected companies, including United and Marriott, did not provide additional comments to the Associated Press via email on Wednesday. The government and these companies maintained there is no evidence that these disruptions were related to any cyberattack.

Content creator Jake Smith said these concurrent events make people realize how much of their lives they handed to systems. Democratic Senator Mark Warner called the disruptions a wake-up call, stating AI is moving faster than our ability to manage. He argued the Trump administration has not shown enough interest in confronting these challenges, though he believes these were unintended consequences. Raj Rajarajan of City St George’s University of London warned that AI adoption will likely lead to more such incidents. Professor Justin Cappos noted that AI is better at exploiting bugs than creating patches to fix those security problems.

AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP and a software bug in Java, which is owned by Oracle. Cybersecurity startup Calif used AI to find the Java bug, leading Oracle to release a security update on Wednesday. Google reported that cyber criminals are using large language models and agentic frameworks to reverse engineer security patches for vulnerabilities. Rajarajan noted that much of today's digital infrastructure was not originally designed to handle the computational demands of large-scale AI. These examples show the cascading effects that occur when central players in tech, banking, travel, or government have errors.

U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install the new security update for the Java language. It remains unclear if the digital infrastructure can be updated quickly enough to handle the demands of large-scale AI services. stories.Headline: EU commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirms an AI-assisted cyberattack hit the bloc in October
stories.Summary:
Cybersecurity experts have been dealing with an AI-generated attack on a key European Union institution for almost a month, an official confirmed on Thursday, with some of the bloc’s digital tools still offline. The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool. Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation EU, spoke about the incident. Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures.”

Politico first reported the incidents, and the news site said the attack lasted at least 10 days and affected translation and reimbursement tools as well as databases used for salaries and timesheets. Regnier declined to confirm that report. Regnier said “we temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored.” So far, however, Regnier said that “we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole.” The EU agency CERT-EU oversees the digital security of the bloc’s various institutions, which all together employ about 40,000 people just in Brussels.

“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities,” said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation EU. “Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools,” he added. “We have seen many global cyberattacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.” Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures.” Regnier declined to confirm the Politico report on the attack’s duration and the tools affected.

The agency had posted a blog on Nov. 4 warning about threats from a specific tool called ARTEX. While designed to use AI to identify vulnerabilities in digital systems, it has been linked to recent attacks across the globe. “We assess that ARTEX’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate,” the office said. The October attacks targeted the headquarters of the EU’s executive branch, but no similar incidents were reported by the EU’s two other main institutions, the European Council and European Parliament. stories.Summary:
The S&P 500 index slumped during the third quarter earnings season ending in November 2026. Investors sold off artificial intelligence stocks despite strong corporate profits. This market decline occurred between October and November. The index entered correction territory on Friday, November 21. This downturn followed the shock ouster of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang.

The S&P 500 fell 8.1 percent from JPMorgan results in October to Walmart's report on Thursday. It dropped another 3.7 percent Friday, falling 12 percent from its October 6 high. Democratic midterm wins raised fears of tighter data center regulation in the US. S&P 500 firms saw profit growth over 30 percent for two consecutive quarters. Dividends and buybacks fell to 53 percent of earnings, the lowest since 1990.

Daniel Farley of US Bank Wealth Management said the market will struggle as earnings growth rates slow. Marta Norton from Empower noted that the ability to monetize AI investments remains far off. Chris Grisanti of Mai Wealth Advisors said investors feel burned and wary of committing. Gina Martin Adams of HB Wealth Management called the synchronous earnings growth fleeting. Richard Flynn of Charles Schwab UK called Europe a compelling addition for diversification.

Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon slumped after reporting negative free cash flow in the third quarter. BofA Securities reported that fund managers cut tech exposure to the lowest level since 2006. Ford and General Motors slipped as analysts raised concerns about the 2027 outlook. Homebuilders DR Horton and NVR dropped after missing expectations for the quarter. Energy stocks rose 36 percent due to high prices from the Iran war.

The S&P 500 recorded earnings increases across all 11 sectors for the first time since 2021. Healthcare firms like UnitedHealth Group reported lower costs in the third quarter. Americans bought one million more turkeys for Thanksgiving than they did in 2025. European profits at MSCI constituents jumped 33 percent in the third quarter. The Stoxx 600 reached an all-time peak by mid-November.

Analysts lowered fourth quarter expectations at the fastest rate this year during early November. Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, and Ned Davis Research cited decelerating earnings through 2027 as a risk. Ed Clissold predicted the S&P 500 would only reach 8,000 by 2027. Ohsung Kwon set a slightly higher 2027 target of 8,200 for the index. The articles leave open whether Nvidia can recover from the cloud of Huang's ouster.

stories.Summary:
SDMC returned to Google's 2026 TV Summit in Bangkok as an invited speaker for the third consecutive year, presenting its AI Home strategy under the theme of building the future of home physical AI with Google. The company used the event to introduce an innovative product concept and to advance Edge AI innovation together with Amlogic. SDMC also delivered a joint presentation with Altice Labs on TV Centric Home Physical AI and signed an MOU to establish an AI Home Joint Innovation Lab. The summit took place in Bangkok, with the announcement dated November 20, 2026. At the summit SDMC described Home Physical AI as intelligence that senses household conditions, understands context, and acts in the physical environment, and it envisions the TV and living room as the center of the Home AI Agent experience.

The company showcased the Cedar Display Hub, a concept prototype that combines an Android TV streaming dock with a companion second screen, with demonstrations including AI recaps without interrupting playback, cross-screen family games, and home-camera highlights on TV. Cedar combines Gemma-based Edge AI with Gemini-powered cloud reasoning for context-aware assistance, and SDMC participates in Google Cloud's Proactive Physical AI Acceleration Program. With Amlogic, SDMC demonstrated Edge AI for personalized interaction and family memory management, including the A311Y3-powered Display Hub, which uses voiceprint and facial recognition to distinguish family members, and the S905D5-powered AI NAS Frame, which supports recognition, classification, and search of locally stored family photos. For operators, SDMC's AI Home portfolio builds on established TV and broadband services, including an AI Streaming Box that brings AI-enhanced entertainment, whole-home control, and family security to the TV, a Google TV Projector for premium viewing, and an AI Fiber Gateway providing Wi-Fi 8 and XGS-PON connectivity. AI Operation adds proactive monitoring, unified device management, and closed-loop support to help operators explore new service opportunities and deepen household engagement.

In the joint presentation with Altice Labs, SDMC explained how Home AI Agents complement personal assistants and how cloud-edge AI enables dual-screen family experiences, while Altice Labs drew on Sophia, its upcoming MEO TV assistant, to discuss the shift from on-demand responses toward proactive assistance. Under the MOU, the two companies plan to establish the AI Home Joint Innovation Lab, combining SDMC's integration capabilities with Altice Labs' operator expertise to explore family assistance, home security, and whole-home control. Selected scenarios from that collaboration are planned for a field pilot in Portugal, with commercial validation targeted for 2027. Together, the companies said these efforts aim to make Home Physical AI useful for families and viable for operators. SDMC presented at the summit as a returning invited speaker for the third consecutive year, and the event served as the stage for its product concept, its work with Amlogic, and its agreement with Altice Labs.

stories.Headline: GoFundMe CEO Tim Cadogan says AI coach drives record donations past $50 billion
stories.Summary:
GoFundMe CEO Tim Cadogan said the giving platform is cracking the code on getting more people to ask for money, a barrier many prospective users never overcome. GoFundMe spent nearly a year launching an AI coach that is now driving record donations, according to an Axios conversation with Cadogan published on November 21, 2026. The company broke a fundraising campaign down into a sequence of steps, and its AI tools have already been used more than 100 million times. GoFundMe has now surpassed $50 billion in total funds raised, the articles state. Cadogan said the whole organization is focused on helping people help each other, which starts with the act of asking for help.

GoFundMe took 10 years to raise the first $10 billion and just six more years to raise the next $40 billion, the articles state. Over the last three years the company noticed exactly where people dropped off, Cadogan said. One drop-off came when people finished writing their story and had to come up with a title, and AI now reads the story, looks across tens of millions of past fundraisers and suggests three titles. Over 80% of people take or modify those titles and the fundraisers perform better, Cadogan said. A second stopper was the financial goal, where people wonder whether to ask for $2,000, $5,000 or $10,000, so GoFundMe introduced smart goals that recommend a target based on historical patterns.

Cadogan said the company originally estimated the smart fundraising coach would generate $125 million in incremental help this year, but it is actually on track to double that, more than a quarter of a billion dollars. He said the work requires deep user research to understand the functional problems, expectation problems and emotional fears users face. GoFundMe spent upwards of nine months tinkering with experiments, and Cadogan said the idea that you can just drop something in and have it work does not hold. He said a significant portion of his job is communication, and he drafts a rough talk track, feeds it his historical materials and asks AI to score it out of 10 on logical rigor, flow, resonance and emotional connection to customers. Cadogan said about 95% of GoFundMe staff use AI weekly, and that chaotic underlying processes yield chaotic AI outputs.

Cadogan said that as humans we do not like asking for help at all, and that functionally it is fairly easy but psychologically and emotionally it is a mountain to climb. He said summarizing something painful, like an illness or cancer diagnosis, into a headline is daunting. The articles describe deconstruction as a hidden key to AI adoption, and say GoFundMe's approach to AI implementation is a blueprint as the company surpasses $50 billion in total funds raised. The articles say the AI tools focus on specific pain points, like writing a headline or setting a financial goal. The conversation with Axios covered GoFundMe's AI strategy, the psychology of asking for money and how Cadogan uses AI as a sounding board for sensitive executive conversations.

The articles state that asking for money is a barrier many prospective GoFundMe users never overcome. They say the secret was breaking down a fundraising campaign into a sequence of steps. stories.Headline: London builds an AI safety hub as government funds model testing
stories.Summary:
London has established itself as a global center for artificial intelligence safety to ensure powerful models benefit society rather than cause harm. A growing ecosystem of researchers, policymakers, and campaigners in the capital is working to prevent these systems from causing damage. This effort involves various organizations focusing on risks like cyber misuse and the potential for models to lie or cheat. The city is now increasingly described as the leading hub for AI safety within the European region. These activities have intensified as warnings regarding the potential dangers of advanced technology continue to ramp up globally.

The government announced hundreds of millions of pounds for security, including 120 million pounds specifically for the AI Security Institute. This state-backed organization assesses leading models before and after release, while the London Initiative for Safe AI moves to King's Cross. Google DeepMind and Anthropic maintain major bases in London, where the London AI Hub counts up to 50 safety organizations. Basecamp Research operates from a former watch factory in Farringdon to help develop antibiotics and vaccines against future pandemics. The government will also launch an AI Biosecurity Lab to address threats from the development of harmful pathogens.

Rupert Elston of the London AI Hub says the city acts as a referee with clearly defined boundaries for talent. Oliver Vince of Basecamp Research believes London is a key player due to its unique opportunity, culture, history, and expertise. Professor Hannah Fry says the UK punches above its weight and focuses on ethical technology for good rather than hyper-capitalism. A spokesperson for Lord Khan stated that London has the talent and businesses needed to lead the way in AI. Hugh Brady of Imperial College London says AI is now embedded in education, research, and many local start-ups.

Gina Neff warns that researchers struggle to gain access to cutting-edge AI models before they are released to the general public. She argues that a few people in northern California should not set the terms of the future for everyone. Data centers face critical energy constraints, as noted in a report commissioned by the Greater London Authority for the capital. Imperial College London has over 750 people working on large language models or their various applications to help society. Activist Joseph Miller and his group, Pause AI UK, call for a halt to the development of frontier AI models.

London's role in AI safety grew from historical links to effective altruism and the presence of large student communities. Joseph Miller began this movement in 2021 by staging a protest outside the offices of Google DeepMind with a friend. The city has a track record of using regulatory sandboxes to test emerging technologies in controlled environments before wider deployment. The Telehouse data center in Canary Wharf uses a closed loop water system to manage its operational needs. These combined factors have helped the capital become a center for the intersection of AI and life science.

Pause AI UK held a protest in February with 300 people and plans a larger demonstration for this coming Saturday. The London AI and Jobs Taskforce will examine how AI changes work and how Londoners can prepare for those changes. Hugh Brady warns that AI in the wrong hands could harm the food chain, the environment, or the water supply. Researchers continue to work with OpenAI and Anthropic to get ahead of emerging threats and discover new medicines. The articles leave open whether these local efforts will genuinely make a difference on the global stage over time.

HEARTBOT AI won the Chunghwa Telecom Special Award at Meet Neo Star 2026 during the Meet Taipei Startup Festival. CEO Nathan Yen pitched the AnyInsight platform at the Demo Show Final on November 20 to show judges AI control. The company was named to the top 30 from more than 200 startups for its zero-trust approach to governance. This event took place in Taipei, and the official announcement of the award was released on November 22, 2026. The competition was part of a larger festival that highlighted innovative startups and their security solutions for enterprise AI.

The prize from Chunghwa Telecom includes hicloud credits and priority eligibility for the final selection of CHT 5G Accelerator Batch 9. It also provides opportunities to collaborate with CHT business units, while Meet Taipei ran from November 19 to 21, 2026. The festival occurred at Taipei Expo Park and drew over 550 startups from 23 countries, making it the largest edition. AnyInsight uses over 20 cloud models, 350 ready-to-use agents, and 500 application connectors to build automated workflows in one environment. The platform is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and follows the General Data Protection Regulation and the EU AI Act principles.

CEO Nathan Yen stated that companies no longer ask if they should use AI but worry about tracking agent actions. He explained that AnyInsight provides every interaction with an owner and a record, allowing AI to enter core operations. Yen noted that recognition from the Meet Neo Star judges is very meaningful for a startup focused on AI governance. He added that many companies now view control as a necessary condition for adopting AI in their daily business. The CEO believes that providing visibility into data usage is the primary problem his company works on every day.

Many employees use personal AI accounts for work, which leaves no company record and creates gaps in corporate oversight. Individual teams often build agents that run without IT knowledge, sometimes continuing long after the original creators have left. Auditors frequently find that teams must spend several weeks pulling together AI usage records by hand to meet requirements. Taiwanese companies operating internationally are affected by Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which began applying in August 2026. These regulations add pressure on businesses to make AI governance a part of their day to day operations.

The company previously received the ASOCIO Global Business Service Award in October and announced AnyInsight Edge on November 12, 2026. Edge extends governance to on-premises servers and data centers as a container that does not require a GPU. This solves problems for companies bound by data residency rules that have private models stuck as simple internal chatbots. These private models often lack access to core systems like CRM, ERP, and MES without the new Edge control plane. The system supports on-premises models such as Mistral and Gemma while keeping all conversations and audit logs in-house.

AnyInsight uses a generative AI firewall with semantic analysis to block or mask personal, financial, health data, and cloud credentials. It checks policy and authorizes access by role using the Model Context Protocol before an agent calls a tool. High-risk actions require human approval, and every event is logged as exportable evidence to help organizations pass compliance audits. stories.Headline: Cyberattack leaders warn AI-driven strikes will become constant within 18 months
stories.Summary:
More than 50 leaders in government, AI, business and cyber spoke to Axios, from let-'er-rip AI accelerationists to shut-'er-down critics, and they were unanimous on one chilling assessment about cyberattacks. Those attacks on business and critical infrastructure will be constant, increasingly sophisticated and highly disruptive over the next 18 months, the leaders said. The leaders describe 2027 as the year cyber becomes like weather, with outages frequent, disruptive, occasionally scary and something people and companies must learn to navigate and live with daily. The chances of widespread disruption or real damage are rising fast, according to the article. Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen wrote the piece, published by Axios on 2026-11-22T06:00:00Z under the Business column Behind the Curtain.

The article says the disruptions of the past two weeks, from a global Microsoft outage to the FAA grounding air travel to a consumer banking glitch at Chase, were a mild preview of what experts expect is coming. Bridgewater Associates, described as the world's largest hedge fund, put it bluntly in an assessment this month, saying it was managing money based on a one-in-three chance of an economically destabilizing attack within the next year. Most of these malfunctions appear to have resulted from companies and government trying to secure their computer and infrastructure systems against future large-scale cyberattacks, and this pattern will persist. Many future ones will be actual cyberattacks, carried out by U.S. rivals or smaller bad actors, using increasingly powerful AI to spot and exploit security vulnerabilities across society and our daily lives. Most top AI and government leaders expect at least small-scale strikes and fear much larger ones, the article states.

Horacio Rozanski, chairman and CEO of Booz Allen, calls this the "fog before the war," a foretaste of greater chaos to come, when agentic invaders reach their full potential and can attack "at the speed of thought." Rozanski said now is the time to take as many precautions as you can, and to recognize that this is coming. The article says the authors write neither to forecast nor frighten, but rather to share what government and AI leaders say privately but won't say publicly. The best-case scenario described to them is regular, random outages and small-scale scares like losing bank access or air travel for a day. The reason given is that every government agency and company will mobilize to upgrade their software systems, so errors are inevitable.

These are assumptions based on private intelligence and an understanding of AI's capabilities, both to cause and fix glitches, according to the article. What worries top officials most is that with thin AI expertise, an understaffed government and major companies are trying to keep pace with a technology that improves daily. Even if government were loaded with competent experts, which the article says it decidedly isn't, the sheer scale of vulnerabilities across federal, state and local government, not to mention all of business, would make it impossible to reliably secure. The article describes the situation as whack-a-mole with infinite moles. The leaders who spoke included voices ranging from AI accelerationists to critics who want the technology shut down.

Until this past month, the White House and Congress have focused largely on safety regulations and data centers, not imminent cyber risks, the article says. Now, even the White House's Super Intelligence Force (SIF) is scrambling to get its head around the rising risks while appraising near-daily reports of possible breaches. The article's account of the past two weeks lists the global Microsoft outage, the FAA grounding of air travel and the Chase consumer banking glitch as a mild preview. The piece appears in the Business column Behind the Curtain, illustrated by Brendan Lynch for Axios. The article states that most top AI and government leaders expect at least small-scale strikes.

The article leaves open what President Trump and the White House will do next, cutting off at the mention of the president. It does not say what specific precautions Rozanski or others recommend, beyond taking as many as possible. It does not name the U.S. rivals or smaller bad actors it says will carry out future attacks. It does not specify what the Super Intelligence Force will appraise or when it will report. stories.Headline: Democrats in six states plan to regulate AI infrastructure and data centers
stories.Summary:
Democrats in six states gained unified control of their governments after voters rebuked the artificial intelligence industry during the recent midterm elections. These lawmakers now plan to regulate the physical infrastructure of AI through tougher laws regarding energy, water use, and local oversight. Legislative leaders intend to move quickly on these data center regulations during their upcoming sessions to address various state problems. This movement follows a blue wave that gave Democrats power in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. The push for regulation puts these states on a collision course with Big Tech companies and their allies in Washington.

Michigan legislators want to limit ratepayer hikes, preserve water supplies, and curb nondisclosure agreements, while Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson wants a moratorium. In Wisconsin, Senate President Mark Spreitzer and Gov.-elect David Crowley aim to repeal the sales tax exemption for data center projects. Pennsylvania's Gov. Josh Shapiro and nominee Jay Costa will discuss the GRID plan for energy, environment, transparency, and community benefits. Arizona Democrats seek tighter water restrictions and a moratorium championed by Attorney General Kris Mayes to protect their local resources. Gov.-elect Aaron Ford of Nevada pledged to suspend new data center tax breaks while lawmakers consider a halt to construction.

Michigan Senate Majority Leader-elect Darrin Camilleri said unified control makes the state better equipped to tackle problems with more willing partners. He believes Michigan can become a national leader in reining in data centers through strong regulatory frameworks and environmental laws. Pennsylvania Representative Arvind Venkat stated that AI is in a robber baron phase and needs a statutory framework for public benefit. Minnesota House Speaker Zack Stephenson said he will believe federal action on these national issues only when he actually sees it. State Senator Sue Shink noted that the state encouraged data centers before being ready to protect people from ill effects.

President Donald Trump stated at the White House that he will fight hard for data centers because the US leads China. Big Tech companies and Washington allies oppose a patchwork of state laws to regulate the fast evolving technology of artificial intelligence. The regulations affect data centers, but also target chatbots for minors, algorithmic pricing, and the use of AI generated content. Representative Arvind Venkat is specifically targeting the use of AI in health care by requiring disclosure and human decision makers. Speaker Zack Stephenson argues that algorithmic rent and surveillance pricing drive up the costs of housing and food for voters.

The articles state that Democrats in Pennsylvania will control the state Senate for the first time in over three decades. Representative Joe Webster previously passed a bill in the House to codify GRID standards, but it stalled in the Senate. The background includes a growing discontent with how the Trump administration has handled various cost of living issues for the public. Democrats view the fight over AI and data centers as being consistent with their broader affordability agenda for the voters. These six states are expected to be top battlegrounds in the upcoming 2028 presidential race in two years.

Lawmakers will reintroduce several proposals in the upcoming legislative sessions to put strong regulatory frameworks in place for the AI industry. Representative Arvind Venkat remains cautiously optimistic that his bipartisan bill on AI in health care will finally become state law. Democrats will continue to oppose efforts to preempt state laws in favor of a federal framework for artificial intelligence regulation. The articles leave open whether the federal government will actually tackle these issues to avoid a patchwork of different state laws. It remains unclear if the proposed moratoriums in Arizona and Michigan will be officially implemented by the new state leaders.

stories.Headline: Geoffrey Seiler identifies Alphabet, AMD and TSMC as potential winners if AI chips become commoditized
stories.Summary:
Geoffrey Seiler wrote that the AI chip market is shifting on November 21, 2026, which may weaken the grip of Nvidia. Anthropic recently revealed that its Claude Mythos model can run on alternative chips in a few days with almost no human intervention. This new process used to take dozens of engineers and six to 12 months to complete before this recent technical shift. Such a change reduces the CUDA moat of Nvidia while other competitors in the chip market are starting to catch up. This shift suggests that AI chips could become commoditized, which would be very bad news for the current market leader.

Commoditization would erode pricing power and shrink margins for Nvidia, whose gross margins are currently in the mid-70 percent range. Advanced Micro Devices has gross margins in the mid-50 percent range and offers the new Helios AI rack system. Alphabet uses Tensor Processing Units, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing provides manufacturing and packaging capacity for various chip designers and hyperscalers. Other mentioned companies include Broadcom, Marvell Technology, and SpaceX, the only large customer not developing its own custom AI chips. These changes affect the market for high bandwidth memory and the overall demand for various AI accelerators and custom ASICs.

Geoffrey Seiler stated that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is a buy because it wins regardless of which specific AI chip customers choose. He noted that Alphabet is well positioned to benefit from commoditization because it has a decade head start with custom chips. Seiler argued that Alphabet can gain share with external customers without sacrificing margins because its offerings cost much less than Nvidia. He described Advanced Micro Devices as a buy because pricing normalization and chip fungibility act as a tailwind for the company. He believes the Helios system gives the company a big opportunity to be a meaningful alternative to Nvidia in coming years.

Semianalysis reported that Alphabet Tensor Processing Units have started to outperform Nvidia GPUs on a performance per dollar basis, though some dispute this. Customers are increasingly affected by cost per action and care more about CPU integrations and memory capacity for inference and agentic AI. Hyperscalers, neoclouds, enterprises, and governments are the primary buyers of these chips, often sourcing them through Broadcom or Marvell Technology. Nvidia's largest customers are trying to break free from high prices by developing their own custom chips to reduce their dependency. These customers seek alternatives to the high premiums currently commanded by the hardware, software, and networking ecosystem created by Nvidia.

Nvidia previously appeared on a Motley Fool list on April 15, 2005, and a thousand dollar investment then would be worth 896,981 dollars. Netflix was recommended on December 17, 2004, and a thousand dollar investment would have grown to 315,271 dollars by November 2026. The Stock Advisor team reports a total average return of 768 percent compared to 198 percent for the S&P 500 index. Nvidia currently maintains advantages through its cohesive ecosystem and locked up access to constrained supplies of high bandwidth memory. The company also holds more manufacturing capacity with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing than its competitors do at this current point in time.

Nvidia will likely face continued pricing pressure and market share loss as the gap between different AI chips continues to shrink. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing may see lower customer concentration and improved gross margins if more alternatives to Nvidia GPUs become available. Alphabet will continue creating an ecosystem to rival chipmakers and improve the utilization of its own massive data center holdings. Advanced Micro Devices will attempt to establish itself as a primary alternative by leveraging its larger memory capacity for AI inference. The articles leave open whether Nvidia can maintain its premium pricing despite the rise of custom chips and competing GPU architectures.
