stories.Headline: Dragos researchers uncover data theft and security flaws in cheap AI inference services
stories.Summary:
Security researchers at Dragos uncovered major security flaws in AI services between July and November 2026 using two million test requests. Attackers stole credentials and keys undetected for several months, including hundreds of AWS keys harvested from a single provider. Some attackers used an AI tool called ARTEX to search S3 storage and establish persistent access to systems. Other actors on residential connections in France used intercepted passwords to attempt SSH logins.

The investigation identified compromised providers including Novita, Phala, and Together, while others like AtlasCloud and StreamLake acted as intermediaries for MiniMax models. OpenRouter responded by removing three providers and revoking Zero Data Retention approval for 125 endpoints. A Chinese AI lab accessed secret test URLs in over half of the requests, even those routed through US providers. One US provider continued crawling a test URL for two months, and another link appeared on Feishu in Beijing and Shanghai.

Chief Research Officer HD Moore stated that users must decide where their prompts go or the lowest price will decide for them. Dragos warned companies against sending credentials to intermediaries and recommended using canary tokens to detect data theft. OpenRouter emailed affected users to warn them that third parties might have read requests sent to MiniMax models. The researchers urged organizations to control their routing and verify privacy settings to avoid these vulnerabilities.

These findings mirror a pattern where intermediaries sit between users and developers to view requests and pass data to third parties. An analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed similar behavior in Chinese proxy services routing requests to models like Claude. While it is unclear if the providers share personnel, both systems allow data to reach Chinese actors despite privacy promises. The researchers suggest that the current supply chain for cheap AI inference creates significant risks for user data.

Articles.Title: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

stories.headline_source: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

stories.Headline: US ecommerce decision-makers trust AI more for demand forecasts than purchasing decisions
stories.Summary:
Fifty-eight percent of US ecommerce decision-makers in the Linnworks Market Survey 2026 would trust AI to generate demand forecasts, while just 37% would trust it to make purchasing decisions. Linnworks released the survey on Nov. 12, 2026, and OnePoll ran the online poll from July 28 to August 4, 2026. OnePoll surveyed 500 ecommerce decision-makers, 250 in the US and 250 in the UK, selected at random from its panel. Each respondent has a say in choosing operations and fulfillment software at a business making most of its sales through ecommerce, with annual revenue of approximately $1.3 million to $130 million. Every figure in the release comes from the 250 US respondents, and the results are unweighted.

Among US respondents, 62% report an AI assistant already acts for them, for example by sending messages or updating records, but only 37% would trust AI to communicate with suppliers. Forty-three percent cite poor integration between systems as a barrier to greater automation, against 37% who name cost, and 21% name integration complexity as the most common barrier to wider AI adoption, while 10% cite unclear return on investment. For 64% of respondents, AI ranks among the most important factors in picking operations software, and 46% expect AI and automation included as standard rather than paid for as an add-on. Fifty-three percent describe AI as scaled or broadly adopted across their organization, 34% have grown more cautious because of data and security concerns, and 3% say their business needs no more automation anywhere.

Linnworks CMO Hilary Smith said ecommerce businesses have stopped debating whether to take up AI and are now deciding which tasks they are willing to let it lead. Smith said AI can help teams make smarter calls about demand, stock levels and daily operations, and added that companies still have to be able to trust the data those decisions rest on. Smith said the next stage of AI adoption is not about handing over control but about giving teams the right intelligence to act faster and make better decisions. Linnworks says it has been in business for 20 years, serves 4,000+ brands and retailers and connects inventory, orders, warehouses and listings. Linnworks builds the kind of software these respondents buy.

On Oct. 19, Grafana Labs released findings from its State of Observability 2026 report, covered by David Ramel for Redmond, and Grafana worked with research firm ETR to poll 300 senior IT and engineering decision-makers overseeing observability spending. ETR ran the survey in June 2026, limited it to director level, vice president level or above, and drew 150 respondents from the United States and 50 apiece from Japan, Latin America and Western Europe. In that survey, 85% of IT leaders are comfortable with AI doing read-only investigation, 84% with AI recommending a fix, 56% with AI making code or configuration changes and 52% with fully autonomous remediation, while 50% are comfortable with AI deploying production changes. Grafana Labs co-founder Anthony Woods said having AI diagnose a problem is meaningfully different from allowing it to change something in production.

Reliability is the top barrier to adoption at 26%, followed by regulatory or compliance constraints at 23% and customer trust at 21%, and explainability and a proven track record of accuracy tied at 45% each as what would make respondents trust AI more. Over the past 12 to 18 months, 47% of US respondents have moved into new sales channels or marketplaces, 41% name inventory accuracy and stock synchronization as a top area where added automation would help, and 57% now use EDI with their trading partners. In research published Nov. 18, 2025, MIT Sloan Management Review drew on a global survey of more than 2,000 respondents plus executive interviews and reported agentic AI reached 35% adoption in two years, with another 44% of organizations planning to deploy it soon. The same research put traditional AI adoption at 72% after eight years and generative AI at 70% in three, and said vendors were adding agentic capabilities as features, so organizations put agentic AI in place before building a strategic management framework for it. The MIT Sloan authors, Sam Ransbotham, David Kiron, Shervin Khodabandeh, Sesh Iyer and Amartya Das, name supervision versus autonomy as one of four tensions in adopting agentic AI, and write that traditional oversight models assume either full human control or complete automation.

The MIT Sloan figures come from a global survey across industries, not from ecommerce sellers, so the link to the Linnworks findings is a parallel in how features arrive, not a measure of ecommerce adoption. The researchers argue competitive benefits will come not from early access to agentic AI but from superior organizational design around it. The Linnworks release leaves open what buyers expect the AI in that software to do, and the gap between the 58% who would trust AI to generate demand forecasts and the 37% who would trust it to make purchasing decisions is the number to watch in any follow-up research. Whether approval thresholds can be set separately for forecasting, reordering and supplier messages, and whether the system will show the stock data and logic behind a purchase recommendation so a buyer can check it, remain open questions. Whether inventory reconciles across every channel and trading partner before the forecast runs is also left open.

Articles.Title: Just 37% of US ecommerce decision-makers would trust AI to make purchasing decisions

stories.Headline: Developer fits 367K-parameter AI question-answering model Tiny 2.1 onto a floppy for 486DX and Pentium PCs
stories.Summary:
A developer has squeezed an AI language model onto a floppy disk for 486DX and Pentium PCs, according to a Tom's Hardware report dated November 22, 2026. The project is called Tiny 2.1, and it is a question-answering transformer with 367K parameters. It needs 540KB of memory to run and speaks its answers through the PC speaker. The report describes the machines it targets as stalwarts of the 486DX and Pentium era.

The model is a question-answering transformer, which means it takes a question as input and produces an answer rather than generating open-ended text. Its 367K parameters and 540KB memory footprint are the two figures the article gives for its size. The floppy format is the delivery method that lets the software run on the older hardware. The PC speaker is the only output channel mentioned for its spoken answers.

The article names no individual developer and gives no direct quotes, so responsibility for the project rests with the unnamed dev behind Tiny 2.1. The report does not say what license the software carries or how it is distributed beyond the floppy. It also does not describe the training data or the process used to shrink the model. Those details are absent from the article as published.

The context is the growing effort to run AI models on constrained hardware, though the article does not frame it in those terms beyond the floppy and the old PCs. What happens next is not stated, and the report gives no release date, price or availability details. No benchmarks or accuracy figures for the model appear in the article. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tribe AI CEO Jaclyn Rice Nelson leads firm past $100 million annual revenue
stories.Summary:
Tribe AI said on Nov. 18 that its annualized revenue had crossed $100 million, up 3.8 times from a year earlier. Jaclyn Rice Nelson, 41, is cofounder and CEO of Tribe AI, which was founded in 2019. The company helps organizations including Fortune 500s like Hyatt and MetLife and multibillion-dollar private conglomerates like Koch Industries put AI to work. Nelson grew up in New York City with a single mother raising two children. After graduating in 2008 with a degree in political science from the University of Michigan, Nelson spent two years as an analyst at Citigroup before moving to Silicon Valley to work for Google.

Tribe AI has grown to a $100 million annual run rate by helping companies move AI projects out of the pilot stage. The company has roughly 250 employees after its team grew fivefold this year, all while raising less than $10 million in venture funding and reaching profitability. Koch Industries employs about 130,000 people and generates more than $125 billion in annual revenue. Working with Tribe, a Koch project went from an idea to a launched product in just five months. The result is an AI-powered coaching tool designed to help employees put Koch's bottom-up management principles into practice, and employees can describe a challenge at work and receive personalized guidance on how to approach it.

Nelson said the hard part is getting AI into production inside a complex business. She said she does not think anxiety around AI is unwarranted and that it is very real. She said AI is ours to shape, and the only way to shape it is to understand it, and the only way to understand it is to use it a lot. She said the goal is not just to scale AI but to make people better and help them lean in on the things they are most uniquely suited to do. She said she believes AI is giving people superpowers and that this is a good example of that.

Chase Koch, executive vice president of origination and partnerships at Koch and son of Charles, said many businesses run through the smartest guy in the room telling people what to do, and that Koch is the opposite of that. Koch said he tried the tool himself after his boss told him he was taking on too many responsibilities, and talking through the problem with the AI helped him develop a plan to prioritize his work, delegate more effectively, and focus on his strengths. Koch said people should understand their comparative advantage and what their gift is combined with what they are passionate about learning. Nelson said she is looking for people deeply curious about AI, willing to take on difficult challenges, and humble enough to recognize how much they still have to learn. She said people have to be humbled by how little they know every day and motivated by learning and getting better.

Nelson's mother transitioned from teaching to business and managed to send both kids to private school in Manhattan. As a teenager, Nelson started babysitting and grew the side hustle into what she once described as a babysitting empire, becoming the go-to babysitter for entire New York apartment buildings. She said she became a trusted, fairly scarce asset, with parents competing to book her on Saturday nights, and that it taught her to be the trusted person and be dependable. She moved to a new city where she did not really know anyone and worked banking hours at Google, always the person still in the office waving her hand to get the light sensors to go back on. Her willingness to take on responsibilities outside her core role led her to Google's growth equity fund, CapitalG, then known as Google Capital, in 2015 as its first business-focused employee among a team of dozens of engineers, and three years later she left to pursue an opportunity of her own.

Nelson said young professionals should figure out what makes them uniquely valuable and then learn how to use AI to make the most of it. She said that if people understand the technology and how it works, they can find the places to use that power and strength to change the trajectory of how it is used and its impact on people, workforces and society. Koch said people should understand what their comparative advantage is and what gets them excited and out of bed in the morning. The articles do not say what Tribe AI plans next or how the Koch tool will be expanded. The articles do not say what Nelson will do with the company's growth or how the hiring search will proceed.

stories.Headline: Investors question AI profitability as tech stocks lose 4 trillion dollars in market value
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence sector experienced a significant market downturn in November 2026 as investors began questioning the profitability of massive technology spending. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index plummeted 5.28 percent on Friday, November 21, which effectively erased every gain the index had recorded since the beginning of the year. This decline followed the November 19 initial public offering of Anthropic, which raised 91 billion dollars but admitted it might need to borrow more money later. The downturn was further fueled by the resignation of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang over several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

The market shift resulted in a combined loss of over 4 trillion dollars in market capitalization for the Magnificent Seven stocks over six weeks. These influential companies include Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta, and Tesla, with their total loss exceeding the annual gross domestic product of France. This financial correction follows U.S. midterm elections where Democrats prevailed and voters supported various local measures to restrict the growth of data centers. The European Central Bank also issued a warning regarding the opaque nature of AI debt and the complex, circular ownership links between different firms in the supply chain.

Financial analyst Steve Sostick of Interactive Brokers stated that a huge repricing is occurring because markets were previously too euphoric about the technology. He noted that investors are now questioning if the ballooning capital expenditures are being spent wisely since the returns on these investments remain unclear. Adam Sarhan from MarketTerminal.com suggested that the AI bubble has already deflated and questioned how much further the market will fall. Additionally, Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management observed that the investment boom shifted from a promising technological story into a capital markets extravaganza.

stories.Headline: Italian citizens moderately accept farm AI but show uncertainty, Turin-led survey finds
stories.Summary:
The articles report only one study, so this is a breaking story with limited detail. A nationwide survey published in Smart Agricultural Technology found that Italian citizens show moderate to high acceptance of artificial intelligence in agriculture, while their favorable attitudes often coexist with measurable response uncertainty rather than firm convictions. An interdisciplinary research team from institutions including the University of Turin conducted the investigation, which explored public attitudes toward eleven distinct artificial intelligence tools used across modern agri-food systems. The study examined consumer evaluations as a behavioral continuum where positive sentiment can mask hesitation, ambivalence, or unfamiliarity, rather than as a simple choice between acceptance and rejection. Using advanced statistical modeling that separates genuine preference from underlying decision-making uncertainty, the researchers found acceptance indices consistently above moderate thresholds for every evaluated technology.

The clarity with which respondents expressed their views varied widely by application, educational attainment, household income, and age bracket. The survey was administered through computer-assisted web interviewing between July and August 2025, developed with a specialized market research enterprise, with formal ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of the University of Turin and adherence to the Declaration of Helsinki. The instrument underwent two-stage pre-testing with expert feedback from consumer science specialists and a pilot trial of ten non-project participants, and eligibility was restricted to adults aged 18 or older residing in Italy. It yielded 1,039 completed questionnaires with a completion rate of 96.10 percent, and after removing 39 straight-line responses with identical Likert ratings, the final sample comprised exactly 1,000 Italian citizens structured to reflect national demographic distributions. Participants rated eleven technologies on a seven-point Likert scale from not at all favorable to very favorable: robotics and automation, drones and unmanned aerial vehicles, machine learning, convolutional neural networks, genetic algorithms, artificial neural networks, computer vision, digital twins, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, and big data analytics.

They also evaluated benefits across four dimensions, organoleptic and nutritional quality, contamination risk reduction and food safety, healthiness through reduced agrochemical residues, and environmental sustainability via resource efficiency and emissions cuts, using standard reference sheets. The researchers analyzed responses with the Combination of Uniform and shifted Binomial model, known as the CUB framework, which disentangles preference intensity from decision uncertainty across ordinal categories. The model decomposes responses into feeling, denoted xi, and response uncertainty, denoted pi, both bounded between zero and one, reported as one minus xi for preference intensity and one minus pi for uncertainty. Goodness-of-fit was satisfactory across all eleven technologies, with dissimilarity indices from 0.06 to 0.10, below the 0.15 adequacy threshold. Acceptance was universally moderate to high, with feeling values above 0.70 for all tools and response uncertainty generally below 0.50.

The Internet of Things and machine learning reached the highest acceptance parameter of 0.81, but the Internet of Things registered significantly lower uncertainty at 0.29 than machine learning, indicating more stable public evaluations. Genetic algorithms recorded the lowest acceptance at 0.73, while digital twins generated the greatest response uncertainty at 0.39, and robotics and automation and computer vision occupied identical positions with equivalent liking and uncertainty. Chi-square tests within the CUB framework showed neither gender nor household composition had statistically significant effects on acceptance or uncertainty. Age significantly shaped acceptance for ten of the eleven technologies, cloud computing being the lone exception, with respondents aged 60 to 70 consistently highest, followed closely by young adults aged 18 to 30, while intermediate groups aged 31 to 59 generally showed lower acceptance. The Internet of Things remained most accepted across all age cohorts except participants aged 31 to 44, who favored deep learning.

Older respondents showed greater response uncertainty than younger cohorts, while participants aged 18 to 30 combined strong favorability with the lowest uncertainty scores. Educational attainment was an exceptionally influential determinant, with primary-educated participants recording the lowest acceptance values, frequently below 0.60, alongside elevated uncertainty, while those holding master's degrees or postgraduate credentials regularly exceeded 0.80 with markedly lower hesitation. Statistically significant education-related differences in uncertainty materialized specifically for machine learning and Internet of Things tools. Higher income brackets showed greater acceptance, most prominently for robotics, automation, and Internet of Things devices, while lower-income respondents experienced significantly greater uncertainty across five tools, robotics, drones, computer vision, Internet of Things networks, and cloud computing architectures.

Correspondence analysis mapped applications to benefit dimensions, with Dimension 1 accounting for 85.99 percent of total inertia and establishing a primary contrast between quality and health versus monitoring-oriented safety. Computer vision, deep learning, and Internet of Things clustered around quality and healthiness, drones and big data analytics aligned with food safety, and machine learning and cloud computing gravitated toward environmental sustainability. The articles describe the contemporary agricultural sector facing accelerating structural pressures to enhance productivity, safeguard environmental sustainability, and reinforce economic resilience against climate shocks and shifting market conditions, pressures they call primary catalysts for sectoral digitalization. They define artificial intelligence as the processing of massive operational datasets paired with sophisticated predictive algorithms, a frontier for addressing bottlenecks in soil functionality, disease outbreaks, complex data streams, and knowledge gaps separating producers from technical innovations.

Specific applications include refining irrigation scheduling, guiding localized spraying of plant protection chemicals and herbicides, and streamlining labor allocation, while machine learning and deep learning support precision farming through systems that sense field conditions, learn from measurements, and adapt routines. Previous empirical studies showed automated equipment managing field weeds without continuous human intervention, and drone imaging with smart sensors enhancing traceability and supply chain sustainability. Technical benefits such as real-time field monitoring, predictive equipment maintenance, and enhanced food safety management are widely discussed among industry experts, yet the extent to which everyday citizens understand and value these technologies had remained largely unmeasured. The articles state that the study's findings rest on the 1,000-person sample and the CUB modeling, and they end mid-sentence in the final paragraph on correspondence analysis, leaving the remaining benefit associations unreported.

They give no date for when the survey results were released beyond the November 22, 2026 publication timestamp, and they do not say how the findings will be used or whether further analyses are planned. The articles leave open the full correspondence mapping beyond the applications named, and they provide no response from farmers, policymakers, or technology developers. No follow-up survey, policy step, or implementation plan is mentioned. More to follow.

stories.Headline: METR warns AI systems improve faster than experts can reliably test their safety
stories.Summary:
The AI research organization METR warned on November 22, 2026, that AI systems are improving faster than experts can reliably test whether the new systems are safe, according to The Decoder. METR found that AI models are rapidly getting better at AI research tasks, and that those gains are becoming harder to measure over time. The organization said current public data is not enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That gap could leave humans unable to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems, METR warned.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found. The systems have not yet outperformed large groups of top experts, according to the organization. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts the models at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027. METR's analysis shows a steady rise in capabilities of leading AI models up through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra.

The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, METR said. They also struggle with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to the organization. METR warned that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments. The organization is responsible for the analysis and its warnings about testing and safety.

The findings come as AI models show steady capability gains across the leading systems METR examined. METR's warning centers on the difficulty of measuring those gains reliably as the models improve. The organization said public data cannot yet rule out a sharp acceleration in AI research in the coming years. The articles do not say what steps, if any, regulators, developers, or METR plan to take next.

stories.Headline: Ben Lovett's Domino venue replaces an AI-made website with a human-made one after errors surface
stories.Summary:
Domino, an upcoming music venue in Brooklyn founded by Mumford & Sons' Ben Lovett, drew attention after Business Insider reported that its website was filled with errors generated by artificial intelligence, and the site was changed after the outlet pointed them out. The site, which is set to open next year, leaned into the old hipster era of Williamsburg and included references to The Strokes and warehouse parties. The AI-generated graphics included a ticket for a Strokes concert that never happened, blurry text and typos, and an artificial texture added on top that gave everything a nostalgic feel. In the middle of the site was a postcard with the text "Human Made," which the article called ironic given the errors around it.

After Business Insider flagged the errors, a Domino representative said the site's designers ran out of time on the venue announcement and used AI as an "interim tool" until their "hand-made" version was complete. The representative wrote that this "falls short of what Domino stands for" and said the website had been replaced with something "completely human made." The representative also said the concert hall wanted to "honor the venues that shaped the Brooklyn music scene," citing Glasslands and the Music Hall of Williamsburg, and said the ethos of Domino is "a celebration of all that is human made." The article noted that the former venue shuttered over a decade ago, while the latter is set to close by the end of the year.

The venue will sit on the ground floor of The Refinery at Domino, a renovated office building where 75% of the occupants are tech companies, many of them AI startups, and ads for OpenAI and Polymarket surround the building. The building sits across from a padel court, a sport popular among the tech set, and TVG, Lovett's hospitality group behind the venue, is backed by tech founders including Slack's Stewart Butterfield and Airbnb's Joe Gebbia. The article described the site as a proxy for a broader shift in Williamsburg, where residents are attempting to marry tech and art, and noted that the neighborhood's early-aughts aura had been dissipating for years as rents rose. The concert hall, which will open in 2027, aims to revive that grungy, artistic spirit in some form.

Articles.Title: An upcoming music venue's AI flubs tell the story of a changing hipster neighborhood in Brooklyn

stories.Headline: Sean Williams says record margin debt and a high CAPE ratio raise crash odds for the AI-driven bull market
stories.Summary:
Sean Williams of The Motley Fool published the article on Yahoo Finance on November 22, 2026, asking whether a stock market crash is imminent for the AI-driven Trump bull market. The article says history weighs in with an unpleasant answer. It reports that the S&P 500 stood at 6,910.39, down 265.44 or 3.70%, and the Dow 30 at 48,147.33, down 949.77 or 1.93%. The Nasdaq was at 22,617.73, down 1,261.47 or 5.28%, and the Russell 2000 at 2,581.79, down 73.32 or 2.76%. The VIX was at 35.89, up 7.45 or 26.20%.

The article says the S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings Ratio, also called the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio or CAPE Ratio, entered this year at its second-highest valuation since January 1871. It says the CAPE Ratio has exceeded 30 only six times over 156 years, including the present. It says the previous five instances were all eventually followed by declines of 20% to 89% in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and/or Nasdaq Composite. It says outstanding margin debt hit a record high of $1.502 trillion in June 2026. It says margin debt soared 77% between April 2025 and June 2026, the fourth time it has skyrocketed by at least 65% since 1998 over 12 to 19 months.

The article attributes the analysis to Sean Williams of The Motley Fool. It says he has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. It says The Motley Fool has no position in any of the stocks mentioned and has a disclosure policy. It says the article was originally published by The Motley Fool. It says Stock Advisor returns are as of November 22, 2026.

The article says the prior three margin debt surges immediately preceded the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000, the start of the financial crisis in 2007 and the onset of the 2022 bear market. It says some of these events featured crash-like moves. It says AI is a $22.5 trillion addressable opportunity through 2031, according to IDC. It says the businesses deploying AI solutions aren't particularly close to optimizing them. It says it took until several years after the dot-com bubble burst for internet-driven companies to maximize the technology.

The article says few presidents since the late 1890s have overseen higher average annual stock market returns than Trump. It says the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq gained 57%, 70% and 142% respectively during Trump's first term. It says every next-big-thing technology since and including the internet in the mid-1990s has navigated a bubble-bursting event. It says investors persistently overestimate the pace of adoption and/or optimization of new technologies. It says AI doesn't have an adoption problem.

The article says none of the three history-backed events or metrics guarantee that a Trump bull market crash is imminent. It says the odds of a jaw-dropping downturn appear to be growing by the day. It says the Shiller P/E Ratio doesn't tell investors when downturns will begin or if a crash will occur. It says the ratio has a knack for foreshadowing substantial downside. It says the article's related coverage includes pieces from one month, four months, five months, 29 days, two months, 23 days, 27 days and six months earlier.

stories.Headline: Apple develops its own AI agent as it competes with Anthropic and OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Apple drew a week of headlines across product design, leadership, insider selling and artificial intelligence, with Palmer Luckey questioning the iPhone’s influence on how people learn to use technology. Luckey, the creator of Oculus and co-founder of Anduril, criticized Steve Jobs for helping popularize technology that requires less expertise to operate. Speaking with Jobs biographer Walter Isaacson on The Builders podcast, Luckey said that Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone. Fortune published excerpts highlighting his argument that simplified interfaces reduced opportunities for advanced users to master technology.

Apple has reportedly selected company veteran Corey Fugman to oversee Apple Pay and Wallet, marking another leadership transition under CEO John Ternus. Fugman has spent 26 years at Apple, beginning in retail operations, and before the reported appointment he served as senior director of Apple Pay and Wallet. Apple’s leadership structure changed in 2026, with John Ternus serving as CEO and Tim Cook becoming executive chairman. Former Chairman Arthur Levinson, now lead independent director, filed to sell as many as 90,000 Apple shares through The Homeplace Trust, where he is listed as a trustee. The proposed transaction, which could be worth $32 million, was disclosed in a Form 144 filing.

The report placed Apple’s AI ambitions alongside its rivalry with those firms. The articles did not say how the agent would work or when it might arrive.

The articles did not say what happens next with the reported Apple Pay and Wallet appointment or with Levinson’s proposed share sale. stories.Headline: Review finds only two of fourteen tuberculosis studies directly integrate GIS with AI modelling
stories.Summary:
A systematic literature review published by Nur Adibah Mohidem and Sharifah Norkhadijah Syed Ismail in the International Journal of Health Geographics found that only two of fourteen eligible studies directly embedded spatial structures within artificial intelligence modelling frameworks for tuberculosis research. The authors searched Scopus, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, and Taylor & Francis for literature published up to July 7, 2025, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. After systematic screening, eligibility checks, and quality appraisal using the MI-CLAIM framework, fourteen primary studies met all criteria for final analysis. The review examined how geographic information systems and artificial intelligence currently converge in tuberculosis research, a field marked by persistent spatial heterogeneity in incidence, mortality, and healthcare access.

Most of the included studies concentrated on tuberculosis incidence and case counts, while others examined diagnostic procedures, medical treatment, mortality patterns, community-based public health applications, and the geographic distribution of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains. Researchers used geographic information systems for spatial mapping, spatial autocorrelation, hotspot analysis, spatial clustering, spatial regression, general spatial modelling, and spatial accessibility assessments including network analysis of healthcare access. The artificial intelligence methods spanned neural networks, deep learning architectures, tree-based and ensemble machine learning, kernel-based machine learning, Bayesian modelling, time-series and regression-based frameworks, and explainable artificial intelligence. However, twelve of the fourteen studies applied the two approaches independently, in parallel, or through sequential pipelines rather than integrating them into unified structures.

The authors concluded that combining geographic information systems and artificial intelligence in tuberculosis investigations is an emerging field with limited technical integration. They said future research must prioritize standardized spatially incorporated artificial intelligence frameworks to translate analytical outputs into operational real-time disease surveillance. The review emphasizes the need for high-resolution geocoded data, spatially sensitive validation protocols, and emerging concepts such as GeoAI, digital twins, explainable artificial intelligence, and tailored implementation strategies. The article was published on November 22, 2026, with a DOI of 10.1186/s12942-026-00506-1.

stories.Headline: Taxonomists and search leaders at KMWorld 2026 detail practical work on taxonomy, enterprise search and AI adoption
stories.Summary:
KMWorld 2026 was held at the JW Marriott in Washington D.C. from November 17 to 19, 2026, with pre-conference workshops on November 16. The conference had four additional co-located events: Taxonomy Boot Camp, Enterprise Search & Discovery, Enterprise AI World, and Text Analytics Forum. Sam Stringer, information architect at Factor, presented Domain Modeling as a Foundation for Taxonomy at Taxonomy Boot Camp. Jennifer Kaari, catalog manager at OpenSesame, presented Creating a Human-Driven, AI-Assisted Source of Truth for Taxonomy Definitions. Joseph Busch, principal analyst at Taxonomy Strategies, and Ahren Lehnert, senior taxonomist at Genentech, spoke in Taxonomies for Humans and Machines: Language, Politics, and AI.

The theme of Taxonomy Boot Camp was Practical Taxonomy for Search, AI, and Findability. Stringer discussed a project to create new information architecture for a cloud computing company's website, whose landscape she called a mess. Kaari and her team needed to quickly connect a taxonomy of 4,000 skills, and her team came up with a four-step workflow. Busch noted there is a role for taxonomists in constructing prompts using natural language and said prompts should be precise and free of jargon. Lehnert said taxonomies are not inherently political but contextually can become so when the term is something like "African Americans."

Stringer defines domain modeling as a representation of information objects and the relationships between them, and said a domain is a conceptual subject area with relationships that should be universal within a domain. Kaari said their custom GPTs inconsistently used definitions, which would undermine confidence in the company's catalog. Busch reviewed the different types of mapping and noted that LLMs help identify gaps. Lehnert noted taxonomies are rigid hierarchies and said that in society, hierarchies are power structures. Lehnert said taxonomists are uniquely positioned to help LLMs improve, for example by using diverse data sources.

The Enterprise Search & Discovery theme was Making AI-Powered Search Real for the Enterprise. Randall Smith, chief revenue officer of Forefront Technologies, and Jeff Fried, director of platform strategy and innovation at InterSystems, featured in Agentic AI, AI-Ready Documents, and Search: Real-World Applications. Smith spoke first, with his talk Corralling the Silos, and said we're in a Wild West of enterprise information spread across organizations. Smith listed AI readiness milestones of information: chaos, discover, clean, understand, protect, govern, and modernize. Fried, who participated via live stream, presented Agentic AI and Search: Real-World Applications That Deliver Results and said text-based embeddings have had breakthroughs with AI, in addition to non-text embeddings.

The Enterprise AI World theme was Driving Real AI Adoption Across the Enterprise. Shubhatha, a software engineer at Northwest Bank, presented AI-Driven Promotion Platforms: Increasing Customer Engagement and said AI can close the gap where traditional marketing falls short. Whitney McDonald, senior manager of KM, and Karen Romano, senior director of customer content, both from Okta, lamented fewer content views because of zero-click search in From Clicks to Citations: The Human-AI Partnership Fueling the "Atomic Brain." The Text Analytics Forum theme was Turning Text Into Actionable Insights With AI and Analytics. Lauren Clark Hill, expert solutions engineer at Squirro, presented Governing Known and Novel Entities to Reduce Hallucinations in Gen AI, and Kyle Garcia, technical solutions lead, and Urmi Majumder, chief architect, both of Enterprise Knowledge, LLC, presented How to Augment Taxonomy Change Management With Statistics.

Smith introduced questions to ask at the beginning, such as what is redundant or obsolete and whether sensitive data is where it shouldn't be, and said organizations need to survey their landscape, connecting repositories and searching across them. Fried said KM is coming into its own with context engineering, so understanding the structure of the knowledge is key. Shubhatha said AI can offer real-time personalization, scalable segmentation for more granularity, automated knowledge creation, and closed-loop improvement from customer responses. McDonald and Romano's Atomic Brain model has pillars of a foundation, optimization, and AI scaling, and Okta now has robust, AI-ready content that agents are using. Hill introduced label-based resolution, which consists of the collapse concept and the fragmentation concept, and said GraphRAG needs to be governed to ensure more accuracy.

KMWorld Europe & Taxonomy Boot Camp London is scheduled for 13-14 April 2027, with a code SUPERTXT offering savings of up to £300 for a limited time. KMWorld 2026 is part of a unique program of five co-located conferences. The articles list sessions including From Knowledge Expert to AI Hero: A Hands-On Workshop on Transforming Raw Documents into AI-Ready Knowledge, Standardize, Comply, Innovate: How Enterprise Information Architecture Helps Businesses Meet Industry Standards, and The Enterprise Semantic Backbone: A Foundation for Reliable and Scalable Agentic AI. The articles leave open what happens next beyond the listed London dates and the named sessions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong deploys AI tools and a new storage tank to improve flood prevention
stories.Summary:
The Drainage Services Department recently implemented several new flood prevention measures to protect Hong Kong from extreme weather events. These updates include the construction of a stormwater storage tank in Ping Che and the deployment of artificial intelligence tools. The city introduced these defenses following heavy rains during the summer months to better manage sudden water surges. These initiatives aim to reduce overall flood risks as the region faces more frequent and severe storms.

The new Ping Che facility provides a storage capacity of 2,000 cubic metres to hold excess rainwater during peak periods. To improve monitoring, the department integrated SmartView CCTV analytics and specialized drainage robots into the city's infrastructure. These AI tools utilize big data to enhance the accuracy of flood predictions and real-time monitoring across the territory. Such technological upgrades are designed to bolster the city's resilience against the ongoing challenges of climate change.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho detailed these advancements in a blog post published on Sunday, November 22, 2026. She explained that the Development Bureau is encouraging various works departments to use innovative thinking and cutting-edge technology. Linn noted that the increasing frequency of extreme weather poses immense challenges to the city's existing flood prevention efforts. By leveraging these new tools, the government hopes to create a more robust defense system for the public.

stories.Headline: Startup claims AI agents designed Frostbite CPU architecture with 4.59x performance per watt in pre-silicon tests
stories.Summary:
A startup claims that AI agents have designed an entirely new CPU architecture from scratch, according to a report published by Tom's Hardware on November 22, 2026. The company says the design, called Frostbite, reached 4.59 times the performance per watt of an in-order core in pre-silicon tests. Those figures come from testing done before the chip was manufactured, not from a physical processor. The report does not name the startup behind the claim or list the agents involved. No independent party is said to have verified the results.

The claim rests on pre-silicon tests, which means the architecture has not yet been built as working silicon. The 4.59x figure compares Frostbite's performance per watt against an in-order core, a simpler class of processor design. The article gives no details on how the tests were run, what workloads were used, or how the in-order baseline was configured. It also does not say when, or whether, the design will be fabricated. Everything reported so far comes from the startup's own account of its results.

The startup is the source of the claim, and the article attributes the design work to AI agents rather than to human engineers. The report does not say what role, if any, people played in the process or how the agents were directed. It also gives no statement from the company beyond the performance figure and the description of the architecture as entirely new. Because the article names no executives, researchers, or outside experts, there are no further comments to paraphrase. The claim therefore stands on the company's word alone.

The context is a wider push to use AI tools in chip design, though the article offers little beyond this single result. Pre-silicon numbers are an early stage of any processor program, and they often change once a design reaches manufacturing. The article does not say whether the startup plans to tape out the chip, seek partners, or publish more data. It also does not say whether the 4.59x figure will be submitted for outside review. On the record given, the next step is simply more testing or fabrication, and the article does not confirm either.

stories.Headline: Knowledge management leaders tell KMWorld 2026 that AI adoption requires human validation and trust
stories.Summary:
Experts and industry leaders gathered at the JW Marriott in Washington D.C. from November 17 to 19, 2026, for the KMWorld conference. The event included pre-conference workshops on November 16 and was part of a larger program featuring four other co-located conferences. Various speakers addressed the integration of artificial intelligence into existing business processes and the necessity of building trust within organizations. These sessions focused on how knowledge management professionals can adapt their roles to survive and thrive in the era of generative AI.

Luke Goetting explained that leadership must evolve because two-thirds of the workforce are digital natives while the average leader is 61 years old. He suggested that leaders should adopt influencer styles by being authentic and using short-form video to connect with younger employees. Sandra Moffett and Justin Elker emphasized that humans must always validate AI outputs to ensure that the technology scales existing knowledge foundations. Dan Rasmus listed 19 responsibilities for professionals, noting that prompts should be treated as knowledge assets and that AI requires a structured knowledge architecture. Julie Mohr, the new VP and research director at Forrester, argued that trust functions like metadata and requires visual signals to prove the validity of information.

Justin Elker from Kenvue stated that AI does not replace people but instead forces their professional skills to evolve over time. Sandra Moffett added that businesses cannot afford to wait to implement AI or they will be left behind by their competitors. Dan Rasmus claimed that human expertise remains essential because judgment and undocumented exceptions cannot be fully replicated by machines. Julie Mohr suggested that leaders can reduce employee anxiety about job security by providing the training necessary to excel. She further noted that a human in the loop is essential to ensure that AI agents produce the desired outcomes.

The conference highlighted that the essence of knowledge management is delivering the right information to the right people at the right time. Participants discussed the need for shared ownership between knowledge roles and departments like engineering, security, and compliance. Future efforts will focus on preparing knowledge for both generative and agentic AI through clear boundaries and validation parameters. Organizations are encouraged to create incentive structures that reward longtime employees for sharing their institutional knowledge with newer staff. These strategies aim to bridge the gap between different generations of workers while leveraging the power of modern technology.

stories.Headline: Civil Guard arrests four for using AI to spread jihadist content and radicalize youth
stories.Summary:
The Civil Guard has arrested four people in three provinces and in the autonomous city of Melilla for spreading jihadist content on social networks with the aim of indoctrinating people in terrorism, in an investigation that also detected the use of artificial intelligence to improve radicalization processes. In a first action, officers arrested three people in San Sebastián in Guipúzcoa, Vilanova i la Geltrú in Barcelona and Fuengirola in Málaga, after confirming that they had become radicalized over recent years, especially because of greater access to terrorist propaganda spread on the internet. A parallel operation in Melilla led to the arrest of a young man for his active work in spreading jihadist ideology, and he is attributed with large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially content used by young people. The detainees also recorded videos in which they expressed their jihadist affiliation and displayed bladed weapons, according to material seized during the investigation.

Among the analyzed materials are content related to Daesh and Hamas, used with the aim of indoctrinating for terrorist purposes, and the investigation has also located material that justifies violence and the carrying out of attacks. The Civil Guard considers this terrorist propaganda material to be of special danger because of the intrinsic risk of fostering jihadist radicalization, especially among a young and vulnerable group. The operations were carried out with the cooperation of the National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States, within an investigation focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for the recruitment and radicalization of users on social networks. The report was published on November 22, 2026, and the arrests were made in San Sebastián, Vilanova i la Geltrú, Fuengirola and Melilla.

The General Directorate of the Civil Guard provided the information on the analyzed materials, and the force described the propaganda as especially dangerous because it can foster radicalization among young and vulnerable people. The investigation attributes to the Melilla detainee large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially material used by young people, and the seized material shows that the detainees recorded videos expressing their jihadist affiliation and displaying bladed weapons. The National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States cooperated in the operations, which focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for recruitment and radicalization. The articles do not say what charges the four detainees face or what happens to them next.

stories.Headline: Researchers review drying methods and AI for preserving kaffir lime leaves
stories.Summary:
A scientific review published in Food Science and Biotechnology examines advanced drying technologies and computational tools meant to preserve kaffir lime leaves and extend how long they keep after harvest, according to a summary of the work released on November 22, 2026. Kaffir lime leaves are valued for their distinctive aroma and recognized medicinal properties, but their high moisture content often causes them to spoil quickly once picked. Drying the leaves is described as a dependable way to slow spoilage, maintain microbial safety and lengthen commercial shelf life. The review was written by N. N. Safie, F. Adam, N. H. Ramli, M. R. Abu Bakar and N. F. Abu Bakar, and it carries the title Sustainable drying solutions for kaffir lime leaves, addressing technological challenges and artificial intelligence assistance.

The review treats the retention of marker and bioactive compounds, especially citronellal, citronellol and sabinene, as a main measure of how well processing works. Evidence gathered across experimental studies shows that drying methods strongly affect both compound retention and the appearance of the leaves, and that low temperatures with reduced humidity preserve marker compounds better than conventional high-temperature methods. The researchers assessed ambient and convective hot-air systems, solar-assisted drying, microwave-based processing and far-infrared dehydration, and they note that far-infrared drying removes moisture quickly while keeping high retention rates of sensitive bioactive compounds. Scaling these technologies up commercially requires balancing energy consumption, drying times and industrial throughput.

To address those hurdles, the review identifies the integration of artificial intelligence as a new and potentially transformative strategy. Machine learning architectures, deep learning models and artificial neural networks are being used to monitor leaf quality and to adjust drying parameters dynamically during operation. According to the review, these optimization models can support the production of premium dried botanical products while improving energy efficiency and sustainable food production in line with global development targets. The review was published in Food Science and Biotechnology under the DOI 10.1007/s10068-026-02322-6, and the summary was reported by Scienmag.

stories.Headline: Joint select committee releases AI report on datacentres and copyright
stories.Summary:
A joint select committee on artificial intelligence is expected to release a report on Monday, November 22, 2026. This report will signal Labor's direction on datacentres and copyright. It arrives as the final four days of parliament for 2026 begin. The government wants to pass several key reforms and savings measures by Friday. This timing coincides with the potential fracture of a bipartisan consensus on AI.

The report addresses datacentres, energy use, and how creatives are paid for AI theft. Other pending Senate issues include the domestic gas reserve and changes to trusts and capital gains tax. The government also seeks changes to private health insurance and the digital duty of care bill. Labor promised a carveout for Western Australia regarding gas to satisfy a key Coalition demand. The digital duty of care bill may include a private right of legal action for citizens.

Labor sources say they are open to amendments on the digital duty of care bill. Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong will speak on Tuesday about AI as a national security issue. She will urge a shared global endeavour that does not reward speed over prudence. Labor figures like Richard Marles, Tim Ayres, and Michelle Rowland have rejected the copyright status quo. They suggest that current copyright laws have shortfalls that need to be addressed.

The Greens want bigger fines, a big tech ombudsman, and gambling restrictions for the duty of care bill. Creative industries were flabbergasted by reports of a music carveout for AI companies. Rightsholder groups have rubbished the need for copyright changes. The Greens say they feel no pressure to cave on trusts or capital gains tax. One Greens source expects very little will actually pass this week.

Liberals Jonathan Duniam and Aaron Violi recently said AI is too important for partisan contests. However, Shadow Attorney General Michaelia Cash called a potential music carveout a ham-fisted tactic. MP Garth Hamilton suggested AI is old-fashioned theft and proposed a levy on companies. Former Nationals leader David Littleproud stated that Anthropic can afford to pay for copyright. These views contrast with the earlier hopes for a bipartisan alliance.

Parliament will determine if several key policies get over the line by Friday. Anthony Albanese is expected to intensify deal-making after visiting Manila and Shenzhen. The report will show if AI policy remains a bipartisan endeavour or fractures. It remains unclear if Labor and the Greens will reach a deal on fossil fuels. The final outcome of the negotiations on private health and treasury bills is unknown.

stories.Headline: Apple's Siri AI in CarPlay handles directions, recipes and lessons in iOS 27 beta
stories.Summary:
With iOS 27, Apple has transformed Siri into a more capable, powerful, and versatile AI assistant that can be used in the car via Apple CarPlay, PCMag reported on November 22, 2026. The new Siri can handle complex requests, answer open-ended questions, and engage in back-and-forth conversations, unlike the old Siri. PCMag's author tested the new Siri AI from behind the wheel in CarPlay. The author asked it to do ten things, including giving directions to a contact and explaining a complex topic. In the author's experience, the new version also handles ordinary tasks more effectively than its predecessor.

Apple's new Siri requires a phone compatible with Apple Intelligence, which means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer. You also need to be running iOS 27 or higher, so go to Settings > General > Software Update and install any available updates. For now, Siri AI remains in beta, so you'll also need to join the program first by opening Settings > Siri and tapping Try Siri AI (Beta). Apple's iOS will then need to build and optimize the search index, a process that kicks off automatically but can take time and has been known to drain battery life. With that done, you'll need to connect your phone to the car through Apple CarPlay.

The article is by a PCMag writer who has been working for PCMag since early 2016 writing tutorials, how-to pieces, and other articles on consumer technology. The writer spent seven years writing breaking news for CNET as one of the site's East Coast reporters. The writer has also written two books for Wiley & Sons, Windows 8: Five Minutes at a Time and Teach Yourself Visually LinkedIn. The writer uses an iPhone 16 Pro, iPad Pro, and iPad mini as well as an Apple Watch. PCMag editors select and review products independently, and if you buy through affiliate links, we may earn commissions, which help support our testing.

In the past, Siri would often give random matching names found on the web instead of consulting contacts, but Siri AI always checks the contacts list when asked for directions to a specific person or business. The author drove to Binghamton, New York, in August to attend a Rod Serling festival, and while driving to the hotel asked Siri to tell something interesting about the town. It told why Binghamton is the carousel capital of the world, how the city played a role in aviation and computing, and how it's the birthplace of a regional sandwich known as the spiedie. Where the original Siri might have trouble with messy speech, Siri AI is built to handle corrections and more natural language.

Siri AI automatically pulls requested music from the iPhone's library unless a specific source is specified, whereas the old assistant would fire up the Beatles Channel on Sirius XM instead of playing from the library. The author asked Siri to find a recipe for lentil soup on the internet, create a shopping list with the ingredients, and then text the list, and it followed each step correctly and ended with the list of items in Messages. Siri AI will look across the apps on the phone until it finds a match, even if the author doesn't remember if the information is in an email or text. The author asked regular Siri to explain Einstein's special theory of relativity, and it provided a short, one-paragraph answer taken from a single source on the web, while Siri AI served up a full and thorough explanation and then asked if the author wanted to explore how this differs from Einstein's general theory of relativity.

The author asked Siri AI how to silence group text alerts on CarPlay, and it explained three ways: turn off the switch to show text notifications in CarPlay, silence alerts for a specific conversation, and use Driving Focus mode, and the author then asked Siri to turn on Driving Focus mode, which it did. The classic Siri told the author it could search the web for a language lesson when finished driving, while the AI-powered Siri asked what language the author wanted to learn, Italian, then offered basic, conversational phrases in both Italian and English, explained what each one meant, and continued the lesson by giving more words and phrases. Siri AI isn't as chatty as other chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, but it's certainly more conversational than its predecessor. The author told it he wanted a back-and-forth conversation about a specific topic, and it asked which topic, and the author suggested American films from the 1930s.

It gave an overview of the topic and then asked if the author wished to narrow it down, and the author said he wanted to talk about screwball comedies. From there, the conversation focused on It Happened One Night, one of the author's favorites from the era, and they were able to discuss various aspects of the film, leading to an interesting conversation. PCMag tests, rates, and reviews more than 1,500 products each year to help people make better buying decisions and get more from technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Burnham announces US defense AI partnership as UK growth relies on American cloud capacity
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a new defense artificial intelligence partnership with the United States in September 2026 during a visit to the United Nations in New York. This strategic move follows a pattern where British technological growth relies heavily on American cloud capacity, graphics processing units, and data center infrastructure. The Prime Minister also stated that Britain intends to act as an honest broker for AI due to its strong global ties. He further intends to place artificial intelligence at the center of the G20 presidency that Britain will host next year.

The government previously launched the Tech Prosperity Deal, which it valued at 31 billion pounds, including 22 billion pounds from Microsoft over four years. Microsoft's commitment includes investments in land and equipment, though the company withdrew from a Loughton data center project in October 2026. Google has contributed a 5 billion pound package that includes a data center at Waltham Cross and research for DeepMind. Additionally, the US investment firm Blackstone has put 10 billion pounds behind an AI Growth Zone located at Blyth in Northumberland. These efforts are complicated by grid issues, as the Loughton site may not receive sufficient power until the early to mid-2030s.

Microsoft officials stated that their large scale investment was possible because of government work on electricity capacity and planning reform. However, critics argue that relying on American firms means the US government can access data under the CLOUD Act, regardless of where servers are located. This concern mirrors issues in France, where Microsoft representatives could not guarantee that citizen data would be protected from US authorities. The current landscape shows that AWS and Microsoft each control 30 to 40 percent of UK cloud revenues, while the British provider UKCloud went into liquidation in 2022.

The European Union is responding to similar dependencies by proposing the Cloud and AI Development Act to reduce reliance on foreign firms. This legislation would require high risk public sector cloud providers to be European owned and controlled rather than just located in Europe. In Britain, OpenAI previously planned to use Nvidia chips at Nscale sites through Stargate UK but put the project on hold in April. The company blamed this decision on restrictive UK regulations and high energy costs. Future success may require the government to support platforms that utilize idle compute capacity across distributed networks.

stories.Headline: Egypt's EGPC and SLB hold workshop on AI for subsurface exploration
stories.Summary:
The Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation and the global energy technology provider SLB co-organized a two-day AI and Subsurface Workshop that brought together specialists from both organizations and representatives of petroleum production companies, according to a report published on 22 November 2026. The workshop examined how artificial intelligence and advanced data analytics can improve subsurface interpretation, reduce geological uncertainties and raise the success rates of exploration operations. Participants looked at how AI-powered technologies can improve exploration workflows, support investment decisions and identify promising hydrocarbon opportunities. The event forms part of the digital transformation strategy of the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, which focuses on integrating advanced technologies into Egypt's oil and gas operations and improving the efficiency of geological and geophysical studies.

Ahmed Kamal, Deputy CEO for Exploration at EGPC, emphasized the need for AI models designed specifically for the petroleum industry, and he highlighted the importance of developing specialized foundation models capable of understanding geology, well logs and reservoirs while adapting to the technical challenges and data requirements of individual operators. Yasser El Tawansy, Managing Director for Egypt and the East Mediterranean at SLB, highlighted the role of data analytics, AI and advanced technologies in improving operational efficiency, enhancing recovery rates and accelerating geological and geophysical interpretation, saying these applications can support more accurate and confident assessments of subsurface resources. Technical sessions addressed the application of AI across different stages of exploration, from data management and geological interpretation to risk assessment and opportunity ranking. One session examined exploration priorities and digital technology requirements, including current technical challenges and opportunities to improve exploration strategies, while another focused on data management and AI-supported exploration decisions and highlighted SLB's Lumi data and AI platform alongside data governance, standardization and enterprise data management.

The Lumi platform integrates subsurface and operational data to support AI and machine-learning applications, including seismic processing, interpretation and reservoir modeling, and it is designed to provide operators with a unified data environment to accelerate analysis and improve decision-making. Further discussions addressed the use of AI in geological and geophysical interpretation, particularly seismic data processing and the integration of technical workflows from interpretation to simulation. The workshop also included a practical case study on applying AI to Egyptian petroleum assets, presented jointly by specialists from Belayim Petroleum Company, known as Petrobel, and SLB. In July 2026, Karim Badawi, Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, met with SLB Egypt executives to discuss expanding AI applications in exploration and production and upgrading the Egypt Upstream Gateway, with the talks covering the integration of AI and advanced data analytics into the platform to improve the assessment of investment opportunities, reduce exploration risks and accelerate decision-making.

stories.Headline: Pictet strategists stay constructive on AI and tech stocks for 2027
stories.Summary:
Pictet Asset Management's chief strategist Luca Paolini and senior multi asset strategist Arun Sai shared their asset allocation outlook for 2027, joined by other wealth managers who offered views on sectors, market capitalisations and regions. The group's stance on investment prospects for 2027 was more positive than it had been a year earlier, according to the outlook. The strategists weighed equities, bonds, alternatives and commodities as they set out how portfolios should be positioned for the year ahead. One wealth manager said she remained reluctant to invest in Brazilian assets, while another pointed to the semiconductor ecosystem that supports the buildout of artificial intelligence capacity. The outlook also touched on record levels of peacetime debt, which the contributors described as not a zero risk for investors.

The 2027 outlook sets out a constructive position on artificial intelligence and technology stocks, with allocations spread across equities, bonds, alternatives and commodities rather than concentrated in a single asset class. The strategists framed the balance of risks around record peacetime debt, which they said is not a zero risk even as they stay positive on the year. The reluctance to invest in Brazilian assets was noted alongside the more favourable view of technology and AI related holdings. The semiconductor ecosystem supporting the AI buildout was cited as a reason for confidence in the sector. The discussion of sectors, market capitalisations and regions indicates that the allocation views are meant to be applied across a diversified portfolio rather than to one market alone.

Paolini and Sai, as chief strategist and senior multi asset strategist at Pictet Asset Management, are the named authors of the outlook, and other wealth managers contributed their own allocation views. One contributor said she was reluctant to invest in Brazilian assets, and another described the semiconductor ecosystem as supporting the buildout. The strategists said the balance of risks should be struck with an appropriate time frame such as the one covered by the outlook. They described record levels of peacetime debt as not a zero risk, a caution that sits alongside their constructive stance. The comments were paraphrased in the coverage rather than given as direct quotations beyond a few words.

The outlook arrives as wealth managers weigh how much of their 2027 allocation should go to AI and technology stocks, and the coverage points readers toward further research on private markets and family offices. Related items listed alongside the outlook include Tiedemann Global's explanation of its investment formula and its view that private markets have more headway, and guidance on how family offices should address private markets when valuations are stretched. A separate item covers bankers' fears that so called Bitcoin treasuries are an accident waiting to happen. The coverage also invites readers to gain access to regular and exclusive research on the global wealth management sector, along with industry events such as breakfast briefings and summits in major wealth management centres and industry awards programmes.

stories.Headline: Ireland's Data Protection Commission blocks or delays nine AI launches over five years
stories.Summary:
Ireland's Data Protection Commission published a report on September 25, 2026, regarding its reviews of artificial intelligence. The regulator examined roughly 180 AI products and services between 2021 and 2025. Most of these reviews occurred before the products reached users in Europe. Nine of these launches were delayed or cancelled because of interventions by the regulator. These reviews were conducted by the Technology Multinational Supervision Unit.

The report, titled Responsible Artificial Intelligence Innovation, covers companies including Meta, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, TikTok, and X. It includes other firms like Airbnb, Apple, Deepseek, LinkedIn, and Pinterest. The DPC noted that 59 percent of AI products launched in 2024 and 2025 received recommendations. Transparency problems appeared in 72 percent of those recommendations. The regulator requires a minimum lead time of 8 weeks for substantive engagement.

The Technology Multinational Supervision Unit is responsible for engaging with large multinational tech companies based in Ireland. This unit operates separately from other regulatory functions like complaints or inquiries. The DPC stated that this voluntary process acts as a quasi-regulatory sandbox. The regulator noted that recommendations are non-binding in nature. However, the DPC may use other regulatory powers if redline issues are not addressed.

The report affects large platforms that sell advertising in Europe because the DPC is their lead regulator. Some companies, such as X, refused to stop training AI models when requested. The DPC applied to the Irish High Court on August 8, 2024, regarding X. Eurostat data shows 52.7 percent of EU firms avoiding AI due to privacy concerns. AI use among EU enterprises rose from 13.5 percent to 20 percent in 2025.

Generative AI drove most growth, accounting for 79 percent of all engagements. The DPC counted 25 generative AI engagements in 2023, 36 in 2024, and 82 in 2025. Non-generative AI engagements totaled 37 over the whole period. AI engagements with large technology controllers grew tenfold from 2021 to 2025. This activity included technologies like facial recognition, age assurance, and large language models.

The DPC now says training AI on private messages faces a very difficult legal threshold. The regulator believes training new AI models will likely require a Data Protection Impact Assessment. Future monitoring will include how mitigations, such as objection forms, work in practice. The report does not name most companies involved in the specific case studies. It remains open whether companies can justify training AI on private messages under legitimate interests.

stories.Headline: Experts say AI speeds up planning of cyberattacks on industrial equipment
stories.Summary:
Experts say artificial intelligence has made it faster to plan cyberattacks on industrial equipment, according to a report by Tom Wilson in the Financial Times dated 22 November 2026. The article states that AI helps attackers read manuals and research past accidents more quickly than before. The report was published under the headline that the AI cyber threat is already here. The available text of the article is limited to its headline and summary, because the full piece sits behind a subscription.

The report does not give the names of any attackers, the equipment targeted, or the dates of any incidents in the text available. It also gives no figures on how much faster planning has become or how many attacks have been carried out. The article does not say which manuals or accident records the attackers study. No specific industrial sector or country is identified in the available material.

The experts quoted in the summary attribute the speed-up to AI tools that help attackers work through technical documents and past accident research. The article does not name those experts or set out their remarks beyond that summary. It does not say what the attackers are said to be planning or whether any campaign has been detected. No response from equipment makers, regulators or governments appears in the available text.

The wider context in the summary is that the cyber threat from AI is already present rather than only expected in the future. The article does not say what happens next, whether defences are being changed, or how companies should respond. Because the full article is not available, the details beyond the headline and summary cannot be reported. More to follow.
