stories.Headline: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on November 22, 2026 by Jiaxin Shi, Ziyuan Chen, Jian Huang and Hansheng Wang sets out a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks held under a split spectral norm product constraint. The authors write that weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. They add that existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are not sufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. Their theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed.

The paper then proposes a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The authors state that the resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still reaching the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, they establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and give robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies reported in the abstract show the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to classical deep network methods. The work is listed under machine learning in statistics, machine learning in computer science and statistics theory in mathematics.

The abstract names stability under input perturbations as necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. It presents the fixed norm-product bound as the setting in which earlier approximation results fell short of optimal statistical rates. The authors describe their contribution as a sharp approximation theory together with an estimator that keeps the Lipschitz constant uniformly bounded. The abstract does not give the size of the logarithmic factor, the constants involved or the specific numerical results of the studies.

The paper is identified on arXiv as 2611.23979, and the posting page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The abstract does not state where the work has been published or accepted, nor does it give a date for any later version. It also does not say what experiments or applications will follow from the results. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers present MPG-DPO, a method that personalizes LLM alignment using multidimensional user preference data
stories.Summary:
Zhen-Yu Zhang, Jerry Huang, Gang Niu, Takashi Ishida and Masashi Sugiyama posted a paper to arXiv on November 22, 2026 describing a method for personalizing large language model alignment with multidimensional user preference data. The paper is titled Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data and carries the identifier 2611.22210. The authors note that preference alignment has become a central tool for aligning large language models with human values and desired behavior. They add that the online variant of preference alignment can advance model capabilities beyond what static data alone offers by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback.

The paper states that costly, time-consuming annotations limit the scalability of online preference alignment, which makes sample efficiency essential. Existing methods typically try to improve sample efficiency by expanding coverage of the response space or by selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. The authors argue that although these methods are effective, they quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the language model, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user. They give the example that a pair can appear highly uncertain to the model even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering.

In response, the authors propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization, or MPG-DPO, which uses low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user's historical comparisons to build a personalized preference cone that guides response selection for online preference alignment. The method first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet show the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis in the paper shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple language model families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

The paper appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share new features directly on the website. arXiv states that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have embraced and accepted its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv is committed to these values and only works with partners that adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next with the method beyond the reported experiments.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose SpatialMind to adapt geometric fusion to spatial task needs in multimodal models
stories.Summary:
Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang and Jinqiao Wang posted a paper titled SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models to arXiv on 22 November 2026. The paper addresses the limited 3D spatial reasoning of Multimodal Large Language Models, which show promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding. The authors report systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion and find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels, such as distance estimation versus route planning, require geometric representations of different granularities. That finding reveals that a fixed fusion scheme cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements, which the authors say earlier approaches either used across all tasks or adopted regardless of task-specific needs. To bridge this gap, the authors propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations.

SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. The authors further introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse, and gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. The authors report that experiments demonstrate SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Computational Geometry, and the source code is publicly available at a URL given in the abstract.

The abstract presents the work as a response to the gap left by recent studies that explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. Those approaches, the authors write, either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. The paper appears on arXiv with the identifier 2611.22415, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, with the abstract page naming all nine authors. The articles give no further details on the benchmarks beyond VSI-Bench, no training details beyond the gating network and the regularization loss, and no publication venue beyond the arXiv posting. The articles also say nothing about planned follow-up work, so what happens next is not stated.

stories.Headline: Graham Dumpleton builds Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for Python apps
stories.Summary:
Graham Dumpleton, who created mod_wsgi twenty years ago, has started a new project called Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for running Python web applications, and Simon Willison linked to it on 21st November 2026. Dumpleton has spent two decades thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web apps in production since he began mod_wsgi. Muru aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps in both development and production. As he did with an earlier project called wrapture, Dumpleton is publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the work as part of his development process.

The project is written in Rust and relies heavily on AI assistance, though Dumpleton says deciding what is not good enough yet remains his job. He credits twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi as useful experience for that judgment. He says he is prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something he would trust and something users would trust too. The articles give no release date, version number or availability details for Muru.

Dumpleton is the person responsible for the project, and his stated position is that the AI may do a lot of the work on the surface but the standard-setting stays with him. He frames the twenty years of mod_wsgi mistakes as an asset rather than a liability for judging the new server. He commits to continuing the polishing work until the server meets a bar he would trust himself. The articles do not say who else, if anyone, is involved in the project.

The context is that Muru follows the same open, detailed development write-up approach Dumpleton used for wrapture. Willison's link post appeared on 21st November 2026, and the article carries a timestamp of 22nd November 2026. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Dumpleton's stated intention to keep polishing Muru. No timeline, funding or adoption information is given.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu and FamilyMart pilot causal AI to analyze purchases of decarbonized innerwear
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Limited announced on November 22, 2026, that it has launched a pilot study with FamilyMart Co., Ltd. to analyze consumer purchasing behavior and establish a demand creation model for decarbonized products. The study combines Fujitsu Causal AI, a core technology of the Fujitsu Kozuchi AI platform, with LLM causal technology. The initiative is part of the Model Project for Creating Demand for Decarbonized Products, a program publicly solicited by Japan's Ministry of the Environment. The two companies will focus the pilot on environmentally friendly innerwear sold by FamilyMart. The study will analyze sales data and survey results collected through FamilyMart's Famipay app to clarify how information and consumer touchpoints help customers understand a product's environmental value and lead to a purchase.

The companies will then implement in-store initiatives to verify their effectiveness and aim to establish a robust demand creation model. The insights and analytical methods gained are expected to be applied to other categories beyond apparel, including food, daily necessities, and household goods. The Ministry of the Environment's model project aims to promote investment and innovation in decarbonization and to encourage consumer selection of these products, thereby fostering market formation. The featured items are made with recycled polyester fibers that reduce CO2 emissions compared with conventional synthetic fibers, by 15% for inner T-shirts and 8% for REHEAT products. The Ministry of the Environment describes the project as one that appropriately displays the decarbonization value of products and services and develops an environment where consumers and procurement entities can understand and evaluate such value, assessing tolerance for price premiums and impacts on purchasing behavior.

LLM causal technology is described as a technology that discovers intervention points by having an LLM complement intermediate factors not present in the quantitative data, based on causal relationships estimated from the data. Fujitsu reported consolidated revenues of 3.5 trillion yen, or US$23 billion, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. The companies will continue to discuss methods for effectively communicating environmental value and optimizing retail environments, and they will explore applying Fujitsu Causal AI to other product categories. By doing so, the partners aim to contribute to the creation of demand for decarbonized products and enhance customer value in the retail sector through advanced, data-driven marketing. Fujitsu states that its purpose is to make the world more sustainable by building trust in society through innovation, with 100,000 employees working to resolve challenges facing humanity.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce VEX framework to help AI agents learn computer use from tutorial videos
stories.Summary:
Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, and Chao Zhang introduced a new framework called VEX on November 22, 2026, to improve how computer-use agents learn. This system allows agents to learn directly from the audio and visual information found in tutorial videos instead of relying on simple screenshot trajectories. The agents follow a specific watch-act-rewatch paradigm to extract guidance from spoken explanations and visual demonstrations before executing tasks. After performing the actions, the agent verifies its own progress by rewatching its execution as a video to ensure accuracy.

The researchers instantiated this framework as video-SALMONN-VEX, which is a 9B-scale agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture using a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. To enhance performance, they developed Action-Grounded Guide Optimization, a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for predicting future actions. The team augmented the AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym benchmarks with more than 24,000 real-world tutorial videos to provide better training data. These technical changes allow the agent to unify external learning from demonstrations with internal reflection on its own behavior.

The authors reported that video-SALMONN-VEX achieved a 22 percent relative increase in task success over the Qwen3.5 backbone when tested on OSWorld. They also found that the guidance generated by their system improved the performance of Gemini-3.5-flash by 10 percent relatively on the same benchmark. The researchers stated that these results demonstrate the strong potential of using audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning. By integrating these capabilities, the agents can better perceive graphical user interfaces and reason over complex instructions to execute tasks.

stories.Headline: Trump threatens taxes on US firms building AI data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced on November 20 that he intends to stop American companies from building data centers in other countries. He threatened to impose very heavy taxes on any domestic firms that continue to invest in these infrastructures outside the United States. This announcement occurred during a press conference at the White House while Wall Street faced one of its worst weeks in recent years. The move specifically targets the development of artificial intelligence infrastructures by giants such as Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.

The new policy requires that strategic computing infrastructures remain within the United States to maintain a technological advantage over Beijing. Trump predicted a huge tax for companies that ignore this directive, though the administration has not yet specified the tax amounts or the application process. These threats coincided with a financial downturn on Friday, November 20, where the Nasdaq lost 5.3 percent and erased all gains from 2026. The S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent and entered correction territory by dropping more than 10 percent below recent highs.

President Trump is responsible for this decision and stated that he will not allow data centers to be placed in other countries because China would take them all. He explained that the goal is to prevent Chinese firms from accessing American computing capacity through facilities located in third countries. The president admitted that he had not yet communicated this specific plan to his collaborators before making the public announcement. He believes these measures are necessary because the United States already limits the export of advanced semiconductors to China.

The European Union may face slower or more expensive data center construction as it tries to reduce its technological dependence on foreign nations. Financial markets are also struggling because investors worry that the rush to build infrastructure is proceeding faster than actual revenue growth. Some analysts fear a bubble exists regarding the enormous investments earmarked for artificial intelligence and data centers. It remains unclear how the administration will implement these restrictions or which specific investments will be affected.

stories.Headline: G2 finds 46 per cent of buyers exceed budget on AI agent production costs
stories.Summary:
A G2 report published in October 2026 found that 46 per cent of companies deploying AI agents in production report higher operating costs than they expected, according to TechGig. The overruns stem from three main factors, which are integration work that was not covered in the initial budget, insufficient support after agents go live, and a lack of visibility into costs on a per-agent basis. Gartner's September 2026 forecast projects that global spending on AI agents and assistants will reach US$29 billion in 2026, which shows the growing financial stake in these deployments. The report was covered by TechGig on 22 November 2026. Several studies point to operational friction as a driver of these costs.

MIT NANDA's "The GenAI Divide" from 2025 found that only 5 per cent of organisations successfully implemented generative AI for specific tasks. MuleSoft and Salesforce's Connectivity Benchmark from 2025 surveyed 1,050 IT leaders and found that 95 per cent faced integration challenges when adding AI to existing processes. Deloitte's "State of AI in the Enterprise" from 2026 reported that only 21 per cent of respondents had a mature governance model for AI agents. Together these studies suggest that AI models often struggle when they interact with real-world systems, data, rules and processes. The report says buyers should demand specific provisions from vendors before signing contracts to avoid cost surprises.

These include cost visibility per agent, per session and per call, with execution details that can be recorded and queried through a console and an API. Buyers should also insist on a spending cap per agent that halts execution when the cap is reached, even when the agent runs on the buyer's own provider key. Using one's own provider key, such as for Anthropic, OpenAI or Google, with no vendor markup on tokens, ensures transparent billing directly from the provider. Vendors should also provide regular reports on AI costs and points of attention to decision-makers before the bill arrives. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these recommendations for buyers and vendors.

stories.Headline: Google Antigravity lets developers pick among Gemini 4 and Claude models for coding tasks
stories.Summary:
Google's Antigravity platform gives developers a selection of AI models, including Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Neon, Argon and Carbon, alongside Claude Sonnet and Claude Opus, according to a TechGig guide published on November 22, 2026. The platform also features Orchestrator, which allows two AI models to collaborate on a single task. The guide says the choice of model depends on the complexity of the development task, with simpler models suited to routine work and more capable ones reserved for demanding problems. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is recommended for quick changes, routine coding and simple debugging, while Gemini 4 Neon is better for difficult debugging and complex coding tasks. Antigravity groups its models into categories it calls Everyday Workers, such as Gemini 4, Orchestrators, which pair models together, and Alternative Models from Anthropic.

Orchestrator uses one model for planning and another for implementation, typically Gemini 4 Neon for planning and Gemini 4 Hydrogen for execution. Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's heavyweight option for complex software architecture and major migrations. Claude Sonnet and Opus offer alternative approaches when Google's models are not producing the desired results, particularly for frontend work or in-depth analysis. The platform also lets developers adjust thinking levels for models, from Low for speed to Extra for demanding tasks. The guide recommends a workflow that starts with Hydrogen for small tasks, moves to Neon for complicated problems and uses Orchestrator for substantial feature development.

Developers should prioritise specific prompts, define what should not change and ask for investigation before implementation, according to the article. It also advises working in manageable steps and varying approaches when a prompt fails. The article says developers can optimise their AI-assisted development workflows and resource usage by selecting the appropriate model for each coding task. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hitachi Digital launches HARC Compose to govern agentic AI engineering
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Digital Inc. launched HARC Compose on November 18, 2026, in Santa Clara, California, according to a release dated November 22, 2026. Hitachi Digital is the global digital services company recently unveiled by Hitachi, Ltd. The product combines technology and services to govern the lifecycle of agentic engineering across complex, AI-driven systems. It does so through enterprise specific context, guardrails and intent. The release says it helps companies orchestrate AI from development to deployment through to operations and continuous improvement in a closed loop.

HARC Compose builds on Hitachi's experience and uses standardized, failure-conscious engineering. Hitachi Digital FDEs, forward deployed engineers, use it to build trustworthy AI-native applications faster and to maintain and improve AI agent performance once deployed. It strengthens Hitachi Digital's recurring service model, giving FDEs end-to-end support from ideas to outcomes. It is compatible across multi-vendor environments, and enterprises can use it entirely or opt for individual capabilities. It strengthens HMAX by Hitachi and augments HMAX Foundry solutions including HMAX Data Fabric, HMAX AI Operations, and HMAX Cyber.

Hitachi Digital is the unified brand of GlobalLogic, Inc. and Hitachi Digital Services LLC, and its legal entity is scheduled to be established on April 1, 2027. A press release on September 3, 2026 covered Hitachi expanding HMAX to accelerate deployment of Physical AI. Anand Birje, CEO and Chairman of Hitachi Digital, said HARC Compose is Hitachi Digital in action. He said the true promise of AI is not just writing code faster but shifting human ingenuity toward composing resilient, mission-critical systems. He said eliminating the divide between build and run closes the feedback loop and delivers governance and trust.

Premkumar Balasubramanian, Chief Technology Officer of Hitachi Digital, said speed is expected and trust has to be earned in an era of AI-generated software. He said customers need clarity on what a change is meant to improve, proof that it worked, and confidence in the process behind it. He said forward deployed engineers direct AI agents to build, test, and coordinate changes while maintaining strict human oversight over what goes live. He said live production evidence verifies outcomes. The release says AI has made code development faster and more productive but not necessarily trustworthy across enterprise systems.

The release says that without the right context, enterprise knowledge, company goals, policies, systems, and risk requirements, fast code becomes fast failure. HARC Compose carries enterprise intent from planning through production while keeping human experts in control of critical decisions. It includes CAKE, the Context-Aware Knowledge Engine, which connects enterprise intent, domain knowledge, systems, policies, risks, security, decision and production history and flags gaps and contradictions before agents act. An Orchestration Engine coordinates multiple agents across build, deploy and operate as one system and supports various AI agents and tools selected by customers. Failure-conscious Engineering uses failure mode and effects analysis to identify how a proposed change could fail and to decide what to test before release.

Universal capabilities include Responsible AI, which guards against system deviations such as agent drift, and guided and autonomous work that maintain human engagement. HARC Compose is built on OFE, outcome-forward engineering, a methodology used by Hitachi Digital's own FDE teams, which treats Define, Build, Deploy and Operate as one continuous system. Delivery is considered complete only when a system yields intended business outcomes in the real world, not at system release. The release lists principles including Fidelity, which establishes intent, constraints, failure risks and guardrails before work begins, and Throughput, which uses coding agents to turn clear intent into operable change. HARC Compose is available to enterprises worldwide, and deployments supported by Hitachi Digital FDEs are already underway in the finance, healthcare, and technology industries.

Hitachi Digital is a wholly owned subsidiary of Hitachi, Ltd. with approximately 35,000 professionals in 27 countries. Hitachi revenues for FY2025, ended March 31, 2026, totaled 10,586.7 billion yen, with 606 consolidated subsidiaries and approximately 290,000 employees worldwide. The release says HARC Compose capabilities are expected to expand as Hitachi Digital grows its technical talent base and ecosystem alliances. The release does not give pricing, customer names, or a general availability date beyond saying deployments are underway. More to follow.

stories.Headline: CERT-In warns agentic AI frameworks divert funds by altering payment records
stories.Summary:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team issued an advisory on November 20, 2026, warning that hackers are manipulating business records and payment approval workflows in order to divert funds. These attacks use open-source agentic AI frameworks to automate reconnaissance and intrusion across government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India. CERT-In observed that unauthorised financial transactions are not limited to BFSI entities, because they also affect technology service providers supporting government-linked payment processes. The agency further noted that platforms handling vendor or partner payouts are affected as well, and it described the use of an AI-driven agentic offensive framework against enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. Threat actors alter business records or approval processes to steal money through legitimate payment processes, rather than targeting payment APIs directly.

This approach allows transactions to pass the usual application and approval checks, even when records have been changed without authorisation, without immediately raising suspicion. The agentic offensive frameworks conduct automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems and rapidly prepare exploitation methods, according to the advisory. They use multiple agents or automated workers for parallel intrusion tasks, which shortens the attack stages, and the advisory was published by TechGig on November 22, 2026. CERT-In recommended that organisations identify service provider systems and accounts that can approve payments or access sensitive information. It also urged them to recheck payment instructions and business records against independent authoritative records.

The agency advised organisations to establish agreements with service providers covering incident detection, access to logs, investigation, and timely notification of shared compromises. The advisory places responsibility on organisations to verify payment-related records independently and to secure their arrangements with the service providers they rely on. The advisory covers government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India, and it states that unauthorised financial transactions extend beyond BFSI entities to technology service providers and payout platforms. CERT-In attributed the attacks to open-source agentic AI frameworks that automate reconnaissance and intrusion, and it said the offensive frameworks target enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the recommendations the agency issued to organisations.

stories.Headline: MBZUAI releases PAN 2 world model to enable simulative reasoning for AI agents
stories.Summary:
The Institute of Foundation Models at MBZUAI released the PAN 2 world model on November 17, 2026. This open 29-billion-parameter model allows agents to practice simulative reasoning by imagining and rendering plans. It generates up to 20 seconds of video from text actions and optional images. The model was published on Hugging Face at the IFM/PAN2 repository. It uses Generative Latent Prediction to help agents act on the best simulations.

The system requires Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.12.1, flash-attn 4, and CUDA 13.2. It combines a Qwen3.5-9B conceptual reasoner with a 29B MMDiT diffusion backbone and Wan 2.2 VAE decoder. Videos are rendered at 704 by 1248 pixels at 24 frames per second. Users must download weights from IFM/PAN2 and models from Qwen and Wan-AI into HF_HOME. Default settings use 50 steps and a CFG of 2.5 for 241 frames.

MBZUAI researchers stated that the model handles symbolic planning through language and pixels through diffusion. They noted that the perceptual backbone was trained on hundreds of millions of videos with structured annotations. The team admitted that long plans often fail, with two in three containing a missed step. They warned that appearance drifts across clips and the model may shortcut physics. MBZUAI requested that users report any misuse to the pan@ifm.ai email address.

Robotics teams comparing PAN 2 to Figure or Unitree demos are affected by these physics limitations. The model is suitable for agent plan scoring but weak for marketing clips due to caption requirements. It is considered entertainment-grade physics and should not be confused with lab instruments. Users needing verifiable numeric benchmarks are advised to pair it with NVIDIA Nemotron for Science. The model is not a replacement for NVIDIA Isaac Sim or production digital twins.

The model follows research threads including VibePrevisBench 4D scenes and embodied AI exposure benchmarks. It is based on the Critique of World Models paper and the GLP framework. The model card includes 300 single-action tests and 100 multi-step tasks with 456 steps. Performance was measured using Physics-IQ Verified, PhyGround, RBench, and 1,400 human pairwise judgments. The system uses a Bradley-Terry model centered at 1500 Elo for these comparisons.

Next, builders should run the pan2-guardrail as a sidecar container to prevent deepfakes and misinformation. Users can fork the model in air-gapped labs or use it for short agent planning. Continued pretraining is possible for labs with proprietary teleoperation logs using provided YAML configs. The articles leave open whether the model can run on consumer GPUs without heavy quantization. They also leave open how it compares to DeepMind world models in specific benchmarks.

stories.Headline: Google blocks 41 AI crawlers from accessing Google Maps pages
stories.Summary:
Google updated its robots.txt file on google.com to block 41 AI crawlers from accessing Google Maps pages. This change occurred between November 17 and November 22, 2026, according to an analysis of archived files. The company placed these bots under a shared AI training opt-out token. Google's own AI control, Google-Extended, remains in the default group to keep Maps open.

The new rules apply to 41 named crawlers, including OpenAI's GPTBot, Anthropic's ClaudeBot, and ByteDance's Bytespider. These bots are now shut out of every Google Maps page on the domain. The group uses the __usage_ai-training token, which Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic committed to honor on October 30, 2026. The list includes Japanese bots Cotoyogi and SBIntuitionsBot, as well as Applebot-Extended and img2dataset.

Japanese SEO specialist Masahiro Tsuji first flagged the update in a post on X at 14:03 UTC on November 22. He initially claimed Google blocked search results and goto pages, but later revised this claim. Tsuji noted that the update makes the stance of refusing scraping clear in the robots.txt file. He expressed surprise at seeing a crawler from Japanese academic institutions on the list.

Barry Schwartz of Search Engine Roundtable replied that some of these rules were added back in July. The change affects various model builders, including Amazonbot, Meta's FacebookBot, and developers from China like DeepSeekBot and QwenBot. Other affected entities include Mistral, Cohere, the Allen Institute for AI, and the Common Crawl archive. These crawlers now lose access to business listings, directions, and contributor profiles on Maps.

The robots.txt file uses a protocol where crawlers follow the most specific user agent group that matches them. Google rewrote an internal comment to ensure new named groups are paired with either the default or AI training group. This design prevents the default group's longer allow rules from overriding the training group's single disallow for maps. Most other pages, like search results, were already off limits to every crawler.

Microsoft will begin honoring these training preferences on February 1, 2027, based on the shared token. Google plans to support the token in early 2027, though private agreements may override these rules. The draft specification states that the policy token is not a directive for crawling behavior. The articles leave open why Google split its own Gemini control from the other 41 bots.

stories.Headline: US restricts Chinese access to remote computing to block AI model training
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration issued new rules this week to restrict Chinese access to cutting edge chips. These rules follow the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after an alleged affair with a spy. Chinese technology firms are now bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans. The US government aims to curtail the ability of China to train capable AI models. This move comes as the technology race between the two superpowers continues to intensify.

The rules restrict remote computing access through data centres located in third countries to close a loophole. Nvidia is no longer shipping the H200 chip, although the Trump administration greenlighted some other sales. Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore based Megaspeed, is alleged to be a Chinese spy. These restrictions follow a House committee report that the US signed off on 900,000 chips. The rules target the use of advanced Nvidia chips for training increasingly capable artificial intelligence models.

Tencent President Martin Lau said the new US rule on chip access sets everyone back in China. Lau stated that everyone is having less advanced compute regardless of when they started building capacities. He noted that training timelines for the next versions of Tencent AI models would probably be impacted. Lau believes Chinese players must eventually rely on domestic supply chains and fast progressing domestic chips. He mentioned that the industry is progressing very fast toward achieving this necessary domestic self sufficiency.

Alibaba warned that the new US rules could affect some of its global data centre expansion plans. James Chai of the ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute said Chinese firms are heavily dependent on Nvidia. A study by the Institute for Progress estimated remote access could be one third of compute. Beijing rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy and called the US rules economic coercion. Analysts say these tightening export control measures will accelerate China's push to make its chip industry self sufficient.

Alibaba reported a 53 per cent revenue surge for AI cloud services to nearly 61 billion yuan. Total revenue for the July September quarter rose 10 per cent to almost 272 billion yuan. Capital expenditures jumped 60 per cent to 50.5 billion yuan due to increased AI infrastructure buildout spending. Alibaba recently launched its Qwen4 Max AI model and the Zhenwu V900 chip, called China's most powerful. Jacob Cooke of WPIC Marketing noted significant untapped demand for AI from various Chinese enterprises.

Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following the ouster of Jensen Huang from his leadership role. US officials suspect Alice Huang was recruited to influence Nvidia to make advanced chips more available. The US is expected to step up chip export control policies due to national security concerns. Alibaba is still assessing the repercussions of the rules on its global data centre expansion plans. The articles leave open how many other chips the US will block from being shipped.

stories.Headline: Investors sell off artificial intelligence stocks as S&P 500 enters a correction
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks fell on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, for a fourth consecutive session as a sell-off in artificial intelligence shares deepened. Investors sold off these stocks ahead of the quarterly earnings report from Nvidia, which was released after the closing bell that day. A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks continued on Friday, November 20, 2026, pulling the S&P 500 down by 3.7 percent. This Friday decline capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest string of losses since the COVID-19 pandemic began in the year 2020. The sell-off in technology stocks spread globally, causing Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi to each fall more than 5 percent overnight.

The Dow Jones fell 848.75 points to 50,759.42 on Tuesday and dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33 on Friday, while the S&P 500 hit 6,910.39. The Nasdaq Composite shed 181.37 points to 24,328.38 on Tuesday and lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73 on Friday, November 20. The S&P 500 entered a correction after falling over 10 percent from its October 6 all-time high, a state not seen since March 2025. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 sank 76.06 points to 7,340.53, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74 percent and the Dow Jones fell 1.64 percent. All 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the red, with financials down 1.87 percent and utilities down 1.6 percent on Tuesday.

Baird market strategist Michael Antonelli said the idea that AI can spend unlimited money to support the stock market is ending right now. He stated that he does not believe the overall bull market, which started in October 2022, has come to an end yet. The Commerce Department reported that U.S. retail sales rose 0.2 percent in October, following an unrevised 0.8 percent increase in September. The National Association of Home Builders reported its housing market index fell to 25 in November from 29 in October, its lowest since 2012. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom after a major air campaign in Yemen.

The sell-off affected chip stocks like Micron, Advanced Micro Devices, and Intel, while Broadcom gained 2.46 percent on Tuesday before falling 12.1 percent Friday. Software stocks declined on Tuesday, with Salesforce falling 9.45 percent and ServiceNow dropping 6.51 percent, while Nike, IBM, and UnitedHealth Group lost over 4 percent. Home Depot fell 2.45 percent after a disappointing outlook and the announcement that Richard McPhail would succeed Ted Decker as the company CEO. Walt Disney slipped 1.48 percent after reporting revenue of 25.9 billion dollars and adjusted earnings of 1.77 dollars per share, beating expectations. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI tool, tumbled 9.1 percent to 88.30 dollars on Friday after its record-breaking initial public offering.

The S&P 500 last had a correction in March 2025 when the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market and escalated in April 2025. The Nasdaq composite experienced its worst weekly loss since March 2020, when the global economy ground to a halt due to the pandemic. AI stocks drove Wall Street's big gains this year, but fears of a bubble grew after recent midterm elections at state and federal levels. The University of Michigan index of consumer sentiment rose recently, though it remains below February levels before the start of the war with Iran. Brent crude oil rose 0.6 percent to 92.57 dollars per barrel amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

The Federal Reserve is scheduled to release the minutes of its October meeting on Wednesday to provide more insight into current economic policy. Traders have increasingly priced in a quarter-percentage-point rate increase at the December meeting because of persistent inflationary pressures currently affecting the U.S. economy. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.93 percent from 5.04 percent, while General Mills rose 3.7 percent and homebuilder Lennar gained 1 percent. Nvidia has fallen 17 percent since last week and dropped more than 25 percent since the scandal involving former CEO Jensen Huang erupted. The articles leave open whether the AI buildout will recover or if the current market correction will lead to a longer downturn.

stories.Headline: Asia-Pacific business leaders call for increased cooperation to turn AI into economic gains
stories.Summary:
Global business leaders gathered at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, on Tuesday to discuss artificial intelligence. These executives called for increased cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region to turn technological advances into real economic opportunities and productivity gains. They emphasized that the next phase of adoption depends on how effectively companies translate deployment into better decisions and measurable customer value. The goal is to achieve tangible improvements in business performance rather than pursuing automation for its own sake.

Robin Li, the cofounder, chairman and CEO of Baidu, noted that while investment in cloud resources and computing power has risen, many firms have not seen higher profits. He warned that AI could become a bubble if companies fail to identify specific scenarios where the technology is truly suited. Yang Ting, the vice-president of Agilent Technologies and general manager for Agilent China, explained that her company integrates AI into laboratory workflows to improve data quality. Fang Ling, the president of Alstom's Asia-Pacific region, stated that rail technology requires combining AI with deep engineering expertise and rigorous validation for safety.

Poh-Yian Koh, the president of FedEx China, argued that scaling AI responsibly requires high-quality data, connected systems, and clear governance. He suggested that employees must combine AI-driven insights with their own professional expertise and sound judgment to be effective. These leaders viewed China's AI Plus initiative and its diverse industrial scenarios as key opportunities for multinational companies to develop solutions. They urged APEC economies to share practical experiences and expand digital skills to make these applications more accessible across various industries.

stories.Headline: Yasir Mahmood lists ways to access paid AI models for free through developer tools and student offers
stories.Summary:
Yasir Mahmood, a mechanical engineer and technology writer for MakeUseOf, published a guide on November 22, 2026, regarding free access to paid artificial intelligence models. He noted that free chatbot options became more restrictive throughout 2026, including the October 2026 move by Google to shift free Gemini app accounts to Flash-Lite. Additionally, the free sign-in options for Gemini CLI and Qwen Code were ended entirely during this period. Users can access Gemini 4 Hydrogen, released on November 12, 2026, for free through Google AI Studio without providing a credit card. GitHub Copilot Free offers 2,000 monthly inline code completions and uses Copilot Fusion to route tasks to models like GPT-6 Luna.

OpenRouter provides 11 free models as of November 22, 2026, allowing 50 free requests per day for users who skip the payment method. Eligible United States college students aged 18 or older can claim 12 months of Google AI Pro, worth 19.99 dollars monthly, if they redeem the offer by December 31, 2026. Yasir explained that while these routes work, they each have specific drawbacks that users should consider before relying on them. He warned that Google AI Studio may use prompts for training purposes, and OpenRouter models can disappear without notice as promotions end. For the student offer, he advised setting a reminder because Google will charge the monthly fee after the free year expires.

He suggested that AI Studio is best for general prompts, while Copilot Free is the strongest choice for coding tasks. The author noted that free access is now primarily found through developer tools and student promotions rather than standard chatbot applications. He mentioned that GitHub Education provides free Copilot access for verified students, though sign-ups were paused from April until June 2026. He also clarified that a previous offer for four months of free ChatGPT Plus for students ended on October 31. Because free tiers are often temporary, he recommended comparing paid plans after a month of actual use.

stories.Headline: Salesforce leads US-backed Super Intelligence export consortium under Commerce program
stories.Summary:
Salesforce was selected by the U.S. Department of Commerce to lead a government-backed Super Intelligence export consortium, according to a Simply Wall St report dated November 22, 2026. The designation comes under the new American SI Exports Program, which was created to promote governed Super Intelligence technology packages globally. Salesforce is expected to coordinate with public agencies and private partners to support international adoption of U.S. Super Intelligence systems. The report says the export role should be weighed alongside other business fundamentals and risks before any investment decision, and it notes three warning signs worth knowing about at Salesforce.

The export designation puts Salesforce closer to governments that are standardising on governed data, model choice and agents, the report says. That aligns with its existing subscription and workflow platforms and can support more usage based AI revenue if public sector customers route more services through Agentforce, Data Cloud and related tools. Salesforce earns most of its money by selling customer relationship management software that helps organisations handle sales, service and marketing, and the report describes it as a large US$148.7b software provider to enterprises across the US, Europe and Asia Pacific. The consortium role lines up with the view that Salesforce wants its data products to be the context layer for AI and that Agentforce style bundles can support higher contract values, while raising the stakes on previously highlighted risks around security and reliability because more government workflows would run through those same agents.

The report says the clearest near term checkpoint is how much SI related business Salesforce reports in upcoming earnings, especially any disclosure of American SI Exports Program deals inside its public sector segment. Investors can track references to Super Intelligence packages and governed AI agents in fiscal 2027 and 2028 guidance updates, according to the report. The article was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and it states that it is general in nature and not intended as financial advice. It also says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

stories.Headline: Unauthorized party downloads stored prompt samples from Together AI
stories.Summary:
An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples from Together AI during June and July of 2026. This security incident occurred after an AI coding agent named xorl committed a private repository credential into a public GitHub repository. The leaked data consisted of prompt samples from the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models. These specific samples were primarily collected on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.

The company is now implementing several changes to strengthen its development workflows and customer data controls. These updates include using keyless access or short-lived credentials and checking all pull requests for sensitive information. Together AI has also made zero data retention the default setting for all new accounts. The organization is currently reviewing the affected data to identify which customers require direct notification regarding their exposed information.

Together AI apologized for the incident and stated they are working with law enforcement and an external forensic firm. They noted that the unauthorized party searched the samples for other credentials, though five tested keys were only canary credentials from a Dragos security experiment. The company claimed they have found no evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this specific event. They advised customers who handle sensitive data to enable zero data retention in their account settings.

stories.Headline: NSPCC campaign addresses how under-16s are protected from and prepared for AI
stories.Summary:
The Times published a report on 22 November 2026 asking what school children hope and fear about artificial intelligence, framed around questions of cheating and deepfakes. The article describes how the question of protecting under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it is being addressed through an NSPCC campaign. Alice Thomson, writing for the paper, saw how students reacted to that campaign. The piece sets out the tension between guarding young people against harm and equipping them to work with the tools.

The report presents the issue as a choice between protection and preparation, asking how under-16s should be shielded from new technology and helped to use it at the same time. It names cheating and deepfakes as among the concerns the discussion covers. The NSPCC campaign is described as the vehicle for addressing the issue, and the article follows Thomson as she observes students responding to it. No further figures, dates or names appear in the available text.

Responsibility for the issue is placed with the NSPCC, whose campaign the article says hopes to address it, and with the wider question of how under-16s should be protected and helped. The article does not record what the students themselves said, so their views are not set out in the text available. Thomson's role is limited to seeing how the students reacted to the campaign. The paper frames the matter as one of balancing protection against preparation.

The context given is the arrival of new technology, with cheating and deepfakes cited as the specific worries in view. The article does not say what happens next, beyond the campaign's stated hope of addressing the issue. It offers no timetable, no figures and no further named individuals. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Reco predicts AI agent security will merge with SaaS posture management in 2027
stories.Summary:
Reco, a security vendor, published five predictions on 19 November 2026 about how enterprises will manage AI agent security in 2027, arguing that agent security will merge with the established SaaS Security Posture Management market, known as SSPM, rather than remain a separate category. The company expects security teams to treat AI agents, model context protocol connections and AI-driven workflows as the same governance challenge as users, applications and OAuth permissions. Gal Nakash, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer at Reco, said the distinction between SSPM and agent security will blur because agents increasingly operate inside the same SaaS platforms that SSPM products already monitor. He said enterprises will increasingly expect SaaS security platforms to account for agents, MCP connections and AI-enabled workflows alongside users, applications and OAuth grants. The second prediction is that agent security posture management will move closer to runtime enforcement, so that findings such as unnecessary access rights or risky connections may trigger direct action while an agent is operating rather than being left as alerts for later review.

Possible responses include blocking a tool call, requesting approval, quarantining an agent or restricting access to certain systems, which Nakash said means more platforms will use posture context to make decisions while an agent is acting. For Chief Information Security Officers, that could mean defining more clearly which actions can be blocked automatically and which still require human sign-off. Reco also argues that AI-assisted integration work will become central to maintaining visibility, because the number of enterprise applications, agent platforms, MCP servers and AI-enabled features is growing too quickly for vendors to build and maintain connectors manually. Nakash also expects large software vendors including Salesforce, Microsoft, ServiceNow and Anthropic to strengthen governance features for agents running on their own platforms, but Reco argues that native controls will not remove the need for an independent cross-platform view. He said those tools will raise the baseline but cannot fully address agents that connect across applications, identities and vendors.

The final prediction is that AI itself will play a larger role in investigating and remediating agent risk, tracing permissions, mapping connections, identifying likely causes of risk and recommending specific changes to access rights. Nakash said using AI to summarise alerts will no longer be particularly differentiated, and that platforms will increasingly use AI to investigate why an agent represents a risk and, in lower-risk situations, carry out remediation automatically. That leaves enterprises with a governance question about how much authority to give the security agent itself, especially when it comes to revoking access or making changes without direct human involvement. The cross-platform concern is becoming more relevant as enterprises test autonomous workflows that depend on several identity systems, APIs and software layers at once, and security teams may need to understand how an agent's relationships change across the wider estate rather than only whether it is controlled inside one application. Reco's predictions cover 2027, and the article does not say what happens next beyond those expectations.

stories.Headline: Reticket founder Aniket Chaudhary says ticket scalping in India still relies on scripts and fake accounts rather than AI
stories.Summary:
Raye’s registration for her concert at London’s Royal Albert Hall attracted 1.8 million sign-ups for just 5,000 seats, and she wrote on X that scalpers using AI bots created hundreds of thousands of fake registrations. She said she had never witnessed bots on this scale, and her team decided to manually review registrations. When Coldplay came to India last year, BookMyShow saw nearly 13 million fans vying for 150,000 tickets. A large number of tickets appeared on resale platforms such as Viagogo and Gigsberg with astronomical markups, and the culprit was bot-driven ticket scalping, where operators used bots trained to mimic human behaviour to bypass checks.

India’s live and concert market is worth ₹20,000 crore. Reticket uses zero-knowledge Transport Layer Security through Reclaim Protocol to obtain cryptographic proof that booking details came directly from the issuing platform’s servers and were not altered. The verification checks the event, payment, and booking status, each ticket can be listed only once, and a listing is locked when a buyer begins payment. Reticket holds sellers’ payouts until 72 hours after the event, and where a transfer or wristband delivery is delayed, sellers must set up a refundable UPI mandate deposit ranging from ₹499 to ₹4,999 to compensate the buyer. Reticket caps resale prices at the amount originally paid by the seller.

Aniket Chaudhary, Founder of secondary ticket marketplace Reticket, said most ticket scalping in India still runs on old methods: scripts that check out faster than a human can, lots of accounts on different phone numbers, and people hired to wait in online queues, none of which needs AI. He said anyone can now make a booking confirmation that looks exactly like a real one in about a minute. He explained that the bigger problem is real tickets, since more scams involve someone holding a genuine ticket than an AI-made fake. He said Reticket’s verification already works without any formal tie-up because sellers prove ownership from their own accounts, but the original platforms can do things Reticket cannot. He said that soon many people will simply ask an AI assistant to book tickets for them, and that is completely fair.

Anuj Gupta, Founder and CEO of AI research lab KiteFishAI, said the real issue is that ticketing systems were originally designed around human interaction, while automated systems can operate at a completely different speed and scale. He cautioned that a bot written with the help of ChatGPT is not necessarily an AI agent. He argued that ticketing platforms need to treat tickets as verifiable digital assets rather than images or documents, and that every ticket should be associated with a valid transaction and a unique cryptographic identifier that can be verified against the issuing platform. He said the distinction should be based on identity, authorisation, transaction behaviour, and intent rather than simply whether a browser or an AI agent is involved. Events discovery platform MeraEvents identifies bulk registrations, duplicate accounts, unauthorised resale, and copied booking confirmations as potential risks, but cautions that automation alone does not establish AI involvement.

Earlier, scalper bots could be blocked by simple IP blocks and “traffic light” tests, but now scalpers use thousands of generated digital identities, continuously scraping through resale demand and seat availability to adjust markups. Conventional bots can refresh availability, navigate online queues, select seats, and submit checkout requests using predefined instructions. Fake booking confirmations can reproduce familiar logos, booking IDs, and QR codes, supported by convincing descriptions and conversations with supposed buyers. A screenshot or PDF cannot establish that a seller still owns a ticket or has the right to transfer it. MeraEvents notes that event organisers need to communicate official booking channels, establish transfer and entry rules, and coordinate with ticketing and on-ground teams when discrepancies arise.

Primary ticketing platforms could notify resale marketplaces when a ticket has been scanned or transferred, and could also reissue tickets to buyers, invalidating the seller’s original copy and making double-selling harder. Dynamically refreshing QR codes, digitally signed ticket credentials, and controlled transfers could also make screenshots and duplicate tickets harder to reuse. Chaudhary argues that linking purchase limits to verified individuals rather than accounts could make bulk buying harder. Gupta argues that platforms should not automatically treat all automation as malicious, which could require systems that establish which customer an agent represents, what actions it is permitted to perform, and whether a specific transaction has been authorised. Without those checks, the same tools that help a fan book a ticket could also be used to coordinate purchases across multiple accounts.

Articles.Title: From Raye to Coldplay, How AI Scalpers are Pricing You Out of Concert Tickets - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: IT leaders prioritize data streaming over AI to feed real-time systems, Confluent survey finds
stories.Summary:
IT leaders are now prioritizing the infrastructure that feeds artificial intelligence over the technology itself, according to a report released on November 22, 2026. This shift indicates that enterprises are focusing on data streaming platforms to ensure information moves continuously rather than remaining locked in disconnected systems. The trend suggests that organizations are becoming more realistic about the foundational work required to make advanced technology successful. The 2026 Data Streaming Report from Confluent surveyed 4,625 IT leaders across 14 countries to identify these changing strategic priorities. In Singapore, 51 percent of respondents ranked data streaming as a top priority for 2026, while only 31 percent chose AI and machine learning solutions.

Security remains the highest overall category at 96 percent, and combined data management, protection, and governance priorities reached 90 percent. Furthermore, 78 percent of leaders reported that insufficient infrastructure for real-time processing is a major challenge, an increase from 62 percent in 2025. Greg Taylor, the senior vice president and general manager for Asia Pacific at Confluent, stated that investing in data infrastructure is essentially investing in AI outcomes. He noted that 81 percent of respondents struggle with data silos and 76 percent face inconsistent data sources. Taylor suggested that framing infrastructure as a prerequisite for performance is more persuasive than treating it as a separate expense.

He emphasized that the real value of data is realized when it is used as and when it is needed. The report highlights that 97 percent of leaders believe data streaming increases the impact of AI investments. Many organizations are seeing significant returns, with 47 percent of Singaporean firms anticipating at least five times return on investment. Beyond AI, 96 percent of respondents expect benefits in customer experience and 95 percent see a reduced time to market for new services. These findings suggest that real-time data infrastructure supports broader business goals while improving the reliability of live operational decisions.

Articles.Title: Why Data Streaming Is Overtaking AI as a Strategic Priority for Enterprises

stories.Headline: Deloitte analyses legal risks of generative AI for businesses across IP, data protection and contracts
stories.Summary:
The articles do not contain a specific news event, so this is not a breaking story. Deloitte published an analysis on 22 November 2026, in collaboration with the Deloitte AI Institute, of the legal implications of Generative AI for corporations, covering intellectual property, data protection, contracts and Generative AI policy. The article notes that enthusiasm for AI adoption is being fuelled in part by Generative AI, and it cites the EU AI Act, Article 28b (4), which defines Generative AI as foundation models used in AI systems specifically intended to generate, with varying levels of autonomy, content such as complex text, images, audio, or video. It says a legal executive's role is to advise stakeholders, including business leaders, executive peers and the board, on the risks of business applications of Generative AI, and that regulatory frameworks in this area are emerging and quickly evolving. On intellectual property, the article says AI can process vast quantities of data and, without much noteworthy human intervention, transform it into an AI-generated output, and that discussion of how to treat rights in both the training input and the AI output is still in its early days.

The report focuses on copyright law, but the same concepts are likely to apply to other sorts of protected IP. Generative AI systems ingest and generate large amounts of data, including images, text, speech, video, code, business plans and technical formulae, and training, testing, uploading, analysing, consulting or otherwise processing such input and output data requires various levels of protection. The report addresses challenges organisations face when using personal and confidential data in Generative AI systems, and measures to mitigate the relevant legal risks. The article says several common personal data principles and protections across jurisdictions are highly affected by Generative AI systems, and organisations should pay specific attention to transparency, data minimisation, lawfulness, sensitive data and individual rights. Given the legal risks of using Generative AI in a business context, it says careful consideration of contract terms is important when licensing or otherwise entering into a contract relating to a Generative AI solution, with key points from liability to AI regulations likely to require attention.

It says adoption of this powerful, differentiating technology demands attention to risks that could imperil an enterprise's brand, reputation, stakeholder trust or compliance with legal and regulatory obligations. The article also links to related Deloitte material, including a piece asking who is responsible for mistakes when AI acts on its own, which says embedding legal oversight and clear accountability into agentic AI from the outset lets businesses harness autonomous technology with confidence and control. It points to a piece on scaling Generative AI deployment, which says scaling responsibly requires navigating legal, ethical and regulatory complexities. It cites Deloitte's 2026 Global Tax Policy Survey, with insights from 1,010 tax and finance leaders across 28 jurisdictions on tax transparency, digitalisation of tax including AI, sustainability, international tax reform including OECD Pillar Two, and trade and tariffs. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Travis Tritt warns fans that AI videos of him commenting on the CMA Awards are fake
stories.Summary:
Travis Tritt posted a warning on social media on the morning of November 22, 2026, after a video that claimed to show his thoughts on that week's CMA Awards went viral and drew hundreds of thousands of views. The video was made with artificial intelligence and carried a watermark disclosing that fact, though the mark was partly cut off in some of the versions that circulated online. In the fake clip, an AI-generated Tritt called the people running the CMA "idiots" for sidelining Ella Langley while celebrating Taylor Swift, who he said did not win a damn thing. The video also claimed that Ella Langley got almost no camera time, which the article calls a dead giveaway that the clip was fake, because she spent much of the show on stage accepting awards for "Choosin' Texas."

Tritt told fans that any recent videos of him supposedly commenting on the latest CMA Awards show are obviously fake and were created using AI, and he asked people to disregard them completely. The article says the fake Tritt video is not even good AI and is clearly fake, yet plenty of people in the replies still fell for it, some supporting the supposed comments and others disagreeing with them. A second AI video is also going around that claims to feature Jason Aldean sharing much the same opinion, bashing the CMA Awards and Taylor Swift, and it has been shared dozens of times and drawn nearly 100 replies from people on both sides of the debate. The article notes that the AI in both the Tritt and Aldean videos is not very good, but that as the technology advances it is getting harder to spot fake content, and people are falling for it regardless.

Tennessee is one of the few states so far that have tried to protect artists from AI-generated uses of their likeness and voice, through a law called the ELVIS Act, which stands for Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security. That law prohibits AI creators from using a person's name, image, likeness, photograph, or voice without consent, and it allows artists and others to sue creators who use their likeness or voice without permission. The article says lawmakers have been slow to respond to the rise in AI, and it calls the problem one that will no doubt get worse before it gets better. Until there are laws not only on the books but actually enforced against the people who make this fake content claiming to be from others, the article says, it is a reminder to verify anything you see online these days.

Articles.Title: Travis Tritt Issues Warning After AI Video Claiming To Be His Thoughts On The CMA Awards Goes Viral: “Obviously Fake”

stories.Headline: Samsung orders more Protec bonding equipment for HBM expansion
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics placed an additional order with Protec for temporary attach bonding equipment as it expands high-bandwidth memory production capacity, and Protec disclosed the contract on Nov. 20. The order is worth 23.41 billion won, which represents 10.2% of Protec's consolidated revenue in 2025. The contract period runs from Nov. 19, when Protec received the purchase order from Samsung, through Sept. 30, 2027. Protec had previously supplied the same equipment to a Samsung mass-production line in 2025, and the initial order placed in September 2024 was worth 24.38 billion won.

Temporary attach bonding equipment is used to precisely align and temporarily attach chips at designated positions before final bonding, and the newly ordered tools will be installed at Samsung's Cheonan facility, a key advanced packaging site. Samsung began construction of its fifth advanced packaging line at its Onyang Campus in Asan, South Chungcheong Province, on Nov. 12, and that line is scheduled to begin operations in June 2028. Samsung plans to invest a total of 46 trillion won in the Onyang Campus in phases, and the expansion of its advanced packaging capacity could lead to additional orders for Protec. Protec's mainstay equipment has traditionally been dispensers that uniformly apply liquid materials during semiconductor packaging processes, and the company began supplying semiconductor die bonders in 2020.

Protec expanded into advanced packaging bonding equipment following its Samsung order in 2024, and annual bonding equipment revenue, previously between 5 billion won and 10 billion won, increased to approximately 30 billion won in 2025. Protec reported consolidated third-quarter revenue of 78.2 billion won and operating profit of 24.4 billion won, up 53.1% and 57.2% respectively from a year earlier. Its operating margin reached 31.2%, and cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters totaled 63 billion won, exceeding the 46.3 billion won recorded for full-year 2025. The articles do not say what Samsung or Protec executives said about the order, and they do not state what happens next beyond the scheduled line start and the possibility of further orders.

stories.Headline: Masayoshi Son drops plan to acquire SK hynix for 1 trillion dollars
stories.Summary:
Masayoshi Son, the chairman of SoftBank Group, recently explored acquiring the memory chipmaker SK hynix. He approached major United States financial institutions to discuss raising money for this massive purchase. The potential deal was reported by The Information on November 20 and 21, 2026. However, the idea appears to have been dropped at an early stage of the process. SoftBank now says it is no longer actively considering the acquisition of the company.

The deal could have reached 1,400 trillion won, which is approximately 1 trillion US dollars. This price reflects a 40 percent control premium over a market value of 577.7 billion dollars. SK hynix is based in Korea and is the world's second largest memory chipmaker. The plan required securing high bandwidth memory to complement SoftBank's other artificial intelligence investments. The acquisition would have involved the largest shareholder of SK hynix, which is SK Square.

A spokesperson for SoftBank stated that the company reviews many opportunities but this one is gone. SoftBank did not confirm that Wall Street banks had discussed providing the necessary financing for the deal. SK hynix issued a statement saying it had no knowledge of the reported acquisition plan by Son. An industry official said the approach showed Son wants to control the entire AI value chain. The chairman has historically relied on borrowing and pledging shares to fund his large investments.

Market observers believe the idea was never realistic due to financing, governance, and industrial security hurdles. The deal would affect the global supply of high bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. These accelerators are monopolized by Nvidia and rely on memory from Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix. The HBM market share for SK hynix was 50 percent as of the second quarter. This concentration of production in Asia has raised security concerns for the United States and allies.

SoftBank already owns Arm, Ampere Computing, DigitalBridge, and SB Energy, and has stakes in Intel and OpenAI. Son previously used Saudi and UAE sovereign wealth funds to launch the 100 billion dollar Vision Fund. He also borrowed against Alibaba holdings to help pay for the 32 billion dollar purchase of Arm. SoftBank's cash position at the end of September 2026 was about 34.3 billion US dollars. In October, the company issued bonds to invest an additional 10 billion dollars into OpenAI.

The Korean government would likely require prior approval because the chipmaker is a key national strategic asset. President Donald Trump determined in January 2026 that semiconductor imports could threaten the security of the United States. Korea can prohibit foreign mergers that involve core national technologies to protect the national economy and security. The articles leave open whether Son will seek other ways to secure the AI memory supply chain. It remains unclear how SoftBank could finance such a large deal given its growing financial burdens.
