stories.Headline: AI tools raise team output but leaders risk burnout by raising workloads
stories.Summary:
Companies that begin using AI tools are definitely seeing a productivity boost, but as team production increases, team performance dips, according to an article published by Entrepreneur on November 22, 2026. The cause is that AI helps to make task completion faster, which at face value sounds beneficial since human workers don’t need to spend as much time getting their work done. But organizations are responding by increasing workloads and expectations, so teams are getting more work accomplished while individual employees aren’t getting any kind of a break. Instead, they’re expected to multiply their workloads, which the article calls a surefire road to capacity strain and burnout.

The article says leaders should teach team members how to think more clearly in disruptive, fast-moving environments, helping them create enough cognitive space to apply judgment, adaptability and emotional intelligence they already possess. It cites human performance company Q Studio, which takes this approach through organization-wide Mind Skills Training, and corporate agile training company Agile Seekers, which teaches team members to show curiosity and skepticism about AI rather than simply accepting what it recommends. It also says leaders should make human connection an expectation, because Thomson Reuters research shows that when employees are given the okay to just turn in AI work, they lose a sense of connection with that work and eventually with each other. The article adds that encouraging team members to role play difficult conversations with each other can be a stronger way to build bonds than using chatbots trained for that purpose.

The article says leaders around the world are laying off team members in the name of AI, though some giants aren’t, and it calls that a tricky move that should be reconsidered even if AI has improved productivity. When people are let go because AI took their jobs, the article says, everyone who remains gets a mixed signal that productivity matters more to the organization than performance. As a result, those employees may stop trying to hand in stellar work and just try to be as busy as possible. The article concludes that productivity will always matter and AI can let employees do more work in less time, but leaders should not concentrate so hard on getting more done that they forget to celebrate the human characteristics and acumen only their team members can provide.

Articles.Title: AI Is Helping Your Team Do More. That Doesn’t Mean They Can Handle More.

stories.headline_source: AI Is Helping Your Team Do More. That Doesn’t Mean They Can Handle More.

stories.Headline: Writer pairs local Ollama and free Gemini models in Obsidian via Copilot extension
stories.Summary:
The article, published on itsfoss.com on 2026-11-22T06:00:00Z, describes how its author set up both local AI and cloud AI inside Obsidian, the personal knowledge management system. The author configured the two kinds of AI for different vaults to suit specific needs. A local AI handles the most private notes and journals, keeping personal thoughts entirely on the machine. Gemini chat, chosen because it is free, serves work-related documents and learning journeys where speed and broader knowledge access are key. The author says this approach gives privacy where it matters most and powerful cloud capabilities for everything else.

The setup relies on Copilot for Obsidian, a community extension that supports both local and cloud AI and offers its own Plus features. The author notes that local AI needs a decent GPU to work seamlessly and efficiently. For Gemini, the author created an API key on the Google AI Studio website, named the key, clicked Create a New Project, clicked Create Key, and copied the key with the Copy key button. In Obsidian's settings, reached with CTRL+, the author opened Copilot, went to the Basic tab, clicked Set Keys, pasted the key, and selected the Gemini 2.5 Flash model from the dropdown. The author set that model as the default chat model, after which Copilot appears in the ribbon menu and opens in the right sidebar, and says the same setup works for other providers like Claude and GPT.

For local AI the author used Ollama, a command-line tool for downloading and running open-source LLMs such as Llama3, Phi-3, Mistral and CodeGamma on the local machine. The author says a GPU is highly recommended, that running on a CPU is possible but not ideal, and that a TPU or NPU would be even better though Ollama may not support all of them. The tutorial used the Llama3.2 3B model, which downloads almost 2GB or more of data and is noticeably faster than larger models on a CPU-only machine. The author checked that Ollama was running on its default localhost port, where it should show the message "Ollama is running", then installed the model and listed installed models to copy its exact name. In Copilot's Model tab the author clicked Add Model, entered that exact name in the Model Name field marked with a red asterisk, chose any Display name, set the provider to Ollama, left the Base URL and API key fields at their defaults, optionally enabled Vision in Model Capabilities to allow image additions, pressed Test to check for configuration errors, clicked Add Model, and set Llama as the default chat model in the Basic tab.

The author says Copilot's chat interface appears in the right sidebar and by default uses the current note as context, while pressing the @ symbol lets the user select multiple notes as context. If the model supports processing images, screenshots can be sent directly through the sidebar, which the author does when writing configs and asking the LLM about an error. Each result in the sidebar has an Insert/Replace at cursor button that adds the chat result exactly where the cursor sits in the note or document. Copilot saves all chat sessions as standard Markdown documents in a dedicated copilot/copilot-conversations folder in the vault, properly backlinked from the active note.

The author says AI can hallucinate and add wrong data, never suggests using it for research purposes, and says core learning and note-taking should always be done manually, though AI can add helpful context and format notes into a better Personal Knowledge Management format. The article says AI is rapidly gaining popularity across various fields and that using AI with notes gives superpower to the notes, while asking whether AI should be given access to a knowledge base. It says AI technology often comes with inherent privacy concerns, that corporate AI solutions typically offer faster queries and results at the risk of privacy, and that local AI can be taxing and slow, especially on moderate hardware. The author says the Copilot name does not mean the extension is exclusive to Microsoft Copilot, and describes Ollama as a command-line tool for running open-source LLMs locally.

The article notes that It's FOSS has helped people use Linux for 14 years and asks readers to become Plus members for ad-free reading and 5 eBooks. It also asks readers to tell Google they prefer It's FOSS so its Linux news and tutorials appear more often in search. The article leaves open whether Ollama supports all TPU and NPU hardware, saying the author is not sure. It does not say which heavier models a given system should choose beyond advising selection based on system specifications.

It does not report whether the author's own machine uses a GPU, a CPU, or a TPU or NPU. It does not give the default localhost port number Ollama runs on. It does not state the price of Copilot's Plus features or what those features include. It invites readers to share in the comments whether they prefer using AI in Obsidian, and it does not say what the author will configure or test next.

Articles.Title: My Hybrid AI System in Obsidian: Local and Cloud AI Integration

stories.Headline: Kraftwerk Berlin apologizes for hosting Helsing military AI launch and vows to revise rental policy
stories.Summary:
Kraftwerk Berlin apologized for hosting a military AI launch on November 11, 2026, after the city's music community expressed strong backlash. The venue hosted the launch of Clarity, a military AI targeting system developed by the European company known as Helsing. This event caused a dispute because the arts complex is closely associated with the experimental music scene in Berlin. The venue called the booking a serious error of judgment and promised to change its commercial booking policy.

The launch transformed the central hall of Kraftwerk Berlin into a setting that resembled a war room with drones hanging overhead. Maps and aerial footage covered the concrete walls, while guards in flak jackets patrolled the area with sniffer dogs. Helsing says Clarity uses AI agents to process sensor, satellite, and drone data to identify targets for human operators to approve. A spokesperson told RBB that the system finds ships, launch pads, and radar systems rather than identifying people.

Managing director Dietmar-Maria Hegemann called the booking unacceptable and stated that staff arranged the event without consulting him. Hegemann also leads Tresor, the techno club in the same complex, which condemned the event for being in community-built spaces. He claimed a staff member at the company responsible for commercial rentals at Kraftwerk Berlin made the arrangement. The venue stated it would revise its commercial-rental policy to avoid such errors in the future.

Curator and DJ Michail Stangl argued that human approval of strikes does not settle the broader concerns regarding this technology. Stangl told the Guardian that the system could eventually be sold to domestic police, authoritarian governments, or the border agency Frontex. He noted that the need for German support for Ukraine should not mean that people abandon critical scrutiny. These points were raised as concerns about future use rather than as evidence of actual sales.

Kraftwerk Berlin hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and shares its complex with the nightclub and record label Tresor. Tresor helped connect the electronic music scene of Detroit with post-Wall Berlin during the 1990s. Commercial rentals are common among former underground venues due to falling bar revenues and rising rents. Kraftwerk previously rejected a Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams before the booking.

The venue must now determine if its promised policy change brings cultural staff into decisions before the next commercial booking. Some Berlin nightlife insiders expressed surprise that Hegemann was not consulted given the planning required for high-security events. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian regarding the controversy. The situation tests how Berlin cultural venues balance their rental income with control over commercial events.

Articles.Title: Kraftwerk Berlin apologizes for hosting military AI launch after music-scene backlash

stories.headline_source: Kraftwerk Berlin apologizes for hosting military AI launch after music-scene backlash

stories.Headline: Lee orders legal overhaul to block AI-assisted exam cheating
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung ordered officials on Sunday to overhaul the legal basis for technology use on tests, review how national certification exams are managed, and consider printing a legal warning and adding identification marks to test papers, according to the JoongAng Ilbo. Lee pledged to close legal gaps that allow test-takers to cheat by using AI, writing on X that the fairness of exams is a principle that can never be compromised. He said concerns about AI-assisted cheating are spreading to essay exams and school tests. He wrote that it is difficult to come up with measures that perfectly address the issue at once, but that does not mean waiting until such perfect measures can be imposed.

He said his government will quickly implement the measures it can take now and keep making up for what is lacking. Lee said he would first order a full overhaul of the legal basis for using technology on exams to block people from photographing test papers and distributing those photos during the exam. He said he would also instruct ministries and agencies to jointly review how national certification tests and others are managed and revise related laws where needed. He added that he would order officials to review printing a legal warning on exam papers and adding unique identification marks, so that if one is photographed or leaked, the government can trace the source.

He wrote that those who cheat will be held accountable to the end, and that no matter how much technology advances, the principle of fairness must not be shaken. He said he would see the measures needed to protect the fairness of exams through. The same day, Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered to resign over the handling of this year's College Scholastic Ability Test, and Lee accepted the resignation, the article says. Choi took responsibility for last-minute changes made to the security measures for the 2027 CSAT, caused by worries of AI-assisted cheating, which drew criticism ahead of the college entrance exam and triggered nationwide confusion.

In a social media post, the president said academic dishonesty on the college admissions test is a crime as serious as corruption involving government officials. The article also says Lee reminded the public that a 100 million won reward for reporting CSAT cheating is still valid, and it credits the prime minister with spearheading anticheating measures for the college admissions test. The article says AI is rapidly changing our lives, but the principle of fairness must not be shaken. It was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools, then edited by a native English-speaking editor.

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three inference providers and drops 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility
stories.Summary:
Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld, according to OpenRouter. OpenRouter said it has been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them. The findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter, the company said. The results of the testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers, and OpenRouter said a live list of the security announcements it has received from providers is below.

OpenRouter said it off-boarded three providers from its platform based on the results of its investigations. It removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility, including providers flagged by researchers plus additional endpoints removed as a precautionary measure. OpenRouter notified all potentially affected customers. It is adapting the researchers' testing approach so it can run these checks on an ongoing basis, and it is conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties. OpenRouter is requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.

OpenRouter said it takes data policy enforcement very seriously as the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers. It said it is grateful for the Dragos report, and that as it integrates similar testing techniques it will keep raising the bar, with providers that want to be on OpenRouter needing to meet it. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, and OpenRouter said it has notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. It is encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and said it will keep the list updated.

stories.Headline: China's top spy agency helps domestic companies acquire advanced AI chips
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of State Security, which is China's top espionage agency, has conducted a campaign for at least two years to help Chinese companies acquire advanced artificial intelligence chips. This operation focuses on overcoming Western barriers to technologies that President Xi Jinping considers essential for the rise of China. The agency has shifted its priorities to gather intelligence and obtain semiconductors that the United States has barred companies like Nvidia from exporting. This effort aims to solve the chokehold problems that currently hold back the development of future industries within the country.

The campaign requires the adoption of extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors, as Xi Jinping told the Politburo in January. A central part of this quest involves the case of Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused by United States officials of working with the spy agency. Officials allege that Ms. Huang was tasked with spying on Jensen Huang, who serves as the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia. These specific allegations regarding the targeting of the Nvidia executive were first reported by The New York Times.

The Ministry of State Security is responsible for these actions, though the Chinese government has rejected the claims of espionage as pure fabrication. Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment regarding her alleged role in the intelligence gathering operation. The agency has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule, but it now prioritizes the acquisition of advanced semiconductor chips. This strategic shift reflects the broader goal of the Chinese leadership to secure technological independence from the West.

stories.Headline: Anthropic integrates Claude Mythos 5.1 into Zscaler endpoint security
stories.Summary:
Anthropic PBC integrated its Claude Mythos 5.1 model into Zscaler Endpoint AI Security for enterprise threat detection, the two companies reported on Sunday, November 22, 2026. The article was published by Bailey Pemberton at 12:07 PM CST on that date. Anthropic and Zscaler report that Claude Mythos 5.1 now supports next generation endpoint analysis for corporate cybersecurity teams. Cofounder Jack Clark says Anthropic's Claude system autonomously designs successor models. Clark describes that as evidence that the Singularity has arrived.

The combination of Claude Mythos 5.1 in Zscaler security tools and Claude self improvement only captures part of Anthropic's current story. The article points to one major warning sign that Anthropic PBC investors should know about. It says investors can compare Anthropic with wider peers through 41 AI small caps. Anthropic PBC develops large scale Claude AI systems for commercial use. The cybersecurity push shows the US software group trying to embed its models directly into enterprise workflows, where reliability, governance and constant model refinement matter as much as raw capability.

For Anthropic PBC investors, the update leans into two very different catalysts, according to the article. Claude Mythos 5.1 inside Zscaler's Endpoint AI Security backs the case that Anthropic's models are being used for concrete, high stakes work. That supports the existing thesis around enterprise adoption and real workloads. Jack Clark's claim that Claude now designs successor models puts pressure on governance, model oversight, and how public markets price extremely fast, partly autonomous improvement. The article describes the stock as having already seen sharp swings and as highly illiquid.

The article says the key reference point from here is Anthropic's first full quarter of reported results as a public company that includes this Zscaler collaboration. It advises close attention to disclosed enterprise security customer metrics and any commentary on Claude Mythos usage. Those figures will show how much this kind of deployment is feeding into the high revenue growth investors are already assuming. The article states it is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. It says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

The article's related coverage includes a Simply Wall St. piece from 3d ago titled Anthropic (ANT) Adds New Claude Integrations As Post IPO Enterprise Traction Builds. It also lists a PREMIUM MT Newswires item from 1d ago titled Zscaler Collaborating With Anthropic, Mistral On AI Security. Other listed items include Anthropic unveiling a cheaper, faster Claude Opus 5.5 model as the AI race accelerates, from Investing.com 1mo ago. A Yahoo Finance item 5mo ago covers Anthropic launching a Mythos-class Claude Fable 5 model available to the public. A Reuters item 7mo ago covers Anthropic touting an AI cybersecurity project with Big Tech partners.

stories.Headline: Joi AI launches AI companions to attract tech workers fearing romantic espionage
stories.Summary:
Tech workers now fear romantic espionage after a scandal involving Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese asset. Matchmakers report that more professionals worry their dates seek corporate secrets rather than romance. This anxiety follows reports that AI companies warned their employees about honeypots. Some men now avoid dating people from Russia or China due to these fears. A cybersecurity firm founder even hired a matchmaker because he worried about spies.

Joi AI launched zero espionage Executive Girlfriends on Tuesday to offer a safe alternative to human dating. Amy Andersen of Linx Dating in Silicon Valley offers vetting and NDAs in bespoke packages. These security services cost between 75,000 dollars and over 500,000 dollars for the Founders Level. One Palantir employee told Blaine Anderson he would not date any Russian or Chinese nationals. Simone Grossman is a Brooklyn matchmaker who sees these fears trickling down to regular professionals.

Isaac Stone Fish of Strategy Risks says it is difficult to tell engineers they are targets. He explains that some people receive attention because of their jobs rather than their personalities. Julie Levin of Joi AI says her platform allows users to discuss secrets comfortably. She claims that the company uses several layers of security and anonymizes all user data. Ira Winkler tells clients that beautiful strangers may not be interested in their personalities.

One anonymous tech worker rates his anxiety about espionage as a seven out of ten. AI workers are particularly affected because their rising net worth increases their perceived romantic desirability. Shannon Lundgren has worked as a San Francisco matchmaker for 15 years and notes heightened skepticism. Many employees previously joked about spies but did not consider the threat to be serious. High profile executives are considered the most at risk but are often the hardest to protect.

Honeypots often target lonely people or those seeking adventure and excitement, according to Ira Winkler. Greg Rinckey says victims are usually groomed over months or years rather than seduced quickly. Catherine Marinis-Yaqub notes that targets may meet spies at conferences or coffee shops. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang through a mutual associate who was also her husband. Rinckey says arrogant executives are easy targets because they love talking about themselves.

Users can now exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without any judgment. Security experts advise that if a romantic situation seems too good to be true, it is. The articles do not say if the number of actual espionage cases has increased recently. It remains unclear how many tech workers are switching to AI partners for security. The text leaves open whether these AI companions truly provide a completely secure environment.

stories.Headline: Cognizant launches NVIDIA-built patient hub operations and expands Qualys AI cybersecurity alliance
stories.Summary:
Cognizant Technology Solutions launched an AI-powered healthcare product called Cognizant Patient Hub Operations, built with NVIDIA, according to a Yahoo Finance article by Mitch Lawler dated November 22, 2026. The offering runs on NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform to automate patient support workflows for therapies. Cognizant also expanded its AI cybersecurity alliance with Qualys to provide AI-driven managed cyber risk and compliance services to enterprises. The article appeared at 06:00:00Z on 2026-11-22 and was updated at 1:06 PM CST. Cognizant trades on NasdaqGS under the ticker CTSH.

Cognizant Technology Solutions is a US-based IT services provider with a US$26.0b market cap that helps healthcare groups and enterprises design, build, and run large scale digital systems. Its commercial mix shifted from time-and-materials toward fixed-price and outcome-based contracts, with these models now at 58% of revenue compared with 48% in 2023. The NVIDIA collaboration puts Cognizant's Narrative into practice in healthcare, where its TriZetto platform already matters. Patient Hub Operations is an AI-heavy, repeatable service that lines up with the thesis that more work becomes digital labor. The expanded Qualys alliance pulls in outcome-linked cyber services that run continuously on client estates.

The article says Cognizant is pitching a simple idea to investors, that AI-heavy platforms and outcome-based work are meant to turn a traditional IT outsourcer into a higher quality, more resilient services business. It states that these partnerships are the latest proof point for that pitch. It quotes that the shift in commercial mix underpins a business model that is increasingly tied to outcomes and digital labor. The article says the expanded Qualys alliance supports the idea of higher quality, recurring work but also concentrates risk if fixed-price deals misjudge effort. stories.Headline: Dragos finds widespread AI supply chain security failures and data theft
stories.Summary:
Between July and November 2026, the research team at Dragos discovered widespread AI supply chain security failures. Chief Research Officer HD Moore led the investigation into how AI providers handle inference data. The team sent nearly two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary token credentials to various AI services. They monitored these secrets to see where they surfaced after the initial inference request. This process revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and failures to protect customer data.

The study found that attackers stole data from three different hosting providers starting in mid July. One breach in late October involved a couple hundred AWS keys stolen at the provider's front door. Some stolen requests were marked as Zero Data Retention, which is the strictest privacy setting. One attacker used a rented server to compromise two providers and employed the ARTEX penetration testing framework. Other leaks involved a Chinese AI lab and U.S. providers that ignored privacy settings.

HD Moore stated that the results showed a disconnect between AI marketing and actual data handling. He explained that AI providers often store prompts for training, safety, or business purposes. The research team noted that attackers used stolen keys to list S3 buckets and search Secrets Manager. They observed that some marketplace resellers used standard logging to view and retain customer prompts. Moore highlighted that some U.S. providers transmitted data to Chinese organizations despite privacy flags.

Marketplace resellers and external attackers affected customers by stealing confidential source code and strategic plans. Individuals using home broadband connections in France and elsewhere tried to guess usernames and passwords. Some customers paid U.S. providers to keep data domestic, but their prompts flowed to China. One secret link appeared in a Feishu company chat twenty four days after the request. These actors targeted private git repositories and used stolen credentials for tens of thousands of API calls.

AI routers offer a single API endpoint to forward requests to a pool of available models. These routers can be open marketplaces where the lowest price seller receives the traffic. Data often traverses multiple organizations, including model developers, cloud operators, and third party resellers. Some sellers use stolen AWS credentials or consumer API keys to offer deep discounts. This infrastructure creates multiple hops where every entity can see the entire prompt and response.

Defenders can use CloudTrail to detect user agents from Kali Linux and the ARTEX framework. The research team notified the three breached providers, who were previously unaware of the thefts. The articles leave open whether the providers have fixed the bugs causing privacy setting failures. It remains unclear how many real customers lost data alongside the Dragos canary tokens. The report does not state if the Chinese AI lab or the resellers were identified.

stories.Headline: Newton police chief Timothy Cohoon backs AI surveillance cameras with privacy safeguards
stories.Summary:
Newton’s Public Safety & Transportation Committee discussed the City Council’s potential role in regulating AI surveillance technology at a meeting on Wednesday. Ward 5 Councilor-at-Large Brittany Hume Charm said the key question was whether the City Council should have a seat at the table if a surveillance technology proposal came before the city. Charm said the matter was certainly not about inviting surveillance technology into Newton and that she wanted to be very clear about that. Newton Police Chief Timothy Cohoon, who was sworn in last March, worked with surveillance technologies in the past and expressed support for bringing them to Newton, Charm explained. Charm said initial conversations with Cohoon showed he had used some of these technologies in his previous cities and roles.

Charm said Cohoon remains supportive of the technologies with safeguards and discussions about the right use of them to balance interest in privacy. In September, after a request from The Heights, the Newton Police Department stated in a notice on its public records portal that it did not have plans to install Flock cameras. Cohoon has now expressed a willingness to implement AI surveillance technologies such as Flock Safety cameras and automated license plate readers. Cohoon said his job is to make sure police give their folks the most modern equipment, systems and investigative capabilities. Cohoon said police should embrace responsible innovation while protecting individual privacy and civility.

Residents of Newton have taken an interest in opposing Flock cameras, and several members of the public were present at Wednesday night’s committee meeting holding up signs reading “No Mass Surveillance.” Charm explained that repeated instances of misuse and threats to public safety involving Flock cameras played a significant role in generating the high level of community concern. Charm cited Texas tracking a woman across state lines who was seeking an abortion, and examples of misuse by police for former romantic partners. Charm said there are examples of this locally across Massachusetts as well. According to Charm, these technologies could be brought to Newton without any notification to or say from the City Council.

Charm said cameras have been installed in many cities without the City Council or even the public being made aware, and that kind of lack of transparency and discussion is quite concerning. Charm said the council would not have to be notified if the police department wanted to implement this currently. Ward 7 Councilor-at-Large Brian Golden said cameras proliferating around a community do cause a sense of anxiety because of the potential for invasions of privacy and sharing information. Golden said he wants to be really sure that the council needs to be involved in that. Ward 8 Councilor-at-Large Jacob Silber said he is no more afraid of this technology than of his cell phone in his pocket because he does not really feel he has an expectation of privacy anymore in this society.

Ward 1 Councilor Maria Scibelli Greenberg said Newton is 43 percent below the national average in crimes, so she wondered how necessary this is. Greenberg said increasing staffing, professional development and developing a crisis intervention program would seem to be better funding than having this type of surveillance in a city that does not have that kind of crime. Several council members believe the risks posed by Flock cameras demonstrate the need for the City Council to take a stand on the issue. Ward 6 Councilor-at-Large Sean Roche said this is a very scary set of technologies and that we should be very careful.

Roche said it is in good judgment for the council to say “Let’s not implement these” and that we should just draw a line in the sand. Roche proposed a moratorium to temporarily prevent AI surveillance technologies from being brought to Newton. Roche asserted that the City Council has the ability to regulate the use of these devices. Roche said a moratorium says that, right now, we are not going to implement that.

Although Cohoon reaffirmed his support for automated license plate readers, he stated that there are no current plans to bring any AI surveillance technologies to Newton. Cohoon said the automatic license plate readers have been a game changer for policing and that there has been abuse, but to throw the baby out with the bathwater is a step too far. Cohoon said he does not have any plans right now to bring this technology to the city. The committee discussed the City Council’s potential role in regulating AI surveillance technology at the Wednesday meeting.

Charm said the key question before the committee that night was whether the City Council should have a seat at the table if a proposal for surveillance technology came in front of the city. Cohoon was sworn in last March. The Newton Police Department’s September notice on its public records portal stated it did not have plans to install Flock cameras. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sheffield philosopher Gerardo Viera argues cognitive science study equips students to understand AI
stories.Summary:
The Hindu published an article on November 21, 2026, by Gerardo Viera, a Lecturer in Philosophy of Science at the University of Sheffield in the U.K., asking why students should study Cognitive Science in the age of AI. The article says emerging AI technologies are playing larger roles in work, entertainment, relationships, health and politics, and are changing how people understand themselves. It says societies approach this technological horizon with a mixture of hope that it will solve problems and fear that it may end life as we know it. Viera argues that simply developing skills for the current state of the art is not enough, because technology moves so quickly that those skills rapidly become obsolete.

He proposes instead investigating how advances in AI relate to puzzles about the nature of intelligence and the mind. The article says Cognitive Science draws on Philosophy, Psychology, Neuroscience, Computer Science and related fields, and that these joint resources offer the best hope of resolving puzzles about how the mind fits into the natural world. It says AI advances promise a better understanding of biological minds, since systems can now reproduce complex behaviours long thought to be uniquely human, such as producing language and novel proofs in Maths. It adds that studying biological minds can help design and understand artificial systems, noting that Computer Science was founded by trying to replicate perception, learning and memory, and that advances in the 1970s took inspiration from the network-like arrangement of neurons.

The article also describes an engineering hurdle: modern data centres can use as much electricity and water as a small city, while a honeybee navigates its environment, learns food locations and recognises faces on around 50 calories a year. Viera says discipline-specific training can reveal only part of these puzzles, and that advances in AI and understanding biological minds will likely come from those who acquire interdisciplinary skills. He says that as people rely on AI systems for information and decisions about health and policy, they start to trust these systems as though they are peers, and that safeguarding ourselves and assessing risks and benefits requires knowing how the systems work and whether they are genuinely intelligent. He says these skills open careers across academia and research, education, law and public policy, computing and technology, journalism, public service and social impact.

He says organisations will need people who understand both the technical possibilities of these systems and their wider implications for individuals and society. The article says Cognitive Science requires integrating findings from various, often conflicting, research disciplines. It says a background in Cognitive Science and AI provides an understanding of the limitations and capacities of emerging AI systems, which is needed to navigate this complex technological horizon and to contribute meaningfully to the organisations and professions shaping the technological future. The article does not say what happens next beyond these points.

stories.Headline: Teenager uses AI chatbot to hack Agniveer test website and tries to sell data on dark web
stories.Summary:
A 14-year-old boy from Ballabhgarh in Haryana was apprehended for allegedly attempting to sell sensitive information linked to around 4,000 Agniveer personnel on the dark web, Delhi Police sources said. According to a senior official familiar with the investigation, the teenager used artificial intelligence tools to identify data that could fetch him money and sought a chatbot's help to hack into a website. He gained unauthorised access to a test website designed for former Agniveers to register themselves and explore employment opportunities in the Indian Armed Forces. Preliminary investigation revealed that the boy managed to breach only the test website, gaining access to names and addresses, the official said. There is no indication so far that information relating to marks, ranks, results or other sensitive personnel records was compromised.

During preliminary questioning, the boy told investigators he was motivated by the prospect of making money, saying he first asked an AI chatbot what kind of data could help him earn and then sought its assistance in finding a way to hack into the system. The exact method used to gain access is still being examined. After accessing the website, he allegedly extracted the information and advertised it on a dark web marketplace, claiming to possess personal records of around 4,000 Agniveer personnel and seeking $500 for the purported database. The Delhi Police's Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations unit has recovered data from the juvenile's digital devices, and investigators are examining the material to establish its authenticity and determine the extent of the suspected breach.

The IFSO unit has written to the National Informatics Centre seeking clarification on the data available on the test website and the information accessed by the boy, and police are awaiting a response to ascertain precisely what may have been compromised. While the NIC provides digital infrastructure and hosts government portals, the ownership and maintenance of Agniveer personnel records rest with the Armed Forces and the concerned ministries, officials said. As the accused is a juvenile, he was counselled and handed over to his parents, and police are consulting the Juvenile Justice Board on the further course of action. Further investigation is underway.

stories.Headline: Northwestern students use AI to prepare for internships as employers expect faster work
stories.Summary:
Simon Benigeri, a French fourth-year artificial intelligence Ph.D. candidate at Northwestern, said he brought hidden efficiency to his internships in the U.S. by making tasks seem to take longer than they did, giving him more time to “chill.” He realized soon after starting an internship with Apple’s Siri Speech and Innovation team that he could no longer pull this off. Benigeri quickly saw how fast AI was changing the culture and pace in the office. He said the team had a big budget for AI and that expectations changed so that people should be getting work done really fast. His experience reflects a broader shift in which students turn to AI to land internships and employers increasingly expect them to know how to use it.

Northwestern Career Advancement encourages students to use AI as a supplementary tool in their job searches, leaving many students to decide for themselves where AI fits as they apply for and complete internships. Benigeri said he has noticed a change in companies’ hiring practices, with many more interviews where candidates are expected to use AI to code during the interview. He said there are also many more interviews where companies set programming aside and try to see how a person thinks and tackles problems. McCormick junior Benjamin Runde secured a job this summer as an investment banking summer analyst at Morgan Stanley and used AI to prepare for technical questions and practice speaking with recruiters. Runde said he would put ChatGPT or Claude on voice mode, give it the 400 questions and a test bank of appropriate answers, and have it grade his responses for precision.

Runde said practicing mock interviews at any time and place ended up being a useful asset in his preparation, though he said he did not know how good the AI actually was at grading and that it just got him to do it all the time. Weinberg sophomore Victoria Wang interned at Concannon Business Consulting this past summer and, like Runde, used AI to prepare for interviews by practicing case interviews, the problem-solving exercises consulting firms use to evaluate candidates. Wang said that as a younger student she found AI helpful when she could not find a “case buddy” or felt too embarrassed to case with people. She said she has learned to match different tools to different parts of the process, preferring Claude for technical case preparation because she said it has a better grasp of the frameworks consulting interviews require. For behavioral interviews and networking, Wang said she would ask ChatGPT to generate a possible scenario of how a behavioral interview would go or how she should lead a coffee chat to get to the questions she wants to ask.

Runde said AI use is not the same in every field, and while he leaned heavily on AI for investment banking recruitment, he rarely used it during engineering internships at companies including Procter & Gamble and L3Harris Technologies. He said that was especially true in defense, largely because the industry is heavily regulated and much of the work his team handled was confidential, and that AI is not as pervasive in defense or consumer goods as it is on a college campus. Medill senior Laura Garcia, an editorial intern at Sunset Magazine, said she built her resume without AI and was thankful because Medill is super extensive in the whole resume process. Garcia used AI as an editing tool for cover letters in her internship applications, asking ChatGPT to identify the main points she should keep and build around after her original draft ran long.

Wang said LinkedIn is a good tool to find and apply for jobs and that AI has been helpful in tightening the bullet points under her experience section, but she drew the line at editing the headshot for her profile picture because she felt the photoshop made it not look like her anymore. Wang said combining LinkedIn and AI use has helped her land coffee chats with current employees to boost her odds in consulting recruitment, and in crafting emails she uses a standard prompt that tells ChatGPT to introduce her, explain how she found the person and mention something specific such as their office location or past projects before closing with a request for a short phone call. She said she puts people’s LinkedIn or a screenshot of their information to AI, has the AI write the email, double checks, and then sends them out. Runde said most of his emails are either written or heavily edited by ChatGPT, and following the release of the AI agent Grok Bot in August, which now acts as his personal assistant, he has it look at his Canvas twice a day and go through every assignment page and calendar page and put everything on his Google Calendar.

Runde said he also has it check his email and organize his day, and he expects tools like the Grok Bot that handle monotonous tasks to become the standard of AI use going forward. Garcia said her editors at Sunset have told her they find it strange that Medill does not teach students how to use AI given its capabilities and potential, and she said she thinks students have to learn as much from it as they can rather than hide it and put it in a box. Benigeri, who once stretched out the time it took to complete tasks, now urges students to do the opposite and said he thinks students should do the work to really understand what they are doing. He said students can use AI later, that it is going to be great and they absolutely should use it, and that it is good not to take shortcuts so they can give themselves the best chance to understand things.

The article also lists other Daily Northwestern pieces, including one on the Northwestern Network for Collaborative Intelligence’s five strategic leaders aiming to expand interdisciplinary AI across campus and one asking who Sharath Narayan is, a former “Jeopardy!” champion continuing cancer research and quizbowl competitions at Northwestern. Other listed pieces cover how an international exchange student lives on $1,000 a month in Evanston and how Evanston artist Val Zee reshapes “her-story” through bold colors. The page carries a 2026 Daily Northwestern copyright notice and credits a FLEX Pro WordPress theme by SNO.

stories.Headline: Mistral opens Singapore science hub and APAC headquarters to build sovereign AI models
stories.Summary:
The French artificial intelligence firm Mistral opened a new science hub and Asia-Pacific headquarters at Asia Square Tower 1 in Singapore on November 20, 2026. This facility aims to create sovereign AI models for robotics, high-tech manufacturing, and the public sector to help organizations keep proprietary technology and sensitive data in-house. To support this expansion, the company intends to increase its regional workforce from approximately 100 to 200 employees by 2027, with most of these new roles based in Singapore. The expansion requires hiring forward-deployed engineers with business acumen and forward-deployed scientists with advanced mathematical training to build unique AI tools. These efforts respond to geopolitical concerns, such as new US rules effective November 19 requiring licenses for certain advanced AI chip exports to Singapore and four other nations.

Mistral also seeks to develop models that reflect Singapore's linguistic diversity and help humanoid robots navigate complex environments. In manufacturing, the technology will be trained on production line images to identify defects and irregularities. Geoff Soon, the vice-president of revenue for Asia-Pacific, stated that governments and enterprises in the region increasingly want to control the technology they depend on for economic competitiveness. Co-founder and chief executive Arthur Mensch explained that the company wants Singapore to be a strategic location for empowering clients to retain ownership of their intelligence. Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How noted that resilience comes from working with strong partners while building deep local capabilities.

Pee Beng Kong of the Economic Development Board added that this investment reinforces Singapore's position as a hub for frontier AI innovation. The company previously collaborated with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency on Phoenix AI models that reflect local laws regarding race and narcotics. Mistral now plans to establish new partnerships within the Singaporean financial sector, although specific details have not yet been released. This growth occurs as companies fear that overseas decisions could cut off access to essential AI models and the chips that run them. Future developments will focus on creating lasting economic value and industrial competitiveness across the Asia-Pacific region.

stories.Headline: Australia reviews competition laws for AI agent shoppers and surveillance pricing
stories.Summary:
Australia is reviewing its competition laws so they can handle more people using personal artificial intelligence agents to shop, pay and manage money on their behalf, the government said on Nov 21, 2026. Andrew Leigh, assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, told reporters in Canberra that the government is doing a whole lot of work to ensure the competition laws keep pace in an AI age. He said more consumers are going to be shopping with AI agents and the government is looking at whether it is important to update the laws there. AI agents are increasingly being designed to shop, make payments and manage money on behalf of users, with retail just one sector among many globally confronting the reality of customers handing over decision-making to agents.

Their growing autonomy is forcing financial institutions to work out how much authority to give them and who is responsible for their actions, the article says. Australians have been shopping online for years, leading to lower footfalls in established retail networks like David Jones, the department store group which has collapsed after almost two centuries in business. Leigh said the government was considering issues such as personalised pricing, also known as surveillance pricing, where different prices can be set for consumers based on their individual data. He cited an example he had heard overseas of people being asked to pay more for a security product because their area was suffering from crime.

Leigh said sometimes that can lead to people paying higher prices, and he stated that the government does not want Australians mucked around by surveillance pricing powered by AI. He said the government wants Australians to get the very best deal in the AI age. The government is also looking at who is responsible for agents' actions as part of its review of whether the laws need updating. The article does not say when the review will finish or what specific changes are being considered.

The article gives no further details on next steps beyond the government's stated work on competition laws and surveillance pricing. It does not name any bill, timeline or enforcement action that would follow from the review. The report was published by The Straits Times on Nov 21, 2026, and was updated the same day. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Australia vows to manage AI agent shoppers, surveillance pricing

stories.Headline: Asahi CEO Katsuki plans $85mn AI cybersecurity upgrade over three years
stories.Summary:
Japanese beverage maker Asahi Group Holdings is investing 13.5 billion yen, or 85 million dollars, into its cybersecurity infrastructure. This massive financial commitment follows a ransomware attack that occurred in 2025 and disrupted business operations for several months. The company intends to spend this money over a three year period to protect its digital assets. These upgrades are designed to prevent similar security breaches from happening again in the future. The investment requires the company to rebuild its existing systems using advanced artificial intelligence technology.

Asahi Group Holdings will also hire more specialized talent to help detect unauthorized access to its networks. These changes aim to create a more resilient defense against the evolving threats of the digital age. The three year plan focuses on integrating these new tools to ensure long term stability. Chief Executive Officer Atsushi Katsuki detailed the spending plans to address the vulnerabilities exposed by the previous incident.

He explained that the company must modernize its approach to security to safeguard its global operations. The leadership believes that combining AI with expert human talent is the best way to monitor threats. This strategic shift reflects a commitment to protecting the company from further operational disruptions. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Asahi pours $85mn into AI cybersecurity upgrades after ransomware attack

stories.Headline: Japan's Noetra AI project faces $5bn cost rise as chip prices and weak yen bite
stories.Summary:
The flagship domestic artificial intelligence initiative in Japan is facing a massive increase in projected expenses. This sovereign project is seeing costs rise by as much as 800 billion yen, which equals approximately 5 billion dollars. The financial pressure on the plan has intensified recently due to the soaring prices of necessary computer chips. A weak yen has further contributed to the rising costs of the technology required for the project. The Noetra initiative now requires a significant amount of additional funding to maintain its current goals.

This sudden cost surge means the Japanese government may be forced to shoulder a much larger financial burden. The project must navigate these economic headwinds to ensure the domestic AI strategy remains viable. These changes are necessary to prop up the initiative against the volatile global semiconductor market. President Hironobu Tamba of Noetra has been speaking about the development of physical artificial intelligence.

He discussed these technological advancements at a government event held in Tokyo on July 16. While the specific response to the cost surge was not detailed, the leadership is managing the project's growth. The government is now evaluating how to cover the multi-billion dollar gap in the budget. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Shachihata launches AI video authentication on X to offset shrinking hanko market
stories.Summary:
A Japanese company that specializes in making traditional carved stamps will launch a new authentication service later this month. Shachihata is moving into the artificial intelligence realm to help users identify videos on X that have been altered. This strategic shift comes as the company seeks new sources of growth to offset its shrinking traditional market. The business is attempting to fight back against the digitalization that is currently devouring the hanko market. The new system requires the use of acoustic watermarks and digital fingerprints to verify the authenticity of video content.

These technical tools will allow users to detect whether a video has been manipulated by artificial intelligence or other editing software. Shachihata is implementing these changes to pivot away from its reliance on physical stamps used for signing documents. The company intends to establish a strong presence in the cybersecurity field by providing these verification tools on the X platform. The leadership at Shachihata is responsible for this transition as they give themselves a mandate to expand their business operations.

They believe that moving into the digital authentication space is necessary because the demand for traditional hanko stamps is declining. By leveraging new technology, the company hopes to protect digital media from the risks associated with deepfakes and altered footage. This move represents a significant departure from their historical focus on physical office supplies and traditional Japanese signing customs. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a Nasdaq IPO to raise over 90 billion dollars for AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to debut on the Nasdaq stock market this coming Thursday to test investor confidence in the global artificial intelligence boom. The five year old company develops the Claude family of models and expects the initial public offering to generate over 90 billion dollars. Technology companies are committing billions of dollars to the offering despite concerns over financing risks and the sustainability of the investment boom. This arrival occurs during a difficult moment for the sector following a decline in technology shares and a leadership crisis at Nvidia. The company reported a net loss of 104 billion dollars during the first nine months of 2026 but holds 132 billion dollars.

The offering price is expected to be 70 to 78 dollars per share with investments of 26 billion dollars from several major firms. These investors include Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, while Amazon holds a substantial stake. Anthropic has over 900 billion dollars in spending commitments, including 110 billion dollars with Amazon over 10 years and 400 billion dollars elsewhere. It will spend 125 billion to 150 billion dollars on Google chips by 2028 and lease a data centre starting 2027. Amazon also built an 11 billion dollar data centre in Indiana for Anthropic using custom chips, and Google guaranteed 19 billion dollars.

Anthropic stated in its prospectus that it previously underestimated computing requirements, which left the company short of capacity and affected product deployment. Joe Fath of Eclipse called the staggering numbers hard to wrap one's head around, while David Tollen called it smart investing. Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google executive, said that everybody knows Anthropic is going to be the future of the Google company. Broadcom provided a financial backstop with a maximum liability of 43 billion dollars to support the rental of artificial intelligence chips. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley offered 63 billion dollars to purchase the racks of chips that Anthropic will rent.

Corey Quinn of Duckbill questioned if the long agreements could remain unchanged, stating that anything past four years is like throwing darts. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent in October, which was its worst monthly performance since March 2025, adding pressure to debt heavy providers. Rising interest rates and new United States ballot measures could further restrict the development of new data centres across the entire country. Investors are also concerned by Nvidia, where shares fell 13 percent after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs. Colette Kress was appointed interim chief executive after Huang was linked to a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.

The company is committing to infrastructure well in advance because it needs computing power to develop advanced models and expand its services. Cloud providers Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31 percent of the contractual obligations listed in the latest official company prospectus. Google is expected to hold an ownership stake of approximately 13 percent following the completion of the initial public offering process. The 10 year agreement with Amazon is twice the length of typical contracts, which has attracted questions about the financial exposure. These investments occur as the broader technology sector faces mounting pressure from indebted cloud infrastructure companies and volatile global stock market trends.

The initial public offering will provide funding for the computing infrastructure needed to operate advanced models and expand the company's current services. The articles leave open whether the long term infrastructure commitments and the 20 year data centre lease will remain financially sustainable. It remains uncertain if the arrangements with cloud providers will be renegotiated before the contracts expire as suggested by some industry experts. The market will see if the 90 billion dollar debut can redefine the scale of technology listings despite the current sector turmoil. Investors must wait to see if the calculated exposure to these staggering costs will result in the predicted future for Google.

stories.Headline: Hideo Kojima warns AI may sap joy of creation while Mamoru Oshii sees no immediate film change
stories.Summary:
Japanese game creator Hideo Kojima and film director Mamoru Oshii discussed the potential effects of artificial intelligence on creative work during a recent event. This conversation took place in Tokyo on November 20, 2026, as part of a celebration for the 150th anniversary of the Nikkei media company. The two leading figures shared their perspectives on how emerging technologies might reshape the boundaries of games and cinema. They examined whether these tools would enhance the artistic process or fundamentally alter the nature of imaginative production. Hideo Kojima warned that while artificial intelligence could be beneficial for business operations, it might sap the joy of creation.

He expressed concern that the widespread use of these tools could make people more passive consumers of entertainment over time. The shift toward automated content might reduce the active engagement and effort typically required to produce meaningful art. This transition could potentially change how audiences interact with stories and how creators approach their craft. The responsibility for navigating these changes lies with the creators and industry leaders who integrate these technologies into their workflows.

Kojima suggested that the efficiency gained through automation might come at the cost of the human spirit in art. Mamoru Oshii offered a different view, stating that he sees no immediate change to the world of film. He believes that in the cinematic arts, the questions surrounding the technology currently outweigh the available answers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: LG Uplus, KT and SK Telecom raise AI data center spending as returns stay uncertain
stories.Summary:
SK Telecom, KT and LG Uplus increased their capital spending as they expand into artificial intelligence data centers, and their combined expenditure reached 3.68 trillion won in the first nine months of this year, up 13.7 percent from a year earlier, according to their regulatory filings on Friday. LG Uplus posted the biggest increase, with capital expenditure on a standalone basis reaching 569.8 billion won in the third quarter, a 30.1 percent year-on-year rise driven largely by its AI data center project in Paju, Gyeonggi Province. The company is building a 200-megawatt facility there with four buildings scheduled to begin operations by 2028, and its first 50-megawatt building is expected to be completed by next June. KT's cumulative capital expenditure, including major affiliates, reached 1.599 trillion won, up 20.3 percent, while SK Telecom's total, including its new AI data center unit SK Hyper, was 1.234 trillion won, up 3 percent.

The push requires large upfront spending on land, construction, power infrastructure and cooling systems, while depreciation, electricity and maintenance costs continue after facilities begin operating. KT plans to invest a total of 6 trillion won in AI transformation infrastructure over the next five years and to expand its data center capacity by more than 1 gigawatt by 2031. SK Telecom's spending declined when SK Hyper is excluded, reflecting its strategy of bringing in external investors to share the financial burden of large-scale data center development. Industry officials said the telecom and AI data center businesses have different revenue structures, because returns on data center investments can vary significantly depending on each facility's ability to attract customers, its utilization rate and contract terms.

LG Uplus says it has secured customer demand for all four buildings in Paju. During its recent earnings call, SK Telecom said a certain level of increase in investment is inevitable, while emphasizing its plan to finance a substantial portion of AI data center development through external funding. The AI investment push comes as the telecom companies seek new growth engines beyond their mobile businesses, with demand for computing power and data storage increasing as companies adopt generative AI and expand their use of AI inference services.

Questions remain over whether the investments can be recouped, particularly over depreciation costs for graphics processing units. U.S. hyperscalers typically depreciate GPUs over five years in their financial statements, but questions remain over whether this is appropriate, because AI accelerator makers such as Nvidia release new products almost every year. This means the period during which existing GPUs can handle cutting-edge AI workloads may be considerably shorter than their accounting lifespan, effectively shortening the time companies have to generate sufficient returns. Securing customers before facilities become operational and maintaining high utilization rates will be critical to recovering investment costs, and long-term contracts can provide more predictable revenue, but profitability will also depend on electricity prices, operating expenses and the timing of equipment deployment.

Articles.Title: Telecoms ramp up AI investment amid questions over returns

stories.Headline: Over half of Korean workers fear workplace photos could be misused in AI sex crimes, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey of 1,000 workers in Korea aged 19 or older found that 53.1 percent worry photos of themselves posted on company intranets or messaging platforms could be used in artificial intelligence-assisted sex crimes, according to results published Sunday by The Korea Times. The survey was commissioned by the labor rights group Workplace Gapjil 119 and carried out by the polling firm Global Research between Aug. 1 and Aug. 7, 2026. Concern was more widespread among women, with 58.2 percent expressing anxiety, compared with 49 percent among male respondents. The poll also asked workers about safeguards at their companies and about the impact of AI on gender inequality in hiring.

Only 11.6 percent of respondents said their employers had rules in place to prevent and respond to AI-related sex crimes, while 48.6 percent said their companies had no such rules. Another 39.8 percent said they did not know whether such rules existed at their workplaces. Asked what measures companies should take, 29.2 percent called for stronger security regulations, and 28.8 percent said employers should establish workplace policies that clearly define digital sex crimes and set zero-tolerance disciplinary standards. The survey also examined how workers view AI's effect on gender inequality in hiring and employment.

Nearly 40 percent of respondents agreed that AI-driven automation could replace jobs in female-dominated occupations first, increasing women's risk of unemployment. Another 36.8 percent said AI-assisted recruitment systems could disadvantage female applicants by learning from male-dominated hiring records. To prevent such discrimination, 42.9 percent called for companies to fully disclose the criteria and details used by AI in evaluating employees. Another 40.4 percent said companies should regularly check AI-backed hiring systems for gender bias and make the findings public.

Kim Ja-yeon, a labor attorney at the civic group, said AI technology is advancing rapidly while digital sex crimes and gender discrimination are penetrating everyday life, and that companies and the government need to take proactive measures to create safe workplaces. The survey report was published by The Korea Times on Nov. 22, 2026, with a publication time of 4:03 p.m. KST, and was written by Lee Hyo-jin. The article presents the findings as a survey showing that more than half of workers in Korea share the concern about misuse of workplace photos.

stories.Headline: SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won calls for universities to teach wisdom over knowledge in the AI-native era
stories.Summary:
Chey Tae-won, chairman of SK Group and of the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies, said at the Tokyo Forum 2026 that universities must build a new educational system suited to the AI-native era. He spoke during the Business Leader session of the forum, held at Yasuda Auditorium at the University of Tokyo in Japan on the 20th and 21st of November 2026. The Tokyo Forum is an event jointly organized by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies and the University of Tokyo, and it has been held annually since 2019. Chey said universities should go beyond teaching knowledge and should focus on cultivating wisdom, and he called for nurturing talent who will steer the direction of change so that the value created by AI can be broadly shared.

Chey defined an AI-native society as a human-centered society in which cyberspace and physical space are fused, and he predicted a society that accepts AI as a naturally given environment rather than merely using it as a tool. He also said that as of now no one has the right answer for how to reach an AI-native society, and he sees education as the starting point for finding that solution. He said AI is new and no one has the answer, so collective intelligence must be pooled to find one, and he added that the answer may turn out to be wrong but that the experience of having designed a system firsthand will become a capability to solve problems when facing real-world challenges. He then introduced SK Group programs to develop talent, support employment, and train data center personnel.

Regarding Aizen, a two-year, non-degree program unveiled last month, Chey explained that it is a model that assigns team projects and lets participants find answers on their own. He said participants will tackle assignments across diverse fields and try out their own designs for solving problems. On collaboration between businesses and universities in the AI era, he said working with people from countries with different cultures, systems, and languages is not easy, but the younger generation strengthened by AI can take on such challenges more readily. He added that it would also be a good approach for companies and universities in Korea and Japan to create and operate joint programs to cultivate AI talent.

Articles.Title: Chey Tae-won, “In the AI-native era, universities should focus on cultivating wisdom rather than knowledge”

stories.Headline: Verónica González Laporte examines Korean society and AI in her novel Peeling
stories.Summary:
Mexican anthropologist and novelist Verónica González Laporte wrote a novel called Peeling about Korean society. She began writing the book in 2020 and completed the work in 2024. The story follows a plastic surgeon named Ji-ho who falls in love with an AI sex doll. Ji-ho faces a family illness and a warning from a shaman during the plot. The author used her personal experiences in Korea to explore beauty, isolation, gender, and shamanism.

The book was originally written in Spanish as K-Beauty before being translated into Korean as Bakpi. It features scenes at Mount Halla and Changdeok Palace, and it mentions the city of Cuernavaca. The plot includes a gay character named Geon-hee and a doll named Seong-mi. González lived in Seoul for over five years with her husband, Bruno Figueroa Fischer, until 2023. The story draws parallels between Latin American women and the haenyeo divers of Jeju Island.

González said she wanted to offer another Korea by looking behind the stage of its polished image. She explained that she aimed to recognize social issues that are difficult to notice because they are familiar. The author stated that younger generations need to recognize patriarchal mechanisms that have been established for many years. She noted that she felt at home on Mount Halla because it resembled her Mexican city. González said that people in different countries are similar even if they do not speak the same language.

The novel explores how gender inequality and women's rights play out within the Korean family structure. Ji-ho's mother represents the vulnerable position of young women and the expectations of their in-laws. The character Geon-hee reflects the social taboos and prejudices regarding homosexuality that the author encountered. The book also examines the contrast between cutting-edge technology and centuries-old beliefs like shamanism. These themes affect the characters as they navigate the tension between fantasy and reality.

Inspiration came from a visit to a dermatology clinic during the COVID-19 pandemic for facial redness. González read reports about bodies in plastic bags in China and a man suing for a sex doll. She observed that Korean brands often have similar windows and colors, creating a sense of visual uniformity. Her background as an anthropologist included studying male shamans in northern Mexico before seeing female mudang. She noticed that Korea is a highly organized society that sometimes lacks fantasy in its decorations.

A Spanish-language edition of the novel is currently in preparation for publication. The author recently visited Seoul and noted that the orange taxis she remembered had disappeared. The text describes how the novel reveals shared values that transcend borders through its various characters. The articles do not state when the Spanish edition will be released to the public. They leave open whether the book will be translated into other languages beyond Spanish and Korean.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Mythos model finds thousands of flaws, driving a global patching surge that causes outages
stories.Summary:
Microsoft patched 3,554 security flaws in the two and a half months before a major November outage. This surge in patching followed the March 2026 release of the Anthropic Mythos model to select firms. The model scanned code for bugs and found hundreds of vulnerabilities, some dormant for decades. These rapid fixes caused outages for Microsoft Outlook, Apple, Workday, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase, and US air traffic control. The NSA also suffered a classified messaging system outage last week due to a PHP programming language upgrade.

The industry found over 100,000 confirmed vulnerabilities this year, more than double the 48,000 found in 2025. New Zealand health sectors faced Microsoft disruptions in January in the upper North Island, July in Waikato, and November. The NCSC recorded 4,673 incident reports and 23.8 million dollars in losses for 2025/26, down from 5,995 and 26.9 million. The Reserve Bank names concentration risk in shared AI, software, and cloud providers as a financial stability concern. Its Operational Resilience Standard will not take effect until 2028.

US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the NSA outage was a fix and not an attack. Retired General Paul Nakasone stated that the current situation of frequent outages is a new normal. Twenty chief executive Joe Lin described a collision between the speed of discovery and the ability to address flaws. US Representative Jim Himes warned that the pace of patching could cause more frequent outages. Health NZ director James Allison insisted disruption was minimal because of satellite phone and Starlink contingencies.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs said all available evidence suggests the recent outage events are not connected. Azul CTO Gil Tene believes AI-driven patch velocity is already causing major incidents. Filigran CEO Samuel Hassine argues updates are pushed onto systems that cannot take much change. Cogent IT expert Tony Grasso criticized the move to the cloud over servers for creating single points of failure. Unions want hospital IT treated as life saving clinical care rather than relying solely on Microsoft.

The acceleration of vulnerabilities began in March 2026 when Anthropic shared its Mythos model with security firms. Most firms moved to the cloud because it was sold as a cheaper and more secure option. The NCSC warns that malicious actors may gain frontier lab AI capabilities by early 2027. This would allow attacks to unfold faster than businesses can detect or respond to them. The RBNZ and FMA are currently urging firms to get the basics right.

Mitiga field CISO Brian Contos recommends using tested rollback procedures, monitoring, and staged rollouts. Business leaders should map vendors under critical functions and build offline fallbacks for processes that cannot stop. Firms are encouraged to ask suppliers how they reverse and stage their updates. The articles leave open how SMEs will handle the risk before the 2028 rules arrive. It remains unclear if the health sector will reduce its reliance on Microsoft.
