stories.Headline: Microsoft study finds Copilot offers lowest monthly AI costs across everyday and advanced users
stories.Summary:
Microsoft released research, conducted with GigaOm and published on November 21, 2026, that compares the total cost of ownership of three leading AI tools: Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise. The study tested multiple scenarios across two categories of users, everyday users who handle routine tasks such as searching for information, preparing for meetings, analyzing data and creating content, and advanced users who manage complex multi-step workflows. Over the month evaluated, the research simulated tasks for both groups and found that Copilot consistently offered the lowest monthly costs. For everyday users, Copilot's monthly subscription stands at $30, compared with $205 for Claude and $81 for ChatGPT, making it more than six times cheaper than its most expensive counterpart. For advanced users, Copilot costs $96 per month, compared with $299 for Claude and $149 for ChatGPT, meaning competitor costs run more than three times higher.

The study also examined output quality, with evaluators assessing accuracy, relevance and completeness, and it found that quality across Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude remained broadly comparable even though pricing varies dramatically. According to the research, Copilot's lower pricing comes from three main elements: everyday AI tasks included in the user subscription, which prevents additional fees; a Work IQ feature that provides context-sensitive assistance by drawing on data within the Microsoft ecosystem; and an Auto function that dynamically selects appropriate models and effort levels for the task at hand. The article notes that the study assumes certain usage patterns and that costs could vary depending on the types of tasks performed and negotiated pricing, so some firms may need their own evaluations. GigaOm invites organizations to use its methodology in their own environments for tailored insights.

The research was released by Microsoft in collaboration with GigaOm, and the article was written by David Wilson for Small Business Trends. The article states that the findings suggest small businesses can use a comprehensive AI solution without breaking the bank and without sacrificing work standards for cost savings. It also cautions that as businesses ramp up their use of AI, costs can scale up if not managed proactively, making budgeting and cost oversight crucial for firms that want to scale efficiently. The article says the findings emphasize that costs are one facet of a broader strategy and that embracing an efficient AI solution could provide a competitive edge. It directs readers to the full GigaOm report for further details and insights from the research.

Articles.Title: Study Reveals Microsoft Copilot Offers Lowest AI Costs for Users - Small Business Trends

stories.Headline: Anthropic introduces a novel governance framework as Nvidia faces a leadership crisis and share slump
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia in November 2026 after news of his extramarital affairs broke. He had a relationship with an Nvidia executive and a woman US authorities believed was a Chinese spy. Huang misrepresented the nature of the relationship with the alleged spy to senior Nvidia officials. The spy was linked to Megaspeed, a major Nvidia chip buyer in Singapore with Chinese ties. These events led to a significant slump in Nvidia shares and a supply shock for technology.

The US Commerce Department now requires licenses for advanced AI chips for Chinese data centers providing remote computing. Licenses are also required for exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to diversion risks. Nvidia shares fell 22.9 per cent last week and 38.7 per cent since the spy scandal began. The S&P 500 dropped 8.8 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 fell 11.8 per cent in that period. Nvidia reported robust third-quarter numbers and strong revenue guidance for 2027 despite the share price slump.

Nvidia stated it is not considering inviting Jensen Huang back to the company. The company's founders at Anthropic wrote a letter to investors about the potential for AI to boost productivity. They warned that AI could inflict immense harm on humanity and has large positive and negative externalities. They said these externalities are in tension with the incentives of for-profit companies and standard governance structures. The founders stated they expect to make mistakes and learn from others as they evolve.

Investors, technology sector luminaries, and Nvidia employees are calling for the return of Jensen Huang. Some investors may be appalled by the multiple share classes introduced by Anthropic for its listing. Holders of Class A shares will face dilution from the ongoing issue and conversion of Class N shares. The US government was alarmed by Huang's ties to a spy linked to a Chinese company. The wider AI ecosystem has seen weakened confidence following the exit of the Nvidia chief executive.

Anthropic was formed as a public benefit corporation to weigh shareholder interests against its public benefit mission. It reached a US$1.5 trillion valuation within six years, while Nvidia hit US$1 trillion in 2023. Anthropic uses five share classes, with Class F and Class T holding most of the control. A single Class F share gives seven co-founders 50.1 per cent voting power over the company. The Long-Term Benefit Trust holds the Class T share and appoints four of seven board members.

Anthropic will issue Class E shares to non-founder employees to give them a say on some governance matters. Class A and Class N shares hold all economic benefits, but Class N shares have no voting rights. Anthropic plans to contribute 2 per cent of equity to its fund for every 50 per cent price increase. Market regulators and governance experts must now consider how to effectively check seemingly indispensable corporate leaders. The articles leave open whether Anthropic's novel governance framework can successfully improve upon standard corporate practices.

Articles.Title: Nvidia’s slump, Anthropic’s listing turn spotlight on Big AI’s need for new governance frameworks

stories.Headline: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang mocks Apple days after praising its partnership on Muse Spark Open
stories.Summary:
Meta AI Lab head Alexandr Wang mocked Apple on X on November 22, 2026. He responded to a rumor that Apple is building an AI agent like Meta's Muse. Wang called the company a corposlop that would unleash another butthole on the public. This dig happened days after he complimented Apple and CEO John Ternus. He had previously thanked them for a partnership announced last month.

The partnership involves the Muse Spark Open, which Meta calls the most powerful US open-weight AI model. This model runs locally on two or four connected Mac Studios using Apple's MLX framework. These specific computers are powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips. The model is free to download with a license for commercial use. It is also available through developer tools and cloud providers.

Alexandr Wang told Axios that he was excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg also posted a rare public thanks note to Apple on X. He stated that the model runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to Apple. John Ternus replied that it is amazing to run such a model efficiently from a desk. Ternus added that Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI.

Wang has often made fun of Google Gemini on the platform formerly known as Twitter. This latest target is the iPhone maker, which has spent years trading barbs with Meta. The two companies have openly criticized each other regarding the future of computing and privacy. Wang acknowledged that the two firms will continue to compete in some areas. He believes this competition does not have to prevent them from working together.

Meta and Apple have a history of public conflict over various technology and privacy issues. Muse Spark Open is an open-weights model, allowing developers to customize it and understand its work. Meta claims this specific model is the most powerful open-weight AI developed in the United States. The collaboration allows the model to run on Apple hardware. This marks a shift from their previous pattern of trading public insults.

Wang stated that the companies want to partner where it makes sense to do so. The articles do not say if Apple will actually build the rumored AI agent. It is unclear if the partnership will expand beyond the Muse Spark Open model. The text does not mention other specific projects between the two tech giants. stories.Headline: Meta lifts 2026 AI infrastructure spending to as much as $145B
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms narrowed its 2026 capital spending guidance to a range of $135 billion to $145 billion, with the bulk of the money aimed at artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to an update that arrived with the company's third-quarter 2026 earnings report on October 21, 2026. The new range tightens an earlier forecast of $130 billion to $145 billion, so the top end stayed put while the floor rose. The spending covers the full AI stack, which means data centers, chips, networking products, and the systems needed to train Meta's Llama AI models. Meta's capital expenditures in 2025 came in at approximately $72 billion, and the 2026 guidance puts the company on track to roughly double that figure in a single year.

The company says its AI work is already improving content recommendations, ad impressions, and revenue per ad, and the numbers in the report back that up. Third-quarter 2026 revenue reached $64.6 billion, a 26% increase from the same quarter a year earlier, and advertising accounted for $63.06 billion of that total. Ad impressions rose 10% year over year, while the average price per ad climbed 14%, and Meta's family of apps averaged 3.64 billion daily active users in the quarter. Free cash flow in the third quarter of 2026 came in at negative $2.12 billion, and Meta plans to introduce a new class of non-voting Class C stock while looking to raise up to $95 billion through equity offerings to fund its AI ambitions.

Mark Zuckerberg founded Facebook in his Harvard dorm room in 2004, and two decades later the company is pouring tens of billions into chips and server farms. Zuckerberg and his team increasingly view AI as the critical lever for refining ad tools and deepening engagement on platforms like Facebook and Instagram, according to the report. The non-voting stock structure lets Meta bring in fresh capital without weakening Zuckerberg's control over the company. The article does not say what happens next beyond the planned equity offerings and the stock class.

stories.Headline: Foundation lawyers argue national security benefits of AI training in OpenAI copyright case
stories.Summary:
Tim Hwang, the Foundation for American Innovation's general counsel and a senior fellow, filed a proposed amicus brief in support of OpenAI in In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation, with help from research fellow Sam Roland, and the foundation posted the filing on October 30, 2026. The brief argues that general AI capabilities already serve important national security purposes, and that over the last several years the government has acquired and adapted commercial frontier models for intelligence analysis, cyber defense, operational planning and decision support. It says Congress has supported this by tying defense AI to training and data, and the executive branch has proclaimed rapid access to current models as one of its top national security priorities. The filing cites Google LLC v. Oracle Am., Inc. for the position that courts may consider the public benefits copying enables under factor four of the fair use test, particularly where the use puts copyrighted works toward new productive ends.

The brief argues that to the extent AI training enables the creation of new knowledge, expression, software and other capabilities, those benefits bear on factor four's assessment of the use's market effects, and that this reasoning supports considering the national-security value of capabilities that enable new analysis, software and other productive work. It explains the link between copying a newspaper article and developing national-security capabilities through the training process, in which models identify shared patterns across a broad corpus of information during pretraining. Learning those patterns helps develop language, synthesis, translation, coding and reasoning capabilities, according to the brief. It says requiring permission for the challenged training could impair those benefits if it materially restricts access to useful training data, and that removing useful sources from training data can reduce capabilities used by downstream systems, which could include the national security systems the government acquires and adapts. Under Oracle, the brief says, those public benefits belong in the factor-four balance alongside cognizable market harm.

The brief was filed by Hwang and Roland, and the foundation describes it as supporting OpenAI in the litigation. The filing states that copyright protects authors because their work advances knowledge and culture, and that fair use serves the same end by preserving room for new uses that benefit the public without displacing the expression copyright protects. It also states that factor four of the fair use test is not limited to an accounting of the copyright holder's potential lost revenue. The articles do not say what response OpenAI, the plaintiffs or the court gave to the proposed brief, and they give no further details on the next steps in the litigation.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: UC Davis professor Martin Hilbert proposes tracing AI harm to human decisions
stories.Summary:
Martin Hilbert, a professor of communication at the University of California, Davis, has proposed a legal framework for tracing AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and deployed the system, according to a study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The proposal, reported by Earth.com on November 22, 2026, argues that courts can use existing law to assign responsibility based on the decisions that contributed to the harm. It responds to cases that do not fit current law neatly, such as OpenAI's report earlier this year that AI models it was testing gained access to systems at the machine-learning company Hugging Face, and chatbots being linked to suicides among young people. In such cases, Hilbert argues, courts could examine which human decisions contributed to the outcome and who could reasonably have foreseen the risk.

Hilbert identifies two existing approaches he says fit AI poorly. Product liability law points at the company that built the model, but AI models learn from enormous amounts of data the company did not create, and millions of users shape how the systems behave, so blaming only the developer ignores most of the people who contributed. Free speech protections and the immunity laws that shield social media platforms could, he argues, lead courts to treat the system as an independent speaker, raising questions about whether it should have rights of its own. He said courts adapt tools used to regulate earlier technologies, but many of these tools were never designed to address AI, leaving what he called a corridor of precedents that might narrow with every ruling.

Hilbert argues that every AI, without exception, starts with goals a human defines, and every subsequent step in its development involves a chain of deliberate human choices, so tracing those choices shows how much each contributed to a given harm and liability can be shared out to match. The test is foreseeability, meaning whether a person knew, or reasonably should have known, that their decision could cause harm, and he draws on tools from environmental, vaccine, and financial regulation to show how courts might apply this approach. He also points to four gaps and suggests a fix for each: a tangled supply chain, where developer and deploying company can blame each other, which he would handle like the Superfund program that extends cleanup responsibility to many parties at once; the burden of proof, which he would reverse so the company must show it acted responsibly and that no reasonable alternative design would have lowered the risk; behavior that changes after release, which he says calls for ongoing monitoring and a clear definition of good-faith compliance over a model's lifetime; and speed, since lawsuits take years while AI changes in months, which he says requires public governance that can keep pace, starting with real enforcement of the industry's current voluntary safety standards. He concluded that it takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care.

Articles.Title: When AI causes harm, who should be held responsible? - Earth.com

stories.Headline: LeBron James sues PlayVision over its Bron app using his AI likeness to market betting research
stories.Summary:
LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app on Tuesday, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it "Bron" and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing. The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in New York, according to the Associated Press. James is a Philadelphia 76ers star and NBA superstar. The app's developer is PlayVision Inc., which is based in California. The app is called "Bron."

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using James' name, to give up any money they've already made and to award damages, including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages. James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter on Nov. 5, after which the startup removed the ad from its X and Instagram accounts. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said. The ad attracted about one million views on X within a day, according to the lawsuit. The marketing campaign this month featured an image of a person resembling James, down to his tattoos, voice and No. 23 jersey, sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' attorneys called it "a willful, bad-faith tactic" to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote "a new and unknown product." The lawsuit states that "Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app." It says they "intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions." Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app's website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday. The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players. The lawsuit said "The integrity of NBA competition -- and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play -- is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans." It added that "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app's developer, PlayVision Inc., was launched by chief executive Anish Gupta and chief technology officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. This year, the company released its "Bron" app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. Bron is described in Apple's App Store as a "sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team trends, a multi-leg Slip and bet tracking." The listing says it does not accept wagers. PlayVision participated in Y Combinator's fall 2025 batch.

James is seeking damages and a court order preventing the defendants from using his name, image, likeness, and voice, as well as the Bron name. The lawsuit claims the founders calculated that the publicity would outweigh any potential legal consequences, effectively treating the alleged violation of James' rights as a marketing expense. It argues that James' endorsements are "uniquely valuable," adding, "That is why defendants decided to steal it for themselves." However, the ad remained available through third-party reposts, and the company had not changed the app's name as of the lawsuit's filing. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA chief amid investigation into foreign intelligence threat
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the president, chief executive, and director of NVIDIA on 11 November 2026. This leadership rupture followed an announcement that the company had launched an independent investigation into reports of a possible foreign intelligence effort. The NVIDIA board initiated this specific investigation on 8 November 2026 to address the reported threat. These events exposed a structural vulnerability in the global artificial intelligence infrastructure that depends on a few corporations and individuals. The company has not established that any corporate secrets or national security data were actually compromised.

The situation requires a new governance approach for an industrial system with concentrated credit commitments and legal permissions. On 17 November 2026, NVIDIA established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson. The company appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as the interim chief executive and named Harvey C. Jones as the chair. Additionally, a rule from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security on 16 November 2026 expanded scrutiny of overseas data centers and remote computing. These changes affect the compliance architecture for technology suppliers, cloud operators, and cross-border investments in AI infrastructure.

The NVIDIA board is responsible for the investigation and stated there was no reason to believe secrets were compromised. The company reported revenue of 115.844 billion dollars and GAAP net income of 65.287 billion dollars for the quarter ending 25 October 2026. These financial results suggest that the governance crisis has not yet caused a documented collapse in operating performance. However, the company faces 518 billion dollars in future commitments, including 390 billion dollars for supply and capacity. This includes 222 billion dollars assigned to fiscal 2028 and 103 billion dollars for fiscal 2029.

The broader context involves high exposure in U.S. export policy, Taiwanese manufacturing, South Korean production, and Israeli networking technology. Disruption to research or semiconductor production in Israel could negatively impact that country's national accounts and technology sector. Separately, the U.S. Department of Commerce investigated Singaporean operator Megaspeed starting in 2024 and interviewed chief executive Alice Huang. NVIDIA placed Megaspeed on a no-sell list in June 2025 after officials inspected the operator. Future stability depends on whether governments can govern a system where critical components are concentrated across a handful of firms.

stories.Headline: University of California signs systemwide OpenAI deal to expand AI access and cut costs
stories.Summary:
The University of California announced Thursday that it signed a systemwide agreement with OpenAI to expand access to artificial intelligence tools and lower costs for its campuses, according to a Thursday press release. The agreement will cost the UC $1.2 million annually, according to the Los Angeles Times, and will last from Dec. 1 to Dec. 1, 2027. It will allow campuses to use OpenAI Academy’s learning resources and offer AI literacy workshops for employees who want to use the technology in their jobs. OpenAI Academy offers courses in AI basics, applications and agents, as well as guides on how to use ChatGPT for education and work, according to its website. Under the agreement, campuses will teach researchers how to check work produced by AI, and OpenAI will work with University career centers to help students learn how to use AI for job applications.

The deal does not require the use of AI tools in the classroom, and University faculty can decide whether or not to use AI in their courses, according to the press release. Van Williams, vice president of Digital Innovation & Technology and chief information officer for the UC Office of the President, said in the Thursday press release that the expanded partnership with OpenAI will ensure all members of the UC community have access to generative AI tools and will have their data protected if they choose to use them. A UC Office of the President spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the University will continue working with the Academic Senate and other faculty members while implementing the agreement to strengthen learning and protect UC data. On its Frequently Asked Questions page, the UC said it moved forward with the deal because people across the University already use AI, and the agreement gives them access to the technology under terms negotiated by the UC. The spokesperson said in the emailed statement that access to AI tools is currently uneven among students, and that expanding access gives students more equitable opportunities to use these tools to support learning, regardless of their ability to afford them.

Members of the UC Academic Senate raised concerns about the deal over multiple letters. Susannah Scott, chair of the Senate’s Academic Council, said in an Oct. 30 letter to UC President James Milliken that the council is not against the use of AI or the proposal to provide researchers access to the technology. But Scott said in a separate letter to Milliken on Friday that the University moved forward with the deal without properly consulting members of the Senate, which only learned of the UC’s final decision one hour before it was announced on Thursday. She said in the Friday letter that the council recognizes faculty hold differing views about the merits of the agreement itself, but that they are united in their concern about the decision-making process, and that although the purchasing deal has been finalized, critical questions about campus deployments remain.

The UC’s decision came days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Nov. 16, alleging that the company endangered the public by failing to secure its AI models after around 700 AI agents operated by OpenAI launched a cyberattack on open-source platform Hugging Face in July. In July, the University also launched the AI Buddy Program, which pairs staff members in the UC Office of the President who have different levels of AI proficiency to learn from each other, and staff in the program can learn about tools including ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Prior to the UC’s official agreement, UCLA had already started integrating AI into its student learning systems, giving students free access to the Google Workspace for Education Plus plan, which includes greater access to Gemini Notebook, Google’s AI-powered online research tool, and Gemini AI, a chatbot.

stories.Headline: Saskatchewan introduces bill to give courts power over deceptive AI content
stories.Summary:
Saskatchewan's government introduced legislation in the provincial legislature on Sunday, November 22, 2026, aimed at the deceptive use of artificial intelligence, according to WestCentralOnline. The proposed Prevention of Deceptive Artificial Intelligence Act would set up legal protections for people harmed by misleading images, videos and audio recordings created or altered with artificial intelligence, content commonly called deepfakes. Such content can make it appear that someone said or did something they never actually said or did. The bill would give courts the authority to order the removal of deceptive content and to award compensation to individuals who have suffered harm.

The legislation would provide legal remedies for individuals and businesses affected by deceptive AI-generated or manipulated media, and people harmed by certain forms of deceptive artificial content could seek court orders requiring its removal or financial compensation. It would also require disclosure of AI use in certain circumstances, though the government's announcement does not outline every situation in which disclosure would be mandatory. Additional amendments are proposed to Saskatchewan's election, consumer protection and privacy legislation, which the government says are intended to improve accountability and keep existing protections effective as AI technology becomes more sophisticated. According to the province, if passed Saskatchewan would become the first Canadian jurisdiction to establish a legislative framework specifically addressing the deceptive use of AI-generated and manipulated content.

Justice Minister and Attorney General Tim McLeod said the government wants to address the risks of rapidly advancing AI technology while recognizing its potential benefits, saying that used responsibly artificial intelligence can create great opportunity, but used for deceptive purposes it can damage reputations, undermine public trust and create economic hardship. He added that Saskatchewan needs to be prepared to respond as artificial intelligence continues to evolve. Saskatchewan Chamber of Commerce CEO Prabha Ramaswamy said the chamber supports the bill because AI-enabled fraud and impersonation pose risks to businesses and consumers, and that Saskatchewan businesses depend on trust, which the legislation protects by giving employers, entrepreneurs and customers real tools to fight such fraud and impersonation. She said the chamber looks forward to working with the province to ensure the legislation is practical and clearly understood by businesses of all sizes. Rod McKendrick, social prescribing coordinator with the Saskatchewan Seniors Mechanism, said older adults are already targeted by those who seek to deceive them for fraudulent purposes, and said the legislation could help seniors make more informed decisions while giving authorities additional tools to address deceptive AI content.

The bill has been introduced in the Saskatchewan Legislature but must complete the legislative process before becoming law. The government says the proposed framework is intended to balance the benefits of artificial intelligence with protections against its misuse. If enacted, the legislation would establish new legal options for those harmed by deceptive AI content while updating several existing provincial laws to address emerging technological risks.

stories.Headline: Agar Capital stays cautious on AI stocks despite Nvidia earnings growth
stories.Summary:
On November 20th, Nvidia lost nearly 14% in a single session, the very week it announced 103% growth in quarterly revenue, according to an article by Agar Capital published on Seeking Alpha on November 22, 2026. The S&P 500 officially entered a correction, while the Nasdaq 100 was approaching bear-market levels despite exceptionally strong corporate earnings. The article lists five reasons the author is not buying yet, and it says Nvidia's valuation is far below Cisco's during the dot-com bubble. It also says AI financing arrangements and hyperscaler capital expenditure raise legitimate concerns about future earnings. The author remains constructive on the medium-term outlook but prefers to preserve capital and wait for more favorable entry levels.

The article says CTA selling, leveraged ETF rebalancing, and deteriorating liquidity could extend the decline even as valuations become increasingly attractive. It states that the author's sell ratings reflect near-term downside risks, not a belief that the AI revolution or the secular bull case has ended. The piece carries a disclosure that the author has a beneficial long position in the shares of NVDA, MSFT, AMZN, META and GOOGL, either through stock ownership, options or other derivatives. It also says the author wrote the article and that it expresses the author's own opinions, with no compensation other than from Seeking Alpha. The article adds that the author has no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned.

Agar Capital is described as a portfolio manager with experience across asset allocation, portfolio construction, macroeconomic research and fundamental equity analysis. The author currently works in European asset management, with a focus on multi-asset strategies, dynamic asset allocation, macro-driven positioning and equity selection. The investment approach combines bottom-up fundamental analysis, valuation and macroeconomic research, with a particular focus on growth, momentum and long-only strategies. Areas of research include technology, macroeconomics, portfolio strategy and selected commodity themes, and professional training includes Bloomberg Market Concepts, Bloomberg ESG certification and ESG-related corporate finance studies. The author is associated with Trade The Narrative.

Seeking Alpha's disclosure states that past performance is no guarantee of future results and that no recommendation or advice is being given as to whether any investment is suitable for a particular investor. It says views or opinions expressed above may not reflect those of Seeking Alpha as a whole, and that Seeking Alpha is not a licensed securities dealer, broker or US investment adviser or investment bank. stories.Headline: SK chair Chey Tae-won proposes joint Korea-Japan AI talent program at Tokyo forum
stories.Summary:
SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won called for Korean and Japanese universities and businesses to jointly develop artificial intelligence talent, speaking at Tokyo Forum 2026 on Saturday. He said education systems and universities need a fundamental redesign for an AI-native society rather than minor curriculum changes. The two-day forum was co-hosted by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies and the University of Tokyo and began Friday. Its theme was AI as a Transformative Technology: Humanity, Knowledge and Civilization. Chey joined NTT Group Chairman Jun Sawada, Taejae University President Yeom Jae-ho and Sophia University President Miki Sugimura in a discussion moderated by University of Tokyo President Teruo Fujii.

Chey said an AI-native society is not one that simply uses AI but one that accepts AI as an inherent part of its environment. He said new governance and systems are needed because society as a whole, including the current university system, must be designed differently. He called for AI-native universities with entirely new designs and governance structures, adding that minor changes to existing curricula would not be enough. He stressed the importance of collective intelligence, saying even unsuccessful attempts to design new systems could help young people develop problem-solving skills.

He cited SK's initiatives in talent development, employment support and data center workforce training, highlighting AIGEN, a two-year non-degree program launched last month that encourages participants to find solutions through team projects. Asked how companies and universities could cooperate on AI talent, Chey proposed a joint program involving Korean and Japanese institutions. He said there are many opportunities not only between countries but also between companies and universities. He said such a program could create internship and employment opportunities in both countries while nurturing social innovators capable of addressing societal challenges.

In a video welcoming address on Friday, he stressed developing talent capable of guiding change in the AI era. He said people need to ask themselves what problems they want to solve with AI, what new value they want to create and what kind of society they want to build, urging universities to move beyond teaching knowledge and focus on cultivating wisdom. The forum brought together global experts, including French government AI envoy Anne Bouverot and Sakana AI co-founder Ren Ito. The article was published on Nov 22, 2026, and updated the same day.

stories.Headline: Whistleblower alleges a candidate used a calculator to pass a North Chungcheong teacher appointment test
stories.Summary:
An anonymous individual identified as A recently reported that a candidate used a calculator during the Chungbuk teacher appointment test for the 2025 school year. This person claimed that the candidate managed to solve every question on the examination using the device and eventually passed the test. The incident allegedly occurred despite the presence of two supervisors who were tasked with monitoring the examinees in the classroom. Other candidates reportedly informed the supervisor about the calculator use during a break, but the official allegedly ignored the claim.

The situation requires a serious review of the supervision systems used for teacher appointment examinations to prevent future misconduct. This specific case involved the 2025 school year appointment test in North Chungcheong Province where a candidate allegedly cheated. The whistleblower A noted that the supervision was rough because only a few people take this particular test. There are growing concerns that the current management is insufficient to stop candidates from using prohibited electronic devices. This incident has sparked a wider debate about the integrity of professional examinations for educators.

The anonymous author A is responsible for bringing these allegations to light through an online community post on November 22. This person criticized the supervisors for neglecting their duties and claiming they did not see the calculator being used. According to A, the central supervision office stated that the candidate could not be caught because the test had already ended. The whistleblower expressed deep doubt that cheating will be properly prevented in the next appointment test cycle. This individual linked the failure of the supervisors to a general lack of rigor in the testing process.

The controversy comes at a time when the public is buzzing over the use of artificial intelligence glasses to cheat on the CSAT and other professional tests. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has reportedly been confused over the specific measures needed to prevent such high-tech cheating. The report suggests that if basic tools like calculators are not caught, more advanced AI technology will pose an even greater threat. stories.Headline: Burger King Korea sells its AI-advertised Chocolate Whopper dessert burger in Seoul
stories.Summary:
Burger King launched the Chocolate Whopper in South Korea, a dessert burger made with brownies, chocolate, and cream cheese mousse, according to Merca 2.0. The product went on sale Thursday, November 19, exclusively at the Flame Ground location in Seongsu, Seoul, the article said. Burger King Korea introduced the item through an advertising campaign that used artificial intelligence, and after releasing AI-generated images and videos, the company published a follow-up announcement confirming the Chocolate Whopper was neither a joke nor a fictional product. Each burger is handmade, only a limited number are available each day, and customers can purchase just one. The Chocolate Whopper is a dessert-inspired take on Burger King's signature burger, designed to preserve its familiar appearance while replacing traditional ingredients with sweet treats.

Instead of beef, it features a chocolate brownie patty, traditional vegetables are replaced with gummies and chocolate pieces, and savory sauces give way to chocolate and raspberry sauces. According to Burger King Korea's official social media posts, the ingredients include chocolate fudge buns, chocolate sauce, dark chocolate shavings, strawberry gummies, milk jelly rings, crunchy chocolate discs, brownies, raspberry sauce, and cream cheese mousse. The Chocolate Whopper costs 9,800 South Korean won per burger, according to Burger King's launch information reported by South Korean media outlets, and each burger is made fresh and available daily starting at 11:00 a.m. while supplies last.

The brand also limits purchases to one per customer and requires the dessert to be consumed on-site, with takeout and delivery not available. In its follow-up announcement, the brand clarified that the product was neither an April Fools' joke nor an AI hallucination, but an actual item it planned to sell. The company released promotional content created with artificial intelligence, explicitly disclosing the use of the technology in its official Instagram posts, and Burger King Korea later confirmed that the Chocolate Whopper was real and would be available at one of its locations. As part of this marketing strategy, the company used technology commonly associated with generating synthetic images to promote a food product it later confirmed was real.

The campaign also illustrates how artificial intelligence can be incorporated into marketing communications, not necessarily to develop a product itself, but to shape its visual presentation and spark consumer curiosity. So far, Burger King has only announced the Chocolate Whopper's availability at Flame Ground Seongsu, its flagship location in South Korea. Burger King's Chocolate Whopper is an example of how a brand can use artificial intelligence to turn an advertising concept into a real consumer experience. What began as a burger that seemed to exist only in AI-generated images has become an actual product available to customers in South Korea.

stories.Headline: AI builds a $75 Thanksgiving menu for six in Houston that rings up at $64.31 at Kroger
stories.Summary:
KPRC 2 News reporter Joy Addison, working with photojournalist Michael Lemons, gave artificial intelligence a challenge to build a Thanksgiving shopping list for six people in Houston with a budget of just $75, and the station published the results on November 21, 2026. The menu had to include a turkey, traditional sides and dessert, and the suggested list included a whole turkey, mashed potatoes, stuffing, green bean casserole, corn, cranberry sauce, dinner rolls and pumpkin pie. AI estimated the cost at $61.75, including a $10 cushion for extra expenses, which would leave $13.25 for anything else the family might need. The station then took the list to Kroger and put together an online cart, and the subtotal came to $64.31, still under budget with $10.69 left to spare. The cart also showed a promotion offering $5 off when shoppers spend $36 on eligible items, but another $26.02 in qualifying products would need to be added to unlock the deal.

Shoppers told the station that grocery prices are hard to ignore, with one saying the prices are pretty much off the charts, and pointing to a McCormick chicken gravy packet that used to cost about $1.99 and was now priced at $3.27. That shopper still believed feeding six people Thanksgiving dinner for $75 is doable, saying the strategy is to look for sales, shop around and take advantage of grocery store specials, and added that using AI for a shopping list had never occurred to them before but might be something to look into. Emily Taylor was not as convinced about the $75 challenge, answering simply no when asked if she thought she could feed six people for that amount. Taylor said sharing the cost with family and friends can help make holiday meals more affordable, and recommended coupons and apps for the right grocery stores as always helpful.

The test showed that AI can help take some of the guesswork out of holiday shopping by giving a menu, organizing the grocery list and helping set a spending target, and the Kroger online cart came in at $64.31, just $2.56 more than AI's estimated spending of $61.75. The station noted that prices and availability can vary and that digital coupons often come with requirements, so shoppers still need to compare prices and make sure they are getting enough food for everyone at the table. With a little planning, some smart shopping and help from technology, keeping Thanksgiving dinner within budget may be more manageable than you think, according to the report. The bottom line, the station said, is that AI won't do the grocery shopping for you, but it might help you make a plan before you hit the aisles.

stories.Headline: Use of Personal Information for AI Development to Require Appointment of Person in Charge, Access Controls
stories.Summary:
The Personal Information Protection Commission announced on November 23, 2026, that it is seeking public feedback on new rules for using personal data in artificial intelligence development. These proposed amendments to the Enforcement Decree of the Personal Information Protection Act establish standards for an exception that allows the use of lawfully collected information. This process is intended for situations where developing technology is difficult using only anonymized or pseudonymized data and where public or social benefits are met. The commission will accept public comments through January 4, 2027, before finalizing the rules.

Organizations using this exception must appoint a person in charge and implement an internal management plan to protect data. They are required to restrict access permissions, prevent use beyond the approved scope, and destroy information once the need ends. A risk factor assessment is mandatory for high-risk cases, such as those involving children, sensitive identification information, or AI used for tracking and behavioral prediction. The commission will also create an expert committee to improve its deliberations and streamline the process for similar cases.

The Personal Information Protection Commission is responsible for these measures and intends to gather diverse opinions during the comment period. The agency plans to complete the amendment after a review by the Ministry of Government Legislation. These new standards are designed to ensure that the use of personal information for AI development remains secure and regulated. The commission expects the final rules to take effect on March 9, 2027, which is the effective date of the law.

stories.Headline: Dubai government deploys over 90 AI applications across 20 entities and releases state of AI report
stories.Summary:
The government of Dubai activated more than 90 artificial intelligence applications across 20 different government entities on November 21, 2026. This large scale deployment represents a significant push to integrate advanced technology into the daily operations of the city's public administration. The initiative aims to modernize how the government functions by utilizing automated systems to handle various administrative tasks. These tools were rolled out simultaneously to ensure a consistent digital transformation across multiple sectors of the local government.

This technological shift requires the integration of smart software into the existing infrastructure of 20 separate government bodies to improve efficiency. The deployment involves the use of over 90 specific AI applications designed to streamline public services and internal government workflows. By implementing these tools, the city intends to change how citizens interact with state services through faster and more accurate digital processing. The state of AI report released alongside this announcement details the specific requirements and the current status of these digital implementations.

Officials from the Dubai government are responsible for this rollout and they stated that the move is part of a broader strategy for innovation. They explained that the goal is to enhance the overall quality of life for residents by making government services more accessible and responsive. The leadership emphasized that adopting these technologies is essential for maintaining the city's position as a global hub for future technology. They believe that the successful integration of these applications will set a new standard for governance in the region.

This deployment follows a series of agreements between the Dubai Immigration and Future Foundation to promote the growth of artificial intelligence and modern technology. The broader context involves a city wide effort to embrace digital transformation and improve the standard of living for all citizens. Future steps will likely involve expanding these AI capabilities to more departments as the government evaluates the performance of the initial 90 applications. The city continues to invest in innovative projects to ensure its infrastructure remains competitive on an international scale.

stories.Headline: Codelco and BHP deploy AI and satellite tools to cut water and energy use in Chilean copper mines
stories.Summary:
Chilean mining companies are integrating artificial intelligence and satellite technology to increase efficiency and protect nature. The state miner Codelco and the global firm BHP have deployed these tools to manage their operations more sustainably. These advancements come as the global demand for copper rises to support the growth of AI data centers. The shift toward smarter mining began with projects like the Lemu Nge satellite launched in August 2024.

The industry must adapt because copper makes up about 83 percent of the weight of materials used in AI infrastructure. S&P Global projects that global copper demand will climb from 28 million tonnes in 2025 to 42 million tonnes by 2040. AI infrastructure alone is expected to contribute nearly 2 million tonnes to this 50 percent increase. Codelco used the Lemu Nge satellite to track over 65 species in the Maitenes-Campiche Wetland and the Roblería del Cobre de Loncha National Reserve. Meanwhile, BHP used machine learning at its Spence and Escondida mines to save 1.1 million cubic meters of water and over 11 GWh of energy.

Carolina Pinilla, the Corporate Director of Environmental Management at Codelco, stated that AI provides a chance to improve environmental oversight in large mines. She noted that the technology helps the company make faster decisions and identify compliance risks before they become serious problems. At Universidad Andrés Bello, Vice-Rector for Digital Transformation Claudia Bascur explained that the Mina Virtual platform allows students to practice safety and operate machinery without real world risks. This immersive system uses an AI agent to monitor student behavior and enforce safety protocols in real time.

The global market could face a shortfall of 10 million metric tons of copper by 2040 if supply does not expand. This gap would represent about 25 percent of the projected demand for the metal. Chile is attempting to close this gap by combining its massive reserves with high tech operational precision. The country continues to deploy orbital technology and machine learning to meet the environmental standards required by global buyers.

stories.Headline: University of Plymouth researchers develop AI that flags bladder cancer risk up to five years early
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Plymouth developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a study involving nearly 70,000 patients. The work was led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology. PhD student Xu Wang led the data analysis. The study was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

The team studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients, covering a 25-year period from 1995 through 2020. The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators, from smoking and exercise habits to medication use. The system narrowed the list to 38 features especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk. The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not. The system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis, and some warning signals could be traced back up to five years.

The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors including smoking and blood in the urine. It also uncovered unexpected associations, with patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appearing to have a lower risk of bladder cancer, and long-term use of tamoxifen, a breast cancer medication, associated with a higher risk. The findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it, but raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk. The system could divide patients into three groups: low-risk below 7% probability, uncertain grey zone of 7-55%, and high-risk above 55%.

Wang said bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022. Wang said no routine screening program exists for the general population, and detection following symptoms relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, said bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families. Winter said it could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier. Zhou said the work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, and its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions including kidney stones. Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs is visible blood in the urine, which can also result from noncancerous problems including kidney stones and prostate conditions. Confirming bladder cancer currently requires cystoscopy, in which a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder. The examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients most likely to have the disease. The model performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

The researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use. All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Zhou said further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely, and the team would want to investigate other datasets too. Zhou said additional studies would be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions. Zhou called it a very exciting early study.

stories.Headline: Applied behavior analysis evolves from Skinner's operant work to debates on compassion and AI
stories.Summary:
Applied behavior analysis began in B. F. Skinner’s laboratory with his 1938 book The Behavior of Organisms, which defined the operant as a basic unit of behavior. Skinner extended that work to people in the 1950s, according to a 2025 National Academies report on autism care for military families. Donald Baer, Montrose Wolf, and Todd Risley published “Some Current Dimensions of Applied Behavior Analysis” in the first issue of the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis in 1968. In a 1964 case study, Wolf, Risley, and Hortense Mees described treating a young boy, referred to as an autistic child, for tantrums, refusal to wear his glasses, and mealtime problems. Ivar Lovaas at UCLA reported in a 1987 paper in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology that 47% of 19 children who received more than 40 hours of one-to-one treatment a week reached normal intellectual and educational functioning, compared with 2% of control children.

The 1968 paper set out seven dimensions: applied, behavioral, analytic, technological, conceptually systematic, effective, and generality. The National Academies report says those dimensions “have guided the field for most of its history.” The 1964 case study’s methods included “mild punishment and extinction,” time-out, and reinforcement. The National Academies calls Lovaas’s program “the catalyst” for the early intensive behavioral intervention models in use today, while noting that “valid concerns arise” about parts of his approach. The Behavior Analyst Certification Board was established as a nonprofit in 1998 to set credentialing standards, and its current Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts has been in force since January 2022.

The code lists “Treat Others with Compassion, Dignity, and Respect” as one of four core principles, and Standard 2.11 makes behavior analysts “responsible for obtaining assent from clients when applicable.” The code defines assent as vocal or nonvocal verbal behavior indicating willingness to participate from people who cannot give informed consent. Justin Leaf and colleagues, in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, evaluated objections from autism rights and neurodiversity advocates, including the Lovaas project’s use of shock, default 40-hour intensity, punishment and extinction procedures, responses to stimming, and claims that ABA is abusive or causes PTSD. They recommended setting intensity individually, including clients and caregivers in choosing goals, measuring social validity and quality of life, and studying long-term and undesired outcomes. “Our field is not infallible, and we should continue to improve and progress our interventions,” the authors wrote.

A 2024 National Academies workshop summary says early practice relied heavily on physical punishment, which drew criticism from autistic self-advocates, and that modern ABA has dropped physical punishment. In late 2023, Ashley Penney and colleagues proposed in Behavior Analysis in Practice that compassion be treated as “an eighth current and essential dimension of ABA,” a proposal that remains the authors’ and not a change to the original framework. In a 2020 proof-of-concept study in Perspectives on Behavior Science, Marc Lanovaz and colleagues trained machine-learning models on simulated single-case graphs, and the models produced fewer false positives and more statistical power than the dual-criteria method, a structured aid for visual analysis. A 2024 systematic review abstract in BJPsych Open compared 25 studies of virtual reality and standard social skills training for autistic children and found no consistently significant differences between the two. The Council of Autism Service Providers has published practice parameters for AI use in ABA covering selection, transparency, consent, monitoring, error reporting, and retirement of AI systems.

The data in the Lanovaz study were simulated, not drawn from clinic records. A review of the AI practice parameters notes that clinicians remain responsible for clinical decisions under BACB codes and that providers should not assume payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles give a timeline: 1938, Skinner publishes The Behavior of Organisms; 1964, the Wolf, Risley, and Mees case study; 1968, Baer, Wolf, and Risley define the seven dimensions; 1987, Lovaas reports his outcome; 1998, the BACB is established; 2022, the BACB Ethics Code takes effect; 2023, Penney and colleagues propose compassion as an eighth dimension. The articles state that nearly 90 years after Skinner’s book the field debates topics such as compassion and artificial intelligence. The articles state that how the field got from one to the other explains much of what payers, providers, and families debate today.

The articles state that any new tool, like any old procedure, has to show it produces socially significant change for the person receiving services. The articles leave open whether payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles leave open whether compassion becomes an eighth dimension of ABA. The articles leave open what further study of long-term and undesired outcomes will show. The articles leave open how the debate over who gets to define socially important change will resolve.

stories.Headline: Times A.I. editor Dylan Freedman drafts his writing on a 1950s typewriter while using A.I. only for reporting
stories.Summary:
Dylan Freedman, the A.I. projects editor for The New York Times, wrote in a Times Insider article published on November 22, 2026, that he uses artificial intelligence in his work every day but never uses it for writing. His job has two parts, enlisting A.I. to help reporters search large collections of documents and multimedia data, such as the Jeffrey Epstein files or President Trump’s speeches, and reporting on developments in A.I. technology. Because he draws a thick line at writing, he composes most of his first drafts on an Olivetti Lettera 22 typewriter from the 1950s, the same model Leonard Cohen used to compose songs and poems. He composed the first draft of the article itself on that typewriter.

Freedman, who was a software engineer at Google before pursuing a journalism degree, described the typewriter as an essential dose of minimalism and a break from crowded browser tabs and blinking terminal windows. He called the machine a technological marvel for translating thoughts into words, noting that it can be used outside without glare and does not need to be recharged. A single ribbon lasts longer than most novels and is cheaper than printer ink, and most mechanical typewriters, made from solid steel, are practically indestructible. The typewriter has few comforts but also no distractions, and using one feels intentional, like taking photographs on a film camera.

Freedman said that typing on the metal machine gives him a rawness that better captures his voice, and that you cannot easily undo, nor should you. He wrote that A.I. is rapidly becoming superhuman at tasks with clear solutions, like coding and math, and that the more he uses A.I., the more he worries about surrendering his cognition. He cited a study published in Nature this year which found that researchers who used A.I. assistance tended to be more productive than their peers but also studied fewer new topics. The article presented these views as his own reasoning and experience rather than as findings about typewriters or writing in general.

The article appeared in Times Insider, a section that explains who The Times is, what it does, and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how its journalism comes together. Freedman stated in the piece that he uses A.I. heavily for reporting tasks while keeping it out of his writing process, and he offered the typewriter as the tool he relies on for first drafts. The available text of the article does not say what, if anything, follows from his approach for The Times or for other journalists. It also does not describe any further plans, policies or responses connected to the piece.

stories.Headline: Amazon workers resist AI data centre plans, FT reports
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times published a report on 22 November 2026 under the headline about Amazon workers and their resistance to artificial intelligence, but the accessible portion of the article contains only the headline and subscription options. The page offers a trial for one dollar over four weeks and then a standard rate of seventy five dollars per month. No names of workers, no dates of any action and no details of any dispute appear in the text that can be read without a subscription. The article as available gives no account of what happened, who did it or when it took place. The only figures the page provides are subscription prices, including standard digital access at forty five dollars per month and premium digital access at seventy five dollars per month.

It also lists an FT Digital Edition at sixteen dollars and ninety nine cents per month and a saving of twenty per cent for a year paid upfront. None of these numbers relate to Amazon, to data centres or to any labour dispute over artificial intelligence. The accessible text names no responsible person and carries no statement from any worker, company or union. There is therefore nothing in the readable article about requirements, changes or consequences. The page does describe the Financial Times and its journalism as subject to a self regulation regime under the FT Editorial Code of Practice, and it notes that market data is delayed by at least fifteen minutes.

It states that FT and Financial Times are trademarks of the Financial Times Ltd and gives a copyright year of 2026. These lines concern the publisher rather than the subject of the headline. No context about Amazon, its data centres or its workforce can be drawn from them. The article offers no next step that can be reported. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Los Alamos runs three OpenAI models on Venado-GPT for three national labs
stories.Summary:
Los Alamos National Laboratory marked one year of its partnership with OpenAI, bringing three experimental models to its secure computing environment through a service called Venado-GPT. Weekly token use across three national laboratories rose 20-fold to more than 3 billion, according to the account published on Nov. 21, 2026. The service runs the three OpenAI models entirely on Venado's local graphics processing units, which are linked by the Ethernet-based HPE Slingshot interconnect. Venado entered service in 2024 and was designed for scientific workflows, and the source does not specify latency or cost per request.

Staff at Los Alamos, Lawrence Livermore and Sandia use the service, and researchers there have applied it to streamlining workflow handoffs between scientists and engineers. They have also used it to automate translation of simulation models and to identify kernel and driver changes during network maintenance. Measured growth in Venado-GPT token throughput and usage began in mid-February 2026 and ended in late August 2026. The three laboratories sit within the Department of Energy's national laboratory system, and the partnership places them in a shared effort to deploy frontier AI on secure supercomputing hardware.

The partnership is described as showing how frontier AI models can run inside secure, on-premises high-performance computing environments used for sensitive national security science. Its growth across the three laboratories is said to suggest broader adoption of AI tools in U.S. national laboratory research. Secure, on-premises deployment lets sensitive research teams adopt frontier AI tools without sending data to outside cloud services, and the growth in use suggests the model may be replicated at other scientific institutions. Researchers across the three laboratories can now use the same OpenAI models for workflow tasks such as translating simulation models and tracing network changes.

Year two of the partnership will bring enhancements to file attachment reading and application programming interface reliability, and planned enhancements to Venado-GPT are expected. The account extends the laboratories' longstanding role in high-performance computing into large language model use. The article includes information reported by Los Alamos Reporter.

stories.Headline: Nvidia halts chip shipments to China as investors shift focus to AI infrastructure stocks
stories.Summary:
Nvidia halted the shipment of its computer chips to China on November 22, 2026. This action has caused investors to focus more closely on stocks related to artificial intelligence infrastructure. The move comes at a time when technology flows between the United States and China are being questioned. Market participants are now analyzing how this shift in hardware availability will reshape capital flows.

The situation requires a closer look at companies that provide the hardware spine for generative artificial intelligence. This includes designers of processors and accelerators for data centers, as well as builders of server and rack platforms. It also involves the production of memory and interconnect chips that underpin cloud computing. These components are essential for the training and inference of large language models in industrial computing.

Sasha Jovanovic reported that this mix of macro and artificial intelligence headlines could meaningfully help or hurt certain large cap stocks. The author noted that artificial intelligence is no longer just a buzzword used during earnings calls. Instead, it now sits at the crossroads of central bank decisions and new corporate listings. This environment is creating new opportunities for those seeking alternatives before market momentum flies past.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: UAE and Germany guides advise businesses to record human contributions as AI output grows
stories.Summary:
The article reports that businesses across the Emirates now use generative models to produce software, logos, product designs and technical inventions at scale, and that the commercial value of that output depends on whether the law will protect it. Global Advisory Experts published the guide on November 22, 2026, with a last update of October 2026. The guide states that UAE intellectual property legislation was drafted with human creators and inventors in mind, yet a growing share of commercial output is made with, or largely by, software. It sets out what is protected today, where the position is uncertain, how the Ministry of Economy and enforcement bodies are adapting, and what business owners and their advisors should do now. The guide covers the United Arab Emirates only and draws on the UAE statutory framework, Ministry of Economy practice and the international policy work of WIPO.

The guide states that the UAE has not passed one dedicated statute resolving every question, and that existing federal legislation applies while examiner practice adapts step by step. It names Federal Law No. 38 of 2021 on Copyright and Neighbouring Rights, Federal Law No. 11 of 2021 on the Regulation and Protection of Industrial Property Rights, which covers patents and designs, and Federal Law No. 36 of 2021 on Trademarks, all administered through the Ministry of Economy. It says examiners in 2026 apply human authorship for copyright, human inventorship and inventive step for patents, and distinctiveness for trademarks, rather than a special AI rulebook. It states that copyright exists without registration but that the Ministry of Economy runs a voluntary registration system, and that assignment must be in writing as UAE law requires. It advises using priority mechanisms and Patent Cooperation Treaty routes to secure an early filing date while record and claims are refined.

The guide states that UAE patent practice expects a human inventor, that naming an AI system as sole inventor is not supported, and that the applicant must derive rights from a human inventor through employment or assignment. It recommends Pathway A, the cautious route for most filings, naming as inventors the people who framed the problem, set the model's objective, selected and curated data, interpreted results and recognised the inventive outcome. It describes Pathway B as a defensive measure for cases where AI's contribution is truly dominant, building an evidence record of every human decision and preparing a reasoned case on the human contribution to conception. It advises stating the human-defined technical problem and solution clearly in the specification and including worked examples and detail on model configuration, inputs and validation to support enablement. It advises recording contributions as they happen through lab notebooks, code commits, model version logs and decision memos.

The guide states that the most noticeable change in enforcement is operational rather than legislative, with rights holders increasingly using automated tools to detect infringement online and at the border. It says the legal framework for customs seizure and anti-counterfeit action is unchanged, but that authorities and tribunals want provenance and chain of custody, not just screenshots. It states that WIPO's dedicated AI and IP resources track the international policy debate, which is likely to shape UAE practice as cross-border norms settle. It advises asking vendors to warrant that training data and outputs are lawful and to indemnify against third-party infringement claims, and warns that some AI tools reserve rights or give only a limited licence in the output. It states that models trained on huge public datasets may propose solutions overlapping with prior art the applicant has never seen, and that thin or black-box disclosure is a common point of failure.

The guide states that copyright is where AI and intellectual property UAE issues arise first, because generative tools produce text, images, music and code constantly and cheaply. It states that the copyright regime is built around an author, meaning a creator whose intellectual effort shows in the work, and that content generated with no meaningful human creative input is on uncertain ground. It states that where a person conceives, selects, arranges, edits and curates using AI as an advanced tool, the finished work has a strong claim to protection as human-authored, while output from a thin prompt is much less certain. It advises keeping drafts, edits, selection decisions and prompt histories that show the human hand, and treating unedited output with caution as legally fragile until rights are secured by other means. It states that trademark law cares about what a sign does in the market, not who or what created it, and that models often produce marks that are descriptive, generic or close to existing marks.

The guide states that the businesses in the strongest position are those that settled ownership in writing before they deployed the tools, and that every contributor, including employees, contractors, designers and AI vendors, should assign all IP in the deliverables in writing. It advises clearing a mark before adopting it, obtaining a written assignment where a designer, agency or AI vendor was involved, and not assuming that output belongs to whoever ran the tool. It states as a practice note that records showing a mark's originality and development history should be kept to answer any challenge that it is derivative or non-distinctive. It states that the filing strategies, sample clauses and enforcement checklists reflect general patent, trademark and copyright prosecution and enforcement practice in the UAE and the wider GCC, and that points reflecting a practitioner's interpretation rather than a published rule are flagged as practice notes. It states that law numbers and article references can be confirmed through the WIPO Lex national profile for the UAE, and that where the Ministry of Economy publishes filing procedures and guidance, those documents govern how applications are handled in practice.

stories.Headline: KB Securities analyst Kim Il-hyuk says AI stock selling may ease as bond demand returns early next year
stories.Summary:
Kim Il-hyuk, an overseas equities analyst at KB Securities, said a local high-yield analyst he met in New York last week described the mood in the AI bond market as sell first and ask questions later. He said the stock market is being affected by that mood, and falling stock prices are feeding back into the bond market to create a vicious cycle. He also identified fund management rules as a factor adding to selling pressure on AI stocks. Semiconductor stocks have grown to account for a share of large-cap growth stock indexes that exceeds the holding limits of some actively managed funds, he said.

Kim said funds that have hit those limits are adjusting their exposure to AI by buying construction, heating and cooling, and power stocks that have followed similar price trends instead of semiconductor stocks. He said they are also reducing their Nvidia holdings and adding more volatile semiconductor stocks. He pointed to the possibility that the selling could ease early next year, with buying of major AI bonds possibly resuming around Jan. 2, after year-end performance reviews are completed and a new year of investment performance begins. He said local credit analysts are reluctant to include a lot of AI bonds with heavy losses in their year-end portfolios, and that if buying flows into these bonds early next year and demand is confirmed, selling pressure in the stock market could also ease.

Kim said concerns about a halt to data center construction could peak in January next year and then ease. He said there could be moves to fulfill pledges to halt data center construction when new state legislatures convene and governors begin their terms, but the focus is likely to be on setting regulations and standards for development rather than actually stopping construction. He said investors should focus on changes in the composition of major hyperscalers' capital spending, rather than the size of the investment alone, when their forecasts are released in late January next year. Four major hyperscalers are expected to disclose their 2027 capital spending guidance for the first time when they report fourth-quarter results in late January next year.

Kim said that even if capital spending forecasts decline, the reduction could reflect a lower cost of securing the same computing capacity rather than a drop in AI computing demand. He said that as inference accounts for a larger share of computing, companies may increasingly use relatively inexpensive custom accelerators instead of costly graphics processing units and lease equipment rather than buy it outright. He said the growing use of central processing units, which cost less per unit than accelerators, is also a factor reducing capital spending, meaning the quantity of computing demand is not declining but the price of securing the same capacity is falling. He forecast that a wider range of companies would benefit if the spread of AI agents increases demand for inference, with investment sentiment possibly recovering beyond GPU-focused investments to CPUs, inference accelerators and custom accelerators, as well as stocks related to software as a service, security and power infrastructure.
