stories.Headline: Researchers find every AI job cluster pairs new tools with established human skills
stories.Summary:
A study published by researchers Irene Spada, Vito Giordano and Antonella Martini examined how employers pair artificial intelligence skills with traditional competencies in online job postings. The researchers analysed millions of job vacancies published in Italy and Germany between 2022 and 2023. They used text analysis and network theory to determine how skill sets take shape in the hiring market. The study found that every identified cluster of competencies pairs artificial intelligence technologies with established occupational proficiencies. The authors said workplace automation relies on functional complementarity between new tools and established human capabilities.

The dataset came from records curated by the labour analytics provider Lightcast. Raw extraction yielded 7,621,326 postings for Italy and 231,681,146 listings for Germany. After duplicates were removed, the Italian corpus comprised 262,943 distinct ads and the German corpus contained 24,263,752 notices. Advertisements averaged 9.34 total skills and 1.6 AI-specific competencies in Italy, compared to 7.02 total skills and 1.47 AI skills in Germany. Competencies were standardized using the European Classification of Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations alongside a Lightcast taxonomy of 249 distinct artificial intelligence capabilities.

The authors conducted all quantitative network and statistical evaluations separately within each country because raw posting volumes differed substantially between the two nations. The protocol treated advertisement observations as relational data, with edges between nodes weighted by co-occurrence frequency of skill pairs. This yielded 324,191 co-occurring skill pairs in the Italian data and 552,668 pairs in the German data. Node-level centrality scores were computed using unweighted network graphs based on unique job listings. The team calculated degree centrality, betweenness centrality and eigenvector centrality, multiplying the three values into a composite complementarity index.

Correlation analyses showed degree centrality and eigenvector centrality correlated at 0.98 in both national datasets, while betweenness centrality aligned with overall vacancy demand at 0.93 in Italy and 0.86 in Germany. The Louvain algorithm uncovered four distinct functional clusters in both economies, with modularity scores of 0.131 in Italy and 0.145 in Germany. Cluster 1 formed a foundational baseline of analytical, technical, linguistic and managerial competencies. Cluster 2 brought together data science and computational linguistics, aligned with project management and prototyping in Italy and with logistics and banking operations in Germany. Clusters 3 and 4 represented technical specializations, with Italy linking Industry 4.0 competencies to engineering and maintenance alongside marketing and sales, and Germany focusing on machine vision, robotics, electricity and customer relations.

In Italy, hiring demand concentrated at European Qualifications Framework level 4, representing secondary diplomas, accounting for approximately 78 percent of notices, or 5,277,117 postings. In Germany, demand concentrated at level 5, denoting short-cycle tertiary education, encompassing nearly 85 percent of notices, or 19,319,681 listings. Chi-square tests returned a statistic of 11,114,988 with 12,872 degrees of freedom in Italy and 40,810,088 with 15,648 degrees of freedom in Germany, both with p-values below 2.2e-16. Spearman rank correlations identified monotonic trends across educational levels, yielding rho values of 0.011 in Italy and 0.035 in Germany with p-values below 2.2e-16. Top-demanded competencies such as machine learning and basic artificial intelligence remained prevalent across all qualification categories, accompanied by teamwork, adaptability and problem solving.

Network Comparison Test pairwise comparisons generated p-values below 0.05 between different tiers in both countries. In Italy, structural distance showed pronounced divergence between vocational tier 2 and doctoral tier 8, registering an M-value of 0.62. In Germany, level 5 exhibited similarity to the aggregate national labour market structure, recording an invariance distance of only 0.08. The authors noted that pre-processed Lightcast data prevented inspection of original posting text, precluding external validation of proprietary text-parsing pipelines. They also noted that their 2022 to 2023 timeframe preceded the full market diffusion of generative artificial intelligence technologies, suggesting subsequent shifts in employer demands may require ongoing structural monitoring.

stories.Headline: Primary Care Artificial Intelligence Research Surged but Implementation Evidence Remains Limited
stories.Summary:
Annual research output on artificial intelligence in primary health care grew from 6 papers in 2015 to 220 in 2024, with steady growth after 2018, according to a bibliometric analysis published in Primary Health Care Research & Development by Chen, Li and Zou in 2026. The authors searched the Web of Science Core Collection for records published between January 1, 2015, and October 19, 2025, and screened an initial yield of 1,481 records to remove studies without specific primary care applications. Using Python-based term lexicons, weighted scoring and manual adjudication, they built a core corpus of 1,123 articles and review articles. A supplementary search found 599 candidate papers, and after screening excluded 457 records, 142 additional papers were added to form a 1,265-paper sensitivity corpus used for keyword-frequency re-evaluations, co-occurrence mapping and annual trend reruns. The year 2025 was kept only as an incomplete-year observation and left out of complete-year growth comparisons.

The analysis found a consistent core of research on machine learning, electronic health records, diagnostic support and clinical screening, while themes shifted over the decade. Model validation became more common alongside initial model creation, governance and regulatory oversight topics emerged after 2018, and between 2022 and 2024 attention turned substantially toward fairness, algorithmic bias and model explainability. The researchers emphasized that the growing publication counts and diversifying themes do not confirm that these computational systems are widely deployed in routine practice or actively benefiting patient care. The article states that the surge in publication volume does not demonstrate routine clinical adoption or improved health outcomes in general practice.

The study was conducted by Chen, Li and Zou and published in Primary Health Care Research & Development, volume 27, Article e134, with the DOI 10.1017/s1463423626102023. The article was reported by Blake Davidson on November 22, 2026, citing Scienmag as the news source. The authors described their work as a focused bibliometric mapping of research trends and changes in thematic attention from 2015 to 2025. The articles do not say what steps, if any, will follow from the findings.

stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marius Hobbhahn calls a 2027 AI takeover plausible and warns OpenAI audit access falls short
stories.Summary:
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and co-founder of Apollo Research, said on the podcast MTS that he has reversed his view on short AI timelines, having called takeover by 2027 "very, very unlikely" two years ago. He said he is no longer sure and called it a negative update over the last two years. He endorsed the timeline Paul Christiano laid out on the Dwarkesh podcast, roughly a one-in-three chance of superintelligence within about a year. Hobbhahn said such an event is "less likely than not" in the next year. He said that if things move that fast, humans would not be able to correct it in any meaningful way.

Hobbhahn described a 6-to-12-month window in which substantial risk of full AI takeover would emerge. He said the risk is a speed problem, a correction lag, not a movie-style robot revolt. He said his earlier worry was "trained-in" scheming, where a model develops goal-seeking during reinforcement learning and improves itself past human supervision. He said the Hugging Face incident, an investigation Apollo was involved in, pushed him to take seriously a second pathway he calls "on the episode" risk. He said bad behavior in that pathway is committed spontaneously during a single rollout rather than baked in during training.

Apollo is one of four organizations OpenAI embedded inside its operations in November 2026, alongside METR, Transluce and Goodfire. OpenAI gave them access to model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems and technical documentation, framed as part of commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. Apollo's pilot tests four claims: training-process subversion, evaluation robustness, historical deployment review and monitorability. OpenAI supplies a whitelist of approved employees for Apollo to interview, and Apollo cannot speak with other OpenAI staff about the assessment or anything in scope. Apollo's public statement calls the pilot "an ambitious first step" whose access and disclosure rights "don't yet meet our bar for full embedded evaluations."

Hobbhahn said he understands why broader access would cede a lot of control to an outsider. He argued that science has always advanced through the informal channel, through "coffee chats" and things "heard over lunch." He said the field has to be robust enough that even if any particular developer was trying to hide something, the external evaluator would find it. He said that is a necessary condition for a field like this to exist, and that "Right now, we're just nowhere near that."

He wants embedded evaluation to become a professional field with nuclear-inspection-grade powers, analogous to nuclear inspections, food inspections or cyber security. The Verge reported a six-person Apollo team spending four months inside OpenAI, with conversations logged and no access to internal messaging tools such as Slack. The research community has read that as well short of the employee-level access Sam Altman previously promised. Hobbhahn said he expects little internal effect, because only a handful of lab staff would interact with the evaluators.

He said he expects a real external effect, with a trusted outside voice able to correct public misreadings in both directions. Anthropic was preparing a listing with an IPO expected to raise as much as $85 billion. Earlier in November the S&P 500 slid 10% from its October peak into correction territory, a seven-day losing streak reaching back to February 2020, and even NVIDIA's strong earnings and Anthropic's listing failed to bring buyers back. SoftBank's Masayoshi Son, who has poured roughly $64.6 billion into OpenAI for about a 13% stake, publicly conceded that skipping Anthropic was a mistake.

Asian family offices have reportedly been paying premiums of 30% for fund stakes that merely touch Anthropic or OpenAI paper. The articles say to watch whether OpenAI's approved-interviewee list widens to direct employee access. They also say to watch whether METR, Transluce and Goodfire adopt Apollo's same four-claim template. The articles say Hobbhahn's 2027 timeline is the headline, but the access terms decide whether anyone outside the building can constrain anything at all.

stories.Headline: UNESCO and the EU launch training for 18,000 Nigerian teachers in digital pedagogy and AI
stories.Summary:
UNESCO and the European Union, working with the Government of Katsina State, launched a training program for 18,000 teachers on November 10, 2026. This initiative focuses on digital pedagogy and the responsible use of artificial intelligence to improve teaching and learning across Nigeria. The national flag-off ceremony took place in Katsina State and included various education stakeholders and traditional leaders. Training activities began on November 10 and will continue through the end of November 2026.

The program requires teachers in Adamawa, Bayelsa, Enugu, Katsina, Oyo, and Plateau states to develop practical digital competencies. It utilizes 13 training modules that were developed after an assessment of more than 10,000 teachers. These modules teach educators how to use technology for lesson preparation, the creation of learning materials, and student assessment. This effort is part of the second phase of the Education and Youth Empowerment Initiative in Nigeria, which is funded by the European Union.

UNESCO Representative Dr. Isaías Barreto da Rosa stated that technology should support teachers and learners without replacing human relationships. Governor Malam Dikko Umaru Radda, represented by Commissioner Yusuf Sulaiman Jibia, noted that these digital tools improve instructional delivery and learner engagement. Ambassador Gautier Mignot of the European Union reaffirmed a commitment to helping Nigeria prepare its education sector for the digital age. These leaders emphasized that professional judgment and empathy remain essential to the learning process.

The initiative adopts an inclusive and ethical approach to ensure that digital transformation does not increase existing inequalities. By strengthening teacher resilience and capacity, the program aims to improve the overall quality of education in Nigeria. Participating teachers are encouraged to apply their new knowledge directly within their classrooms to boost productivity. Stakeholders are now urged to maintain consistent monitoring and evaluation of the program to ensure its long-term success.

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines Lab releases Inkling 2 Mini multimodal model for local AI setups
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines Lab released the Inkling 2 Mini model on November 20, 2026, to provide cutting-edge performance for local AI setups. This new multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model uses a looped transformer architecture to increase its capacity without adding more physical parameters. It features approximately 26 billion physical total parameters and 3 billion active parameters per token for its processing tasks. The model accepts both text and image inputs and supports a context size of one million tokens for users. A DSpark drafter is included with the release to provide additional speed-up at a small cost to memory.

The model has 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop for 48 logical layers. It uses a hidden size of 2,304 and selects eight experts from 128 per layer, unlike the 384 in Small. Weights are shipped in mixed-precision format using NVFP4 and MXFP8, with support for transformers, MLX, Llama App, and SGLang production deployments. The decoder runs layers 0 to 5 once, layers 6 to 17 three times, and layers 18 to 23 once. Each six-layer block contains five sliding-window layers with 1,024 tokens and one full-attention layer using dynamic key and value convolutions.

Thinking Machines Lab stated that this model is a refreshingly new great local model designed specifically for smaller AI setups. They noted that in their vibe tests, the performance is at least comparable with the Qwen 3.8 27B model. The developers mentioned that more validation is needed, but they are super excited about the release of this specific model. They provided a research artifact called TML-d24-varloop-research that allows users to set a variable number of loop passes. They explained that setting one or two passes instead of three makes inference faster, though generation quality may drop.

The model leads in 32 out of 48 benchmarks in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, including coding and reasoning. It outperforms Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8 27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL across various knowledge and safety categories. In coding, it leads in FrontierCode v2.0 and ties with Qwen 3.8 27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, but trails on AutomationBench-AA. Users can adjust reasoning effort from none at 0.0 to max at 0.99, with a default high setting of 0.9. The model can also perform tool calling, such as getting the current temperature for a specific city and country.

The developers based this approach on architectures like Nanbeige, which previously explored the concept of looping within a transformer model. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages, and a gating controller decides how much input to forget or add. The router uses SwiGLU experts, and the text decoder width is 2,304 while the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Attention uses 24 query heads and eight KV heads, along with learned relative position logits and a learned sink. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers stored in the checkpoint while maintaining 48 total layer visits.

Next, users can run the model on macOS or Windows via Llama App using GGUF 4-bit or 8-bit quants. Linux users can serve the model from the CLI or use SGLang on SM103 hardware for production datacenter deployments. The research variant allows for further testing of variable loop passes to balance inference speed against the quality of generations. The articles leave open the final results of the deeper evaluation for the variable loop research artifact and further validation. They also leave the full list of benchmark scores to be viewed on the official Inkling 2 Mini model card.

stories.Headline: Baseten releases two open-weight decision models that top the Artificial Analysis Decision Index
stories.Summary:
Baseten released two open-weight decision models called bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 21, 2026. These tools are built on the Gemma 4 backbone and do not write text for users. Instead, they provide calibrated probabilities for score, choice, and yes or no questions. The company designed these models to handle routing, guardrail pipelines, and ticket triage tasks.

The bison-1 model is a 31B dense model, while groundhog-1 is a 26B mixture-of-experts model with 4B active parameters. Both models increase the context window from 16k to 128k tokens and can accept images. Bison-1 scored 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, ranking first among 19 models. This score is one point higher than the 75 achieved by Liquid AI's d1.2-ultra.

Baseten stated that using soft labels in the training mix helped the models report uncertainty more accurately. This method resulted in a Brier score of 0.14, which is the lowest and best on the index. The company noted that bison-1 ranks first on four of six index components. They also reported LongMemEval M scores of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1.

These new releases join the existing Qwen-based lineup consisting of mammoth-1, elephant-1, and joey-1. Baseten describes this new pair as the first models they have built on an American backbone. The weights for both models are available on Hugging Face under MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses. Users can also access these decision models through the Baseten Model APIs.

stories.Headline: Ineffable founder David Silver says superintelligence is near and urges safety work now
stories.Summary:
David Silver, a Google DeepMind veteran and founder of the neolab Ineffable, told the Slush audience in Helsinki that AI could become smarter than humans at virtually everything within a few years, and he described the arrival of superintelligence as a matter of when rather than if. He said he believes the technology is close and that people should take the prospect seriously rather than dismiss it. Ineffable has raised a $4.8bn round led by Lightspeed, with Nvidia and Google among the investors, according to the article. Silver previously led the AlphaGo project at DeepMind, the system that beat the world champion at the board game Go.

Silver said the race requires thinking hard about safety, and he argued that the field needs to work out how to keep powerful systems under control before they arrive. He described the goal as building systems that remain answerable to humans and said the industry should not treat the problem as someone else's to solve. The article says Ineffable is working on what Silver calls "magic" superintelligence, and it notes that the company has not published technical details of how it plans to achieve this. Silver also said the singularity, the point at which machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence, is just over the horizon.

Silver is responsible for leading Ineffable and for setting out its safety approach, and he used his Slush talk to call for serious work on the problem rather than slogans. He said he does not think the risks can be waved away and that researchers should be honest about how little is known. The article reports that he compared the current moment to the early days of other transformative technologies, though it gives few specifics of that comparison. He said the company's investors understand the stakes and that the funding gives Ineffable room to pursue the work.

The context is a crowded field in which several labs are racing toward more capable systems, and the article says regulators and researchers are debating how to oversee them. What happens next depends on whether Ineffable publishes more about its methods and whether the safety questions Silver raised get taken up by others in the industry. stories.Headline: Deep learning models fail to beat standard risk scores for cardiac surgery mortality
stories.Summary:
A systematic review published in The Cardiothoracic Surgeon found that deep learning algorithms do not outperform conventional risk scores or standard statistical models in predicting short-term mortality after adult cardiac surgery. The investigation re-examined the published literature to determine whether complex neural architectures provide measurable clinical discrimination gains over long-standing tools. The review was reported by bioengineer.org on November 23, 2026. The authors concluded that the available clinical evidence supporting deep learning as a replacement for established surgical risk scores remains sparse, inconsistent, and burdened by high or unclear risk of bias. Across four primary studies meeting strict methodological inclusion criteria and comprising five cohort-level comparisons, the deep learning systems failed to demonstrate superiority.

The review compared deep learning models against the European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II, the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality, and refitted logistic regression equations evaluated in identical patient cohorts. In four comparisons reporting numerical discrimination metrics, none favored the deep learning model: one showed identical discrimination and three numerically favored the conventional comparator. None of the observed differences met conventional thresholds for statistical significance. The review was registered in the PROSPERO prospective international register under registration identifier CRD420261354546. The authors systematically searched MEDLINE through PubMed, Europe PMC, Lens.org Scholarly Works, and IEEE Xplore across September 27 and 28, 2026.

The authors noted that institutional access limitations prevented searches of Embase, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, representing an incomplete search relative to their initial registered protocol. Study selection yielded an initial pool of 1,845 records, from which 515 duplicate entries were removed before screening. Of the remaining 1,330 titles and abstracts, 1,254 were excluded, leaving 76 full reports sought for retrieval. The researchers successfully assessed 54 full-text publications after 22 reports could not be retrieved. Of the 54 candidate papers, 35 were excluded for specific deficiencies, and ultimately only four studies representing five distinct cohort-level comparisons satisfied every eligibility requirement.

Raghu and colleagues developed a 42-layer Inception v3 convolutional neural network fine-tuned on preoperative chest radiographs at a single United States medical center. When tested against STS-PROM among patients undergoing STS index procedures, the chest-radiograph model yielded lower area under the receiver operating characteristic curve discrimination values in both a temporal test cohort of 2,300 patients (0.829 versus 0.884; difference -0.055, P = .20) and an external validation cohort of 1,905 patients at a second hospital (0.738 versus 0.803; difference -0.065, P = .14). Salikhanov and colleagues assessed a two-hidden-layer perceptron against logistic regression among 3,483 patients undergoing isolated coronary artery bypass grafting at a Swiss center. Lippmann and Shahian examined neural networks alongside logistic regression across 80,606 patients from the 1993 STS national database, showing areas under the curve of 0.761 and 0.762, respectively. Benedetto and colleagues evaluated a two-hidden-layer perceptron against logistic regression refitted to EuroSCORE predictors in 28,761 procedures at a United Kingdom center, yielding an area under the curve of 0.77 compared with 0.80 for logistic regression.

Methodological quality appraisal using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool for artificial intelligence, known as PROBAST + AI, demonstrated that every study in the primary synthesis exhibited high or unclear risk of bias in at least one domain. In Raghu and colleagues, inclusion required a posterior-anterior radiograph available in only 70 percent of patients, and the cohort was 96 percent non-Hispanic White. Salikhanov and colleagues analyzed only 87 total mortality events and omitted calibration analysis entirely. Lippmann and Shahian relied on single-value mode or median imputation and analyzed clinical data from 1993. Benedetto and colleagues treated missing predictors as absent and did not report formal comparative significance tests for discrimination differences.

In Benedetto and colleagues, every evaluated model was miscalibrated on the calibration belt, and the neural network exhibited a 64.2 percent increase in its goodness-of-fit statistic compared with just 15.9 percent for logistic regression. A critical secondary synthesis examined fifteen studies whose neural network depth could not be verified from the source text. Twelve of these reports provided numerically extractable discrimination data, and across these twelve comparisons the neural network achieved a higher area under the curve in four instances and a lower area under the curve in eight, with a median difference of -0.004 and an interquartile range from -0.024 to 0.027. The sole notable comparison favoring artificial intelligence emerged from Allou and colleagues, who evaluated an adapted TabBERT tabular transformer against EuroSCORE II in 165,640 patients across 43 French centers.

stories.Headline: Singapore SMEs use artificial intelligence to scale operations and reduce resource limitations
stories.Summary:
The Infocomm Media Development Authority and Singapore Business Federation organized the inaugural SME AI Impact Awards 2026. Thirty winners were named from 290 nominations across 21 different industries. These small and medium enterprises used artificial intelligence to scale their operations. The awards recognized firms for creating their own solutions or deploying customized products. This event highlighted how AI helps smaller firms tackle work requiring bigger budgets.

Oceanus Media Global won the SME Innovation Excellence Award for its AI integrated production pipeline. IYLA Collective and You Tiao Man both received the SME Adoption Excellence Award. IYLA Collective uses Claude tools costing 3,000 dollars a year for its beauty business. You Tiao Man built an AI Operations Co-Pilot using Claude and n8n. These companies are based in Singapore and operate in media, beauty, and food.

SBF chief executive officer Kok Ping Soon said AI provides capabilities previously requiring larger teams. OpenAI international managing director Oliver Jay suggested employees build tools around work they know best. Oceanus Media Global chief executive officer Nick Tan said AI allows co-owning films with partners. IYLA Collective founder Lim Yi Ying stated AI changed what her small team can take on. You Tiao Man founder Audrey Chew noted the tool helps track orders across channels.

The awards affected 30 winning firms that now face fewer resource limitations. IYLA Collective customers can now use a customized product bundle page for National Day. You Tiao Man clients benefit from fewer missed deliveries and better order consolidation. Oceanus Media Global partners with firms from South Korea and Australia on movie projects. These SMEs now compete in areas that once demanded specialist expertise or manual effort.

Oceanus Media Global launched in 2020 and shifted toward original content and hybrid filmmaking in 2024. IYLA Collective sold through its own online store for more than three years before retail. You Tiao Man struggled with six different order formats from Shopify, TikTok Shop, and WhatsApp. IYLA Collective began testing AI tools in early 2025 to analyze sales and content. Oceanus Media Global drew inspiration from Hollywood productions like The Mandalorian and Oblivion.

Oceanus Media Global plans to take on as many as 12 multi-location projects annually. IYLA Collective will launch a customer app built with Claude Code by year end. Lim Yi Ying aims to expand into the region and launch own-brand products. You Tiao Man staff will continue maintaining AI workflows to reduce reliance on external vendors. The articles leave open how other SMEs in the 21 industries will adopt AI.

stories.Headline: Nvidia falls 14% as AI stocks plunge and Huang prepares for Senate testimony
stories.Summary:
On Friday, 2026-11-21, the US stock market suffered what the article called a "Black Friday" overnight, with the AI sector crashing sharply, according to a November 21 report from Zhidx. Nvidia's share price plummeted 14%, Dell dropped 11%, Anthropic fell 9%, Oracle, SpaceX and Tesla all slumped 8%, Meta declined 6%, and Amazon shed 4%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 10.7% on Friday, marking a cumulative 43% drop from its peak in June. SanDisk plunged 16%, Micron Technology dropped 14%, AMD fell 13%, Western Digital, Broadcom and Marvell all slumped 12%, Applied Materials declined 11%, Lam Research shed 10%, TSMC fell 9%, Intel and Texas Instruments both dropped 8%, and ASML tumbled 7%. The VIX index once surged to 40 points, hitting its highest level since April 2025, and according to CoinGlass a total of 271,500 users were liquidated in the past 24 hours, with total liquidation amounts reaching 1.79 billion US dollars.

As of the latest US market close, Nvidia had recorded declines for 7 consecutive trading days, and from its peak on October 6 its share price had fallen by a cumulative 47.5%, its longest losing streak since 2008, wiping out 2.74 trillion US dollars (about 18.30 trillion yuan) in total market value. Since Jensen Huang's resignation was announced on November 12, Nvidia's market value had evaporated by approximately 1 trillion US dollars (about 6.68 trillion yuan). Anthropic, which just went public this Thursday, saw its share price fall close to its IPO offering price at one point, then narrowed its decline to close down 8.5%, with its total market value dropping to 1.18 trillion US dollars (about 7.88 trillion yuan). The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index plummeted 5.6%, marking its 7th consecutive trading day of decline, with a cumulative 10.4% drop this week, the largest single-week decline in more than 6 years, and the index has fallen 20% from its intraday high on October 6. The S&P 500 Index fell 3.7%, with a cumulative decline of more than 10% from its high in October, and the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note fell 0.1 percentage point to 4.94%.

According to Reuters, two people familiar with the matter said the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating possible accounting issues at Nvidia. An aide to U.S. Republican Senator Tim Scott released a statement on local time Friday saying that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify at a public hearing of the U.S. Senate. Jensen Huang has also agreed to attend a closed-door meeting with three committees of the U.S. House of Representatives on December 1. U.S. President Trump said at a White House press conference on Friday that "we have to protect our brilliant people, and Jensen Huang is one of them," adding that he would love to see Jensen Huang come out with a big apology and come back. Trump said he really wants Jensen Huang to come back and wants to see him get a second chance, and that if the company is smart it will bring that brilliant man back, accept the apology, and let him go back to work.

During the latest earnings call this week, Colette Kress, interim CEO and CFO of Nvidia, said the company will be more cautious about AI industry financing transactions in the future. Nvidia's latest quarterly financial report exceeded expectations, raised its performance guidance for fiscal year 2028, and promised to give employees pre-emptive pay raises and additional stock grants, but these failed to stop the sell-off. Nvidia used to be the company with the highest market value in the world, but now its market value has dropped to 3.03 trillion US dollars (about 20.23 trillion yuan), ranking after Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet, the parent company of Google. The last time Nvidia's market value stood at around 3 trillion US dollars was in May last year. According to CNBC reports, the last time Nvidia saw such a severe consecutive weekly decline was during the 2008 financial crisis, when Nvidia's quarterly revenue was less than 1 billion US dollars, while today Nvidia earns more than 1 billion US dollars in a single day.

Concerns about the AI bubble began to spread around the middle of this year, and it was not until last month, as the trend that major economies such as the United States need to raise interest rates further to curb inflation became increasingly obvious, that the sell-off really began to accelerate. This week the sharp plunge in global financial markets deteriorated drastically, with concerns over AI and U.S. interest rates triggering large-scale sell-offs across assets from stocks to copper and gold. According to Reuters, since hitting its peak in August this year, the total market value of global stock markets has evaporated by nearly 9 trillion US dollars (about 60.10 trillion yuan). This sharp plunge is the latest sign that enthusiasm in the AI sector has shifted into concerns over the massive spending and borrowing by tech giants to invest in AI infrastructure. Investors are increasingly worried about Nvidia's future after Jensen Huang's departure, and are paying growing attention to circular AI financing transactions.

If the hearing proceeds as planned, this will be Jensen Huang's first public testimony since his resignation. For investors, questions remain over whether Nvidia relies more on Jensen Huang's vision and adventurous spirit, or has become a company that places greater emphasis on rigorous financial planning, and whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and maintain its strong influence in the AI market without Jensen Huang. The article states that every move of AI giants and semiconductor giants such as Nvidia may trigger market turmoil at a time when investors are extremely sensitive to AI spending and returns. The article leaves open the outcome of the SEC investigation into possible accounting issues at Nvidia. The article also leaves open whether the Senate hearing and the December 1 closed-door House meeting will proceed as planned.

stories.Headline: Former DeepSeek core member Tony Zhang founds Simplex AI to develop personal computer agents
stories.Summary:
Tony Zhang announced the open source of his personal agent product Linger on November 19. He is a former Project Lead of DeepSeek-VL and a core member of that lab. Zhang founded Simplex AI to develop this new AI technology for personal computers. He started his entrepreneurial journey in 2025 after leaving DeepSeek in March 2024. This move marks the first public case of a DeepSeek core author starting a company.

Linger runs on personal computers to operate software, process emails, and enable multiple AI assistants. It uses PolyStrata, a local inference project created by an 18-year-old developer named VecSzn. Simplex AI, also known as Hangzhou Topology Lingxi Technology Co., Ltd., was established February 24, 2025. The company has registered capital of 1 million yuan and secured 6 million US dollars. GL Ventures led this seed round of financing announced in January 2026.

Zhang Bo said he learned the importance of focusing on one thing from DeepSeek's founder. He told his research team to pursue quality over the number of papers they publish. Zhang hopes to bring AI back to personal computers to change the current data center model. He noted that users currently pay per Token for usage of most large AI models. He wants users to have an AI assistant that keeps working without cloud reliance.

Users on the X platform asked if the product could connect to mobile phones. Some users reported encountering model download problems during the installation of the new software. Linger affects ordinary computer users by reducing the cost of running large AI models. The product allows users to avoid paying Token fees to cloud model service providers. However, users must still bear their own costs for electricity and necessary computer hardware.

Zhang earned a bachelor's degree from Zhejiang University in 2013 and a doctorate in 2019. He worked at Microsoft Research Asia on projects like VQ-Diffusion and Rodin before joining DeepSeek. At DeepSeek, he helped develop the first-generation large language model and the DeepSeek-VL project. He later became a PhD supervisor at the State Key Lab of CAD&CG at Zhejiang University. DeepSeek's core team is stable, with only 6.4 percent of paper contributors having departed.

Simplex AI plans to support mobile phone functions within one month of the Linger release. The team is working to fix a reproduced bug regarding the model download process. Simplex AI also plans to launch a hosted version, though the price is not announced. The articles leave open whether ordinary users can actually use the technology in practice. It remains to be seen if third party developers will verify the enterprise test data.

stories.Headline: Apple develops autonomous AI agents to perform tasks across apps independently
stories.Summary:
Apple is developing its own autonomous AI Agent to perform tasks across apps and plan workflows independently. The company is the last tech giant to enter this market during the first year of AI Agents. Two job postings related to these agents appeared on the official Apple website in mid-November. Apple wants Siri to evolve from giving verbal commands to taking actual actions on its own. This move follows a trend started by generative AI access for ordinary users in 2023.

The system requires a senior engineering manager to develop assistants with proactive service capabilities that operate computers like humans. It must browse the web, run commands, write code, and coordinate multiple specialized sub-agents to execute multi-step tasks. A senior applied AI engineer must establish personal intelligent evaluation benchmarks and use feedback mechanisms to optimize performance. Candidates are required to use Claude Code and Codex in their daily work. macOS 27.3 Beta 2 adjusts authorization for device control and full disk access permissions.

Bloomberg reports that Apple is developing this autonomous AI Agent to enable independent planning of workflows. Apple's job postings describe a vision where AI can select the appropriate tool for each step of a task. The company emphasizes the need for privacy, security, sandbox isolation, and permission management in these roles. Apple aims for the agent to find ways to complete tasks on its own and become more reliable. The company wants to prevent agents from accessing user data and devices at will.

Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, Tencent, and ByteDance are already pushing AI Agents into real work and life scenarios. Meta's Muse has over 10 million setup users in the US and Canada, with 25 percent using it daily. OpenAI launched Dots in September, which connects to over 4,000 apps and works continuously in the background. Anthropic offers Claude Code and Claude Duet, with the latter currently open for research preview. These competitors have already accumulated millions of users and started generating actual revenue.

Apple relies on a huge ecosystem consisting of the iPhone, Mac, and the App Store. The company is now preparing for the deep involvement of AI within its operating system. Recent updates allow users to authorize specific apps and folders and provide status prompts during AI control. This follows the success of Meta's Muse, which handles travel planning, restaurant reservations, and document sorting. Other agents like Dots and Claude Duet now have their own working environments and external service connections.

Apple considered launching these related products as early as the end of 2027. Development of the autonomous AI Agent is still in the early stage. The company must solve the balance between agent capability and data security together. The articles do not state the exact date the product will be available to the public. It remains open how third-party Agents will be affected by the new macOS permission rules.

stories.Headline: Dispatchers and bank staff quietly override AI systems as accountability stays with humans
stories.Summary:
At the end of 2022 a multinational bank approved an AI system to automate routine credit decision-making, and during the pilot phase the system processed applications faster than human staff, made fewer errors, and promised significant cost reductions. The bank's risk management department endorsed it, the compliance department signed off on it, and the CEO publicly promoted the system as strong proof of the bank's march into the future. Six months on, the AI system continued to score users' credit applications and generate recommendations, but most application documents still required manual review, and exceptions were piling up. Measures originally designed as temporary safety safeguards, such as dual-review thresholds and manual confirmation flags, gradually solidified into permanent process steps. Although the AI system was integrated into the bank's workflow, in reality most final decisions were never made by it.

The justifications offered were that the organization was not fully ready, the model needed further optimization, employees required more training, and change is always difficult, yet the technology is already practically viable, the economic benefits are clear, and the AI system received formal and enthusiastic approval from the organization. The only thing it never truly obtained is empowerment, the full backing of the organization to make decisions within clearly defined boundaries. A multinational manufacturing enterprise launched an AI-based demand forecasting system, but its planning department still stuck to old workflows and only treated the AI's forecasts as reference points. A healthcare network introduced an AI-assisted triage system that shortened patient waiting times and improved triage consistency, and clinicians recognized the accuracy of the AI model, yet they still insisted on manually reviewing most of the AI's recommendations. As a result, the triage system was mostly used for archiving rather than supporting decision-making.

The problem is not that the pilot project failed, but that accountability and legitimacy within the organization failed to evolve in tandem to support the application of the AI system. The author calls a legitimacy architecture a consensus within an organization about who has the authority to make decisions and whose decisions can be trusted. Many organizations are continuously raising their level of intelligence, yet they have not reshaped their organizational structures around this change. Previous waves of automated decision-making, such as ERP systems and credit scoring, exposed the same organizational inertia, in which enterprises introduced systems capable of making better decisions yet retained their existing human decision-making authority structures, which often led to the rejection of decisions made by the systems. In the 1990s, when ERP systems such as those from Oracle and SAP emerged, they promised centralized, transparent management and operational optimization across the entire enterprise.

Nestlé USA's experience implementing an ERP system is highly illustrative, because before it the company's various departments operated independently, each responsible for its own production, costs, and supplier contracts. When the ERP system required departments to give up this autonomy and follow unified business processes, employees who were still accountable for local business outcomes naturally had good reasons to insist on making their own decisions. Even though the system generated unified, consolidated forecasts, the accountability mechanisms at the time rewarded local adjustments to or override of the system's recommendations. Tom Davenport of Babson College pointed out that the company treated the ERP system at the time purely as a technology deployment, rather than as a comprehensive management process reshaping. Studies on auto loans show that compared with manual underwriting, algorithmic underwriting not only delivered higher loan profits but also reduced default rates, and the most significant performance gap between the two occurred precisely in segments where loan officers, out of self-serving considerations, fiercely guarded their discretionary power.

Other studies found that loan officers manipulated input data and scoring results to push borderline applications across the approval threshold, in order to earn performance bonuses tied to transaction volume, so it looked like approval authority had been delegated to the model, but ultimate responsibility still rested with the relevant human staff. The airline industry's experience with revenue management systems offers a useful contrasting case, because airlines clarified the scenarios suitable for human intervention, standardized the escalation process for issues, adjusted performance evaluation methods, and established the professional legitimacy of following the system. The system's authority was not established because of the algorithm's perfect performance, but because airlines changed their organizational governance mechanisms for automated systems. Davenport, Erik Brynjolfsson, and others have pointed out this phenomenon before, and the article reveals the root cause behind it: as long as individual employees are still required to take responsibility for the outcomes of system operations, decision-making authority will never truly shift. Enterprises must resolve this disconnect between rights and responsibilities, otherwise employees will continue to bypass AI systems, not out of resistance, but purely out of self-protection.

No amount of training or communication can bridge this gap, and enterprises may successfully implement changes yet permanently relegate the technology to an advisory role, or provide employees with ample psychological safety yet still penalize employees who follow the system's instructions when decision errors occur. Some argue that organizational inertia creates resistance, but in AI applications what is often seen is superficial compliance: dashboards are running, workflows have incorporated the system, and employees are all using it, yet the AI system never truly gains decision-making power. Research on automation complacency suggests that humans tend to defer to machines too easily, but this phenomenon does not apply here, because the company's accountability system makes it professionally risky to blindly follow AI systems. Research on the productivity paradox, while pointing out that information technology investments fail to translate into performance improvements, mostly does not explain the organizational mechanisms that lead to this outcome. Ethan Bernstein's research on transparency shows that employees under surveillance will hide their actual operations to avoid scrutiny, but they also use explicit compliance mechanisms, such as archived exception operations, escalation procedures, and multi-level review processes, as tools to maintain their own control.

In most cases enterprises adopt some kind of AI system and promote it vigorously in internal corporate demonstrations, but in reality whenever AI and humans disagree, humans quietly prevail in the end. Out of prudence, experts always reshape the boundaries of AI systems by adding more review links, slightly lowering trigger thresholds, increasing the number of archived override operations, and enabling new flagging mechanisms for sensitive cases, and individually each of these settings and adjustments is justifiable, but taken together the consequences are catastrophic. UPS's deployment of its ORION route-planning system vividly illustrates this tension, because when the system was first rolled out in 2013, many drivers treated the routes it generated as advisory suggestions, preferring to rely on their own local experience and customer relationships. Over time UPS adjusted its performance evaluation criteria so that drivers were no longer compared against their own past performance but assessed against the routes set by ORION, with the system tracking their compliance with the routes, and as a result following the algorithm became a legitimate part of the drivers' job responsibilities.

Recently the author observed the same dynamic at another multinational logistics company that handles high-value cargo transportation for enterprise clients, where during the pilot project an AI route-planning system drastically reduced cargo delays and improved asset utilization, and the company immediately approved the system for adoption. Dispatchers privately admitted that the system often generated better routes than the ones they devised themselves, but after the full rollout dispatchers kept adjusting routes in their daily work, for long-standing clients, cargo with internal political importance to the company, and drivers they trusted more. At first these adjustments were seen as fine-tuning, but over time the AI system no longer functioned as a decision engine, and its outputs only served as the starting point for discussing subsequent plans. When senior management pushed for full adoption of the AI route-planning system, dispatchers neither argued that the system was flawed nor refused to use it, and instead they added measures: flagging sensitive cargo, adding escalation links, and lowering the thresholds for triggering reviews.

One dispatcher explained the logic with disarming candor, saying that if a decision made by the system goes wrong his name is the one signed on the report, and if a mistake is made in a decision he made himself at least he can explain it. This dispatcher was neither troubled by the AI system nor felt a lack of security, he simply accurately interpreted where the responsibility lay. Research on professional identity threat shows that when practitioners' professional skills face automation substitution, they experience genuine anxiety about their social status, professional value, and future career prospects, and this anxiety affects their behavior, and these behaviors are neither irrational nor trivial. stories.Headline: A CIO says organizational culture and clear responsibilities, not AI tools, determine enterprise efficiency
stories.Summary:
A CIO friend of a company in Lao Yang's group posted on November 20, 2026, that organizational efficiency cannot be improved by tools alone, and that an agile organization can be efficient even via emails. The same passage said that those who pass the buck all day cannot make good use of the best software in the world even if it is given to them free. Lao Yang wrote the article in Xiangjiang Digital Review, published with authorization from 36Kr, and 36Kr said the views are the author's own. Lao Yang recalled that a CIO friend from a manufacturing group was called out by the general manager that day about arguing over cross-departmental account reconciliation in WeChat groups for three days after adopting AI and buying collaboration software. The CIO replied that the problem was not the system but that no one was responsible for the result of the account reconciliation in the first place.

Lao Yang said the ceiling of organizational efficiency usually lies not in tools but in culture, consensus and collaboration mechanisms, and that technology is advancing while collaboration mechanisms stay stagnant. He said top leaders understand digital transformation as deploying systems, purchasing SaaS and installing models, while efficient organizations have transparent information, decentralized decision-making and clear responsibilities. He said that with these three points even primitive emails, asynchronous, traceable and group-sent for synchronization, achieve high efficiency because everyone knows who to turn to, what to respond and when. He said that with fragmented information and ambiguous rights and responsibilities, AI only makes wrong decisions faster and makes buck-passing reasons more technical. He described an enterprise that deployed an intelligent report system where, when data was wrong, everyone blamed the underlying calibers not being aligned and no one took responsibility.

Lao Yang said the tool did not improve efficiency but gave buck-passing a set of professional terms, and he thought of the word entropy. He said to judge an organization's entropy by one small thing: for a cross-departmental demand from initiation to closed loop, how many groups are created, how many hands it passes through and who makes the final decision. He said the more steps and the more chaotic the groups, the higher the entropy, and that in high-entropy organizations AI is not an antidote but an amplifier. He said enterprises must sort out information flow, rights and responsibilities before talking about tools, and that buck-passing reflects a lack of trust and result-oriented contractual spirit. He said AI and digital tools are levers that amplify executive power in healthy organizations and destructive power in organizations used to shirking responsibilities.

Lao Yang said AI's prediction reports become evidence for departments to attack each other and automated processes become an excuse, with people saying the system judged it automatically. He said the primary premise of AI implementation is a matter-oriented rather than person-oriented data culture, and without the courage and consensus to tell the truth with data, advanced AI tools can only write weekly reports or become an excuse. He said tools are neutral and what the organization turns them into depends on the organization itself. He said email suits teams with high self-discipline and high consensus, while many enterprises stuck in the agricultural era deploy interstellar battleship level collaboration software and AI middle platforms, so employees create small WeChat groups to complain and fill in data no one reads. He said AI implementation failures are often caused not by inaccurate algorithms but by collaboration maturity that cannot support tool complexity, which is production relations failing to adapt to advanced productivity.

Lao Yang said AI implementation should advance in small steps and reject the Great Leap Forward, starting with a small scenario with clear pain points and clear responsibility boundaries, such as financial invoice recognition or automatic classification of customer service work orders. He said light tools should come first and a heavy middle platform at the start is useless except for showing off. He said employees pass the buck mostly because of ambiguous areas in the process, and AI intervention only solidifies these holes with code, deeper and harder to find, while managers use diligence in AI technology to replace laziness in management. He gave the example of an approval process with unclear rights and responsibilities where, after AI intelligent approval, people argue about why AI judged this way and who set the rules, so the buck-passing shifts from people to algorithms and the algorithm takes the blame. He said AI is the accelerator of processes, not the repairman, and business process reengineering must come first, cutting off points that cause artificial buck-passing and clarifying responsibility boundaries with systems and SOPs before AI enters.

Lao Yang said the first step of process reengineering is often to write who on earth is responsible for the result into the system, and execution is the key. He said efficient organizations using emails have every sentence correspond to clear action items and responsible persons, a kind of mental digitalization with a common logic. He said the goal of AI is not to teach employees to operate software but to train the organization's best practices and consensus into the default workflow of AI, and without consensus on what a good solution is, AI solutions are picked on and rejected by departments based on their own interests. He said the highest state is system as code, consensus as algorithm, with 80% of efforts to unify business logic, precipitate knowledge assets and clarify evaluation criteria and 20% for purchasing computing power and training models, solidifying review standards into a reusable knowledge base and review checklist. He said not to let the IT department take the blame for poor organizational efficiency, and suggested that before any major AI or digital project, a team be asked whether it could push the matter forward with only emails and Excel without internet and software, solving people's problems first and then letting AI amplify efficiency.

stories.Headline: Major tech firms use existing ecosystems to compete in AI office software as models become commoditized
stories.Summary:
Major Chinese companies recently adjusted their organizational structures for AI office business to concentrate resources and use existing advantages in channels and ecosystems. ByteDance integrated Doubao, Feishu, and Volcano Engine in July, while Liang Rubo explained this arrangement at the September Feishu Conference. Tencent incorporated QClaw into WorkBuddy, and Alibaba merged three products into Tongyi Office under the DingTalk team. Baidu integrated internal products into Baidu Dazi, and Kingsoft Office shifted its main focus toward AI.

Tencent WorkBuddy connects to Hunyuan, DeepSeek, Zhipu GLM, Kimi, and MiniMax, while Doubao Work accesses Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, and two Doubao models. Tongyi Office launched ten models in mid-November, including self-developed Tongyi, DeepSeek, Kimi, and MiniMax, after briefly accessing external models in August. Microsoft Copilot adopts both OpenAI and Claude models, and packages AI functions into the E7 plan for 99 dollars per user monthly. Alibaba popularized the data mid-platform concept around 2015, but the company began weakening this specific approach around 2020.

Large enterprises claim that holding massive data provides a competitive advantage, but the author says getting departments to coordinate interests is difficult. These companies also argue that connecting systems to core processes creates customer reliance, though this can make product modification very slow. The author notes that the labor cost saved in some RPA projects is not even enough to maintain the software. Satya Nadella integrated OpenAI capabilities into the Office suite rather than making AI an independent product.

Users of WorkBuddy are partly driven by point subsidies and free traffic from WeChat, though this may not translate into long-term usage. Tencent relies on WeChat and WeCom traffic, while Alibaba uses DingTalk enterprise customers and Kingsoft uses government and enterprise channels. Baidu utilizes its search, cloud disk, and intelligent cloud systems, while Microsoft relies on the customer base from Windows and Office. These companies use traditional software industry tactics, making their AI office products increasingly similar to one another.

The articles state that many people initially thought new AI products would replace industry leaders and allow small companies to rise. However, big companies with existing customer relationships and complete product systems still occupy a favorable position because models are now accessible to all. The author explains that sorting messy data into usable information requires long-term accumulation that cannot be solved by simply switching models. This suggests that AI is currently being used by old companies to complete upgrades to their original systems.

The winner among these five major companies remains unknown because it is too early to tell who will prevail in this competition. The articles leave open whether a balance can be struck between product stability and the flexibility needed for models that update every half year. It remains unclear if a new player, developing outside the attention of leading enterprises, will emerge to re-divide the market. The realization process of technological change is described as more tortuous than initially expected.

stories.Headline: Angel Robotics lets people build and control robots without code through its phact and phorce platform
stories.Summary:
Angel Robotics, a wearable robotics company founded in 2017 by Kong Kyoung-chul, is pursuing a physical AI business strategy built on two technologies, the phact actuator and the phorce control platform of circuit boards and algorithms. Kong, who is also a professor of mechanical engineering at KAIST, described the goal as letting anyone build and control the robot they need without writing a single line of code. The company became the first Korean wearable robotics company to go public on the KOSDAQ in 2024, and its flagship products include the Angel Legs M20 and Angel Suit H10 rehabilitation robots. Those products combine phact, which works like a muscle, phorce, which controls movement, and AI that reads users' movement intentions in real time to assist them.

The company has secured coverage under Korea's national health insurance system for its products and has expanded into overseas markets including Malaysia. The platform's potential was shown at the first Robot Hackathon at KAIST in August, where all 10 teams of undergraduates from KAIST and Seoul National University, most without a formal robotics background, built robots with phact and phorce in just 100 hours. Their projects included robots for packing boxes and grilling lamb skewers, and some students went on to launch startups based on their creations. Kong said physical AI has a wide range of applications, noting that a robot filling containers with rice and one filling them with red beans require separate development because they involve different data.

Kong said the company spent years studying the resistance and friction of rehabilitation robots to help treat patients, and that this research has become a competitive advantage in the era of physical AI. He added that as the physical AI ecosystem expands, advances in data and lower component costs will create synergies with the wearable rehabilitation robot business. He also said there will be sufficient demand for the platform, and that the company will dramatically lower the barriers to physical AI so ordinary people can use it without difficulty. He said the company aims to become a leader in the "robots for all" ecosystem.

stories.Headline: Asian developers adopt Chinese open-weight AI models to lower costs and keep data onshore
stories.Summary:
Asian developers are adopting Chinese open-weight artificial intelligence models to obtain affordable and capable tools. This trend involves using models that allow anyone to download, fine-tune, and self-host trained parameters. These developments have become prominent through 2025 and 2026 across various Asian nations. The process allows startups and governments to keep data onshore and reduce costs. This adoption does not automatically create a state of dependence for the users.

In January 2025, India's Electronics and Information Technology Ministry allowed DeepSeek models on Indian servers. AI Singapore released SEA-LION in 2025, which was built on Alibaba's Qwen model. Thailand's OpenThaiGPT is fine-tuned on Qwen2.5, and DeepSeek's V4 was adapted for Huawei Ascend chips in April 2026. Alibaba opened a third Malaysian data center in 2025 and planned a second for the Philippines. Alibaba also launched an AI centre in Singapore to provide compute and token credits.

Karthik Nachiappan says that real lock-in occurs in the compute and cloud layers of the stack. He states that open weights are fungible and cannot be revoked once they are downloaded. He notes that Chinese models carry political and linguistic assumptions from their training. He argues that dependence is not inevitable but depends on what the region builds. He claims that China's head start may harden into dependence if Asia fails to act.

Many adopters use both U.S. and Chinese models to avoid being beholden to one vendor. Washington has barred DeepSeek from federal systems, which creates risks for firms with U.S. customers. Perplexity retrained the DeepSeek R1 model to remove Chinese state censorship from the system. Indian firms are affected by the trade-off between Chinese models and U.S. hardware export controls. Most businesses without spare engineers or GPUs cannot afford to host these models themselves.

Chinese models account for over 80 percent of open-model usage on OpenRouter. By August 2025, Qwen derivatives made up over 40 percent of new language-model derivatives on Hugging Face. Llama derivatives accounted for 15 percent of new language-model derivatives on Hugging Face during that time. India is investing 1.2 billion dollars in the IndiaAI Mission to deploy 38,000 subsidized GPUs. Sarvam AI developed models with 30 billion and 105 billion parameters to create a hedge.

Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max now require commercial agreements from large firms. Asia can preserve choice by building diversified compute and model-evaluation capacity. The region must also develop credible local alternatives to avoid long-term dependence. It remains unclear if demand for models is converting into cloud contracts in Asia. The articles leave open whether Asia can build the means to scrutinize and replace these models.

stories.Headline: PLA Daily writers urge China to grant frontline commanders more autonomy for AI and drone warfare
stories.Summary:
Since July 2026, commentators writing for the PLA Daily have urged the People's Liberation Army to grant frontline commanders more autonomy during combat. These writers argue that the rapid pace of drone warfare and artificial intelligence requires faster decision making on the battlefield. They suggest that subordinates should be able to act without waiting for orders from the centralized command structure. This shift is intended to help the military adapt to the evolving speed of modern electronic warfare.

The proposed changes would allow senior officers to set general objectives while letting lower level commanders decide how to achieve them. This approach mirrors the Western military concept of mission command, which is especially useful when communications are disrupted. The goal is to delegate tactical authority while ensuring that major military operations remain under strict central control. Such a system would allow for greater flexibility when battlefield conditions change unexpectedly during a conflict.

Analysts believe these articles reflect a long standing interest in flexible decision making based on lessons learned from the war in Ukraine. However, these experts question whether Beijing will actually loosen its grip on the tightly controlled military system. They remain uncertain about how much authority the central government is willing to give to officers in the field. The tension exists between the need for tactical speed and the desire for absolute political control.

Articles.Title: Can China’s top-down military adapt to the speed of AI and drone warfare? - South China Morning Post

stories.Headline: UN conference agrees watered-down deal on autonomous weapons rules
stories.Summary:
A United Nations conference focused on regulating autonomous weapons concluded with a weakened agreement after facing opposition from major arms producers. The United States, Russia, and Israel resisted stronger measures during the diplomatic talks that took place in Geneva. These discussions officially began on November 16 and eventually stretched into overtime due to various diplomatic disputes. Russia specifically objected to the participation of observers from the European Union and other civil society organizations. The final agreement involves one hundred and twenty-eight countries that are currently party to the Convention on Conventional Weapons.

These participating nations have pledged to develop a new set of rules for AI arms within two years. This timeline establishes a window for member states to negotiate the specific legal frameworks for autonomous systems. The resulting deal is described as watered-down because it lacks the stringent restrictions some nations desired. The responsibility for the outcome lies with the participating member states and the major powers that blocked stricter language.

These nations disagreed on the level of control required for weapons that can operate without human intervention. The delegates struggled to find common ground while balancing national security interests against global safety concerns. No specific quotes were provided, but the tension between arms producers and other nations defined the talks. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI arms safety: UN conference to regulate autonomous weapons ends with watered-down deal - CNA

stories.Headline: Flagship Pioneering invests £100 million to build AI-driven biotech companies in the UK
stories.Summary:
Flagship Pioneering said on Monday that it is opening its first lab for creating companies outside the United States, putting £100 million, or about $131.94 million, behind a new UK-based effort to fund and build AI-driven biotech companies. The move is a first for a firm that has created more than 130 companies, including Moderna, and that had operated only from the United States for more than 25 years. The announcement came after three years of groundwork in Britain, during which the company opened a London office in 2023 near the Francis Crick Institute in King's Cross. Its local team has since built partnerships with academia, government and regulatory groups.

The Flagship Origination lab will be anchored at the firm's London office, and the company hopes its £100 million will attract £500 million or more from partners. Flagship expects to recruit about 50 scientist-entrepreneurs and operators in Britain initially, and it said it will not buy into existing companies. Instead it plans to cast a wide net for partnerships with universities, corporations and funders. AI will run through every stage of the lab's work, from invention to clinical trials, according to the firm.

Noubar Afeyan, founder and CEO of the venture firm and chairman of Moderna, told Reuters that the company concluded this might well be the right next step in its evolution. He said the country's main draw is the National Health Service and the patient data it has gathered, which lets researchers begin with real-world evidence to find disease targets before developing drugs. He cautioned that the use of AI in the field is still early, saying he thinks AI's most fundamental contribution in the first instance will be to shed light on what is happening mechanistically in diseases. Flagship companies are already testing that approach, including drug developer Generate Biomedicines, which completed an early-stage trial of an AI-designed drug for asthma in Manchester.

Articles.Title: Venture firm Flagship bets £100 million to build AI-driven drug companies in Britain - CNA

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s record IPO coincides with a deepening AI selloff as Nvidia and chip peers slump
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed the largest IPO in history on November 19, 2026, a debut that was supposed to restore confidence in the artificial intelligence trade but instead coincided with a deepening selloff, according to The Wealth Advisor. The Nasdaq has surrendered its gains for the year, Nvidia has lost 42% of its value in four weeks, and the departure of CEO Jensen Huang has compounded that decline. Rival chipmaker AMD has fallen roughly 20% over the past month, while Micron Technology has lost more than a third of its value over the same period and now trades 50% below its June peak. The excitement surrounding Anthropic's offering could not overcome mounting concerns about data center financing, regulatory restrictions and the economics of AI investment.

Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James Investment Management, sees an opportunity in the wreckage and believes investors are selling high-quality companies alongside more speculative AI investments, creating what he calls a fire sale. He said the IPO may ultimately help investors distinguish between the businesses building AI infrastructure and those developing the technology itself, and that public disclosures from companies such as Anthropic should provide greater visibility into the economics of AI development. Speaking on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang, he said investors were finally getting details about what is underneath the curtain, and he hopes they will eventually recognize that many companies caught in the selloff remain fundamentally attractive. Orton also rejects comparisons with the dot-com collapse of 2000, noting that today's AI developers raised substantial private capital before entering public markets and that some recent selling may reflect portfolio managers protecting earlier gains as the year approaches its end, and he described the market as really healthy.

Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott is considerably less comfortable, having observed that money is leaving stocks altogether and moving into cash and Treasury securities rather than simply rotating out of expensive technology shares into defensive equities. The distinction is visible in the bond market, where the 10-year Treasury yield fell 14 basis points Friday to 4.91% as the equity selloff accelerated. McElligott is watching the coming week for signs that systematic investment strategies, including volatility-targeting funds, might begin buying again, since their participation could help stabilize prices, while a continued inability to rally would suggest the selling reflects something more persistent than a routine correction. UBS has downgraded U.S. equities from Attractive to Neutral, and David Lefkowitz, the firm's head of U.S. equities, still expects the S&P 500 to reach new highs in the months ahead, although he acknowledges that the balance between potential returns and risks has become less favorable.

The disagreement leaves investors confronting two very different interpretations of the same market, with Orton seeing fundamentally sound companies marked down indiscriminately and McElligott looking for evidence that investors have begun abandoning positions rather than merely taking profits. Both interpretations can be true for a time, and the difficulty is determining whether the selling has already created the bargains Orton anticipates or whether prices still have further to fall before buyers regain confidence. Anthropic's IPO was supposed to provide that confidence, and its failure to do so has left Wall Street with an uncomfortable possibility: even the companies best positioned to benefit from artificial intelligence may not be immune to a market reconsidering how much that future is worth.

Articles.Title: AI Stocks Are on Fire Sale. Wall Street Can't Agree Whether It's a Bargain
