stories.Headline: Greg Abel says Berkshire Hathaway can fund AI power needs through its utilities and energy businesses
stories.Summary:
The article, published by The Globe and Mail on November 22, 2026, was written by Motley Fool and appeared at 6:35PM CST. It says Berkshire Hathaway's next big AI bet could be hiding in plain sight. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is not exactly seen as an artificial intelligence play. It says the company may have more exposure to this emerging technology than you realize. The article states that the company's large utility and energy operations present opportunities for AI-related investment.

The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is usually classified as a finance business. It says the company is really a massive conglomerate with businesses including insurance, utilities, energy, manufacturing, housing, and retail. In Greg Abel's first annual letter as CEO, he reported that the company had 51 non-insurance operating businesses. In a previous letter, former CEO Warren Buffett said the company owned 189 operating businesses. The article says the definition of an operating business is probably responsible for the two different numbers.

The article states that Greg Abel is the CEO of Berkshire Hathaway. It says his acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison Home for $8.5 billion suggests he is not going to suddenly shift directions. The article states that Greg Abel noted at the start of 2026 that infrastructure built for hyperscalers and data centers must be paid for by those customers. It says he said this infrastructure must reflect the risks tied to step-changes in long-term demand. The article states that former CEO Warren Buffett long focused on acquiring boring businesses that were well run and attractively priced at the time of purchase.

The article states that the company's utility operations provide the electricity that powers AI. It says the energy business helps supply the natural gas that lets utilities, and increasingly AI companies, generate electricity. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway could easily afford to buy a technology business with its cash hoard of more than $370 billion. It says Chevron, a longtime holding in Berkshire Hathaway's stock portfolio, has agreed to build a power plant that will use Chevron-produced natural gas to supply dedicated power to data centers. The article states that data center operators appear increasingly willing to pay for infrastructure built for them.

The article states that it would be exciting if Berkshire Hathaway went out and bought a giant U.S. utility such as NextEra Energy. It says it would also be exciting if the company bought a large pipeline business such as Enterprise Products Partners. The article states that Greg Abel probably would not target companies of that scale. It says the CEO could certainly afford to buy smaller players in either sector. The article states that both the utility and midstream sectors are capital intensive.

The article states that utilities own massive power plants that take years to build and require huge sums of money. It says midstream companies are no different, with their pipelines, storage, refineries, and transportation assets. The article states that it is not unusual for a utility or midstream company to have multi-billion-dollar capital investment plans extending as far as five years into the future. It says Berkshire Hathaway could make very large capital investments within its existing operations, and that this is probably the most likely outcome. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is unlikely to start buying up AI technology businesses.

stories.Headline: Etsy lets third parties train AI on seller artwork as artists close shops in protest
stories.Summary:
Etsy updated its terms of service to allow AI training using artwork posted on its platform. This policy change caused an uproar among independent artists and small business communities. Some artists with tens of thousands of followers closed their shops in protest. These creators shared their decisions through posts on X and Instagram. The new terms of use go into effect on December 16.

The updated language appears under Section 5, titled Your Content, in the terms of use. It allows Etsy and third party partners to develop, train, test, and improve machine learning technologies. This follows clearer restrictions on AI use that the company released in October. The older terms, effective through December 15, contained no mention of artificial intelligence. The new policy grants a worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, and perpetual license to use content.

James Ossman, the vice president of customer operations, addressed the changes in a November 16 blog post. He stated that Etsy does not use content to train models designed to copy original work. Ossman claimed the company does not claim ownership over the creations of its sellers. He said the goal is to connect unique items with buyers. He argued that these broad rights are necessary to keep the platform going.

Some artists claim the terms allow Etsy to train generative AI on their artwork. One post with nearly 100,000 likes alleged that Etsy can resell data to third parties. Many vendors rely on the marketplace to make sales and feel their art is being scraped. These creators are affected by the potential for AI to replace their creativity. They worry that staying on the platform means their art belongs to the company.

Etsy previously stated it does not claim ownership over shop names, profile pictures, or listing photos. The company uses content to resize listings for its mobile app and translate descriptions. It also uses seller content to feature listing photos in marketing campaigns. The company trains models to identify fraudulent accounts and provide tailored recommendations to buyers. It also builds AI-powered tools to help sellers run their businesses more efficiently.

Etsy has not clarified if it uses generative AI to create advertisements from listing photos. The company has not responded to requests for further clarification on these specific practices. While the terms mention opt-out rights, the privacy policy shows no way to opt out of training. United States users can only opt out of the sale of their personal data. Courts are still deciding if it is legal to scrape copyrighted content for AI.

stories.Headline: AI surveillance software creates false movement narratives by inventing journeys between camera gaps
stories.Summary:
Burak Oktenli wrote an analysis on November 23, 2026, about AI surveillance risks. He explained how multi-camera tracking can create false narratives of a person's movements. This happens when software joins authentic clips into a continuous route despite gaps. The system may invent a journey that the cameras never actually recorded. Such errors can occur when cameras lose sight of a subject.

The author mentions Hong Kong activated AI facial-recognition in its SmartView network on 16 November. The Metropolitan Police reported a 2026 pilot using live facial-recognition on existing street infrastructure. In India, AI-assisted face matching at a Delhi protest led to a legal dispute. The Metropolitan Police September 2025 report recorded 2,077 alerts and ten false classifications. Six people were approached after those false alerts, but none were arrested.

Oktenli says that high scores on existing evaluations do not prove reliability in real deployments. He argues that detection and facial recognition are different tasks from multi-camera tracking. The author claims that a strong result on one task does not establish reliability on others. He suggests that systems must flag uncertainty when they are guessing a person's path. He believes that human corrections must propagate to every downstream report before actions are taken.

The US Federal Trade Commission alleged a false match led to searching an 11-year-old girl. This 2023 Rite Aid case showed how innocent people experience consequences before corrections occur. Researchers Ergys Ristani and Carlo Tomasi noted that appearances vary with angle, light, and occlusion. They stated that similar-looking people may be joined into one route by the software. A single person may also be split into multiple tracks by the system.

The US National Institute of Standards and Technology excluded cross-camera tracking from its Face in Video Evaluation. MOTChallenge assesses tracking within a single camera and assigns fresh identifiers when people reappear. The European Union AI Act restricts certain law-enforcement uses of real-time remote biometric identification. These rules provide safeguards for exceptional uses in publicly accessible spaces. The author notes that HOTA metrics improve measurement but do not eliminate deployment testing.

Procurement should start with end-to-end trials using consenting participants and independent ground truth. Tests must count incorrect joins and broken tracks separately under ordinary working conditions. Reviewers should deliberately reject mistaken links to test if corrections reach all searchable records. Organizations must limit the retention and unnecessary dissemination of surveillance footage. The articles leave open how non-biometric tracking will be regulated under the AI Act.

Articles.Title: When AI Cameras Invent A Journey Nobody Took – Analysis

stories.Headline: Geoff D argues that people should work with AI rather than just prompt it
stories.Summary:
The article argues that people should spend less time learning to prompt AI and more time learning to work with it, and it makes this case through two experienced creative professionals who use similar AI tools but get dramatically different results. One of them gets predictable ideas, polished presentations and the occasional useful shortcut, while the other gets sharper thinking, unexpected perspectives and work that moves forward at a completely different pace. The article says most conversations about AI still treat it like a sophisticated vending machine, where you put the right instructions in and get the right output. It acknowledges that AI can write, summarize, research, generate ideas and produce work at remarkable speed, but calls that a very limited view of what it can contribute.

The article says creative and strategic thinking rarely happens in a straight line, because ideas evolve, assumptions get challenged, perspectives shift and the first answer is rarely the best one. It says the real opportunity is moving beyond isolated requests toward something more cumulative, a way of working where context, critical thinking and intellectual exchange make the collaboration increasingly useful. It states plainly that AI does not magically become smarter with every conversation, but that the combination of human judgment, AI capabilities and relevant context can create something more effective than either working in isolation. It says much of the conversation around AI focuses on efficiency, doing more, working faster, saving time and producing more content, which it calls valuable but only half the opportunity for strategists, marketers and creatives.

The article says AI should not simply help execute an idea but should be capable of contributing to the thinking behind it, by questioning assumptions, exploring alternatives, connecting seemingly unrelated observations, making an argument stronger or explaining why it does not hold up. It says sometimes that means thinking with us and sometimes it means doing substantive thinking for us, and that the opportunity is not choosing between better thinking and faster execution but combining both. It warns that the more personalized an AI experience becomes, the easier it is to confuse familiarity with intelligence, and that an AI which consistently tells you what you want to hear could become the world's most efficient echo chamber. It calls that a serious risk for creative and strategic work, where the most valuable contribution is often the one that challenges the original thinking, and says a good collaborator should sometimes make you realize your favorite idea is not very good.

The article says that as AI becomes more powerful and accessible, the competitive advantage may increasingly come from the quality of the human-AI collaboration rather than simply the technology itself. It says the best model will still matter, and so will the skills of the person using it, but that knowing how to get an answer and knowing what to do with that answer are two very different things. It closes by suggesting the question is not whether you are good at prompting AI but whether you have developed a way of working that allows AI to tell you something you did not want to hear. The article is by Geoff D. and was updated on November 22, 2026.

Articles.Title: Stop Prompting AI. Start Working With It.

stories.headline_source: Stop Prompting AI. Start Working With It.

stories.Headline: The Information asks whether the AI bubble is deflating and puts Dell and Workday on deck
stories.Summary:

The article carried a timestamp of 06:00:00Z on that date and appeared under the headline asking if the AI bubble is deflating. The piece was published by The Information, a technology business publication, and its headline paired Dell and Workday with the question about the AI bubble. The article's text as provided consists of the headline, a promotional line about early access to a Black Friday sale offering savings on two years of a subscription, and site navigation and marketing material. No further details about Dell, Workday or the state of the AI bubble appeared in the article text.

It invites readers to search, find and engage with others who are serious about tech and business, and to follow and join discussions about tech, finance and media. It also offers in-depth insights in seconds through a tool called Ask Deep Research.

The article as provided does not name any person who did anything in connection with Dell, Workday or the AI bubble, and it contains no statements from executives or other officials about either company. The only figures in the text are the subscription offer of up to $500 in savings on two years of The Information and the years attached to the publication's lists and projects. Because the text carries no account of what Dell or Workday did or said, there is no responsible party to identify and no paraphrase of comments to report.

The article provides no context about the AI bubble beyond the question in the headline, and it does not say what happens next for Dell, Workday or the wider market. It does not state whether either company was scheduled to report results, make an announcement or appear at an event, and it gives no indication of when any such development might occur. The publication date of November 22, 2026 is the only timing the text supplies, and nothing in it describes consequences or follow-up. stories.Headline: Beijing pushes AI from scientific innovation to industrial use to drive economic growth
stories.Summary:
Beijing is accelerating the transition of artificial intelligence from scientific innovation to industrial use to drive economic growth. By September 24, 2026, the city had completed the filing process for 319 large generative AI models, which is the highest total in the country. The core AI industry in Beijing reached approximately 450 billion yuan in 2025 and included more than 2,500 related companies. These two figures represented about 40 percent of the respective national totals for the industry.

The city aims to become the world's leading AI city during the opening year of the 15th Five-Year Plan. Officials intend to expand the value of the core AI industry to more than 1 trillion yuan within two years. Beijing E-Town established the first facility in the country for producing embodied AI training data based on real-world environments. This facility covers more than 30 scenarios and houses over 150 mainstream robots in 40 configurations to reach a goal of 1 million hours of high-quality data.

The Beijing Shuimu Dongfang Medical Robotic Technology Innovation Center uses a manufacturing and services model to accelerate the commercialization of research. This platform has handled nearly 600 client engagements and helped 22 products obtain registration certificates from the National Medical Products Administration. LY iTech's Beijing Embodied Intelligence Super Factory plans to produce 10,000 units in 2026 and 500,000 units by 2030. These initiatives are designed to turn technological progress into a tangible source of economic growth for the region.

stories.Headline: Grimes criticizes Elon Musk for his fixation on AI generated women
stories.Summary:
Grimes publicly opposed the artificial intelligence interests of her former partner Elon Musk in November 2026. Musk wrote on X on Tuesday, November 17, that super intelligence will hack the limbic system. He shared this message while resharing an announcement about the first AI generated influencer. Grimes responded in the comments section of the post on the X platform. She criticized the fixation on fake women as a form of cope.

Grimes, 38, mentioned that the AI influencer Claudia is an alien creature without a Birkin deal. She referenced the 1883 concept of the last man by philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche regarding lazy nihilism. Musk, 55, has eleven children with three other women besides those he shares with Grimes. Their children include sons X Æ A-Xii, 6, and Techno Mechanicus, 4, and daughter Exa Dark Sideræl, 4. The couple were together from 2018 to 2022.

Spokesperson Mitchell Jackson stated that Grimes opposes the unelected power held by Elon Musk. Jackson said Grimes believes it is ridiculous for Musk to promote AI slop in his free time. He noted that Grimes is disappointed by the lack of leadership from tech giants. Jackson claimed that tech leaders do not care about AI safety for humans or machines. He stated that Grimes welcomes the discourse surrounding her tweets.

Grimes expressed grave concern in March 2025 about her children living public lives on the internet. She claimed she begged Musk and the public to keep the faces of her kids offline. The singer believes there is no way to deal with the dismantling of privacy. She hoped a law would allow a parent to veto children from living public lives. Grimes believes we cannot afford aggressive nihilism from those in power.

Musk and Grimes made their red carpet debut in May 2018 shortly after relationship reports surfaced. They were together for four years before they called it quits in 2022. During their relationship, they weathered split rumors and a public feud with Azealia Banks. They have since gone back and forth about social media guidelines for their three children. Grimes, whose real name is Claire Elise Boucher, continues to coparent with Musk.

Grimes will address her tech safety concerns in a forthcoming record and her single DeepSeek. The song DeepSeek is about machine welfare according to her spokesperson Mitchell Jackson. Grimes intends to continue speaking out about these important issues and aggressive nihilism. Musk has not publicly addressed the criticism from Grimes at the time of publication. The articles leave open whether Musk will ever respond to her concerns.

stories.Headline: Antropics closes Nasdaq IPO at $97.17 per share after raising $81.3 billion
stories.Summary:
Antropics, a U.S. artificial intelligence company, closed its initial public offering on the Nasdaq on the 19th local time at $83 per share, above its initial offer price of $70 to $78. It raised about $81.3 billion through the public offering. Its closing price on the first day of listing was $97.17, up 17.1% from the public offering price. Information signs were installed outside the Nasdaq market site in New York ahead of the IPO. Related companies are drawing attention in the domestic stock market.

SK Telecom invested $100 million in Antropics in 2023 and also participated in Series H investment this year, with cumulative investment of about $200 million. Yuanta Securities estimated the value of SK Telecom's stake at about 5 trillion won based on the closing price of the first day of Antropics listing. Compared to the book value of 3.5 trillion won at the end of June, the valuation has jumped by about 1.5 trillion won. Compared to the initial investment, it is about 18 times larger. SK Telecom plans to decide whether to sell its stake and how to use it in consideration of future market conditions and demand for investment resources.

SK Telecom said it can also consider investing in mid- to long-term growth such as AI data centers and ways to enhance shareholder value. An investment prospectus submitted by Antropics to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission states that SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics are major producers of high-performance memory, including high-bandwidth memory. Samsung SDS has entered into a strategic partnership with Antropics, and the two companies decided to introduce Claude, verify technology, and build and operate services together for domestic companies. Samsung SDS has already provided Claude Enterprise to about 70,000 executives and employees of 20 Samsung affiliates. LG CNS has also signed a contract with Antropics to introduce Claude Enterprise.

LG CNS plans to apply Claude to LG Group affiliates and expand its service to customers of external companies. LG CNS also invested in Antropics shares through LG Technology Ventures in 2023. Naver is known to have indirectly invested in Antropics through a U.S. investment company. Antropics mentioned the supply constraints of high-voltage transformers, distribution boards, power generation facilities, and transmission equipment needed to operate the data center as business risk factors in its prospectus. HD Hyundai Electric signed a business agreement with LG CNS to build a smart factory with data center power infrastructure.

HD Hyundai Electric decided to jointly promote a project to supply power devices and distribution systems to data centers. LS ELECTRIC is expanding its business to supply power facilities for data centers in North America. The two semiconductor companies are also linked to Antropics in equity investments and reportedly participated in Antropics' Series H investment this year. However, since Antropics' corporate value was already formed at a high level at the time, the return on investment may be limited compared to SK Telecom, an early investor. Equity investment companies can expect valuation gains from rising stock prices, but equity sales are necessary to realize actual profits.

Semiconductor companies should also check the supply volume, price, and contribution to sales by customer. For IT service companies, the key is whether the introduction of Claude leads to actual orders and profits. The listing of Antropics does not immediately lead to improved performance of domestic related companies. How much Antropics' stake value will be reflected in SK Telecom's corporate value is considered a variable in future stock prices. It is difficult to expect direct benefits at the same level as SK Telecom and LG CNS for Naver, as the investment route and stake size have not been clearly disclosed.

stories.Headline: EEG study links ChatGPT essay writing to weaker brain connectivity in 54 participants
stories.Summary:
Researchers conducted a study of 54 participants who wrote essays using three different methods. One group used ChatGPT, one used a conventional search engine, and one used no tool. The researchers recorded brain activity using electroencephalography to see how participants performed. This study was reported in a segment by Deutsche Welle titled AI Cheating.

The experiment required participants to write essays under one of the three specific setups. The ChatGPT group used the chatbot, while the search group used a traditional engine. The no-tool group wrote without any external aid to isolate the tool's effect. EEG sensors on the scalp measured brain connectivity among the 54 people involved. The results are currently a preprint and have not been peer-reviewed by a journal.

Deutsche Welle asked if relying on chatbots for answers weakens knowledge and critical thinking. The broadcaster framed the issue as outsourcing brains and questioned if AI makes people think less. The reporting noted that the claim about weakening critical thinking is a paraphrase of research. It stated that the viral version of the story goes beyond what reporting supports. The segment was filed under the SHIFT banner regarding life with digital technology.

The findings affect students, parents, and employers who use chatbots instead of working things out. ChatGPT users showed the weakest brain connectivity, while the no-tool group showed the strongest. Search engine users fell in between these two extremes of reported mental engagement. ChatGPT users also reported lower ownership of their writing and had difficulty recalling text. These participants struggled to quote their own work immediately after finishing the task.

The articles describe cognitive offloading as passing a mental task to an external aid. This practice is common, such as writing a grocery list or saving a phone number. Generative AI is different because it can generate reasoning, structure, and prose for users. A separate survey from Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University also looked at workplace habits. That survey associated greater confidence in AI with less self-reported use of critical thinking.

The study found an association during the task but did not prove causation. It remains unconfirmed if AI permanently weakens intelligence, memory, creativity, or critical-thinking ability. The small sample size and narrow task limit broad claims about human cognition. Future steps require replication and peer review to stress-test the methods and statistics. The articles leave open whether these findings indicate long-term changes in mental ability.

Articles.Title: AI Made 54 Students Think Less, EEG Study Finds

stories.Headline: Benj Edwards runs a small ChatGPT model on the SNES using a Super FX 2 chip
stories.Summary:
Vintage Computing blogger Benj Edwards created a chatbot for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. He released this project on November 19, 2026, to run ChatGPT on the console. The system uses a Super FX 2 chip to accelerate the chatbot replies. This project allows a 35-year-old console to process a small language model. It is available as a ROM for real hardware or emulators.

The model is a 2.2-million-parameter distillation of OpenAI's GPT-OSS-120b. Users can choose a 4MB model or a 19MB version with Wikipedia data. The larger version includes opening sentences from 150,000 Simple English Wikipedia articles via MSU-1. It runs on a 21.47 MHz RISC CPU inside the Super FX 2 chip. This is faster than the 2.68 MHz Ricoh 5A22 main CPU.

Benj Edwards is responsible for the project and used GPT-6 Astra and gpt-oss. He stated that the model is millions of times smaller than standard ChatGPT models. He noted that the small knowledge base leads to some fun and weird results. Edwards admitted that the usefulness of the app is very limited beyond curiosity. He presented the project as an unofficial version of ChatGPT for the SNES.

The project affects vintage computing enthusiasts who can use a flashcart system for hardware. Users can also interact with the chatbot through the SNES9x emulator in a browser. These users experience chip-tune soundtracks and input sound effects while they type on keyboards. The articles do not mention other people who commented on the project's utility. The chatbot can make mistakes during interactions with the users.

The Super FX 2 chip originally debuted with the game Yoshi's Island for the SNES. This coprocessor was manufacturer-installed on cartridges to enhance 2D and 3D graphics. It retained the polygon capabilities of the original SFX but ran at full speed. The chip also supported larger ROM sizes than the previous version of the hardware. It was also integrated into the cartridge for the game Doom.

Users can download the ROM to play it on a real vintage SNES console. They must have a flashcart with Super FX and MSU-1 support for all features. The articles do not state if Edwards plans to expand the model size. It is unclear if other vintage consoles will receive similar AI acceleration projects. No further development dates or future software updates are mentioned in the text.

stories.Headline: Simply Wall St identifies Amplitude, Pony AI and Ambarella as small cap AI stocks for investors to watch
stories.Summary:
Sasha Jovanovic wrote an article on November 22, 2026, about small cap AI stocks. The author identified three specific companies that investors should watch closely. These businesses apply machine learning and automation to their products. The report highlights how these players might be mispriced by the market. This analysis focuses on companies with different risk and reward profiles.

Amplitude integrates machine learning into product analytics tools to create automated decisions. It has a market value of roughly US$2.1b and generated US$396 million. Pony AI develops autonomous driving software for robotaxis and robotrucks in China. It carries a market value of about US$1.44b and operates in international markets. Ambarella reports US$418 million from semiconductors and has a market value near US$2.3b.

The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St is responsible for the analysis. They stated that Amplitude's shift to a multiproduct platform supports higher pricing uplifts. The analysts noted that Pony AI is scaling robotaxi fleets in China's Tier 1 cities. They claimed that edge AI now accounts for 80% of total revenue for Ambarella. This shift toward on device intelligence is the key driver for Ambarella.

Investors are questioning if massive spending on data centers and chips will ever pay off. This uncertainty has hit AI stocks hard and punished the largest companies. Digital teams at Amplitude are affected by the shift from static reports to automation. Urban mobility and logistics sectors in China are affected by Pony AI's technology. Users of portable video and robotics are affected by Ambarella's low power chips.

The articles state that AI stocks have faced a selloff due to spending concerns. Amplitude's current valuation assumes continued expansion of annual recurring revenue per customer. Pony AI focuses on scaling in Changsha, Hangzhou, and the Greater Bay Area. Ambarella develops software that lets hardware run AI at the edge of networks. These three companies were selected from a screener that surfaced 41 small caps.

Investors are watching if pressure on Amplitude's path to stronger margins will ease. The market is monitoring Pony AI's capital needs and its path to profitability. Ambarella must turn its richer product mix into consistent margins and earnings. The articles leave open how these pressure points will affect future value creation. It remains unclear if these companies can achieve accelerating operating leverage over time.

stories.Headline: AI bone age tool matches atlas medians but varies more in individual children
stories.Summary:
A retrospective study at Independent Public Clinical Hospital Number 1 in Zabrze, affiliated with the Medical University of Silesia, evaluated how artificial intelligence compares with radiological reference atlases for bone age. The analysis covered 376 pediatric patients whose skeletal maturity was assessed by the Greulich and Pyle Atlas, the Pocket Atlas of Skeletal Age, and the Stanford University Hand Bone Age artificial intelligence web tool. Archived DICOM radiographs were retrieved from the hospital picture archiving and communication system for cases collected between April 2024 and June 2025. The initial screening identified 473 clinical cases evaluated during routine hospital care for short stature, precocious puberty, delayed puberty, and growth hormone deficiency managed with recombinant growth hormone therapy. An experienced pediatric radiologist performed the atlas evaluations, while the automated web tool independently predicted age values from identical digital radiographs.

Inclusion required radiographs of the non-dominant hand with proper positioning and complete records of chronological age, sex, and pediatric endocrinologist-determined pubertal status. Exclusion criteria eliminated acute hand or wrist trauma, insufficient image quality, contradictory data, and diagnosed skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia. Because the Stanford platform operated within a validation boundary of 72 to 192 months of skeletal age, both atlases had to produce estimates within that six-to-sixteen-year span, yielding 376 patients. Chronological age averaged 142.9 months with a standard deviation of 35.0 months, a median of 146 months, and an interquartile range of 114 to 173 months across an absolute range of 47 to 220 months. Twenty-two participants fell outside the 72 to 192 months range chronologically, with four children younger than 72 months and 18 older than 192 months.

The study group comprised 188 female and 188 male patients, and 250 patients, or 66.5 percent, were clinically categorized as pubertal, whereas 126 patients, or 33.5 percent, were classified as prepubertal. Statistical evaluation in R software version 4.5.3 showed the Pocket Atlas, the Greulich and Pyle atlas, and the Stanford algorithm all yielded an identical median bone age estimate of 144 months. Interquartile ranges were 114 to 165 months for the Pocket Atlas, 120 to 162 months for Greulich and Pyle, and 120 to 156 months for the artificial intelligence application. Shapiro-Wilk testing showed significant departure from normality for the Pocket Atlas at W equals 0.96, Greulich and Pyle at W equals 0.96, and the automated model at W equals 0.93, with all probability values below 0.001. A global paired comparison using the Friedman test detected significant divergence among the modalities, with a test statistic of 29.55 and a probability value below 0.001.

Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank testing with Bonferroni correction showed the global differences were driven by the automated application rather than disagreement between human atlas evaluations. The Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence comparison reached significance with an adjusted probability value of 0.001, and Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence yielded an adjusted probability value of 0.044. The direct comparison between the Pocket Atlas and the Greulich and Pyle atlas showed no statistically significant difference, recording an adjusted probability value of 0.13. Median pairwise discrepancies were centered at zero months across all comparisons, but mean pairwise differences were 0.69 plus or minus 6.82 months for the Pocket Atlas relative to Greulich and Pyle, 2.22 plus or minus 13.66 months for the Pocket Atlas relative to artificial intelligence, and 1.53 plus or minus 12.73 months for Greulich and Pyle relative to artificial intelligence. The two-way mixed-effects intraclass correlation coefficient for absolute agreement, ICC(A,1), was 0.93 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.92 to 0.94.

Pairwise intraclass correlation values reached 0.98 with a confidence interval of 0.97 to 0.98 between the Pocket Atlas and Greulich and Pyle, 0.90 with a confidence interval of 0.89 to 0.92 between the Pocket Atlas and artificial intelligence, and 0.92 with a confidence interval of 0.90 to 0.93 between Greulich and Pyle and artificial intelligence. Bland-Altman analysis revealed an average bias of 0.69 months between the two visual atlases, with 95 percent limits of agreement from minus 12.68 to positive 14.06 months, while comparisons pairing artificial intelligence against the Pocket Atlas and Greulich and Pyle produced wider limits of agreement spanning minus 24.55 to positive 28.99 months and minus 23.43 to positive 26.48 months. Under a predefined threshold of agreement within plus or minus 12 months, the two human atlas approaches agreed in 363 out of 376 cases, an agreement rate of 96.5 percent with a confidence interval from 94.2 to 98.0 percent. Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence dropped to 83.8 percent, representing 315 out of 376 children with a confidence interval from 79.7 to 87.2 percent, and the Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence registered 77.4 percent across 291 patients with a confidence interval from 72.9 to 81.3 percent. Under a stringent threshold of plus or minus six months, the two reference atlases sustained agreement in 77.9 percent of cases, encompassing 293 patients, while concordance fell to 44.4 percent across 167 cases for Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence and 43.6 percent across 164 cases for the Pocket Atlas against the automated tool.

Locally estimated trend lines indicated the Stanford model tended to underestimate bone age relative to visual atlases among the youngest and oldest participants, a deviation absent in the direct atlas comparison. After controlling for quadratic age trends, Breusch-Pagan testing confirmed significant age-related heteroscedasticity for comparisons involving artificial intelligence, with probability values below 0.001, whereas the two atlas methods maintained homoscedasticity with a probability value of 0.52. Spearman correlation between chronological age and absolute residuals showed weak but statistically significant negative associations for the Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence at r equals minus 0.14 and Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence at r equals minus 0.18, compared to r equals 0.006 and a probability value of 0.90 between the two manual atlases. Patient sex exerted a profound effect on method agreement, creating pronounced divergence in female patients that was largely absent among males. Wilcoxon rank-sum testing with Bonferroni correction established significant associations between sex and pairwise differences for the Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence and Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence, both displaying adjusted probabili More to follow.

stories.Headline: Dragos researchers find widespread user data leakage across AI service networks
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by HD Moore from the security firm Dragos identified significant security vulnerabilities within the artificial intelligence supply chain on November 22, 2026. The team planted 2 million digital tripwires using unique, trackable credentials to monitor how various AI services handled sensitive information. Their study revealed that AI routers and inference providers frequently expose user data to potential threats. The investigation found that at least three AI providers suffered breaches that allowed attackers to siphon prompts directly from the services.

The findings show that multiple resellers log user prompts despite privacy settings like Zero Data Retention policies. One Chinese AI lab systematically scraped secret URLs from prompts, even when those requests were routed through providers in the United States. This widespread leakage occurs because prompts are decrypted at every hop within the complex network of inference resellers. To mitigate these risks, the research suggests that users should host models on-premises or contract directly with first-tier providers to reduce intermediaries.

HD Moore stated that the current AI ecosystem has a systemic failure regarding the protection of customer data. He believes this situation poses a significant challenge for any users who rely on third-party services for sensitive tasks. The researchers used the seeding of prompts to prove that sensitive data is not being handled securely across the supply chain. This evidence highlights the danger of using intermediaries that may ignore privacy agreements or suffer from poor security.

Articles.Title: Researchers uncover widespread data leakage in AI service networks

stories.Headline: AI helps uncover a Ghostscript flaw that exposes Google and Zoom to attack
stories.Summary:
A series of major technology failures across the United States over the past two weeks slowed banking transactions, interrupted Microsoft and Apple services, disabled a classified National Security Agency network and temporarily grounded commercial air traffic nationwide, the New York Times reported on Saturday. U.S. officials said they had no evidence the incidents were caused by malicious cyberattacks. Instead, they attributed several of the disruptions to software patches intended to strengthen systems against newly discovered vulnerabilities. The disruptions came as confirmed cyberattacks on systems in the U.S. and Europe underscored the growing vulnerability of interconnected networks. Hackers had already targeted American municipal water systems and European refrigeration infrastructure.

The Times reported that Iranian hackers targeted scores of municipal water systems in the United States this summer, exploiting weak or default passwords on computers controlling operations. Recent cyberattacks against refrigeration systems in Europe showed how even relatively unsophisticated hackers can disrupt equipment essential to commercial operations. Cybersecurity researcher Paulos Yibelo, founder of PWN AI, discovered a serious software vulnerability called Upload2Shell using artificial intelligence to examine file-upload processes. The flaw involved Ghostscript, decades-old software widely used to process documents and images, and could potentially have allowed attackers to compromise systems at major companies including Google and Zoom by uploading a specially crafted file. Yibelo reported the discovery to the software developer and affected companies, which issued patches.

Microsoft reportedly released more than 1,400 security patches in October, roughly 10 times its historical baseline. The NSA experienced a days-long outage of a classified network after installing faulty updates designed to address vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, which officials cited by the Times said had been identified with the assistance of artificial intelligence. Retired Gen. Paul Nakasone, the former director of the NSA and U.S. Cyber Command, said at a Washington conference hosted by Vanderbilt University's Institute of National Security that the past week is "the new normal." Nakasone, who also serves on OpenAI's board, called artificial intelligence "the most disruptive technology" in history and said, "We are in an era where we've got to think differently about how we're going to be more resilient."

He said industries and agencies are trying to rapidly modernize and at the same time defend themselves, and that "A.I. is driving all of this, the opportunities and the challenges." Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., warned the White House that existing cybersecurity defenses were struggling to keep pace, writing that "A.I. is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace." Michael Yeh, Microsoft's vice president of customer security and trust, said some of the most frequently exploited vulnerabilities were discovered years ago and that "None of those are A.I.-driven attacks," adding that "These are people exploiting existing legacy vulnerabilities" that can be decades old. Rob Joyce, a former senior NSA cybersecurity official, said at Cyberwarcon on Friday that AI was not "inventing brand new ways to hack" but was intensifying pressure to repair existing weaknesses, comparing the situation to a forest fire in which "All that tech that's on fire and going to burn down" while "all the little things that are down in the forest floor" will grow stronger and more capable.

The disruptions affected consumers who suddenly could not access banking services, businesses experiencing interrupted operations, and travelers stranded by computer failures. Experts disagree about whether artificial intelligence will ultimately make the internet safer or produce an endless cycle of newly discovered vulnerabilities and emergency repairs. Repeated disruptions affecting financial transactions, communications, transportation and national security systems risk undermining confidence in the institutions responsible for protecting them. Public skepticism does not prove that officials are concealing cyberattacks, yet the combination of confirmed intrusions, aging infrastructure and increasingly frequent outages creates a difficult credibility problem, especially when technical explanations are not accompanied by detailed public findings.

The distinction between a failed software update and a deliberate cyberattack is increasingly difficult for ordinary Americans to assess, particularly when the consequences can look nearly identical. The incident illustrates a growing dilemma in which security teams must respond quickly to newly discovered weaknesses, but rushing to install protective updates can itself trigger serious disruptions. The incident also illustrates how AI is dramatically accelerating the discovery of security flaws in technology that businesses and government agencies have relied upon for decades. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Government Blames Glitches as Cyber Threats Are 'New Normal' With AI

James Demmert, the chief investment officer for Main Street Research, analyzed a significant selloff in artificial intelligence stocks that occurred during the previous week. He characterized this sudden market decline as a period of panic within a standard correction for the technology sector. Demmert believes that the current cycle for artificial intelligence is only approximately halfway finished. He suggests that investors should view this downward trend as a strategic buying opportunity.

The current market situation requires a shift in perspective toward cheap valuations and strong earnings to discount negative news. Demmert expects the Federal Reserve to reduce its interest rate increases to a 25 basis point hike. He maintains that the probability of a global recession occurring at this time is extremely low. These factors combined suggest that the market will eventually stabilize as the initial panic subsides.

James Demmert is responsible for these insights and explained that the recent volatility is typical for tech cycles. He argued that the fundamental strength of the industry remains intact despite the short term price drops. By focusing on earnings, he believes the market will move past the current fear. He views the current price levels as an attractive entry point for long term investors.

stories.Headline: Google's Maxwell Minckler says marketers must frame why they use AI before adopting it
stories.Summary:
Maxwell Minckler, the insights lead for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Google, wrote an article published on 22 November 2026 on Think with Google about why mindsets drive value in AI transformation in marketing. He described how a character he called “The Great Cat Detective”, invented with his eight-year-old son at bedtime, was brought to life with Gemini Omni, and how his son reacted to seeing it. He said he spends his days researching how marketers are weaving new technology into their work. He wrote that marketers at leading companies feel empowered to reimagine their workflows and roles using AI, but that the deeper question of why organisations use AI in the first place is a crucial first step.

The article says there is an emerging disconnect between why many organisations push for AI and why individuals actually use it. It says a clear organisational purpose rarely shows up on its own, and that individuals need to know why they should implement AI in their day-to-day work and why the business values that implementation. It says operating without a clear why at both the organisational and individual levels paralyses progress on AI transformation, and it explains this roadblock through the behavioural science concept of loss aversion, in which people who cannot see what a change means for them default to protecting what they already have. To overcome this, it says, leading companies turn to cognitive reframing, a technique used to challenge and replace negative thoughts with balanced, realistic ones, and it offers the reframe that AI is a revealer that commoditises what can be commoditised while revealing the parts of a job that truly matter.

Minckler gave his own job as an example, saying that if he frames his job as conducting research, AI feels poised to replace him, but if he reframes his role around its real value, helping people make better decisions using research, he is empowered and can focus on the human value of his role. The article describes how leading AI companies enable this shift in practical ways, including reframe sessions, which are long-form, manager-led conversations with no slides and no training manuals, built around three honest questions about what parts of a role people want to enhance, what can be automated and what the blockers are. It also describes AI Spotlights, unpolished, real-world before-and-after stories shared where people actually communicate, such as team newsletters or chat groups, and says these work because they model a mindset shift in action rather than showcasing a toolset or teaching a skill set in isolation.

The article says mindsets matter, and that because AI toolsets and skill sets are more tangible and have clearer owners, organisations often place most of their focus on them, yet AI mindsets are equally critical in driving sustained AI adoption. It says Google's research has shown that a clear focus on maximising advantages, which it calls FOMA, is the AI framing and mindset that drives value within leading companies, and that framing the why is the crucial but often skipped first step. To help organisations move from the wow of AI to tangible business value, Minckler says Google has developed the FOCUS playbook, a five-part behavioural science framework based on multi-year research, in which marketers frame the why, own the loop, cultivate capability, uncover the unsaid and stoke the system, moving from isolated experiments to an integrated AI strategy. He says the future of marketing depends not only on adopting new technology but on how well we understand and empower the humans wielding it, and that the real magic lies in the combination of the technology and the people using it to reimagine what is possible.

stories.Headline: Santa Lucia Asset Management warns of a demand reset for AI infrastructure in Asia
stories.Summary:
Florian Weidinger, the chief executive officer of Santa Lucia Asset Management, recently warned that the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure across Asia is facing a potential reset in demand. He suggested that this shift is occurring as China moves toward using domestic hardware for its artificial intelligence needs. This transition could significantly limit the access that Nvidia has to the Asian market. Such a change in procurement patterns puts the overall buildout of technology in the region at risk.

The situation requires a reassessment of how hardware is sourced and may change the financial outlook for major chip producers. Weidinger noted that the entry of more chipmakers into the competitive market could put downward pressure on profit margins. Furthermore, he indicated that weaker demand for these high end components may lead customers to revise or reduce their existing orders. These adjustments would impact the scale and speed of the infrastructure deployment across the continent.

Florian Weidinger is responsible for these observations and shared them during a recent discussion regarding the regional tech landscape. He explained that the preference for home grown technology in China creates a barrier for foreign suppliers. He believes that the current trajectory of the market is unstable due to these shifting geopolitical and economic priorities. The CEO emphasized that the reliance on domestic alternatives is a primary driver of this potential demand reset.

stories.Headline: Egyptian firms boost AI and fintech investment to drive growth and regional expansion
stories.Summary:
Egyptian companies are increasing their investments in artificial intelligence and fintech as drivers of growth and competitiveness amid rapid shifts in global markets, according to discussions by experts at the fourth edition of the Executive Education Summit organized by ESLSCA University on November 21 and 22, 2026. During a session titled "From Chaos to Sustainable Growth," representatives from technology, financial services, and education companies said that building flexible business models and investing in technology and human resources are critical to turning economic challenges into opportunities for growth and regional expansion. Malak El Baba, Vice President and General Manager of Visa in Egypt, Libya, and Sudan, said artificial intelligence is reshaping commerce and digital payments, citing the "Stay Secure" study showing that 91% of consumers in Egypt use artificial intelligence in shopping and 88% trust its role in fraud protection. She added that more than 83% of Egyptian companies plan to invest in agentic commerce over the next two years, and she stressed the importance of integrating payment and financing solutions into the purchasing experience as commerce grows across social media platforms and digital gaming.

Ahmed Nader, CEO of Geidea, said the company grew over five years from a team of 3 to 4 individuals to nearly 1,200 employees, with the number of merchants it serves reaching approximately 100,000. He said Geidea broadened its services from point-of-sale solutions to e-commerce, restaurant, and retail services, up to lending and embedded finance powered by artificial intelligence, and he affirmed that digital payment solutions and faster financial inclusion drive corporate growth, particularly for small and medium enterprises. Mohamed Tawfik, Managing Director of TP in Egypt and Chief Operating Officer for English-speaking African markets, said investment in technology and specialized talent helps companies operating in Egypt compete regionally and export services to global markets. He noted that attracting talent in computer science and medical sectors is one of the most prominent expansion challenges while serving clients in the United States and Europe, and he said the company cooperates with the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Information Technology Industry Development Agency (ITIDA) to address the repercussions of regional tensions and ensure business continuity.

Karim El Hennawy, CEO and Secretary-General of ESLSCA University, said rapid technological evolution forces organizations to retrain leaders and employees and to develop strategic thinking and crisis management skills. He explained that the COVID-19 pandemic and remote work accelerated shifts expected by 2030 and 2040 into a reality within three to four years, reinforcing the importance of practical skills and adaptability to labor market changes. Omar El Shenity, Founder and CEO of Qaf Education, said organizations need to move from reactive management to flexible operating models based on data and proactive planning amid continuous changes in labor market needs and its trend toward specialized disciplines. The summit was held with more than 1,200 participants, 60 speakers, and 50 partners, under the auspices of the Ministries of Industry, Higher Education and Scientific Research, Communications and Information Technology, and Health and Population, and it discussed the future of leadership, management, and organizational development amid technological and economic transformations.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT predicts XRP reaches $5 by the end of 2029
stories.Summary:
ChatGPT predicted on November 21, 2026 that XRP could reach $5 by December 31, 2029, about 460% above the forecast's 89-cent starting price. The prediction was published by Sam Daodu, editor of the Crypto Desk at 24/7 Wall St., in an article dated November 21, 2026. XRP was trading around 90 cents, having fallen 22.4% over the past two weeks and 32.1% in the last 30 days. Its close of nearly 91 cents on November 20 was its lowest close of the past year, far below its January 5 high of $2.35. ChatGPT's $5 target is far below Standard Chartered's forecast of $19.60 for 2029.

ChatGPT assigns a 55% weight to the $5 base scenario, a 30% weight to a $1.50 low scenario and a 15% weight to a $15 high scenario. The low scenario of $1.50 is about 66% higher than XRP's current price, and the scenarios imply market values of about $112 billion, $373 billion and $1.12 trillion. These values assume 74.6 billion XRP in circulation by the end of 2029, starting from the current 63.5 billion and adding 300 million new coins each month for 37 months, mainly from Ripple's escrow. XRP reached its all-time high of $3.65 in July 2025 with fewer coins in circulation, and its market value stands at about $57.2 billion, ranking sixth among all cryptocurrencies. The base scenario needs market value to grow about 6.5 times, and the high scenario of $15 could match Bitcoin's current market value of around $1.17 trillion.

ChatGPT forecasts XRP finishing 2026 at 85 cents, a 6% drop from current levels, then rising to $1.55 in 2027, $2.75 in 2028 and $5 in 2029. The model says XRP must stay above $1 consistently in the second quarter of 2027, hit $2 in the first quarter of 2028, exceed $3 in the third quarter of 2028, surpass the all-time high of $3.65 in the second quarter of 2029, about a 310% increase from 89 cents, and reach above $5 in the fourth quarter of 2029. The first hurdle is $1, about 11% above current prices, and XRP must reclaim its 20-day moving average of $1.08 and its 200-day average of $1.24, about 20% and 38% higher. ChatGPT estimates a 12% chance of XRP reaching Standard Chartered's $19.60 target by December 2029, a level implying a market value of around $1.46 trillion. The model gives a 25% chance for a $10 target and a 15% chance for $15.

Standard Chartered anticipates XRP could hit $12.60 in 2028, $19.60 in 2029 and $28 in 2030, and its 2028 forecast is higher than any other major prediction in the comparison. ChatGPT connects the $19.60 target to steady inflows pushing US spot XRP funds into the $15 billion to $20 billion range, with the Bitwise XRP ETF (NYSEARCA:XRP) as a notable example. According to SoSoValue data, total net assets in these funds dropped to $989.6 million as of November 20, down approximately 35% from $1.51 billion on October 28. Investors pulled out $10.4 million on November 9 and around $5 million on November 20, with no net inflows so far in November.

The second condition is that banks and payment companies would have to use XRP as the bridge currency for cross-border transfers. The article says the possibility of XRP reaching $5 by the end of 2029 seems less likely than ChatGPT's 55% weight implies, because ETF outflows and Bitcoin's slide could push prices lower. Bitcoin is trading around $58,084, below its June 30 closing low of about $58,566, and XRP has tended to follow Bitcoin's downward movements. After past declines of 70%, XRP continued to fall to 92% and 95% below its peak, and it already trades about 75% below its all-time high.

A major U.S. bank or payment network using XRP for cross-border transactions at scale could raise the price prediction to as high as $15. If Bitcoin falls below $40,000, the forecast for XRP could drop to around $1.50, which the article calls a reasonable basis for anyone trying to gauge the value of 3,000 XRP. An encouraging sign that $5 remains possible would be total assets in XRP funds climbing back above $1.51 billion. To maintain ChatGPT's optimistic outlook, XRP needs to stay above $1 by mid-2027, then break through $2 and surpass its all-time high of $3.65.

The article leaves open whether ETF outflows and Bitcoin's slide will push prices lower than the forecast assumes. It also leaves open whether a major U.S. bank or payment network will start using XRP for cross-border transactions at scale. The article does not say when XRP funds might return above $1.51 billion. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Homelabber uses two RTX 3090s and a RAM drive to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi AI model
stories.Summary:
A homelabber detailed improvements to a second generation Optane AI build on Reddit. This person used two RTX 3090 GPUs to run a large AI model. The project was reported by Shane Downing on 21 November 2026. The build runs the 2.8 trillion parameter Moonshot Kimi K3 model. It achieves a generation speed of 3.11 tokens per second.

The system uses 45 of 94 shards, or 414 GB out of 865 GB, on a RAM drive. This setup uses Linux tmpfs and DAX for the Optane portion. The model file is a Q2_K version that shrinks the size to 865 GB. Two RTX 3090 GPUs provide 48 GB of total VRAM for the build. The model is a mixture of experts with 896 experts and 104B active parameters.

The builder stated that the persistent Optane memory gets very hot. Because of this heat, the builder says the Optane sticks still need fans. The builder also noted that DRAM is faster than the Optane memory. This distribution of the workload allows the model to avoid slower memory reads. The builder used llama.cpp to measure the performance of the hardware.

The RAM drive boosted generation speed by 41 percent and prompt evaluation by 26 percent. Prompt evaluation reached 16.8 tokens per second compared to 13.3 tokens per second without the drive. Without the RAM drive, generation speed dropped to 2.20 tokens per second. The GPUs handle attention, shared experts, the KV cache, and the current conversation context. These components are used on every token to maintain high memory bandwidth.

The original build was designed to save money by using Optane instead of DRAM. The model is a mixture of experts where only a few experts run per token. Sixteen routed experts and two shared experts are chosen for any given token. A 16 bit precision version of the model would take about 5.6 TB. Moonshot released a 4 bit MXFP4 format version that is about 1.56 TB.

The GPUs manage the dense feed forward network layer that is not split into experts. The routed expert tensors stay on the CPU side in Optane and the RAM drive. The RAM drive is volatile but appears to the system as a disk. Not every enthusiast has enough free system memory to create such a drive. The articles do not state if the builder will add more GPUs.

stories.Headline: Brevo offers AI email tools that generate content and personalize campaigns
stories.Summary:
Brevo, an all-in-one customer relationship management and marketing platform, offers AI-powered email marketing tools that help businesses create, manage and optimize email campaigns more efficiently, according to an article by Jason Will published on vocal.media on 21 November 2026. The platform combines artificial intelligence with marketing automation so that businesses can generate email content, personalize customer experiences, analyze campaign performance and improve engagement. Brevo says its tools suit any company, whether a small startup, an online store or an established organization. The article describes the offering as a way for marketers to reach the right audience with the right message.

The features include AI-assisted content creation that helps marketers generate email copy, improve subject lines and develop promotional messages, which the article says saves time. Brevo also allows businesses to customize emails using customer information, preferences and behavior, and it provides automation tools that send emails based on customer actions and predefined conditions, such as welcome emails for new subscribers, abandoned-cart reminders and follow-up messages after purchases. Campaign analytics and reporting tools let marketers monitor metrics including open rates, click-through rates and conversions, while smart audience segmentation divides contact lists into specific groups based on customer details and engagement. The article lists the benefits as saving time, improving personalization, increasing engagement, supporting business growth, providing valuable insights and simplifying marketing management.

The article names no individual responsible for the platform and carries no statement from Brevo or its representatives, attributing the described capabilities to the platform itself. It advises that AI-generated content should always be reviewed to ensure accuracy, brand consistency and a natural communication style. Businesses across industries can use the tools, the article says, with e-commerce stores recovering abandoned carts and recommending products, educational institutions sharing course updates, newsletters and admission announcements, and service-based businesses sending appointment reminders, promotional offers and customer follow-ups. Small businesses can also maintain regular communication with customers without requiring a large marketing team.

The article presents Brevo as an alternative to traditional email marketing, which it says often involves manually creating messages, organizing subscriber lists and monitoring campaign results at a cost of time and resources. By combining automation, personalization, customer management and AI-assisted tools, Brevo lets marketers streamline their campaigns and focus on developing better marketing strategies, according to the article. It concludes that as artificial intelligence continues to transform digital marketing, platforms like Brevo make it easier for businesses of all sizes to create customer experiences, strengthen relationships and support long-term growth. The article gives no release date, pricing or independent performance data for the platform.

stories.Headline: EU researchers find most high-automation farm tools rely on offline rule-based software
stories.Summary:
The articles report that researchers on the European Union-funded Horizon Europe OpenAgri project published an inventory of open-source agricultural digital solutions in the journal Smart Agricultural Technology. The inventory mapped 191 digital software and hardware technologies designed for modern agricultural production. The researchers found that tools delivering the highest levels of direct farm automation depend predominantly on deterministic rule-based algorithms and offline edge computing rather than cloud-based deep learning systems. Candidate solutions were identified between 2024 and June 2026 through consortium expertise, targeted keyword queries across GitHub, and specialized community resources. The articles were published on bioengineer.org on 2026-11-21T06:00:00Z.

Of the 191 qualifying solutions, software platforms constituted approximately four-fifths of the catalog and the remaining entries were open-hardware implementations. Farm management information systems made up roughly one-quarter of the database, followed by systems for precision irrigation, livestock monitoring, chemical fertilization, and crop disease diagnosis. Using the European Commission's nine-level Technology Readiness Level framework, 114 solutions, or roughly 60 percent, fell in levels four through six, 62 solutions, or 32 percent, reached levels seven through nine, and 15 entries, or 8 percent, sat in levels one through three. Among the 160 GitHub-hosted solutions, the median repository recorded 17 community stars, six forks, two contributing developers, and zero commits over the preceding twelve months, while 42 percent showed active code modifications in the preceding year and nearly one-fifth logged more than 100 recent commits. Only 28 of the 191 solutions, or approximately 15 percent, had corresponding peer-reviewed scientific publications.

The researchers constructed a standardized empirical baseline to categorize software maturity, deployment architectures, connectivity demands, and legal licensing terms. They implemented a systematic mapping review that treated public code repositories, developer manuals, and hardware schematics as primary evidentiary records, and extracted GitHub metrics on a fixed reference date of August 31, 2026, using the platform's REST application programming interface. They emphasized that publicly accessible source code does not automatically constitute open-source software under copyright law. They observed that advanced neural networks remain a distinct minority within agricultural open source. They noted that autonomous operational intervention does not require advanced machine learning or high-speed cloud infrastructure.

The study cited an independent audit from the European Court of Auditors showing that publicly funded digital tools and decision-support platforms frequently disappear from public access once consortium grant agreements expire. The authors observed that publicly accessible agricultural source code has historically failed to translate into proportional real-world adoption or systematic software reuse. They highlighted a persistent structural divide in which digital assets remain scattered across GitHub, GitLab, institutional servers, and individual project websites without uniform metadata or centralized discovery mechanisms. They cited limited digital literacy among farming demographics, infrastructural gaps in rural telecommunications, and concerns about technical complexity and data governance.

Prospective adopters are forced to navigate inconsistent documentation and unclear technical specifications. The investigation found that 51 solutions, or 26.7 percent of the catalog, published accessible source code without any formal software license. Among licensed projects, developers used frameworks ranging from the MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses to the GNU General Public License and the European Union Public Licence, while hardware repositories used the CERN Open Hardware Licence or Creative Commons terms. On connectivity, 44 tools, nearly one-quarter of the inventory, operate entirely offline after installation, 66 technologies, or 34 percent, require only minimal connectivity, and cloud-native architectures demanding continuous maximum connectivity represented 21 percent of the catalog.

Exactly half of the surveyed solutions, or 95 projects, incorporated no artificial intelligence, 53 relied on deterministic agronomic rules, mathematical threshold models, or simulation logic, 27 used machine learning models, and 16 used advanced deep learning architectures such as convolutional neural networks and YOLO object detectors. Of the nine solutions classified as delivering very high operational intervention, eight functioned using classical control-theory mathematics and rule-based software logic, including autonomous tractor autosteering, and only one employed advanced deep learning, while 23 fully offline solutions delivered high operational intervention. Representative solutions ranged from farm records platforms like farmOS, autonomous tractor guidance packages like AgOpenGPS, and smart robotic platforms like FarmBot, to optical spot-spraying weed locators and drone-based pest detection models. The survey also cataloged cross-domain communication tools including the Zenoh protocol.

Niche agricultural applications and localized farm tools were typically sustained by single developers or small research teams, whereas domain-agnostic communications frameworks, databases, and middleware engaged broad international communities exceeding 50 active contributors. The articles state that 73 percent of open-hardware designs operated completely offline or with minimal connectivity, whereas software platforms were more evenly split across cloud-dependent SaaS infrastructures and local on-premise execution environments. The articles do not state what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: A Brooklyn family makes a personal readiness plan as AI and cyber warnings raise outage risks
stories.Summary:
The warnings are coming thick and fast, according to a New York Times article published on November 21, 2026, which reports that Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said the Iranian government has its sights on U.S. energy, water and financial services systems. Senior executives at A.I. companies say their tools could act on their own and wreak similar havoc, or human hackers could deploy A.I. against the same kinds of targets. The article asks readers to imagine a nationwide power outage, or a municipal water system that turns off or becomes unsafe, or the internet stopping for a while. It notes that a lot of important things people are used to accessing on the fly, such as Waze for a teen driver to get home or Venmo to pay a caregiver, would suddenly be unavailable.

The article says there is no way to know the odds of any of this happening, but they are probably higher than they were a year ago. It cites an Anthropic security executive who recently described a vulnerability tsunami headed our way, and it concludes that some preparation seems prudent right about now. Millions of people who are familiar with extreme weather already know the basic outlines of personal readiness, while the rest of us probably do not. That included the article's author and his underprepared family of four, in their midsize Brooklyn apartment building, until they made their own plans in recent weeks.

The article does not name a single official responsible for personal readiness beyond the author himself, who describes his own household as underprepared before it made plans. It paraphrases Mullin's warning about Iranian intentions toward U.S. energy, water and financial services systems, and it relays what senior A.I. company executives say about their tools acting on their own. The Anthropic security executive is quoted only for the phrase vulnerability tsunami, with no further statement attributed to that person. No other named person is given a direct comment in the available text.

The context the article offers is that the warnings are arriving quickly and that the risk is probably greater than a year ago, though it states plainly that the odds cannot be known. It frames the problem around everyday dependence on services like navigation and payment apps that would fail in a wider outage. The available text ends before the article's own planning guidance, so what specific steps the author and his family took is not described here. What happens next, in the article's account, is simply that some preparation seems prudent right about now.

stories.Headline: Researcher Tommy He releases tufazip, an AI tool that losslessly compresses one gigabyte of Wikipedia to 105.39MB
stories.Summary:
Researcher Tommy He built a tool called tufazip that losslessly compressed one gigabyte of Wikipedia data. This achievement was announced in a research post on November 19, 2026. The system reduced the text to 105.39MB using a self-learning AI transformer model. It does not use any hand-built models to achieve this specific result. The process relies on a neural network as its only predictor.

The system requires two Nvidia B200 GPUs and two Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPUs. Compression takes 631,548 seconds, while decompression takes 645,748 seconds, which is about a week. The full package includes a quantized 4.33MB pre-trained starter model with 34 million parameters. The full model is a 12-layer Transformer containing 163 million parameters. Total memory use peaked at 68,525 MiB for compression and 73,748 MiB for decompression.

Tufa Labs is responsible for the project and the resulting research. They stated that tufazip is the best entry on the Large Text Compression Benchmark using only a neural network. The company noted that other entries mix transformers with hand-built models. They explained that the predictor updates must be fully deterministic to ensure no data is lost. Tufa Labs also clarified that the tool is for research purposes and not a product.

The Large Text Compression Benchmark is the primary metric affected by this new entry. As of November 19, the 105.39MB version of tufazip ranked 13th on this list. Twelve other hybrid compressors currently beat its score by mixing different model types. The benchmark is strictly for text, meaning it does not apply to media files. Users would need massive hardware resources to actually run the current version.

The tool uses a self-contained language model that learns on the fly rather than using a cloud. Training occurs in two stages, starting with an offline phase for the starter model. The full model then learns online by predicting and training on each token. The unpacking side repeats these steps to rebuild the model alongside the text. This method allows the model to be rebuilt without storing the full trained version.

The first online-only version of the tool ranked second when submitted in early September. That earlier version resulted in a file size of 105.98MB. It required 647,595 seconds to compress and 630,136 seconds to decompress the data. The GPUs for that version peaked at 43.37 GiB of VRAM between them. The articles leave open whether this research will ever become a commercial product.
