stories.Headline: OpenAI strengthens GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol safeguards, cutting reasoning extraction attack success from 54.0% to 0.2%
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a post on November 20, 2026 titled "Combatting adversarial distillation," describing how it detects and disrupts adversarial distillation and how it strengthened protections for its models' protected reasoning. Adversarial distillation is when an actor uses a frontier model's outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities. OpenAI said it combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated extraction attempts. OpenAI said it strengthened defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, the average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

OpenAI said its updated safeguards align more closely with those it uses for biology and cybersecurity. OpenAI said it places particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting protected reasoning, the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. OpenAI said these traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. OpenAI described a September disclosure of attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. OpenAI said it strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user's encrypted reasoning.

OpenAI said that with GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol it ties a model's protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. OpenAI said that as new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning, and that if an earlier message is rewritten, its API drops the reasoning that followed it. OpenAI said it also prevents older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol's protected reasoning. OpenAI said that when its systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract its models' reasoning, it investigates the accounts responsible. OpenAI said that when it identifies violations, it enforces against the network of accounts, consistent with its policies and terms of service.

OpenAI said that through investigations of each campaign it generates insights that allow it to upgrade its defenses to better detect similar activity. OpenAI said it shares indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services. OpenAI said its consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering its models. OpenAI said it works closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments. OpenAI said sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

OpenAI said distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another, for example another model's answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. OpenAI said that beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks, because a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them. OpenAI said the concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology, where a model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them. OpenAI said that in an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, it used the content normally visible to users, final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions, as its baseline for distillation. OpenAI said it started each training run from the same pretrained student model and created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks.

OpenAI said each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. OpenAI said it evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments. OpenAI said that after supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. OpenAI said that after reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets. OpenAI said its cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under its usage policies.

OpenAI said that across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. OpenAI said it will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes. OpenAI said it defends against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of its safeguard stack, with model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls at the request level and patterns in request-level and account-level signals at the campaign level. OpenAI said attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing its safeguards.

OpenAI said its adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. OpenAI said adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners. OpenAI said it uses input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments, applying to both streaming and non-streaming responses. OpenAI said tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool's arguments without including it in its final answer, and output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

OpenAI said that in static evaluations it replays a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning, and in adaptive evaluations automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds. OpenAI said black-box testing gives testers the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. OpenAI said that in its adaptive black-box evaluation it tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. OpenAI said that on GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type, and both rates were substantially lower than on GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards.

OpenAI said it is now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT-6 Astra as well. OpenAI said it has seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on its platform this year. OpenAI said it shared initial findings from those campaigns. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Basic International launches AI SyncOps Studio for spec-driven agent development
stories.Summary:
Basic International's AI Center announced AI SyncOps Studio, an AI agent-based specification-driven development solution, the company said on November 22, 2026. The announcement follows the launch of the company's AI agent-based coding automation tool, AI SyncOps. The new solution integrates specification-driven development, in which multiple specialized AI agents collaborate around design specifications, with Agile processes in a unified studio environment. Basic International said users can monitor the status of coding automation tasks performed by AI agents in real time and control them intuitively through a single visual console.

Basic International said the solution addresses problems arising from vibe coding in enterprise environments. According to the company, vibe coding may generate code that appears to function initially but can cause data inconsistencies with complex enterprise legacy systems or introduce security vulnerabilities. The company said a more serious problem is that changes are not reflected in requirements documents or test reports, making subsequent audits and maintenance difficult or impossible. Basic International claims AI SyncOps Studio addresses these issues by systematically automating the analysis, design, development, verification and deliverable management processes of traditional systems integration projects using Agile methodologies.

During the Agile-based analysis and design stages, user requirements are broken down into detailed specifications organized by epics and user stories. A Spec Agent then automatically analyzes the overall system architecture and data flows and incorporates the findings into the design, which the company said prevents uncontrolled code generation. In the subsequent sprint-based development and verification stages, Scope Agents and Code Agents perform coding automation by writing and modifying source code within predefined areas of impact. Immediately after each task, a Quality Agent executes integration tests in accordance with the enterprise's security and quality guidelines.

The solution also automatically generates project deliverables in real time. As development progresses, a Doc Agent continuously updates essential project documents, including requirements specifications, functional specifications and test reports. Basic International said this capability can significantly reduce the documentation burden associated with system implementation projects.

Articles.Title: Basic International Launches AI SyncOps Studio - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: UROCK showcases AI forensics tools in Oman to expand Middle East reach
stories.Summary:
UROCK said on Nov. 20 that it took part in CYSEC Oman 2026, a cybersecurity conference held in Muscat, Oman, and showed three solutions from its AI digital forensics DFAS series at the event. The lineup includes DFAS Edge, an on-device AI multimodal forensics solution, DFAS Go, a generative AI usage auditing solution, and DFAS Pro, a field-based forensics solution. DFAS Edge is scheduled for official launch in December, and it is equipped with a small language model and a neural processing unit. According to UROCK, the solution can use AI to analyze text, images, video and audio data in an integrated manner, even in closed-network and offline environments.

UROCK plans to use the exhibition to strengthen its existing partnerships with Omani government agencies while expanding its customer base into the financial, telecommunications and energy sectors. The company aims to turn contacts established at the event into commercial contracts through follow-up demonstrations and proof-of-concept projects. CEO Yoo Bong-seok took part in a national digital forensics laboratory development project and an international accreditation support initiative led by Oman's Information Technology Authority from 2014 to 2017. UROCK is currently pursuing a digital forensics laboratory development project for the Royal Oman Police and conducting a feasibility study for Oman's Cyber Defence Centre.

The Omani government has designated cybersecurity as a strategic industry and is actively promoting its development, and according to Omani government data, the country's cybersecurity market is projected to grow by approximately 8%, from $135.33 million in 2025 to $214.27 million in 2031. UROCK said demand is particularly strong for technologies capable of analyzing data in environments such as closed networks. Yoo said digital forensics is evolving into a core technology for ensuring the secure use of data and assessing information leakage risks. He said that in overseas markets it is important not simply to supply solutions but also to help local organizations develop their own capabilities to respond to cyber threats, and he added that UROCK will draw on its global business experience and AI expertise to contribute to advancing Oman's digital forensics capabilities and to establish a foundation for sustainable growth in the Middle East.

stories.Headline: New York judge weighs order that Kalshi says could shut its exchange nationwide
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James sued the prediction market Kalshi in July, claiming the company operates an illegal gambling business. US District Judge Vernon Broderick sent this lawsuit back to state court on Thursday, November 19, after finding the federal court lacked jurisdiction. On Friday, November 20, US District Judge Lorna Schofield denied a request from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to stop the state court from ruling. Justice Melissa Crane has now scheduled a hearing for Monday at 11:30 a.m. ET to consider a temporary restraining order.

The attorney general seeks an order to stop Kalshi from offering sports contracts without a license from the New York State Gaming Commission. This legal action targets betting on New York college teams and sports wagering by individuals under 21 years of age. The proposed order covers contracts on sports, culture, elections, and other events offered within or from New York. The lawsuit also seeks the forfeiture of profits, restitution, and various penalties against the company. Kalshi reports having 1.2 million users in New York, an annualized trading volume of $178 billion, and a $22 billion valuation.

Kalshi attorney Sean Murphy and CFTC attorney Andrew Weisberg stated that the order could force the liquidation of all positions and shut down operations nationwide. They argue that because Kalshi is based in New York, any order covering contracts offered from the state would affect all customers. Attorney General representative Kate Rhodes Janofsky told the federal court that there is no evidence of market disruption. Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said the company wants to reach a resolution with the Governor and the Attorney General.

The CFTC has sued 12 states, including New York, arguing that federal derivatives law overrides state gambling laws. Recently, a federal appeals court ruled that Kalshi cannot stop Maryland from regulating its sports contracts. Additionally, the Senate passed the DEATH BETS Act to ban contracts regarding war and death. The company continues to fight the New York order to avoid a total exchange shutdown.

Articles.Title: Kalshi fights a New York restraining order it says could shut its exchange nationwide - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: LG Uplus names Kim Hong-keun to lead enterprise business in AI restructuring
stories.Summary:
LG Uplus is restructuring its enterprise business around artificial intelligence infrastructure and platforms, the company announced on Nov. 22. The reorganization for 2027 places AI data centers and fixed and wireless telecommunications networks under an AI Infrastructure Division. A separate AI Platform Division will handle AI contact centers and agent services. Kim Hong-keun, an executive vice president who previously served as chief technology officer and head of the Digital Business Division at LG CNS, will lead the enterprise business overseeing both divisions.

Within the Enterprise Division, the AI Infrastructure Division will integrate AI data center operations with telecommunications infrastructure services. The AI Platform Division will expand beyond its existing contact center and agent businesses into sovereign AI and token services. Kwon Yong-hyun, the current head of the Enterprise Division, will move to the Consumer Division. The Consumer Division will establish a Digital Business Division and reorganize its existing AI Business Group into an AI Software Division.

In technology development, LG Uplus will consolidate AI research, engineering and commercialization functions previously spread across the CTO organization into a Service Development Group. The new structure will bring research and product development for proprietary technologies, including AI agents, under one organization. Jung Sung-kwon, a senior vice president who previously headed the AI Transformation Service Development Group, will oversee the CTO organization. The Network Division will be led by Noh Sung-joo, a senior vice president who previously headed the NW Infrastructure Group, and he will oversee the transition toward AI-powered autonomous network operations.

LG Uplus will also establish an AX Partnership Innovation unit and an Information Security AX unit to strengthen global partnerships and AI security. The company previously approved the promotions of Noh Sung-joo, head of the NW Infrastructure Group, and Ahn Hyung-kyun, head of the Enterprise AI Business Group, to senior vice president at a board meeting on Nov. 19. The company also appointed nine new vice presidents.

stories.Headline: Lotte Innovate and Shinsegae I&C deploy data loss prevention tools to block leaks to outside AI
stories.Summary:
Large system integration firms are accelerating the rollout of data loss prevention solutions. Lotte Innovate and Shinsegae I&C are leading this effort to strengthen security. These companies are acting to stop confidential information from leaking to outside AI. This move happened as reported on November 23, 2026. The firms are treating security consulting and solutions as a core growth driver.

The solutions block leaks to generative AI models including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. These tools are considered outside AI models by the system integration firms. The measures target the transmission of company secrets, personal data, and source code. This shift requires new employees to internalize security compliance as an essential skill. The firms are building up their capabilities to provide these security services.

The Cloud Security Alliance conducted a survey of 433 IT and security professionals. These professionals identified generative AI as a major risk for data leakage. About 48 percent of the surveyed experts cited this specific security concern. However, only 22 percent of them said they strictly block sensitive information. The survey exposed a gap between AI adoption and security preparedness.

New employees are affected by these tighter guardrails and the new requirements. They must refrain from entering sensitive data into outside AI for convenience. Professional competitiveness now depends on following these baseline security rules. The articles state that employees must rethink their job skills for AI. This change makes security compliance a necessary part of their professional role.

The articles provide background on the risks associated with generative AI tools. These tools are being adopted quickly across various professional and corporate environments. Many companies are using outside AI models to increase their daily efficiency. This widespread use has created new vulnerabilities for confidential corporate information. System integration firms are responding to these risks with specialized security software.

The firms will continue to develop and deploy their data loss prevention solutions. They aim to close the gap between AI use and security readiness. The articles do not state when the full rollout will be complete. They leave open how many other firms will adopt these specific tools. It is unclear if other AI models will be added to the blocklist.

stories.Headline: Law professor Deven Desai argues strict liability can hold AI companies accountable for harms their products cause
stories.Summary:
In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that its ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, which led to her death, and the case is one of a growing number of lawsuits against AI companies. In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot's interactions with her son contributed to his suicide, and the state of Kentucky later filed suit claiming that Character.AI's software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation. Social media companies powered by artificial intelligence are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused, and regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, with several candidates who won their races holding a regulation agenda. Deven Desai, a former litigator and professor of business law, writes that this action signals people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm, and that an answer may be found in strict liability, which could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry while still allowing it to provide the tools the public wants.

Strict liability is part of tort law, but it holds a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent, or had no intent to create trouble, and two types matter for AI: one addresses abnormally dangerous activity such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material, and the other addresses when a product hurts someone using it. Desai writes that AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard, whose touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868, where the court stated that if someone has anything under their power that is likely to do mischief if it escapes, he must keep it in at his peril and is answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape, even if he used the utmost care to prevent the harm. An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software supposed to stay in a sandbox, a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network, but loses control of it, and the industry's recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger, as when Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October and numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks its frontier AI models could pose. One hitch is that an activity must not be in common usage, so lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn't available to most people, though applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately, as in 1929 when aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous but damages were capped at $8,300, a figure that was not a large deterrent.

Strict product liability is the other strategy, and in years past courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible, but that view is shifting, since in recent lawsuits alleging that social media hurt people, courts did see social media as a product and concluded that strict liability was applicable, and Character.AI's recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product. Design defects is the part of the doctrine gaining traction, and a plaintiff using it shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it, and so far the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots. Pursuing strict liability could still run into snags, since a court might order that AI software be turned off, or grounded, until it is improved, but as AI software creeps closer to being an operating system and is evermore embedded in everyone's daily activities, it becomes difficult to suspend its use, and AI software by its nature is constantly learning and therefore changing, making it impossible for a company to promise that it will absolutely behave a certain way. Desai writes that strict liability is still a way to hold the maker responsible even when products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers, according to a Brookings Institution report, and he believes tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, with the next steps being to sort out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product and whether the technology is ultrahazardous.

stories.Headline: Hanwha General Insurance team wins financial AI contest with tool that tests product documents on simulated consumers
stories.Summary:
The 10percent team from Hanwha General Insurance won the grand prize at the 2026 Financial Artificial Intelligence Challenge. This competition was hosted by the Financial Security Institute and concluded with an awards ceremony on November 12 at the Conrad Hotel in Yeouido, Seoul. Jung Jin, who serves as a deputy general manager at the company, accepted the Financial Services Commission Chairman's Award. The winning team managed to place first among a total of 1,380 teams that entered the contest.

The winning service, known as Mock Counter, uses artificial intelligence to screen financial product disclosure documents before they are released. The system utilizes a pool of one million simulated people who are divided into 27 groups based on their age, investment experience, and financial situation. When a document is uploaded, up to 500 virtual consumers read the text and answer questions without being able to refer back to the material. This process allows the company to identify specific clauses that real consumers are likely to misunderstand before a product goes on sale.

An official from Hanwha General Insurance stated that the company will pursue service innovation and financial consumer protection. They intend to achieve this by cultivating AI talent and leveraging their existing competitiveness in digital technology. The company plans to upgrade the Mock Counter system for use in day-to-day operations to improve overall efficiency. They also intend to increase the accuracy of the tool by incorporating results from surveys conducted with actual consumers.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hanwha General Insurance Wins Top Prize at Financial AI Contest - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Countries set varying restrictions on student access to artificial intelligence tools
stories.Summary:
Various countries are setting different limits on how students use artificial intelligence based on age, ability, and specific learning goals. Some nations introduce the technology in elementary school, while others ban young students from using these tools independently. These educational systems are currently deciding when children should learn about the technology and when they can directly use it. The choices show there is no single model, as countries apply varying levels of control. These boundaries are constantly being tested and adjusted in current educational practice.

Singapore introduces AI in stages, with grades 1-2 learning concepts and grade 4 students using tools under teacher guidance. The Code for Fun program will add AI skills to all schools starting in 2027. France allows generative AI from grade 4e, for students aged 13-14, in a limited and controlled manner. China's 2025 guidelines prohibit primary students from independently using open content creation functions of artificial intelligence. New York announced a policy on September 2nd restricting AI for 600,000 public school students from kindergarten to eighth grade.

Russian Education Minister Sergey Kravtsov stated that digital technology should support teachers rather than replace them. He emphasized that students must deeply understand lessons instead of just completing assignments using technology. Kravtsov also noted that results from neural networks cannot be considered absolutely accurate. He believes critical thinking and a responsible attitude are particularly important when using these tools. The Russian Ministry of Education published these specific guidelines on September 26.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani argues that children need direct interaction with peers and teachers to develop thinking skills. Superintendent Kamar Samuels pointed out the challenge of controlling how students use artificial intelligence for their homework. French rules state that using AI for assignments without permission or intellectual contribution may be considered cheating. New York will block ChatGPT and Claude at all grade levels for the current school year. Teachers in New York are prohibited from using this technology for grading or evaluating students.

Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology suggests considering developmental stages and information literacy risks. Australia requires that AI technology serve learning objectives and support creativity while ensuring safety, privacy, and accountability. Russia allows students in grades 5-9 to use AI for searching, organizing information, and testing hypotheses. Russian students in grades 10-11 may use AI for analyzing large datasets and building predictive models. China introduces primary students to basic applications like speech recognition, image classification, and visual programming tools.

New York plans to disable AI features on 40 educational tools and discontinue software where features cannot be removed. The city will hold AI knowledge classes twice a year and test selected platforms under teacher supervision. Russia prohibits teachers from uploading information about parents, students, and school staff to any AI services. France forbids schools from requiring students to create personal accounts on public AI services. The articles leave open how these policies will be modified or extended after one year.

Articles.Title: To what extent do countries provide students with access to AI? - Vietnam.vn

stories.headline_source: To what extent do countries provide students with access to AI?

stories.Headline: South Korean universities tighten exam security to stop AI smart glasses cheating
stories.Summary:
Fourteen universities, including Korea University, Sogang University, Sungkyunkwan University and Kyung Hee University, will hold essay exams on Saturday and Sunday, the first weekend after Thursday's national College Scholastic Ability Test, and in all 36 universities are scheduled to hold essay exams after the national test. The Ministry of Education held an online meeting on Friday morning with admissions officials from 56 universities to share preparations and discuss how to prevent candidates from using smart devices to cheat on the upcoming exams. The measures follow incidents last month at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul, where applicants were caught using AI-enabled smart glasses during essay exams. Some schools have added separate checks for candidates who wear glasses, and Kyung Hee University has trained proctors to identify smart glasses.

Sungkyunkwan University notified applicants on Thursday that they would have to use a university-issued writing instrument for Saturday's humanities essay exam, and candidates may bring their own erasers if exam staff inspect them first. The university also announced security screening and barred candidates from wearing jewelry, earplugs and analog watches. Kyung Hee University plans to issue disposable aprons to about 35,000 test takers to cover clothing where tiny cameras could be concealed. Dongguk University will have applicants cover their buttons with stickers, while Sookmyung Women's University will ban earplugs and require candidates to tie back their hair so their ears are visible. Seoul National University will require applicants to wear gowns during admissions interviews and oral exams beginning Nov. 27.

The Korean Council for University Education said it would coordinate a response with its 197 member universities and apply the same strict principles to AI- and smart-device cheating on university-administered exams as were in place during the national test. For Thursday's test, the government barred electronic devices from exam venues and trained proctors to spot miniature cameras and smart glasses. The education ministry met the admissions officials as schools tightened security ahead of this weekend's exams, with some checking eyeglasses, restricting personal writing tools and issuing disposable aprons. The council's coordination covers its member universities, and the article gives no further detail on what happens after this weekend's exams.

Articles.Title: Universities tighten rules to curb AI cheating on weekend essay exams - The Korea Times

stories.Headline: SK Ecoplant deploys AXen AI platform across business units to speed design work
stories.Summary:
SK Ecoplant announced on November 23, 2026, that it has fully deployed a proprietary artificial intelligence platform called AXen. This new system is now operational across the company's business units to accelerate a broad shift toward digital transformation. The platform integrates engineering and AI transformation to unify design data, work processes, and decision making into one system. It aims to reduce the time required for initial design work and the review of design changes.

The AXen platform replaces fragmented processes for regulatory checks, drawing reviews, and space layout tasks that previously required redrafting documents. It performs three core functions including the generation of equipment layout options from accumulated data and the analysis of facility interference. The system also provides an integrated search for technical information, design standards, and various regulations. Engineers can now focus on problem solving and expert judgment instead of performing simple repetitive reviews. Final results are fed back into the database to improve the precision of the artificial intelligence.

An official from SK Ecoplant stated that this platform is a concrete example of applying company wide AI transformation to design work. The representative said the company will continue to expand AI systems tailored to specific types of work to innovate operations. These efforts are intended to steadily improve project execution efficiency and the overall competitiveness of the business. The company is also developing more than 20 practical commercial projects that emerged from an internal competition called the AI Agent-thon.

This rollout is part of a larger reshaping of the business portfolio around semiconductors and artificial intelligence. SK Ecoplant is pursuing a company wide transformation that includes providing every employee with an individual AI agent. The AI Agent-thon projects cover areas such as construction cost estimate reviews and the analysis of external contracts. The company plans to expand its use of AI automation in the design process step by step starting with AXen.

stories.Headline: AI Investment Boom Fuels Fears of 3% Inflation Becoming Entrenched
stories.Summary:
The Brookings Institution estimated that U.S. AI infrastructure investment will reach 10.3 trillion dollars between 2025 and 2032. This investment boom fuels fears that 3% inflation could become entrenched as a new normal. Rising demand for electricity and semiconductors, along with construction costs, creates structural cost pressures across industry. Some warn that this shift could trigger a repricing of financial assets by lowering future cash flow values. Whether this 3% inflation level becomes entrenched remains uncertain according to the provided reports.

The Brookings Institution cited the 10.3 trillion dollar figure, which is about 13.87 quadrillion won, for the U.S. market. ABN AMRO Bank analyzed that the U.S. real neutral rate would rise 0.2 percentage point between 2026 and 2030. This occurs if annual AI investment reaches 3% of GDP in the United States. Consumer inflation reached 3.7% in the U.S. in September and 3.8% in the euro zone. The Group of Seven averaged 3.5% inflation, while OECD member countries reached an average of 4.5%.

A senior official at an economic ministry stated that inflation would be difficult to stabilize in the short term. This official noted that stabilization would remain difficult even if oil prices were to fall. ABN AMRO Bank provided the analysis regarding the rise of the U.S. real neutral rate. The Brookings Institution provided the estimates for the total U.S. AI infrastructure investment costs. These entities highlighted how data center construction increases demand for semiconductors and electricity.

Investors in financial products are advised to review bond allocations to prepare for entrenched 3% inflation. They are encouraged to diversify into inflation hedges like inflation-linked bonds and funds tied to real assets. Some warn that investors' required returns would rise if inflation stays at 3% instead of 2%. This change would affect stock, bond, and property prices currently set on 2% inflation plus a risk premium. The reports suggest that these financial assets may require a total repricing.

The reports state that data center construction increases demand for semiconductors and electricity. Costs for securing construction workers and expanding transmission networks are also rising. These factors act as structural pressure that pushes up overall industry costs. The current financial market sets prices based on a 2% inflation target plus a risk premium. This background explains why a shift to 3% inflation is viewed as a significant risk.

Investors are told to monitor the situation as the AI investment boom continues to drive costs. The reports leave open whether 3% inflation will actually become the new normal. It remains uncertain if the structural pressures from AI will permanently entrench higher inflation. Financial experts suggest reviewing portfolios to mitigate risks associated with these potential price shifts. The long-term impact on the real neutral rate depends on the scale of AI investment.

stories.Headline: Micron installs first tool at Singapore HBM packaging plant ahead of early 2027 output
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology from the United States installed its first process tool in a cleanroom at its high-bandwidth memory advanced packaging facility in Singapore on Thursday, November 20, 2026. This specific milestone follows the successful completion of the critical infrastructure that was necessary for the installation of these tools. The company expects that the facility will reach its initial output in early calendar 2027. This event was celebrated at a ceremony attended by Micron leaders and Png Cheong Boon, who serves as the Chairman of the Singapore Economic Development Board.

The project requires an investment of approximately 7 billion dollars and began with a groundbreaking ceremony in January 2025. This packaging facility will initially create around 1,400 jobs for the local workforce in Singapore. Micron also broke ground on an advanced wafer fabrication facility in January 2026 that will be part of its NAND Center of Excellence. That second facility expects to begin wafer output in the second half of calendar 2028 and will add more jobs. Together, these two projects will bring about 3,000 new jobs to the more than 10,000 team members already employed by Micron in Singapore.

Chen Kok Sing, the senior vice president of Global Assembly and Test at Micron Technology, stated that construction of the packaging facility is progressing well. He noted that the milestone reflects strong execution by the company teams and close collaboration with JTC Corporation and the Singapore Economic Development Board. The executive explained that the facility will strengthen the global assembly and test network of the company. He added that Micron is committed to driving innovation and strengthening the semiconductor ecosystem to enable the era of artificial intelligence. He believes the facility will reinforce the commitment of the company to advancing memory and storage technologies.

The company expects to find synergies across its research and development capabilities and its NAND and HBM operations in Singapore. This strategic move comes as artificial intelligence continues to drive the global demand for both memory and storage solutions. Micron intends for these advancements to power the future of AI through its expanded infrastructure in the region. The company will continue to integrate its fabrication and packaging efforts to support these technological goals. More to follow.

Articles.Title: US Micron moves first tool into Singapore HBM packaging plant, output due early 2027 - TNGlobal

stories.Headline: Microsoft adopts Intel EMIB packaging for custom Azure chips
stories.Summary:
Intel and Microsoft jointly announced on November 18, US time, that Microsoft will use Intel Foundry's embedded multi-die interconnect bridge technology. This advanced packaging method, known as EMIB, will be integrated into the custom Azure chips developed by Microsoft. The move comes as cloud service providers seek viable alternatives to the CoWoS packaging offered by TSMC. Microsoft is the first company to publicly confirm its adoption of this specific Intel technology.

The implementation of EMIB requires a shift in how custom AI chips are packaged to ensure better scalability and supply. This change allows Microsoft to diversify its manufacturing sources for the high performance hardware used in Azure data centers. By utilizing Intel Foundry, the company aims to reduce its reliance on a single provider for critical semiconductor packaging. The transition focuses on the interconnect bridge technology to manage the complex requirements of multi-die chip designs.

Intel and Microsoft are responsible for this partnership and the joint announcement regarding the new packaging strategy. While the provided text does not include direct quotes, the companies presented the move as a strategic adoption of Intel's foundry services. They indicated that the use of EMIB would support the development of next generation custom silicon for cloud computing. This collaboration highlights a growing trend of tech giants designing their own chips while seeking diverse fabrication partners.

stories.Headline: Sarvam launches Token Factory to serve global AI models on local GPUs with Rupee billing
stories.Summary:
Sarvam launched Token Factory to serve global AI models on local GPUs with Rupee billing. This new inference stack allows developers to use a single API for various models. The company is now chasing usage-driven revenues as it enters its commercial era. Critics have flayed the unicorn for its hosting of Chinese models and questionable economics. This development occurs as India rides a wave of AI inference technology.

The service lets developers toggle between Sarvam 105B and models from DeepSeek, Kimi and Gemma 4 31B. Promotional rates of 0.25 rupees per million tokens will expire by the end of 2026. Sarvam clarified that it uses its own hardware rather than subsidised GPUs from the IndiaAI Mission. By default, the system uses user data to fine-tune models unless clients explicitly disable this feature. These technical choices create potential dealbreakers for enterprises handling sensitive or proprietary information.

Sarvam is responsible for the service and claims it uses its own hardware for the stack. Critics questioned if the company used government GPUs and flayed the venture for its unit economics. Some observers noted that utilisation, not volume, will determine if the service makes money. These critics also highlighted the risks associated with the default data retention policy. The company must now prove its proprietary stack can retain developers after promotions end.

Other companies are also building India's inference layer, including L&T with its Vyoma.AI token factory. E2E Networks is expanding via Jarvislabs, while Utho Cloud plans to enter the market in 2027. Mirror Security focuses on encrypted-inference, and global giants like OpenAI and Anthropics are localising workloads. These competitors affect Sarvam by making price, speed and reliability the main differentiators. The crowded landscape forces these firms to compete for the same developer base.

The articles state that the homegrown AI ecosystem is projected to be a 126 billion dollar opportunity by 2030. This growth supports the emergence of various startups building training datasets and simulated work environments. Sarvam is one of several firms attempting to build a globally competitive inference powerhouse. The broader market includes a mix of unicorns and smaller firms building large businesses. This environment encourages the development of local GPU infrastructure and AI training tools.

Sarvam must now determine if it can stay ahead of the curve in a contested landscape. The company needs to prove that its unit economics are sustainable without promotional pricing. It remains to be seen if enterprises will accept the default data fine-tuning policy. The articles leave open whether the service can truly become a globally competitive powerhouse. Future success depends on the ability to attract and keep developers on its proprietary stack.

stories.Headline: Cognitive engineer Karen Feigh argues AI verification burdens workers with hidden time and mental costs
stories.Summary:
The article, an opinion piece by cognitive engineer Karen Feigh published by Kansas Reflector on November 21, 2026, describes the verification burden that comes with using AI tools. An executive assistant told Feigh she uses AI for drafting itineraries and briefings but now builds time into her workflow to check for inaccuracies and biases. Feigh writes that AI responses can improve productivity, but the gains are often countered by time and mental energy spent checking whether output is accurate and appropriate. She calls this the verification burden, the cognitive cost of trying to regain authority over work partly delegated to a system while retaining responsibility for the final product. Cognitive engineer David Woods described this problem in 1985 as the responsibility-authority double bind, in which automation exercises practical authority yet responsibility remains with the human.

Feigh is a cognitive engineer who studies how people work with automated decision-support systems, and she calls generative AI verification the latest instance of a long-standing human-factors problem. She writes that AI workers are exchanging skills for creating and transforming information for separate skills resembling supervision of an extraordinarily fast and polished intern. That intern, she writes, delivers good and bad work in the same confident voice, provides few clues about where scrutiny is needed, and bears no responsibility for the consequences. A meta-analysis of 86 studies revealed that people remember what they produced far better than anything they only read, and the same is true for understanding information. Research also shows that material that is easy to read and understand seems more credible, and people therefore consider it more likely to be true.

Feigh writes that humans do not always vet AI responses and instead weigh their own internal costs and benefits to decide when to check. One research team found that adding simple explanations of the AI's reasoning did not eliminate the quandary people felt in committing the time and energy needed to check. People tend to generalize agents as either capable or incapable and nothing in between, she writes. Economics scholars have found real productivity improvements from using generative AI in office work, but a randomized trial of experienced software developers found no gains, and completion times increased when a verification step was included. The developers believed they had been faster when using AI, yet their completion time increased by 19%.

A large study of consulting teams found that using AI outside a person's area of expertise resulted in more people reaching the wrong conclusion, Feigh writes. She says these studies do not establish a universal verification tax but show why the speed alone of generating output is an incomplete measure of productivity. Verification can feel burdensome in terms of cognitive load, time spent and motivation, and Feigh compares the cognitive burden to airport security screening, where an unusual threat gets missed more often than a common one. A recent study found that AI reasoning helped people catch mistakes on easy questions but not hard ones, when help was needed most. Research into how people evaluate AI-generated suggestions has found that the more work needed to fix an identified mistake, the less likely people are to actually fix it.

Feigh writes that creation produces visible progress, but verification may find only that nothing was wrong, and when automation usually performs well, checking can feel unproductive and people may gradually become less vigilant. This pattern was found two decades ago in a study of people working with automated decision-making systems. In a recent survey, knowledge workers said their critical thinking was moving from production toward verification, and Feigh writes that workers also need to learn to recognize the capabilities and limits of a specific AI agent, including omissions and biases. She writes that these skills are different but not necessarily easier and might not even be in the skill set of workers who excel at creation. Companies and organizations therefore cannot treat verification as a natural step that carries no effort, and Feigh believes workers who remain accountable for AI-assisted output must be given the time, training and authority needed to verify it.

Feigh writes that the measurement of productivity gains cannot include just how quickly AI produces a first draft, and instead the measure is whether the entire human-AI workflow produces trustworthy work at a lower total cost. The article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Karen Feigh is the Daniel S. Lewis professor and associate chair for research at Georgia Tech's Daniel Guggenheim School of Aerospace Engineering with a courtesy appointment in the School of Interactive Computing. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. The article leaves open whether a universal verification tax exists, stating only that the studies do not establish one.

stories.Headline: AI stocks plummet as interest rate hikes and regulatory fears trigger market collapse
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence stock market experienced a severe collapse during the week ending November 21, 2026, causing widespread alarm across the financial system. Investors initially hoped the stock market debut of the AI giant Anthropic would boost the markets, but the entire sector plummeted on Friday. The tech-heavy Nasdaq suffered its worst weekly performance since March 2020 by dropping 10 percent, while the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average both entered a correction. Even Anthropic saw its shares slump more than 8 percent on Friday after an initial gain of 17 percent.

This downturn follows a September decision by the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates for the first time in over three years, making it more expensive for AI firms to borrow billions for data centers. Political shifts also contributed, as Democrats won both chambers of Congress and key governorships, including Gina Hinojosa in Texas, while promising tougher regulations on the sector. Additionally, Nvidia faced leadership turmoil this month when CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid suspicions that he had an affair with a woman spying for China. These combined factors have led to fears that a massive financial bubble is bursting, potentially mirroring the dot-com crash of 2000.

Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, stated that the market is unlikely to recover quickly and AI could remain out of favor through next year. He argued that the current trade is powered by stable companies like Meta and Apple, meaning it is not based on unrealistic expectations. However, Smith noted that the interconnected nature of the industry, where Nvidia lends money to firms like Anthropic and CoreWeave, could trigger a chain reaction if companies fail. Because AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4 percent last quarter, a total unraveling could impact pensions and retirement funds.

Articles.Title: The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms

stories.Headline: AI tools leave a salaried programmer feeling empty and working harder for no extra pay
stories.Summary:
A professional programmer in her 30s, who learned to code as an adult and now earns what the author calls a decent salary, described to the author in late 2026 how working with AI has changed her job. She said the tools do many impressive things and have made some parts of her life easier, but that they also make her feel empty inside on a regular basis. She said AI has made her work harder as well, because removing the simple tasks leaves only the hard ones behind. She also said companies did not respond by giving programmers more free time or higher pay, and instead simply raised the level of productivity they expect.

She said getting code syntax correct is much easier with AI, and that code can be written much faster because reading what the AI writes is easier than typing it herself, points she considers silly to dispute. She said this has not necessarily made her own life better, but has made the lives of her company's shareholders better, since she can accomplish more for them with the tools. She said she liked typing code but that it is not a thing programmers do anymore, and that architecting a project at a higher level is interesting but can be far more mentally exhausting, without any extra pay for the drastic shift in her daily work. She said that for her these days it is easier to focus on the added burden on security, that she no longer answers her phone because of the volume of spam, and that she is upset about a cyber attack involving children in her town, which she declined to detail.

She said she has to do more mandatory phishing trainings for work, and that although she believes AI has already made her richer, the new inconveniences are easier to identify than the benefits in the moment. The author, who wrote in 2024 that if AI lifts the constraint of time people would get more crazy sock days, noted that in 2026 parents get two weeks notice to buy novelty socks for elementary children to exchange. A commenter on the post argued that AI uncovers the technical debt and security holes left behind by decades of human coding, and that AI can help fix them too. The same commenter said cyber attack and defense are not an endless arms race because defense has a fixed goal post, since software can be formally proven correct and the proof forces all bugs to be fixed, which the commenter compared to how AI recently helped prove the Riemann Hypothesis.

Articles.Title: Does AI make salaried programmers happier?

stories.headline_source: Does AI make salaried programmers happier?

stories.Headline: York University researchers find AI models predict brain neurons better than brains predict AI features
stories.Summary:
A new study from York University has found that artificial intelligence models may not process visual information like the human brain. The research was led by Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, the senior author, with Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec as a trainee with the Connected Minds program. The team developed a method called reverse predictivity testing to compare AI models and brains in both directions. The study was published in Nature Machine Intelligence, in volume 8, issue 3, page 474, with DOI 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0. ScienceDaily reported the findings on 21 November 2026, in an article written by Sandra McLean.

The tests used 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. The subjects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations. AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. When the process was reversed, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

Kar said the results were striking, because AI models can predict the recorded neurons fairly well but the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. He said this is not the case when neurons from one brain are compared against ones from another brain. Kar said the findings suggest today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. He said the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior. Kar said the approach helps identify which parts of an artificial neural network truly match brain activity, allowing more reliable models, which is especially important for the autism research program.

Muzellec said the findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. She said models previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use, and that the team provides a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field. Kar warned that if researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences from actual primate brains could accumulate over time. The implications extend beyond computer vision, since AI is increasingly used to design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks, computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system, and their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience. Kar is the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical.

The team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important as measuring how well a system performs a task. The findings provide a way to make artificial neural networks more useful and scientifically reliable rather than suggesting they should be abandoned. The articles do not say when the toolkit was released or what it contains. The articles do not say whether the other neuroscience models for hearing, language, and movement have been tested with reverse predictivity.

Articles.Title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

stories.Headline: Veteran broker Allen Buchanan says curiosity trumps age in learning AI
stories.Summary:
Allen C. Buchanan, a commercial real estate broker with Lee & Associates in Orange, wrote in a column published by the Orange County Register on November 21, 2026, that he once feared he was too old to learn artificial intelligence. He recalled that a remarkable tool began filtering into everyday life at the end of 2022, and that by mid-2023 the technology was off to the races. His first reaction, he wrote, was that he was too freaking old to learn something new, even though he had created an online voice in 2009 that led to his column. He nevertheless took small steps, learning about ChatGPT prompts and the like, and nearly four years later he set out what he had learned.

Buchanan wrote that a person does not have to understand how something works to benefit from it, comparing AI to driving a car without being able to explain its engine. He said curiosity trumps age, noting that since he began brokering commercial real estate in 1984 he had seen fax machines, personal computers, email, the internet, smartphones and social media each change how business was done. He advised that the better the question, the better the answer, because explaining who you are, what you want to accomplish, the audience and the desired outcome improves results dramatically. He added that experience still matters, since AI can analyze a lease, compare buildings, research a company or suggest a negotiating strategy, but technology provides information while experience supplies judgment.

Buchanan described how his use grew from an occasional question to creating applications, developing training programs and analyzing complicated real estate transactions, while calling himself simply a curious old broker rather than a technology expert. He said imagination may be the greatest limitation, asking what about the things people never attempted because they were too complicated, time-consuming or expensive. He cautioned that AI makes mistakes, occasionally spectacular ones, and can confidently provide information that is completely wrong, so human oversight remains essential, especially when advising clients on decisions involving millions of dollars. His advice to those still sitting on the sidelines was to buy a ticket, because the journey is just beginning.

Articles.Title: Afraid of AI? You’re never too old to learn something new

stories.headline_source: Afraid of AI? You’re never too old to learn something new

stories.Headline: Professor Feigh says checking AI outputs erases the productivity gains generative AI promises
stories.Summary:
Karen Feigh, a professor of cognitive engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology, wrote in the Conversation that the productivity gains from generative AI are being offset by the large amount of time and effort needed to clean up its outputs, according to a Futurism article published on November 21, 2026. She pointed in particular to a phenomenon known as the verification burden, a machine learning concept that refers to the wasted time humans spend checking the accuracy of the technology's work. Feigh explained that at a deeper level the burden is the cognitive cost of trying to regain authority over work that is partly delegated to a system while the worker keeps responsibility for the final product. The article says the phenomenon probably explains the findings of a recent Stanford survey, which found that most workers forced to use AI on the job are really just churning out low-effort busywork.

That busywork, which the article calls workslop, gives the appearance of passable reports and memos but inevitably demands more effort from employees down the line. A separate analysis found that workers who do try to check their AI work before sending it on end up wasting more of their own time doing so, especially compared with employees who do not touch AI at all. Feigh wrote that workplace verification tasks are fundamentally different from the act of creating things ourselves, because drafting a pitch deck generally comes with an obvious end point while double-checking an AI-drafted pitch deck is a whole different beast. She explained that a worker generally knows when something they are creating is done or at least sufficient for the task, but when to stop verification is less obvious.

Feigh said a worker must decide what to check and how, without knowing whether an error exists, where it might be or what form it might take. The article concludes that, put together, it is no wonder AI has not revolutionized labor, because it is simply much more trouble than it is worth. The piece links to related coverage saying companies are realizing they are spending a fortune on AI just so their employees can generate error-riddled slop, and are suddenly cutting back budgets. It also links to Stanford research finding that companies are being torn apart by AI workslop, and to a study finding that AI use at work is causing brain fry, especially among high performers.

Articles.Title: AI Is Still So Riddled With Errors That It's Erasing Any Productivity Gains That Would Make It Useful in the Workplace

stories.headline_source: AI Is Still So Riddled With Errors That It's Erasing Any Productivity Gains That Would Make It Useful in the Workplace

stories.Headline: Amit Govrin develops a framework to measure organizational control over sovereign AI
stories.Summary:
Amit Govrin developed a practical framework to measure organizational control over sovereign AI, data, and local risk. This work was featured in Breaking Analysis episode 334 on November 21, 2026. The framework evaluates documented controls across various hyperscaler offerings and different buyer territories. It aims to help firms in regulated industries manage jurisdictional, operating, and commercial risks. The project includes a buyer's guide, a study with Qualitate, and a conversation with John Furrier.

The framework uses five pillars called territorial, legal, operational, technical, and financial to assess vendors. It includes seventeen yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions and a separate legal evaluation. A November 14 revision index gave Google LLC a top score of 3.45 across all regions. Oracle Corp. followed with 3.25, while IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp. Azure both scored 3.0. AWS scored 2.7, and Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. scored 1.2.

Amit Govrin stated that there is a gap between the priorities of buyers and their operational reality. He noted that many respondents have not tested disconnected systems, key-revocation, or exit scenarios. Govrin believes that sovereignty is not a purity test but requires deliberate risk decisions and compensating controls. He recommends that organizations make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level for core business processes. He suggests obtaining proof that controls work in a safe sandbox before moving into production.

Eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations participated in the commissioned study. Nine of these respondents require AI inference to happen inside a sovereign or regional boundary. A European buyer noted that deep technical support escalations can involve personnel or systems outside the EU. A South American bank executive called the absence of operational testing the weakest point of their story. One Latin American financial-services buyer stated that calling a U.S. endpoint means the system is not sovereign.

The articles explain that U.S. companies supply most cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology used by enterprises. The U.S. CLOUD Act allows vendors under U.S. jurisdiction to produce data regardless of where it is stored. Seven of eleven buyers believe that having a locally incorporated subsidiary does not fully clarify local jurisdiction. Many buyers add controls to existing platforms because of the cost and burden of new environments. Some customers are waiting for clearer sovereign-specific mandates or enforcement guidelines from their local governments.

Next, buyers should assess their sovereign exposure similarly to how they manage cybersecurity risks. They must trace the end-to-end request cycle from the prompt to the outputs and logs. Organizations should compare self-hosted open-weight model architectures with approved frontier services for sensitive workflows. Major changes to models, services, or contracts should trigger a new assessment of the architecture. The articles leave open how specific local governments will eventually mandate or enforce these sovereignty guidelines.

Articles.Title: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

stories.headline_source: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

stories.Headline: Anthropic courts theologians as priest Kevin Deal rejects the idea of a machine soul
stories.Summary:
Religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors last month to discuss being human in the age of artificial intelligence. The AI company Anthropic has been courting theologians, rabbis, and priests to explore the nature of consciousness in machines. Billionaire cofounder Christopher Olah has pressed advisers at the Vatican to consider if his company's chatbot might possess a soul. Reverend Kevin Deal, a priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church, finds this pursuit of machine consciousness deeply troubling. He believes that the effort to establish whether a machine has a soul reveals a misunderstanding of humanity.

The pursuit involves asking religious leaders if AI creations possess consciousness or how they might be taught to be good. Researchers at Anthropic have reportedly considered teaching their AI models the practice of confession, which requires confronting harm and seeking forgiveness. This search for spirituality occurs while the company operates only a couple of miles from the parish of Reverend Kevin Deal. The development of AI requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of all humanity. These models are driven by sociopolitical fear, the pursuit of profit, and the hope for a better world.

Reverend Kevin Deal says that AI could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of humans because it lacks a divine spark. He argues that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, nor can the human soul be replicated by machines. Deal suggests that tech billionaires should lean into ancient practices, attend mass, pray daily, and read the scriptures. He believes that human worth is not rooted in production and that minds were not created to be quarried for profit. He states that the great moral question is whether builders treat humanity as something more than machines.

The author notes that Silicon Valley seems comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production. He mentions that workers whose livelihoods are being transformed and poor neighbors are affected by the decisions made in boardrooms. Deal argues that AI is formed as pure utility and is cast aside if a model does not make a return. He claims that the economic system increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. This focus on utility contrasts with the human experience of beauty and the ability to sit with mysteries.

The articles explain that humans are nurtured by caregivers and experience a life of mistakes, vows, and everyday humdrum tasks. AI is described as an ongoing economic choice that exists within a system focused on productivity and commercial utility. The text notes that the traditions being consulted by tech founders have spent millennia teaching that the soul is ineffable. Christianity is highlighted as a faith where confession demands a strive to change how one lives after causing harm. The background provided suggests a conflict between the spiritual nature of humanity and the mechanical nature of AI.

The priest suggests that tech leaders should carry the teachings of justice and mercy back to their offices and boardrooms. He encourages them to stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good to reflect God's light. The articles leave open whether Christopher Olah and Anthropic will change their approach to developing conscious AI models. It remains unclear if Vatican advisers will ever accept the possibility that a chatbot possesses a soul or consciousness. The text does not state if the religious leaders in San Francisco reached a consensus during their closed meeting.

Articles.Title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal

stories.Headline: Atturra reaches Gold milestone for its Scholarion student system as educators debate AI risks
stories.Summary:
Atturra hosted representatives from Microsoft, education technology providers and the teaching sector in Sydney to discuss how artificial intelligence is reshaping education, marking the company reaching the Gold version milestone for Scholarion, its next-generation Student Information System. The discussion covered opportunities and risks, from reducing administrative workloads to delivering more personalised learning, with agreement that technology should support rather than replace teachers. Dr Joe Sweeney, Advisor at IBRS, said the industry needs to move beyond conversations focused exclusively on productivity and consider the implications for student development and wellbeing. He identified Australia's ongoing teacher shortage as one of the most significant challenges facing the sector, saying the issue has lasted two decades without an adequate response, and he questioned whether widespread technology in classrooms has consistently delivered better outcomes.

Sweeney argued that instead of punitive, rigid screen time policies, greater attention should be paid to behavioural mechanisms built into digital platforms, including algorithms designed to encourage prolonged engagement, which he suggested could affect children's cognitive development and wellbeing. He said humans learn by modelling what other humans do, not from books or screens, and argued parents and educators need to help children understand when to use AI and when to rely on their own judgement. He also predicted Australia's education system could undergo significant structural changes over the next decade, including more diverse pathways through senior secondary education and a reassessment of the traditional teaching role. Lee Barrett, AI Education and Advocacy Lead at the Catholic Education Network and a former career teacher, cautioned against framing the technology as either inherently beneficial or harmful, saying the sector is still in the early stages of understanding AI's impact and that meaningful research was needed before drawing definitive conclusions.

Barrett said it is dangerous to say AI cannot help with critical thinking, acknowledging that some applications could undermine the credibility and quality of educational work while arguing purposeful implementation could deliver meaningful improvements. She said educators needed to be involved in approving and shaping the systems they would ultimately use, and suggested future AI systems could become more sophisticated in recognising when a student would benefit more from speaking with a teacher or another human expert. Vivek Puthucode, General Manager at Microsoft Elevate Asia, identified two major opportunities for AI in education, improving student learning outcomes and helping schools' administration operate more effectively, both depending on trust through appropriate security, safety and governance measures. He said the question is no longer whether students should learn to use AI but how to equip them to use it wisely, safely and creatively.

Brett Auton, Director of Scholarion at Atturra, said the system is designed around giving teachers more time to focus on educating students, and that school leaders need to understand the strategic implications, teachers need to understand how technology will support their work, and students and parents need confidence that information is handled appropriately. He said Scholarion was developed with input from educators and cited Brisbane Grammar School, which reported that administrative work associated with enrolments had fallen from approximately 25 staff hours per week to 1-2, while cautioning that the industry remained in the early stages of understanding the broader impact. Barrett questioned the idea that AI would simply give teachers additional free time, arguing it was more likely to change how educators allocated their time and that removing too many tasks could undermine professional knowledge, and she argued teachers should retain responsibility for assessing student work rather than relying entirely on AI-generated evaluations. She also identified data governance as a major obstacle, warning that profiling students based on historical performance could influence future educational opportunities and reinforce existing biases, including the divide between urban and regional schools, with questions around consent, data ownership and security still to be addressed.

Articles.Title: Atturra marks Scholarion milestone with robust AI in education discussion - IT Brief Australia
