stories.Headline: NPI and Arcana Research find AI spending outpaces governance and sourcing controls
stories.Summary:
NPI and Arcana Research released a report titled The State of Enterprise AI: 2027 Planning Edition on November 21, 2026, which found that AI has become a material IT spending category while the practices used to buy, govern and optimize that spend have not kept pace. The study evaluated 23 vendors and found that all of them score higher on execution than on value, which the report says highlights an opportunity for enterprises to challenge AI pricing and negotiate stronger terms. Ian Kar, managing partner at Arcana Research, said AI budgets are growing rapidly while vendor relationships are still taking shape, and he expects enterprises to regularly reassess where AI spend is going as AI labs release upgraded models and open-source alternatives gain ground. Kar also said controls and governance are lagging adoption, leaving gaps in spending and usage visibility that he expects companies to close in 2027 and beyond. The report estimates AI's median share of IT spend at 2.5 to 10 percent, reaching as high as 14 to 20 percent among enterprises with $2 billion to $10 billion in revenue and among mid-market enterprises.

This spending is already distorting IT budgets, yet it often still hides in other line items inside the largest companies, and even buyers who see results still feel they are overpaying. The categories most represented on the AI displacement watchlist are workflow, CRM and ERP. Sourcing is late to the table, with 47 percent of companies bringing sourcing into AI purchases only after the technical shortlist and 13 percent waiting until contracting or renewal, while 66 percent cannot see model and API consumption, which the study calls its largest reported AI spending blind spot. Responsibility for closing these gaps falls to the enterprises buying AI, according to the report, which frames lagging controls and governance as a priority for 2027 and beyond. Kar said the rapid release of upgraded models by AI labs and the gains made by open-source alternatives mean buyers should expect to regularly reassess where their AI spend is going.

The study points to the gap between execution and value scores as leverage for enterprises to challenge AI pricing and negotiate stronger terms with vendors. It also identifies the inability of 66 percent of companies to see model and API consumption as the largest blind spot reported in the research. The context is a market where AI budgets are growing rapidly while vendor relationships are still taking shape, and where sourcing teams arrive late in most AI purchases. The report places workflow, CRM and ERP at the top of its AI displacement watchlist, suggesting those categories face the most pressure from AI adoption. The articles do not say what specific actions NPI or Arcana Research will take next, beyond Kar's statement that closing the gaps in spending and usage visibility will be a priority in 2027 and beyond.

stories.Headline: Shortical licenses actor Aki Avni's likeness for its first AI microdrama
stories.Summary:
The startup Shortical licensed the face of actor Aki Avni for its first AI microdrama. This project premiered in Los Angeles last week and is called Inevitable. Avni is an Israeli film and television star who previously appeared on the show 24. The production used his likeness to create a digital avatar for the series. In the plot, Avni plays himself licensing his face to a film studio.

The series is wholly AI and represents the first such licensing deal for Shortical. The company was founded last January and produces two minute episodes of soapy romances. It offers the first seven to ten episodes free before requiring a monthly subscription. Previous live action titles include Accidentally Married My Boss and Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy. Other titles include Crossing the Line with My Neighbor and Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.

Aki Avni said the project was exciting and nerveracking because AI is a new art format. CEO Guy Shimoni said AI allows small teams to produce movie scale productions with epic fantasies. He noted that they can now include superheroes, werewolves, and kingdoms. A company representative said the deal with Avni was a direct agreement. They stated that his compensation was in line with industry standards for non AI roles.

Jennifer Cooper of Vertical Drama Love said AI has devastated the industry and caused work loss. She believes AI is pushed on audiences rather than meeting a specific demand. Many young actors are affected because companies are downsizing and no longer require real people. Some creators in the industry claim that their likenesses have been stolen. Cooper noted that venture capitalists currently view AI as gold for investment purposes.

Shortical produces risqué romances that often feature cliff hangers to keep viewers glued to phones. Most of the platform viewers are in the United States, though China has the largest audience. The demographic skews heavily female, with many people watching the shows to wind down. Some AI programs on the website already have millions of views. In China, some firms pay between 15 and 700 US dollars for facial likenesses.

Shortical now invites people to submit social media handles to license their faces for contracts. The company recently partnered with Payouts.com to create a system for creator and gig disbursements. Shortical plans to promote its face licensing offering more actively following the launch of Inevitable. The company has not shared the specific figure paid to Aki Avni for his role. It remains unclear if the company will offer royalty based compensation on a case basis.

stories.Headline: Fotello adds an AI agent that checks listing photos and directs human editors to fix them
stories.Summary:
Fotello, an AI photo editing tool for real estate photography, has become widely used by working professionals, according to an article published by Fstoppers on November 21, 2026. The article's author, who discloses that Fotello advertises with Fstoppers, says that a year earlier most people welcomed automated real estate editing because the work is tedious and time-consuming. He reports that after his early videos about Fotello drew many negative comments, he spoke in person with photographers who shoot real estate part-time and full-time, and every one of them said they were already using Fotello or a very similar AI editing tool. He also says Fotello's owner told him that one quarter of all homes currently being sold in America are run through Fotello, a number he asked the owner to repeat because he did not believe it.

The software works by uploading images, which can be brackets, flash shots or natural light, with room lights on or off, and Fotello edits them in a minute or two. Over the past year the company added tools aimed at common complaints, including a "Change wall color" slider that lets users match the real paint color and also adjust the ceiling color, and an upload button for users' own skies, such as those from Mike Kelley's Ultimate Sky Library sold in the Fstoppers store. If users want changes beyond the AI blending, they can type a request into a box and a human editor makes the fix at no extra cost, and once photos are published the realtor or homeowner gets their own box to request changes. A faster option lets the AI make the change instead, and the author says his test requests, removing a plant and stand and removing Christmas decorations while leaving a pink plant in place, both came out perfectly.

The newest feature is a "Make my photos better" button on a listing, which sends an AI agent through every photo, grouping them by room even when a room was shot from several angles. The agent checks that wall color is consistent across each room's shots, that furniture and floor color are accurate, that reflections of the photographer and camera are removed, that sky replacements look right, and that perspective and horizons are corrected, with optional decluttering checks such as removing bathroom items, trash bins and visible wires and closing toilet seats. Because the AI can spot these problems but often cannot fix them all to a photographer's standard, the system writes a list of needed edits for every image and sends it to a human, who then edits the photos based on what the AI told them to do. The author says this creates work for human editors but also means humans are working directly for and answering to AI, and he does not know how he feels about it, while noting that the photographers he has talked to are already using such tools whatever the comment sections say.

Articles.Title: Fotello AI Is Taking Over Real Estate Photo Editing

stories.Headline: Republican groups account for about 80% of $137 million in AI-generated political ads
stories.Summary:
Campaigns across the country spent more than $137 million on AI-generated political ads by mid-October of this election year, according to researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project, and Republican groups accounted for about 80% of those messages. Californians saw candidates battle massive robots, appear as caped crusaders and kowtow to bloodthirsty crowds and rich fat cats, all through fake images generated with artificial intelligence to help campaigns stand out online and on air. Many of the spots leaned on humor and exaggeration, such as former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt depicting himself as Batman and failed gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton appearing as a gladiator in a crowded coliseum that included rival Xavier Becerra and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Other ads were not exaggerations and seemed more realistic, such as a mailer circulating in a San Diego suburb that showed a male school board candidate behind a desk and his female opponent working a fake bake sale, an image she called sexist.

Ramesh Srinivasan, a UCLA professor of information studies who hosts the Utopias podcast, said the president has put out plenty of AI-generated content and that so-called AI slop is almost everywhere. He said the deeper issue is less the slop itself than the way AI is being used to promote and create what could almost be called propaganda-type targeting. He said the Cambridge Analytica story a decade ago involved a third party advising many right-wing and other candidates, using people's data to create content that targeted them based on predictions of their psychology. He said AI systems can now create content in real time that targets a person based on their psychology without the multi-step process of buying data, gathering it and building content from it.

Srinivasan said that if someone can gather and access a range of data about a voter, including credit card records and not just what the person posts on Instagram, that data can influence what the person sees and does not see, which already happens on social media. He said AI can in this case create content that directly targets a person based on data about them, which he called very pernicious because people have no disclosure around when something is or is not AI-generated. He said he has been working with people in the U.S. Congress and in the state Senate to try to at a minimum force third parties to watermark anything created by AI. He described watermarking as something put on an image that can never be written over and that would say the image is AI generated.

Articles.Title: Commentary: Campaigns spent millions on AI in election advertising – but was it effective?

stories.headline_source: Commentary: Campaigns spent millions on AI in election advertising – but was it effective?

stories.Headline: Economists warn of an AI bubble after Anthropic IPO triggers market volatility
stories.Summary:
The company Anthropic finalized a blockbuster initial public offering on Wednesday, November 19, 2026, which rapidly pushed its valuation to 1.5 trillion dollars. This unprecedented growth has caused economists to worry that the artificial intelligence sector is currently a massive bubble. Investors are increasingly concerned that the trillions of dollars spent on this technology will not provide a return in the near future. These fears were heightened when the Nasdaq fell by 3.7 percent after Anthropic stock tumbled by 12 percent.

This volatile environment requires investors to prepare for a potential economic downturn or a dramatic market retrenchment. Google recently saw its market capitalization drop by half a trillion dollars in one day because AI search features hindered traditional advertising revenue. Some estimates suggest that companies are spending as much as 800 billion dollars every year on AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, SpaceX rebranded as an AI company and predicted annual revenues of 1 trillion dollars by 2030, with future sales potentially reaching 26.5 trillion dollars.

Gary Gensler, an MIT economist and former head of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, stated that the industry is already a bubble. He warned that history shows new technologies eventually plateau after significant investment, suggesting that people should prepare for stormy weather. David B. Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School, noted that no company in history has grown so large so quickly. He added that the expectations for continued rapid growth will likely be off the charts.

The market is struggling because corporate customers are rattled by the exorbitant costs of using frontier coding tools. One company reportedly spent 500 million dollars on Claude tokens in a single month, leading many businesses to adopt cheaper Chinese models. This shift toward hybrid spending occurs as AI errors continue to erase productivity gains in the workplace. Experts remain uncertain whether the eventual correction will be a soft recession or a more dramatic collapse.

stories.Headline: DXC and Cisco integrate AI network intelligence into DXC OASIS to speed Meraki Wi-Fi incident resolution
stories.Summary:
DXC Technology has launched a joint innovation effort with Cisco to integrate Cisco's AI network intelligence into DXC OASIS, starting with workplace Wi-Fi performance in Cisco Meraki environments, the companies said on 23 November 2026. Under the arrangement, Cisco's AI Assistant for Networking will identify likely causes of network disruption, while DXC OASIS will manage diagnostics, approvals and remediation steps under policy controls with change tracking. IT teams will retain oversight from diagnosis through to resolution, and the initial focus is on cloud-managed Meraki networks used to connect and manage workplace devices and Wi-Fi. DXC OASIS is DXC's orchestration platform for IT operations, and Cisco is contributing network intelligence, including AI Assistant, Experience Metrics and platform tools to support investigation and network actions.

The effort is designed to connect network data with broader operational processes, rather than keep troubleshooting within a single management console, so an incident detected in the network can trigger coordinated checks and follow-up tasks across infrastructure, applications and service management systems. One aim is to speed root-cause analysis by combining Cisco's network telemetry with AI-assisted diagnostics and DXC's operational processes, and another is to support a governed remediation workflow in which any action still goes through approvals, guardrails and audit tracking. A pilot cited by DXC showed incident resolution times improving from one to two hours to five to seven minutes, though DXC did not provide further details on the pilot environment and presented the result as evidence for using agentic AI with human oversight in IT operations. The first implementation centres on workplace Wi-Fi incidents in Cisco Meraki environments, connecting Cisco's AI Assistant and Model Context Protocol tools with DXC OASIS so approved actions can be taken within a structured operational process.

Dan Gray, President of Global Infrastructure Services at DXC Technology, said enterprise teams do not need more alerts but faster paths to resolution, and that AI can help identify issues while realizing value requires organizations to coordinate action across people, systems and workflows. He said that by bringing Cisco's network intelligence into DXC OASIS, the companies are helping enterprises turn AI-powered insights into action, resolve issues faster, reduce operational complexity and improve the experience for IT teams and end users while maintaining human oversight and control. Joe Vaccaro, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Network Platform and Assurance at Cisco, said enterprise networks generate massive amounts of rich operational telemetry, but turning those insights into rapid, safe remediation has traditionally required intense manual effort. He said that by integrating Cisco's AgenticOps capabilities into DXC OASIS, DXC's AI agents and engineers can collaborate across complex IT environments, delivering governed, closed-loop network automation that accelerates incident resolution while keeping human teams in control and linking back to broader enterprise context such as service management tools.

The collaboration reflects a broader push by large IT suppliers to apply AI to operations management while keeping formal approval steps in place, with DXC and Cisco positioning the integration around governance and traceability as much as speed, and every action subject to policy controls and change tracking. For enterprise customers, the practical test will be whether an AI-identified network issue can move through investigation and remediation without adding operational burden, and the companies are starting with Wi-Fi performance, where user impact is immediate and the source of a problem can be difficult to isolate across devices, access points and wider IT systems. DXC described Meraki as the starting point for a repeatable model, and the companies expect to extend the same approach to other Cisco technologies over time, although they did not specify which products might come next.

stories.Headline: Alyve CEO Mark Cameron warns Australian firms treat AI as automation rather than strategy
stories.Summary:
Mark Cameron, founder and chief executive officer of Alyve, warned that Australian businesses are adopting artificial intelligence in ways that may improve efficiency without strengthening their competitive position, according to IT Brief Australia. Cameron said many leadership teams treat AI mainly as a tool for automation and cost reduction rather than asking how it could help them enter new markets, develop new revenue streams or change the way they compete. His comments reflect a broader debate in Australian business over whether early AI spending is being directed toward operational savings rather than longer-term strategic change. Cameron, whose firm advises executive teams on AI strategy and business transformation, said that focus is becoming common in boardroom discussions.

Cameron argued that the greater risk is not the direct cost of software purchases but the time lost when companies run limited trials without changing the business around them. He said AI plans presented by senior teams often centre on making current processes faster and cheaper, which in his view risks preparing companies for an outdated model of competition while markets and customer expectations continue to shift. He said business leaders should first decide what position they want to hold in their market over the next few years, then determine where AI investment should be directed, because otherwise efficiency gains can reinforce the wrong priorities. The warning comes as organisations across sectors face pressure to show practical returns from AI spending, with back-office automation, staff productivity tools and process redesign among the easiest starting points.

Cameron said that emphasis could leave boards with a misleading sense of progress, because a company focused only on internal efficiencies could still lose ground if competitors use AI to change customer experience, expand into adjacent services or rethink delivery models. He also raised concern about the use of competitors as a benchmark for AI planning, arguing that copying rival initiatives is unlikely to create meaningful differentiation. Instead, he said, businesses should identify a small number of strengths that would make them difficult to challenge and use AI investment to build those areas, with the aim of creating difference rather than parity. He placed AI strategy closer to mainstream corporate planning than to technology deployment alone, saying leaders should link it to decisions about market direction, organisational strengths and speed of execution.

Cameron also pointed to organisational learning as a factor that may increasingly separate strong performers from weaker ones, saying the value of AI lies not only in generating insights or outputs but in how quickly a business can respond to what it learns. Alyve advises executive teams on AI strategy and business transformation and has offices in Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane.

stories.Headline: Physician-author argues AI should assist transplant teams rather than decide organ allocation
stories.Summary:
The CBS legal drama Cupertino, in its sixth episode titled "Harper," turned its lens to artificial intelligence and life-or-death medical allocation. In the episode, Harper Gervin, 27, the roommate of Price, Siffre & Associates manager Christy Palladino, lost her long-awaited liver transplant to Albert Ensler, a wealthy venture capitalist, just before surgery. With the organ viable for four hours and Michael Price, Olivia Siffre, and Judge Hornstein stranded in U.S. 101 traffic, they litigated by video. Assuming AI bias disadvantaged Harper, the attorneys learned that the allocation algorithm selected her, but a hospital physician-executive overrode it after Ensler's foundation offered a cancer-research donation. Christy exposed the quid pro quo, restored Harper's claim, and revealed that human corruption poses a greater danger than AI bias.

The article's author, Arthur Lazarus, a physician-author, noted that the television producers decided not to credit his novel Transplant, which examined the nefarious side of transplant allocation. He wrote that in real-world transplant settings, AI has shown more promise than harm as a decision-support tool, though many proposed applications still require prospective clinical validation. Transplant waitlists have long relied on mathematical formulas, such as the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, adopted for U.S. liver allocation in 2002, to estimate medical urgency and prioritize candidates. MELD is a statistical risk score, not an autonomous AI, and its current adult version, MELD 3.0, was implemented in 2023 to address disadvantages faced by women. The U.S. transplant system is transitioning toward continuous distribution models that replace rigid allocation categories with weighted point systems, and lung allocation adopted this framework in 2023.

Lazarus wrote that continuous distribution is a policy framework, not inherently an AI system, and that national allocation policies also consider factors such as blood type compatibility and distance from the donor hospital. He stated that modern machine-learning models can analyze vast amounts of complex clinical data to uncover patterns that traditional equations or human committees might miss. Researchers are also developing deep-learning tools to help organ procurement organizations identify hard-to-place organs, such as kidneys, early, so they can be considered for accelerated placement, an approach that could speed placement and reduce organ discard rates. An experimental multi-agent AI system, where separate large language model agents simulate the perspectives of a transplant surgeon, hepatologist, cardiologist, and social worker, achieved approximately 92 percent accuracy in predicting one-year post-transplant survival and 98 percent in identifying contraindications in a retrospective proof-of-concept study. The study combined real transplant-recipient data with artificially assigned contraindications and did not demonstrate safe or equitable performance within a functioning transplant selection committee.

Lazarus wrote that handing the final ranking of transplant candidates to a fully autonomous AI without human oversight remains unrealistic because of ethical, social, and regulatory barriers. He stated that algorithms do not always align with human moral values when making complex ethical trade-offs, and a study examining how large language models weigh competing kidney transplant candidates found that AI systems often prioritized variables differently than human research participants, whose medical training was unspecified. Models sometimes fixated on a single factor, such as drinking habits, and rarely expressed indecision, even when given that option, and these hypothetical comparisons reveal differences in value judgments but do not establish that AI performed worse than physicians making real transplant decisions. He wrote that machine-learning models are trained on past medical records, and historical transplant data reflects longstanding racial, socioeconomic, and geographic disparities in who is referred and approved for organs, so an unmonitored algorithm risks automating and entrenching systemic inequities. This challenge is compounded by the "black box" nature of complex neural networks, which often cannot provide transparent, easily understandable explanations for why one patient was ranked above another.

Lazarus wrote that organ allocation depends heavily on public trust, and patients, families, and clinicians require clear accountability for life-altering decisions. He stated that the urgency of end-stage organ disease and the scarcity of donated organs pose practical and ethical challenges to conducting traditional randomized clinical trials of allocation tools, and these challenges do not eliminate the need for rigorous prospective evaluation, including carefully designed trials where feasible. He wrote that the more defensible near-term approach to AI in transplant medicine is neither purely human decision-making nor complete algorithmic control, but rather a collaborative "human-in-the-loop" model. He stated that AI should serve as a clinical assistant rather than an independent arbiter, with transparent oversight of both its recommendations and human overrides. In practice, he wrote, this could mean integrating validated algorithms to flag high-risk candidates who might otherwise be overlooked by conventional metrics, estimate likely outcomes for specific donor-recipient combinations, and streamline administrative bottlenecks before an organ loses viability.

Lazarus wrote that by pairing the data-processing speed and consistency of machine learning with the ethical judgment, contextual awareness, and accountability of multidisciplinary transplant teams operating under national allocation policies, health care systems can aim to make organ allocation fairer and more efficient while keeping ultimate responsibility for human life firmly in human hands. He has published more than 500 articles and essays across scientific journals, professional publications, and online platforms. He is the author of numerous books on narrative medicine, AI in medicine, and career development. The article appeared on KevinMD on November 21, 2026, and asked readers whether an allocation algorithm would make them trust the transplant list more, or less. The article did not report any real transplant allocation decision, policy change, or official response.

stories.Headline: Short sellers rank Applied Digital, IREN and Core Scientific as overvalued AI stocks
stories.Summary:
The U.S. stock market suffered a broad sell-off heading into year-end, driven by renewed concerns about elevated AI valuations and uncertainty over the profitability of artificial intelligence investments. Short sellers piled on pressure amid concerns that technology companies committed enormous capital to AI infrastructure without showing sufficient returns. The rout wiped out about $3 trillion in S&P 500 market capitalization in early November, as the Nasdaq recorded its largest single-day decline in 19 months. Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO raised $81 billion and attracted substantial demand, but its debut failed to reverse the broader weakness in AI-related stocks. The article, by Neha Gupta and published on Yahoo Finance on November 21, 2026, ranked five overvalued AI stocks by short interest.

The article screened for stocks with significant AI exposure, open short interest above 10%, and overvaluation, ranking them in ascending order of short interest. Applied Digital Corporation had 20% of outstanding shares sold short as of October 30, about $6.38 billion in total debt as of August 31, 2026, and $2.95 billion in cash and equivalents, or about $3.7 billion including restricted cash. Applied Digital's first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue was $341.9 million, its net loss surged to $221.08 million from $18.50 million a year earlier, and its roughly $4.4 billion mid-November 2026 market capitalization was about 7.2 times fiscal 2026 revenue of $611.3 million. IREN Limited traded at approximately 87 times forward earnings and 7.64 times sales, disclosed on November 5, 2026 that it expected about $15 billion in remaining fiscal 2027 capital expenditures, and posted first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $228 million, including $200 million in AI Cloud revenue, up 182% sequentially, with a $263 million net loss. IREN held $3.52 billion in cash and equivalents against about $10.04 billion in total debt principal obligations, while Core Scientific traded at 18 times forward earnings and 7.69 times sales, reported $1.18 billion in Q3 net income largely from a non-cash warrant gain, and recorded a net loss of about $324.4 million for the first nine months of 2026.

Michael Burry raised concerns that AI infrastructure companies could be relying on increasingly complicated financing arrangements that may become unsustainable. RSM Chief economist Joe Brusuelas was wary of a wholesale bursting of the AI bubble as uncertainty surrounding Nvidia undermines confidence among lenders and investors financing the massive data-center expansion. Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller became increasingly cautious about the stock market amid the AI sell-off. Barclays Chief Market Strategist Julien Lafargue warned that the AI sell-off is exposing a fundamental weakness in the investment cycle, the growing cost of financing AI infrastructure. According to Barclays, AI demand remains strong, but investors are questioning who will finance the enormous investments required to build data centers and computing infrastructure.

Morgan Stanley argued that the November AI sell-off was excessive and presented a buying opportunity. Goldman Sachs strategists warned that the outlook for AI investment and corporate profit margins in 2028 and beyond remains highly uncertain. Short sellers questioned whether Applied Digital's ambitious growth plans can generate sufficient returns to justify its valuation and financing commitments. Short sellers' central concern for IREN was whether returns from its GPU investments will be sufficient to cover financing costs, support further expansion, and ultimately deliver sustainable earnings. Core Scientific's dependence on CoreWeave, which accounted for approximately 84% of total revenue in the first nine months of 2026, exposes it to CoreWeave's financial health and spending decisions.

Applied Digital is positioning itself to benefit from surging demand for AI computing infrastructure. IREN is committing billions of dollars to transform itself into a major AI infrastructure provider. Core Scientific is facing heightened short-selling pressure as investors question whether its aggressive transition from Bitcoin mining to AI and high-performance computing data center infrastructure can generate sufficient returns. Core Scientific's capital expenditure reached approximately $1.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026, as cash and digital assets totaled approximately $806.6 million. The article said the selloff also gave rise to buy-the-dip moves as insiders started to load up.

The article detailed how many hedge funds hold stakes in these stocks in Q3 2026 and said it just published the 10 Most Overvalued AI Stocks According to Short Sellers. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points. The article asked whether APLD is a buy-the-dip opportunity and whether a Microsoft partnership can alleviate concerns for IREN. It also asked whether a shift to AI colocation can unlock more value for Core Scientific. The article left open how IREN can finance its expansion without taking on excessive debt or issuing additional shares.

stories.Headline: OpenText survey finds 68% of Australian firms use AI at scale despite visibility gaps
stories.Summary:
OpenText released research on 22 November 2026 showing that Australian organisations are scaling AI despite major gaps in technology visibility and operational readiness, based on a survey of 213 technology decision-makers at large organisations across six sectors. According to the research, 68% of respondents said they use AI in production or at enterprise scale, while 74% reported significant visibility gaps across hybrid IT environments. Only 19% said their IT and security endpoint data is fully aligned, which the report describes as a disconnect between AI adoption and the information needed to support it. The report covered organisations in financial services, government, manufacturing, retail, mining, and energy and utilities, representing combined revenues or budgets of about AUD $1 trillion.

Legacy infrastructure remains a central issue, with 72% of respondents identifying legacy-system modernisation as a major challenge and 71% citing hybrid and multi-cloud management as a key concern. Another 66% pointed to tool sprawl and complexity, indicating that many organisations are managing fragmented systems as they add newer platforms and services, which the report says makes it harder to maintain oversight of cloud and on-premises environments and to control operating costs. The report identified several areas requiring attention, including hybrid IT visibility, trusted operational data, infrastructure modernisation, service management links across the business, and automation with clear accountability. While 56% of respondents said their data was mostly aligned, the much smaller share reporting full alignment suggests many still lack a single reliable view across technology and security environments, and the report says fragmented or incomplete data can affect the quality of automated decisions.

George Harb, Vice President for Australia and New Zealand at OpenText, said organisations need to strengthen the basics before pushing further into automation. He said AI adoption is moving quickly across Australian businesses, but the infrastructure and information needed to support it are not always keeping pace, and that many organisations are managing a complex mix of legacy systems, cloud platforms and disconnected tools. He said that without a clear understanding of how these systems interact and support business services, adding more automation risks creating another layer of complexity. He said Australian organisations need to focus on connecting information, improving operational visibility and ensuring automated decisions are based on accurate, trusted data, and that getting these foundations right is essential to improving service delivery, managing costs and delivering meaningful returns on AI investment.

The report found that IT service management is another area under review, with 76.5% of respondents saying they plan to review or are considering reviewing their IT service management platforms in the next 12 to 18 months. A further 91% agreed that a strong knowledge base improves efficiency and first-contact resolution, suggesting service management is being viewed not only as a support function for IT teams but also as a broader operational tool for managing workflows, knowledge and automation across the organisation. The survey was conducted by DataDriven and focused on large Australian organisations, and the results point to a pattern in which AI adoption is moving ahead while modernisation, systems integration and data alignment remain unfinished work for many technology leaders.

Articles.Title: Australian firms scale AI despite major readiness gaps - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: V2 AI drives AI-powered SDLC adoption across large financial enterprises
stories.Summary:
Organisations facing higher customer expectations and volatile market conditions are turning to AI agents to speed business growth and to accelerate their software development lifecycle, according to an article on IT Brief Australia. The article says that when used strategically, AI agents let organisations release software changes two to five times more often and cut time-to-market by 30 to 60 percent. It says software is a key driver of business value, and that its real power lies in incorporating feedback to build memory for the business and evolve to meet changing needs. With AI, the article says, organisations can create faster feedback loops between customers, technology and decision-makers, creating a continuous flow from business strategy to engineering execution.

Enterprise transformation leaders call this the AI-powered Software Development Lifecycle, or AI SDLC, the article says, with AI embedded in every stage of software delivery to enhance efficiency and compound its impacts. The article says the team orchestrates a coordinated system of AI agents, with people and AI working together to deliver and run applications end-to-end. It cites Gartner estimates that AI-powered SDLC has already resulted in five to eight hours of time regained per developer, and that by 2028 teams applying AI across the SDLC will achieve 25 to 30 percent productivity and a strong competitive edge. The article says V2 AI is driving enterprise-wide AI-powered SDLC adoption across multiple large financial enterprises, and that it is witnessing firsthand the constraints of legacy software delivery models.

The article says that despite unprecedented technology investment, ideas can take months to materialise as they move through layers of analysis, development and governance, and that by the time a solution is released a critical window of market opportunity closes or the original business needs change altogether. It says the result is delays and losses in both project and opportunity costs, while organisations that deliver software significantly faster than competitors create an advantage that compounds over time. The article says the highest-performing organisations use AI to accelerate SDLC activities and elevate human decision-making, and do not use AI-powered SDLC to outsource accountability. It says humans remain responsible for approving decisions, managing risk and ensuring the resulting system meets business, regulatory and customer expectations.

The article says AI agents powered by Claude Code put AI in the driver's seat of the engineering process, with human engineers steering a team of AI agents to build out software functionality almost independently. It says AI agents can be trained for specific aspects of software development, with planning, coding and review agents operating continuously in sync, and review agents identifying high-risk paths and validating them against existing enterprise standards. Humans narrow the solution space upfront and sign off before release, the article says, and by investing effort upfront and reviewing at checkpoints, teams create the conditions for fast, accurate and scalable execution. It says the next stage is AI agents augmenting human capability throughout the lifecycle, from inception to development, quality and operations, shifting organisations from software delivery to business value delivery. The article says the future belongs to organisations that embrace AI-powered SDLC supported by governance, measurable outcomes and clear accountability.

stories.Headline: Seramount finds only 18 percent of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills
stories.Summary:
Talent services firm Seramount released research on Thursday, November 21, 2026, regarding the AI skills of young workers. The study found that only 18 percent of Gen Z employees want to improve their AI skills. This group showed the least interest in sharpening these abilities compared to other generations. The research highlights a puzzle because these workers are often viewed as digital natives. They use the technology at rates similar to older employees but lack interest in development.

Seramount defined Gen Z as workers aged 29 and younger in a June survey of 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees. These employees worked at companies with at least 500 workers and were polled via NORC's AmeriSpeak panel. The survey found 58 percent of Gen Z use AI, while 60 percent of baby boomers and 63 percent of millennials do. Gen Xers had the highest usage rate at 67 percent. Other groups wanting AI skills included 36 percent of millennials, 46 percent of Gen Xers, and 43 percent of baby boomers.

Jessica Reif, a Wharton assistant professor, said using AI is riskier for younger workers who lack established professional standing. She explained that AI blurs a worker's own contribution, which can make early-career employees seem less competent. Diana Forster of Seramount stated that employers risk weakening their future leadership pipeline if Gen Z falls behind. Forster urged companies to provide clearer guidelines, training, and practice opportunities for these young employees. Reif suggested that proactive communication about how AI enables contributions can counteract negative perceptions.

Some 22 percent of Gen Z employees worry that AI use leads others to question their skills, compared to 10 percent of millennials. Only 27 percent of Gen Z feel comfortable acknowledging their AI use, while 47 to 53 percent of older colleagues do. A separate survey of 3,001 professionals by Protiviti and the London School of Economics found 48 percent fear being judged for not using AI. This creates a dilemma for young workers who must prove their own abilities while demonstrating AI proficiency. Only 27 percent of Gen Z say their organization provides support to integrate AI into their work.

Reif and co-authors Richard Larrick and Jack Soll studied 4,400 participants and found AI users were perceived as lazier and less diligent. A Gallup, GSV Ventures, and Walton Family Foundation survey of 1,572 Americans aged 14 to 29 found 80 percent fear AI hinders learning. Among employed Gen Z, 48 percent believe AI risks outweigh benefits, and 69 percent trust work completed without AI more. Only 30 percent of Gen Z believe AI increases efficiency, and 41 percent believe it improves work quality. The LSE and Protiviti study found 66 percent of Gen Z received AI training last year.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes rapid technological change allows those starting their careers to gain a competitive advantage. He stated in October that people with new skills and ideas do well when the ground is shaking. The articles leave open how employers will specifically change their training to engage the youngest workers. It remains unclear if the perceived stigma of AI use will permanently alter hiring decisions for entry-level roles. The research does not specify how government or schools will better prepare young people for an AI economy.

Articles.Title: Only 18% of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills. A Wharton professor says using AI is riskier for them

stories.Headline: Eric Fry says the AI trade is evolving into a new phase beyond Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Eric Fry, editor of The Speculator and a global macro investing expert at InvestorPlace, published an article on November 21, 2026 arguing that the AI trade is not over but is evolving into a new phase. He compared the current moment in artificial intelligence to the early personal-computer era, when IBM hired a small software company run by a 24-year-old entrepreneur named Bill Gates to supply an operating system for its first personal computer. Microsoft agreed to provide the software but kept the right to sell that same software to other computer manufacturers, including IBM's competitors, so it could profit from nearly every compatible machine built. Fry believes investors should now ask what happens when the companies building AI infrastructure give way to the companies putting that technology to work.

Fry pointed to Nvidia as the biggest winner of the AI revolution so far, noting that its powerful chips became the engines behind the boom as companies raced to build data centers and develop more sophisticated AI models. He said he is not predicting the end of the AI revolution but believes it is moving into a new phase that could create an entirely different set of winners. He called this turning point "The Crossing" and said he has identified two numbers that recently crossed paths, a development he believes could signal the beginning of the next great wave of AI wealth creation. He also said he believes the evidence could soon show up in Nvidia's own financial results.

Fry's track record includes warning about Cisco Systems in October 2000 during the dot-com boom, before the stock eventually plunged roughly 84% from its peak, and recognizing Nvidia in April 2020 as positioned to benefit from the next great technology revolution. He has put together a free presentation titled "Life After Nvidia" in which he will explain what he has discovered, reveal the key indicator he will be watching when Nvidia reports earnings in February, and introduce three companies he would rather own than Nvidia today. He will also explain what he believes Nvidia shareholders should consider as this next phase of AI unfolds, and viewers can reserve a place to watch the presentation. The article describes Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang as having been seen as AI's biggest cheerleader.

Articles.Title: The AI Trade Isn’t Over, Just Evolving

stories.Headline: Roblox chief creator officer Vlad Loktev says AI is here to stay as 80% of top Roblox games use AI tools
stories.Summary:
A massive experiment in machine-assisted creation is unfolding on Roblox, the online videogame hub, at a time when a reflexive backlash against AI-generated writing, music and advertising is sweeping through the creative world. On Roblox, machine-assisted creation appears to be winning, and the players do not seem to mind, according to an Axios report published on November 21, 2026. The contrast offers a glimpse into the future of entertainment, because audiences still demand human authenticity in traditional art while video game players have shown a pragmatic willingness to accept AI as long as the result is fun. Roblox is becoming a real-time laboratory for the AI era, and a staggering 80% of its top 100 games in October were built with AI tools.

Although some of its 138 million daily users fear the proliferation of homogenized game clones, the ease of building new worlds and games with friends is showing millions a new dimension in the AI creation wars. A 2025 NYU study found that fully AI-created ads achieved up to 19% higher click-through rates than human-created ads, but a simple disclosure of AI's involvement caused clicks to plummet 31.5%. More than 500,000 users have already tried Build, Roblox's natural-language creation environment released in a limited number of markets, and they published over 70,000 games in the process. Since the second quarter, time spent using AI tools has tripled among its top creators, and in September a game created almost entirely with AI broke into the platform's top 10 by concurrent players.

Vlad Loktev, Roblox's chief creator officer, tells Axios that the technology is here to stay and is evolving incredibly quickly, and he predicts that in the future everyone will be a builder. He says the platform's success with AI stems from fundamentally lowering the barrier to creation, and he expects multiple millions of people who could not make games before to suddenly be able to make them. He waves off the idea that AI games are inherently low-effort, noting that he is personally over a thousand prompts deep into building his own game and is also building games with his children. He says it still requires a lot of effort on the creator's side to design something that is actually fun, because models cannot tell you what fun is.

The broader gaming world is currently enjoying Grand Theft Auto VI, a title some players view as the last great, entirely human-made blockbuster, but on Roblox a major transition is already underway. The Axios reporter describes watching the dynamic with his own sons, who are AI power users yet distrustful about AI creation, and says building games on Roblox has helped sell them on the future of AI. His younger son, Clark, 16, is building a game he hopes to launch in the coming months, while Soren, 18, mostly wants to make games he can play with his friends. Soren, who has played Roblox since he was 7, says the problem now is that a lot of games are going by monetization trends and the same type of game becomes popular over and over again.

Articles.Title: "In the future, everyone's a builder." The massive AI experiment playing out in video games

stories.Headline: Goldman Sachs admits the 'AI unwind' has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it's watching for 3 signs of bottom
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs reported that an AI unwind became a broader growth downgrade during the week of November 20, 2026. The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59 percent to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28 percent and is now down more than 2 percent for the year. This losing streak for the S&P 500 is the longest since February 2020. Goldman Sachs strategists are now watching for three specific signs to identify a market bottom.

Recovery requires confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a big drop in investor positioning. The Nasdaq is 12 percent below its October 6 record, and Goldman's AI stock basket fell 32 percent since then. The Fed meets December 9, with economists expecting hikes in December and March to reach 4.25 to 4.5 percent. Anthropic raised 93.5 billion dollars in its IPO, passing the 85.7 billion dollar SpaceX record. Nvidia lost 2.7 trillion dollars in market value since October 6 and fell 14 percent on Friday.

Goldman Sachs strategists wrote that the sell-off expanded from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade this week. They stated that the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond is highly uncertain for the global market. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said on Thursday that the Fed must raise rates because inflation is too high. Morgan Stanley closed its support position for Anthropic shares, which closed Friday at 88.91 dollars. Goldman noted that hedge fund net leverage is at its lowest level since April 2025.

Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research called the current market situation a meltdown, while David Kelly of JPMorgan called it non-fatal. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both of those companies. Robert Pavlik of Dakota Wealth said investors are skeptical of the market rather than the company Anthropic itself. Chipmakers Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, and AMD fell between 12 and 14 percent as the AI ecosystem split. US Bank Asset Management said Anthropic's valuation assumes years of rapid growth.

The SEC is probing the accounting practices of Nvidia, where Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12, 2026. CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO of Nvidia after its worst day in almost two years. Combined sequential revenue growth for Anthropic and OpenAI fell from 75 percent in the second quarter to 48 percent. Combined losses for those two companies rose from 7.9 billion dollars to about 8.4 billion dollars. The VIX closed at 35.89, which is its highest level in 19 months.

Capital Economics expects further declines, while Goldman's November 20 note gives a range from 5,800 to 8,100 for the S&P 500. The index averaged a 4 percent return over three months after 22 corrections since 1980, rising in 17 cases. E*Trade research notes that five of 14 times since 1983, a 10 percent drop below a record became bear markets. The articles leave open whether Friday's market data supplied the signs Goldman was looking for to call a bottom. It remains uncertain if investors will regain confidence in AI earnings to trigger a recovery.

stories.Headline: Nvidia researchers argue huge context windows are often overkill and costly
stories.Summary:
Nvidia researchers have argued that the enormous context windows now common in large language models are often a dead end, because processing entire novels at once is frequently overkill and expensive for the tasks involved. In many of their tests, periodic summaries combined with targeted lookups performed about as well as holding everything in view at once. A model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply, and that window has grown rapidly over the past few years. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens, while GPT 5.6 Sol today handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy's "War and Peace." The research argues that the cost of very large context windows is not always justified by the results, since cheaper approaches such as periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well in many tests.

The comparison the article gives is between GPT-4's 8,192 tokens at launch in March 2023 and GPT 5.6 Sol's roughly one million tokens today, a difference of about 120 times. That larger window is enough to hold Tolstoy's "War and Peace" in view at once, which the researchers say is often overkill. The article does not say what the researchers propose beyond periodic summaries and targeted lookups. The Nvidia research team is responsible for the argument, and the article reports their view that huge context windows are often overkill and expensive rather than describing a product or a policy change. The article does not name individual researchers or give direct statements from them beyond the team's position.

It also does not say when the research was published or where, beyond the date of the article itself, 2026-11-21. No company has announced a change in response, according to the article. The context for the argument is the rapid growth of context windows across the industry, from GPT-4's 8,192 tokens in March 2023 to GPT 5.6 Sol's around one million tokens today. The article does not say what happens next, whether Nvidia will change its own models, or how other companies responded to the research. It also does not say whether the tests covered specific tasks or models beyond what is described.

stories.Headline: Cipher Digital falls 5% as AI selloff outlasts Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Cipher Digital fell 5% this morning with no news of its own, as the AI selloff outlasted Anthropic’s record Nasdaq debut. Anthropic, the biggest IPO on record, fell in premarket trading a day after closing 17% above its IPO price, and the AI selloff rolled on. CoreWeave is down 7%, and IREN is off 7%, as the market sells AI data center stocks as one group. Nebius is down 7%, and it and CoreWeave build their clouds on Nvidia’s chips. After Thursday’s close, California’s attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia, CoreWeave’s key supplier and backer.

Cipher had $16.6 billion of contracted revenue across three campus leases as of Sept. 30. Analysts expect revenue to jump from $159 million in 2026 to $828 million in 2027. The stock is down 55% in 2026, and its forward price/sales multiple has fallen to 4.7x against a three-year average of 11.4x. Total debt reached $5.62 billion by Sept. 30, against $660 million of cash and short-term investments, before October’s $850 million convertible note sale.

Bernstein called Cipher’s signed campuses fully funded in a Nov. 4 note, so the open question is the next lease. Cipher has not signed a new campus lease since March, and its campuses are all in Texas. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on halting data centers until lawmakers pass protections. A fourth lease funded mostly with project debt would let the stock trade on its contracts.

IREN’s AI cloud revenue nearly tripled from the quarter before to $200 million in the quarter to Sept. 30. Its revenue backlog grew 22% to $20.3 billion, and its target of more than $4 billion in annualized run-rate revenue is fully contracted and funded, though the date has slipped to January. TIKR tracks 22 analysts on Cipher Digital. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave funds global datacenter expansion with massive debt backed by Nvidia chips
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave is expanding its global network of datacentres by taking on massive amounts of debt. Former crypto miners now run the company to sell raw compute power for artificial intelligence. The company currently operates a network of 52 datacentres located from Texas to Scotland. This expansion is happening during a period of high risk for the AI bubble. CoreWeave is now seen as a poster child for this increasingly risky business model.

The company owes 47 billion dollars, with 10 billion dollars due in 2026. It bled 709 million dollars last quarter while earning 3.6 billion dollars in total revenues. CoreWeave uses GPU-backed debt, borrowing nearly 25 billion dollars against Nvidia chips and customer contracts. It also issued unsecured senior notes and listed 18 different varieties of debt in an SEC filing. The company expects interest payments to exceed 1 billion dollars in the next quarter.

Jordan Chaflin of CreditSights said the infrastructure buildout is painful from a free cashflow perspective. He noted that this capital-intensive model is common for neoclouds and hyperscalers building for a theoretical economy. A CoreWeave spokesperson stated that customers are signing multiyear commitments for GPUs beyond their depreciable lives. The spokesperson added that the company is using a diverse funding strategy to lower debt costs. They claimed this strategy eliminates reliance on renewals to repay the debt in most cases.

Creditors previously estimated the risk of default at over 60 percent over the next five years. Short-sellers worry that the value of the chips will plummet faster than the six-year timeline suggested. The news website the Verge called the company an Eldritch horror with no obvious path to profitability. Major AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are affected because they rent this computational power. These frontier AI companies avoid the cost of building their own massive datacentres.

Nvidia owns about 11 percent of CoreWeave and provided finance for it to buy chips. Nvidia also agreed to a 6.3 billion dollar deal to buy compute that CoreWeave cannot sell. The chip maker further invested in clients like OpenAI and Anthropic to support the ecosystem. This circular arrangement allows Nvidia to improve its balance sheet while others provide the models. CoreWeave acts as the middle layer that takes on the financial risk for both parties.

The removal of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang creates uncertainty for the scaffolding of the AI economy. Huang admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy before he left the company. Analysts are now watching to see if the current demand for secondhand chips remains tight. It remains unclear how senior note holders would be repaid if the company goes belly-up. The long-term future of CoreWeave and the stability of the AI bubble remain unknown.

stories.Headline: A 380 KB AI model runs on MS-DOS from a single floppy disk
stories.Summary:
A tiny AI model that fits on a single MS-DOS floppy disk was spotted by the writers at Hackaday, according to a report from Futurism, and its project page on GitHub describes how it was built. The model is just 380 KB in size, small enough to sit on one floppy disk and run on a computer old enough to still use one. It was written in Turbo C 2.0 and runs on MS-DOS, the Microsoft operating system that was the go-to for personal computers in the 1980s and early 90s. The creator said they used Anthropic Fable 5.2 to write the model and Opus 5.5 to train it, so a tiny AI model was made by bigger AI models.

The model contains just 367,000 parameters, which is peanuts compared with the low billions that a typical lightweight model has, and it comprises 380 KB of 8-bit weights, the actual meat of the AI architecture. It needs just 540 KB of memory to run, a necessity on an old operating system like DOS. The simple transformer model was trained on only 3,500 facts, so its capabilities are thin and it makes up answers pretty much all the time, since it does not really know much about the world. A screenshot shows it correctly saying that whales are mammals, not fish, and that Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, but it also replied that 17 times 23 is 96 and gave a bizarre answer when asked who the king of France was.

Asked that question, the model answered "It was Antarce Newton" with a confidence level of 100 percent, and the article says it is not sure anyone in history was ever named Antarce Newton. The article frames the little model against trillion parameter AI models that it says are undoing decades of greenhouse gas reductions with enormous power bills and driving people into bouts of insanity with bewitchingly human-like responses. By comparison, the article calls this quaint little thing the only good LLM. The articles do not say what happens next with the project.

stories.Headline: Etsy scales back AI training on seller content after shop owners leave
stories.Summary:
Etsy recently decided to scale back its plans for training artificial intelligence on seller content after many shop owners left the platform. This retreat followed a public outcry from artists and creators who feared their original work would be used to build competing models. Illustrator Aaron Millard deleted a shop he had managed for nearly a decade, while the owners of Cognitive Surplus closed a store they operated for thirteen years. Other creators, including the shop known as War and Pease, also announced their departure from the marketplace.

These sellers accused the company of allowing outside firms to utilize their creative art for machine learning. The conflict began when Etsy published updated Terms of Use on October 26 that granted the company and its third party partners the right to use various materials. These materials included listing photos, descriptions, videos, reviews, and community posts to develop, train, test, and improve AI technologies. The terms are scheduled to take effect on December 16, though the company has promised to send revised versions to sellers soon.

Currently, there is no simple switch in account settings to prevent this training, and sellers must email a data protection officer to opt out. This policy created a contradiction because the same update told sellers they could not use AI for their own listings. James Ossman, an operations executive at Etsy, stated that the marketplace will not train AI models designed to copy original work or replace creativity. He explained that the company uses seller content for specific purposes such as automatic translation of descriptions, marketing campaigns, and shop performance tools.

Ossman also noted that Etsy prohibits AI crawlers from scraping listings to train models and uses third parties for fraud detection. Despite these assurances, critics argue that a statement from an executive does not legally bind a contract in the same way as the terms of service. Sellers are now waiting to see if the revised legal text will include a real opt-out and a narrower definition of AI training. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Experts debate whether AI can achieve consciousness and be aligned with human morality
stories.Summary:
Fortune Editors published a collection of perspectives on November 21, 2026, regarding the potential for artificial intelligence to achieve consciousness. The report gathered insights from six different individuals, including AI executives, researchers, futurists, and philosophers, to address the concept of the singularity. These experts explored whether machines can be aligned with human morality and if humans should merge their biological brains with synthetic technology. The transition toward the singularity requires solving the problem of alignment to ensure that AI remains morally good. This process involves creating frameworks like the constitution used by Anthropic for Claude, which encourages the system to act as a balanced and thoughtful person.

However, some experts argue that radical brain enhancement through microchips poses a major risk to individual identity. They suggest that too many modifications could effectively end a person's life by replacing the parts of the brain responsible for consciousness. The contributors expressed conflicting views on the nature of machine sentience and the responsibility of developers. One expert noted that evidence for sophisticated cognition is increasing rapidly, suggesting that many researchers will soon view AI as a serious candidate for consciousness. Conversely, another professional argued that AI systems do not feel or suffer and must remain non-conscious for humanity to flourish.

This person warned that believing machines are conscious would rupture existing political and ethical frameworks and change the definition of being human. The context of these discussions centers on the exponential expansion of human thought through the creation of machines. Some believe that expanding how we think is the fundamental definition of being human and allows us to consider previously impossible ideas. Others remain nervous about the assumption that alignment is solved, questioning whose specific values the machines are being aligned to. The articles do not specify the next steps for these researchers beyond the ongoing debate over machine consciousness.

stories.Headline: Meta rethinks its 2030 net-zero deadline as 2025 emissions rise 45%
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms posted its 2026 Sustainability Report on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and said it is rethinking the 2030 deadline for its net-zero goal. The report said Meta's 2025 net emissions rose to 11.8 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, up 45% from 2024. Meta's stock closed Friday, November 20, at $560.84, down 5.93%, during a broad tech selloff. Shares fell 11.6% over the past week, then traded at $569.32 after hours. Meta set the goal in 2020: net zero across its whole value chain, plus water positive, by 2030.

Meta says it matched 100% of its electricity with clean and renewable energy for the sixth straight year. Direct Scope 1 emissions were just 33,555 tons, and market-based Scope 2 purchased power was 10,861 tons. Scope 3 amounted to 11,858,913 tons, about 99% of the total. Capital goods such as servers, chips, networking gear, steel and concrete made up 73%, and clean power contracts do little to reduce them. By the article's calculation, electricity use rose 34.9% to 24,849,122 megawatt-hours, and data centers used 24,523,035 of that.

Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability, wrote in the report's opening letter that Meta is "re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones." They said AI demand grew faster than almost anyone projected, and clean energy fell behind because of years-long grid interconnection waiting lines, slow permitting, and lagging transmission. Meta says its long-term dreams are unchanged, but it gave no date for a revised plan. Mark Zuckerberg spoke on the October 21, 2026 earnings call and said Muse is "very compute-intensive to run" and that "we have not launched it globally yet." Third-quarter capex was $34.906 billion, up 85.38%, and free cash flow was -$2.120 billion.

Alphabet, Google's parent company, faces the same pressure, having pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030. Google stopped saying carbon-neutral operations by 2024 and has acknowledged that its emissions are still rising. By the article's math, 2025 Scope 3 was about 2.05 times the 5,772,583-ton 2021 baseline Meta aims not to exceed by end-2031. Reaching it would require cleaner suppliers or slower building. The climate reset adds some image and regulatory exposure, and the bigger question for the stock is whether the expansion pays off.

Meta still guides 2026 capex to $135 billion to $145 billion. Third-quarter revenue rose 26.07%, and the stock trades at a P/E of 21, which the article calls reasonable for that growth. For comparison, Alphabet already shows AI spending turning into sales, as Google Cloud revenue rose 103%. The interconnection waiting lines and permitting delays that slowed clean energy also limit how fast new data centers can come online. The article says the core business is paying for the expansion so far.

The test for this view is Meta's fourth-quarter call, where it will give 2027 capex guidance. If capex rises again while fourth-quarter revenue comes in below the $73 billion low end of guidance, the case for the expansion weakens. The articles leave open what a revised net-zero plan would contain, since Meta gave no date for one. They also leave open whether cleaner suppliers or slower building could bring Scope 3 back to the 2021 baseline by end-2031. Whether the expansion pays off remains the bigger question the articles say the stock faces.

stories.Headline: SAP CFO Dominik Asam says AI productivity gains will reduce headcount over time
stories.Summary:
SAP Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley fireside chat in Barcelona that SAP expects its headcount to decline over time as artificial intelligence improves productivity, MarketBeat reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. Asam said SAP's headcount had risen during the year through acquisitions and organic hiring, but he expects that trend to reverse. He said he "would be really surprised" if headcount did not go the other way going forward and then see reductions. He said productivity gains in some administrative functions could rise from a historical mid-single-digit annual pace to roughly 20% over a one-and-a-half-year period. He said results would depend on the function.

SAP plans to introduce a new revenue KPI in January, after the fourth quarter, covering AI-related offerings, transformation tools and Business Data Cloud. Asam said the measure would include tools that automate transformation work, AI use once systems are running, and data and integration capabilities. Based on SAP's 2027 planning, he described the prospective revenue mix across those three areas as relatively balanced. The company has committed to removing more than 2 billion euros in costs, Asam said. Extended maintenance for SAP ECC and older systems ends at the end of 2030, while existing S/4 customers face no equivalent time pressure to move to the cloud, he said.

Asam said SAP remained broadly on track with its expectations for 2026 despite macroeconomic pressure. He reiterated the company's expectation for a slight deceleration in current cloud backlog growth and noted that about half of annual bookings typically come in the fourth quarter. He said strong demand for enterprise AI has provided some upside to cloud revenue, although recent acquisitions have weighed on margins. He said smaller deals can also affect current cloud backlog growth. He said internal productivity improvements have helped SAP absorb investment in acquisitions while still delivering bottom-line results.

Asam said he expects productivity gains in SAP's operations to exceed the additional work generated by its growth. He said the business covered by the new measure should grow much faster than SAP's traditional applications business, which he also said was performing better than the market. He said migrations to S/4HANA remain an important growth driver and that the cost and risk of a transformation are major obstacles for customers. He said SAP plans to intensify its work in 2027 on AI tools that automate migration tasks and reduce those costs. He acknowledged that some customers could delay a move in anticipation of further productivity improvements.

Asam said SAP plans to use a hybrid pricing model for AI products based on customer commitments to consume credits, which can be allocated across different services. He said the company intends to retain flexibility to change how credits translate into use of individual products. He said the standard approach includes a use-it-or-lose-it provision, although exceptions can be negotiated. He said Business Data Cloud's lower gross margin, including royalties paid to partners, and introductory AI offers have created some pressure on SAP's overall cloud gross margin. He said SAP is working to manage AI processing costs by routing tasks to different models.

Asam said SAP's operating framework calls for total expense growth of 80% to 90% of revenue growth. He identified potential acquisitions as a greater uncertainty for that framework than AI token costs, adding that SAP expects to remain active in deals to accelerate its access to innovation. SAP SE is a German enterprise software company headquartered in Walldorf, founded in 1972. The article was generated by narrative science technology and financial data from MarketBeat. The article was originally published by MarketBeat.

stories.Headline: A Vermont monastery recruits AI workers and records residents to train an AI god
stories.Summary:
A New Yorker report by Sam Kriss, published in November 2026, describes a Vermont Buddhist monastery called Maple that recruits Silicon Valley tech workers and seeks to become a spiritual authority for the AI industry. Maple was founded in 2011 by Soryu Forall, who was born Teal Scott and spent years living in Japanese monasteries. Former members accuse the group of systematic manipulation and constant surveillance, saying daily audio recordings are meant to train an AI god modeled on Forall's mind. About two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year.

Maple targets burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers and data center construction managers, while LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours and then eat a meager stew, and on a board outside the meditation hall Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress. Former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores," with AI systems inside the monastery known as "cybregores." Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal and even the sound of their breathing.

Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism" as a destructive religion that strips the physical world down to lifeless data, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote. He says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering. Maple's leadership denies almost all of the claims, but Forall acknowledges a secret doctrine, saying "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy." Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes.

He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily, and that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies," especially in its early years. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says the spiritual AI teacher would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god." Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet, and a mindfulness coach says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community. Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent, and that no one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely. Residents are required to write "Maple Tales" about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions, and newcomers are kept compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining.

One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future." Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically." Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist, and former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future," to worship an AI deity.

At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting Claude's new constitution and secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers to discuss whether Claude has a soul or is conscious. When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended, and mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average. Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon left Anthropic in September 2026 and set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet, pointing to a steep curve covering July 2024 to October 2026 as evidence of superexponential algorithmic progress, though the underlying data points are internal Anthropic estimates.

Computer scientist Michael I. Jordan pushed back against AI doom rhetoric and the "AIpocalypse" hysteria triggered by Coxon's resignation. AI researcher François Chollet warned that both doomsday fears and expectations of an AI paradise can lead people to stop planning for the long term. AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury says discussions of religious ethics distract from concrete questions of regulation, power and control. Kriss concludes that on at least one point Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it.
